However, Senior Cyber Adviser Gregory Platt intervened, and Plaintiff was instead placed in an S6 role in the 780th MIB, which he began on January 3, 2013.

Plaintiff's work attendance became an issue, as he would often visit family in Georgia and arrive late to work on Mondays, initially being allowed to work late to make up for the lost time. However, on June 17, 2013, Plaintiff was required to submit a request for leave without pay for his late arrival. Plaintiff alleges that he was being singled out and discriminated against based on his race and age regarding the enforcement of leave policy. He contacted an EEO counselor, which led to an EEO Complaint, and discussed his concerns with his supervisor, Michael Young, and Young's supervisor, Major Ross. The EEO Complaint and subsequent discussions led to a change in the work environment, with coworkers testifying that the atmosphere became tense after Young and Major Ross discussed the complaint publicly. Plaintiff was then assigned to open and close the Deer Path Facility, which was being made operational as the headquarters for the 781st MIB and was subject to security restrictions. Plaintiff alleges that he was not formally briefed on these requirements and subsequently violated security protocols by bringing a personal cell phone into the facility and leaving equipment unattended.

Wayne Galbreth, a Louisiana resident, worked for Bellsouth Telecommunications, Inc. (Bellsouth), a Georgia corporation. Galbreth's supervisor was Aaron Begnaud, and during Begnaud's absence, Barbara C. Johansen acted as his supervisor. In March 1995, Begnaud evaluated Galbreth's performance for 1994, giving him a rating that denied him a salary increase. Galbreth alleges that Begnaud's decision was influenced by Johansen's recommendations from 1994. Galbreth contends that Begnaud discriminated against him based on his race, favoring white employees over him in various aspects of his job and in awards and recognition. 

Plaintiff alleges that Begnaud and Johansen, as his supervisors, discriminated against him in violation of Louisiana statutes LSA-R.S. 23:1006 et seq. and LSA-R.S. 51:2231 et seq. Defendant Bellsouth removed the case to federal court, claiming diversity jurisdiction exists between Galbreth and Bellsouth, and that Begnaud and Johansen, both Louisiana residents, were fraudulently joined as defendants to prevent removal. Galbreth opposes the removal, arguing that Begnaud and Johansen were not fraudulently joined and that he has stated a valid cause of action against them under state law.

Galbreth originally filed the lawsuit in Civil District Court for the Parish of Orleans, State of Louisiana, naming Bellsouth, Begnaud, and Johansen as defendants. The lawsuit alleges racial discrimination and seeks relief under Louisiana law. The parties disagree on whether Begnaud and Johansen can be held liable under the relevant Louisiana statutes, with Galbreth arguing that they can be held liable as supervisors and Bellsouth arguing that only the employer, Bellsouth, can be held liable. Relevant pre-litigation events include Begnaud's performance evaluation of Galbreth and Johansen's recommendations, which Galbreth alleges were discriminatory. The parties have exchanged memoranda and the court has reviewed the applicable law, but no decision has been made on the motions to remand and dismiss.

Chandler, a former employee of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), worked at the agency from February 25, 1977, until her retirement on August 30, 2007. During her time at the FDIC, she filed ten Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) administrative complaints and two civil actions against the agency. After her retirement, in 2009, Mir, Mitchel & Company (MMIC), a contractor that works with the FDIC, contacted her about a potential position. Chandler applied and was hired, but despite her repeated requests, she never received a work assignment from MMIC between 2009 and 2013. MMIC allegedly told her there was no work available for her.

In 2015, another FDIC contractor, the SolomonEdwards Group (SEG), offered Chandler a position as an investigative technician on a contract with the FDIC. She accepted and was assigned to work on the closing of the Doral Bank in San Juan, Puerto Rico. However, on March 23, 2015, her supervisor, Doug Thorpe, allegedly told her that he had been ordered to terminate her employment, claiming the order came from the FDIC, not SEG management. Chandler alleges that she was never assigned another project with SEG after her termination. Plaintiff alleges that the FDIC retaliated against her by "poisoning her prospects of working on its contracts" due to her successful litigation of prior EEO complaints during her time as an FDIC employee.

Chandler contends that she was retaliated against by the FDIC, while the FDIC's actions, as described by Chandler, suggest that the agency took no action to assign her work or interfere with her employment opportunities with its contractors. The FDIC's relationship with its contractors, including MMIC and SEG, is also relevant to the dispute. Chandler's EEO complaints and civil actions against the FDIC during her employment, as well as her subsequent attempts to work with FDIC contractors, are central to her allegations of retaliation. The parties' contentions regarding the events surrounding Chandler's employment with MMIC and SEG, as well as the FDIC's alleged involvement in her termination, are in dispute.

Eight states and three private healthcare providers, including Franciscan Alliance, Inc., Specialty Physicians of Illinois, LLC, and the Christian Medical & Dental Society, have sued the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and HHS Secretary Sylvia Burwell. The plaintiffs challenge a new rule issued by HHS, entitled Nondiscrimination in Health Programs & Activities, which implements Section 1557 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA). The rule prohibits discrimination by any health program or activity receiving federal financial assistance on the grounds prohibited under four federal nondiscrimination statutes, including Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972. 

Plaintiffs allege that the rule's interpretation of discrimination "on the basis of sex" under Title IX as encompassing "gender identity" and "termination of pregnancy" will require them to perform and provide insurance coverage for gender transitions and abortions, regardless of their contrary religious beliefs or medical judgment. They contend that the rule's definition of sex does not apply to them because the text of Section 1557 incorporates the religious and abortion exemptions of Title IX, and the rule's failure to incorporate those exemptions renders it contrary to law. 

Defendants claim that the rule does not mandate any particular procedure, but rather requires only that covered entities provide nondiscriminatory health services and health insurance in a nondiscriminatory manner. They argue that the rule does not require the performance or insurance coverage of any procedure, but merely prohibits policies from "operating in a discriminatory manner, both in design and implementation." The plaintiffs, including Franciscan and the Christian Medical & Dental Society, are covered entities under the rule because they receive federal financial assistance and provide employee health insurance. They fear that the rule will require them to perform and provide insurance coverage for abortion- and transition-related procedures, which they believe would violate their religious freedom and medical judgment.

Billy Porter, a black man, began working for the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) in 2013 as a supervisory contracting specialist, supervising employees, assigning and reviewing work, and providing training and direction. Initially, he supervised around sixteen employees in Little Rock, and later, he supervised employees in other states, while continuing to supervise at least five employees in Little Rock until his retirement in 2017. In October 2015, Porter applied for a promotion to division chief, but was not selected for the position after interviews. The VA compiled information about each candidate, including federal contracting experience, supervisory experience, VA experience, and certification level, and each candidate was interviewed by a panel of three people. Porter was not one of the top two candidates, and a white man ultimately got the job.

Porter alleges that a higher-ranking VA employee made a comment that the person who received the job was a "better fit" for the role, which Porter views as a racist remark. Meanwhile, Porter's health issues began impairing his ability to do his job, and he repeatedly requested an accommodation to work from home, providing documentation from medical providers in support of this request. The VA offered alternative accommodations, including an ergonomic workstation, an ergonomic assessment, a sit/stand workstation, hybrid telework, and leave for medical and physical therapy appointments, but Porter rejected these offers, stating that working from home was the only accommodation acceptable to him. Porter contends that the VA's proposed accommodations did not address the impact his disabilities had on his daily life activities, such as caring for himself and attending medical appointments.

The VA denied Porter's requests for advanced leave in April 2016, citing that he had applied for disability retirement and might not return to duty or be able to earn the leave amount by the end of the remaining leave year. Porter's position required him to maintain a certain certification level, and he was temporarily detailed to a position that did not require that certification level after he failed to complete training hours. Porter believes he was subjected to a hostile work environment based on his disability and treated differently than others based on his race, and he also alleges that he was retaliated against for requesting accommodations. The VA and Porter have different contentions about the events and circumstances surrounding his employment, including the reasons for the denial of his promotion, accommodation requests, and leave requests, as well as the impact of these events on his work and well-being.

Borden's, Inc., a New Jersey corporation, closed its Phoenix, Arizona, dairy operation on December 31, 1979, resulting in the termination of all dairy employees except for a few management personnel. Prior to the closure, on July 27, 1979, Borden's had renewed its collective bargaining agreements with two unions representing the dairy employees, which included a severance pay formula in the event of closure. The formula, added to the agreements in November 1979, excluded employees eligible for normal or early retirement, who had to have at least ten years of continuous service with Borden's and be at least fifty-five years old. Fourteen employees, including eleven named in the original complaint, were excluded from receiving severance pay due to their eligibility for retirement.

Plaintiff EEOC alleges that Borden's denial of severance pay to these employees constitutes age-based discrimination in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA). The EEOC contends that the severance pay policy either discriminates against fifty-five-year-old employees or has a disparate impact on them. Defendant Borden's argues that eligibility for retirement, not age, was the determining factor in denying severance pay and that the policy is part of a bona fide employee benefit plan exempt from the ADEA. Borden's also claims that the severance pay policy was intended to provide benefits to employees not otherwise covered by retirement plans.

The parties have stipulated to the facts, including the amounts of severance pay the eleven affected employees would have received under the severance pay formula. The EEOC seeks these amounts with interest, as well as injunctive relief to prevent Borden's from denying severance pay in similar circumstances in the future. Borden's requests that it not be required to pay interest if judgment is found against it and claims that injunctive relief is unnecessary. The evidence shows that there were no fifty-five-year-old employees who received severance pay, and Borden's has not provided evidence of business necessity for the severance pay policy. The EEOC argues that the affected employees were adversely affected by the policy, as they were forced to give up a newly created benefit (severance pay) in exchange for benefits they already had (retirement benefits).

Plaintiff, a Negro employee at Crown Zellerbach's Bogalusa box plant, filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) alleging that the company had engaged in unlawful employment practices, including racial discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that he was denied promotion from "take-off man" to "slitter man" due to his race. He also alleges that the company has a policy of segregating jobs by race, with certain jobs being reserved for white employees, and that the company's testing procedures for promotions are designed to discriminate against Negroes. Plaintiff further alleges that the company's locker facilities are segregated by race.

Defendant Crown Zellerbach contends that it has a policy against racial discrimination in employment and that plaintiff's allegations are unfounded. Defendant argues that each member of the proposed class of Negro employees has unique circumstances, such as seniority and job position, that would require individualized consideration, and that a class action is therefore improper. Defendant also claims that it has taken an affirmative stand against racial discrimination in employment.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with plaintiff being a Negro employee at Crown Zellerbach's Bogalusa box plant. The nature of the dispute is a claim of racial discrimination in employment, with plaintiff alleging that the company has engaged in unlawful employment practices that affect not only him but also other Negro employees. Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff exhausted his administrative remedies by filing a charge with the EEOC, which attempted to conciliate the matter but was unsuccessful. The EEOC's conciliation efforts were directed at eliminating the company's allegedly discriminatory policies, rather than just addressing plaintiff's individual grievance. Plaintiff now seeks to represent a class of Negro employees at the Bogalusa box plant in a lawsuit against Crown Zellerbach, alleging that the company's policies and practices have a discriminatory impact on all Negro employees.

The Plaintiffs, Harding, Goff, and Williams, were employees of the United States Postal Service. They filed compensation claims for injuries allegedly received on the job, but the Postal Service employed a presumption of fraud when processing these claims. Plaintiff alleges that this presumption denied them their Fifth Amendment right to due process. The Plaintiffs had two different grievance systems available to them: one under 5 U.S.C. § 7501, et seq. (the merit system), and another under their union's collective bargaining agreement with the Postal Service, which provided a five-step procedure for resolving disputes. 

Plaintiff Harding and Goff proceeded to final arbitration, while Plaintiff Williams went to step 2 of the arbitration process but then apparently abandoned his claim. The Defendants contend that Williams was dismissed for cause because he could no longer perform his duties as a mail handler and had not worked for the Postal Service for at least five years, which meant he had no right to be assigned to lighter duty. The Plaintiffs argue that the alternative remedies available to them, including the merit system and the collective bargaining agreement processes, have been "perverted by the due process violations" of which they complain, and therefore should not be barred from bringing a constitutional tort claim.

The Plaintiffs' union was initially a party to the lawsuit, but has since been voluntarily dismissed. The Plaintiffs now proceed under a constitutional tort theory, alleging that the Postal Service's use of a presumption of fraud when processing their compensation claims denied them their Fifth Amendment right to due process. The Defendants argue that the Plaintiffs have alternative remedies available to them, including the merit system and the collective bargaining agreement processes, and that these remedies should be exhausted before a constitutional tort claim can be brought.

Joseph Laguana, a part-time Customer Service Representative for United Airlines, Inc., has asthma, which he has had since he was around ten years old. Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020, Laguana had not taken any extended periods of medical leave of absence, and his asthma had not interfered with his ability to perform his work duties. Laguana's employment was subject to a collective bargaining agreement between United and his union, the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers. 

In April 2020, Laguana requested to work remotely, questioned the number of employees at work, and requested to move the location of an operational briefing due to concerns about social distancing. He also asked his doctor, Dr. Scott Wesley Hughes, for a diagnosis of asthma so that he could submit FMLA paperwork, stating that he wanted to utilize his earned hours to excuse himself from work and get paid. Laguana claimed he was trying to avoid contracting COVID-19, as he was not experiencing asthma or COVID-19 conditions at the time. He later emailed United's Employee Advocacy Director, Rahman Henderson, regarding the lack of communication about his request to work remotely and his concerns about retaliation.

In May 2020, Laguana went on a two-and-a-half-year medical leave of absence, which continued until his employment with United ended in November 2022. During this time, United requested additional medical documentation to support his leave, and Laguana expressed concerns about putting himself and his family at risk by going to work due to the continued travel of passengers from COVID-19 hotspots. United became aware of a video depicting Laguana at a bar on June 19, 2020, without a mask and holding an alcoholic beverage, which they believed was inconsistent with his taking of medical leave. This led to an investigation, and Laguana's supervisor, Ellie Sandlin, concluded that he had abused sick leave and was uncooperative during the investigation, violating company policies. 

Plaintiff Laguana alleges that he suffered disability discrimination and was subjected to a hostile work environment, including homophobic and insulting comments. Defendant United contends that Laguana abused sick leave and was uncooperative during the investigation, and that his termination was warranted due to violations of company policies. Laguana claims that his asthma and concerns about COVID-19 led to his requests for accommodations, while United argues that his behavior was inconsistent with his claims of disability and medical leave.

Tammy Ward, an Alabama resident, met with a W & H Voortman, Ltd. employee in Alabama, who encouraged her to apply for a job as the company's products distributor in middle and southern Alabama. Ward alleges that she was offered the job and accepted it, but was either fired or never officially hired because of her sex. W & H Voortman, Ltd. is a foreign corporation with its principal place of business in Burlington, Ontario, Canada. Plaintiff alleges that the company's actions constituted sex discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Defendant contends that it is not subject to suit under Title VII because it is a foreign corporation. Ward admits that W & H Voortman is a foreign corporation, but argues that the company's actions in the United States, specifically in Alabama, are subject to Title VII. The parties' relationship began when Ward was encouraged to apply for the job, and the nature of the dispute centers on whether W & H Voortman's alleged discriminatory actions are covered under Title VII. Prior to the lawsuit, there were communications and a meeting between Ward and the W & H Voortman employee in Alabama, which led to Ward's job application and alleged subsequent discrimination.

The Plaintiff, 545 Halsey Lane Properties, LLC, purchased a 40.747 acre parcel of property in the Town of Southampton in 2003 for $15,150,000. The property, known as Suffolk County Tax Map No. 900-105.000-0001-001.030, is located in the R-80 Residential Zoning District and within an Agricultural Overlay District (AOD) established by the Town in 1972. The property had been utilized as agricultural farmland prior to its purchase by the Plaintiff. In 1980, the prior owners of the property, Raymond G. Wesnofske and Leonard Schulman, entered into an agreement with the Town pursuant to New York General Municipal Law § 247, which imposed certain understandings and agreements concerning the use of the property. This agreement, known as the Grant, reserved numerous property rights to the prior owners and their successors, including the right to utilize the property for farming operations, open space, recreational areas, and the construction of a single-family dwelling and accessory structures.

The Plaintiff alleges that the Grant permits the construction of a barn on the property, and in 2006, the Plaintiff sought to construct an 11,250 square foot barn on the property. The Plaintiff was directed to file an application for a permit with the Planning Board for site plan review. The Planning Board referred the application to the Agricultural Advisory Committee (AAC), which commented that the proposed size of the barn was "disproportionately large" for the proposed agricultural endeavor and that the ball field and playground equipment on the property were not an agricultural use. The AAC also questioned what equipment would be stored inside the barn and asserted that the equipment identified by the Plaintiff was "essentially landscaping equipment," which could not be stored on the property. The Plaintiff addressed the AAC's comments, noting that the ball field and playground equipment were recreational uses permitted by the Grant, and that the proposed structure size was consistent with other permits issued for barn constructions in the Town.

The Plaintiff and the Defendants, including the Town of Southampton, the Planning Board, and various members of the Planning Board and the AAC, have a dispute over the interpretation of the Grant and the Town Code, and whether the construction of the barn is permitted on the property. The Plaintiff contends that the Grant and the Town Code allow for the construction of the barn, while the Defendants argue that the proposed barn is not consistent with the agricultural use of the property and that the Grant does not permit such construction. The parties also disagree over the meaning of "agricultural production" and what structures are permitted on the property under the Town Code. The Plaintiff has submitted various studies and reports to support its application, including a review of public records and a study of the density of barns on parcels within the AOD. The Defendants have raised concerns about the size and location of the proposed barn, as well as the impact on the "view shed" of other preserved farmland.

Professor Janay Garrick was employed as an instructor of secular courses at Moody Bible Institute, a post-secondary Christian educational institution. Moody adheres to a "complementarian" doctrine that forbids women from acting as religious leaders, while Professor Garrick subscribes to "egalitarian Christian" beliefs regarding gender equality in the ministry. Plaintiff alleges that she suffered pervasive sex discrimination during her employment and that Moody ultimately fired her because of her sex, but under the guise that she was "not aligned with Moody's doctrinal statement as it related to gender roles in ministry." Defendant Moody contends that Professor Garrick's claims are barred because she qualified as a "minister" within the meaning of the ministerial exception under Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church and School v. EEOC.

Professor Garrick initially filed a complaint alleging retaliatory discharge and breach of contract under Illinois law, and retaliation under Title IX. Moody moved to dismiss, prompting Professor Garrick to amend her complaint to assert claims for sex discrimination, retaliation, and religious discrimination under Title VII, and hostile work environment under both Titles VII and IX. Moody again moved to dismiss, arguing that principles of "church autonomy" precluded these claims. The court rejected Moody's ministerial exception argument, pointing out that the exception was an affirmative defense and that the facts Moody relied upon came from Moody's submissions, not the complaint.

Prior to the lawsuit, Professor Garrick worked at Moody, where she experienced antagonistic treatment by male colleagues and preferential treatment of male faculty members with respect to job duties and performance. Moody's employment decision-making process and the circumstances surrounding Professor Garrick's termination are disputed. Moody provided a reason for Professor Garrick's termination, stating that she was "not aligned with Moody's doctrinal statement as it related to gender roles in ministry." Professor Garrick disputes this reason, alleging that it was a pretext for gender discrimination. The parties' pre-litigation communications and any relevant employment or workplace documents are not detailed in the provided text, but it is clear that the parties had disagreements regarding Moody's religious views and Professor Garrick's role at the institution.

Chris-Craft, a manufacturer of boats, and Seaward, a former dealer of Chris-Craft products, had a contractual relationship governed by written Dealer Agreements executed at annual sales conferences starting in July 1983 for Seaward's Portland store and in July 1984 for its Seattle store. The agreements described the basic relationship between the parties, with Chris-Craft appointing Seaward as its authorized dealer for the retail sale of its products, subject to the terms and conditions of the agreement. The appointment was non-exclusive, and Chris-Craft reserved the right to appoint other dealers and sell products directly to any person or entity. Seaward agreed to purchase and carry a representative inventory of Chris-Craft products, promote their sale, and maintain an acceptable floor plan and business practices.

Seaward alleges that Chris-Craft failed to adequately reimburse it for warranty repairs, boat show expenses, and advertising expenses, and that Chris-Craft wrongfully terminated the dealership agreements. Seaward claims that Chris-Craft owes it $40,000 in warranty claims and seeks compensatory and punitive damages. Chris-Craft contends that it terminated the agreements due to Seaward's poor sales performance and inability to maintain an adequate financing arrangement, as required by the agreements. Chris-Craft also argues that Seaward's actions, including withholding payment to Borg-Warner, the financing company, were in breach of the inventory security agreement.

The relationship between the parties began to deteriorate in 1985, when Seaward advised Chris-Craft that it wanted to cancel certain boat orders and delay production on others. Borg-Warner notified Seaward that it was delinquent in its payment for two yachts and demanded immediate payment of $185,000. Seaward sent a letter to Chris-Craft acknowledging serious sales problems and asking Chris-Craft to "put the brakes" on boat orders scheduled for 1986. A dispute arose concerning whether Chris-Craft had adequately reimbursed Seaward for certain warranty repairs and expenses, with Seaward demanding $33,843.74 and Chris-Craft offering $9,841.41. Chris-Craft eventually paid Seaward $7,445.83 for warranty claims owed to the Seattle store but demanded payment of $7,038.27 from the Portland store. Seaward withheld payment to Borg-Warner, hoping to pressure Chris-Craft to pay the money due for warranty claims directly to Borg-Warner. Borg-Warner issued another demand for payment to Seaward, asserting that a total of $46,945.86 was past due for interest on the Portland and Seattle inventory. The situation between Seaward and Borg-Warner deteriorated, leading to Borg-Warner filing a lawsuit against Seaward in August 1986. Chris-Craft terminated the dealership agreements with Seaward's Seattle store in November 1986 and with the Portland store in December 1986. Seaward asserts that the agreements were terminated in retaliation for its dispute with Chris-Craft over warranty claims, while Chris-Craft maintains that the termination was due to Seaward's poor sales performance.

Melani Deodhar Beattie, a 64-year-old female resident of Chicago, Illinois, began working as a salesperson for ST Media/HMG, also known as Boutique Design (BD), in March 2013. She worked remotely from her home in Chicago, operating in an assigned sales territory, and earned a salary plus commissions for any sale made within that territory. In October 2018, Emerald Expositions, a limited liability company headquartered in New York, purchased BD, and Beattie's employment transferred to Emerald. 

Beattie alleges that on January 12, 2019, Emerald EVP Joe Randall offered her a new employment contract that mimicked her prior contract with BD and assured her that Emerald intended to replicate her prior compensation structure. Randall emailed her a 2019 Sales Incentive Plan, which she signed, and which specified that she would earn a fixed base salary along with an opportunity to earn commissions on any "cumulative sales" generated by her during 2019. Beattie contends that her job responsibilities included working assigned trade shows and other events within an assigned geographic territory. 

Plaintiff alleges that sometime in early 2019, Emerald EVP Kevin Gaffney gave many of her trade show sales to three younger, less experienced salespeople, and that when she asked Gaffney how those assignments would impact her commissions and sales, she received no clear response. Defendant Gannon Brousseau, an Executive Vice President at Emerald, was not involved in drafting or negotiating the 2019 Sales Incentive Plan. The parties' relationship and the nature of the dispute center on Beattie's employment with Emerald, the terms of her employment contract, and the allocation of sales and commissions. Emerald's actions, including the purchase of BD and the subsequent changes to Beattie's sales territory and commission structure, are at the heart of the dispute.

Plaintiff, a Clinical Laboratory Scientist, was hired by Defendant, Redwood Toxicology Laboratory, with a start date of January 8, 2018. Plaintiff alleges that during her term of employment, a co-worker made one sexual remark to her. She also claims that she was bullied by her co-workers, which led her to resign in May 2018. However, after discussing her concerns with her supervisor, Plaintiff retracted her resignation. 

In July 2018, Plaintiff notified her supervisor that she was experiencing back pains, shoulder hurt, and had sprained her ankle in the lab. Her physician restricted her activity, and Redwood accommodated these restrictions. Plaintiff requested an additional 30 days of leave, which was denied by Redwood, as it had not been requested by her physician. Plaintiff also alleges that she requested a printer at her desk, but Redwood does not have a record of this request. Additionally, Plaintiff claims that two co-workers called her "old" several times.

During her employment, Plaintiff was issued both verbal and written warnings citing several instances of inappropriate conduct or performance issues. Plaintiff resigned from her job on September 27, 2018, and Redwood accepted her resignation. Two days later, Plaintiff tried to rescind her resignation, but Redwood refused to allow her to retract it. Defendant contends that it accommodated Plaintiff's restrictions and did not discriminate against her based on her disability. 

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute involves claims of disability discrimination, harassment, and retaliation. Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and was wrongfully terminated, while Defendant contends that it acted lawfully and reasonably in its treatment of Plaintiff. Relevant pre-litigation events include Plaintiff's resignation and attempted rescission, as well as the warnings and accommodations provided by Redwood. The employment records and communications between Plaintiff and her supervisor are also relevant to the dispute.

Quamar, an Asian American Muslim, is an employee of HHA. On November 30, 2020, Quamar submitted a request to HHA's Human Resources Department for a hardship withdrawal from his pension. By December 8, 2020, Quamar had not received an update on his request and was informed that his application was sent to the Director of HR, Dianne Mitchel. Quamar sent emails to Mitchel over the next several days, but when he asked for updates, he was ignored. On December 14, 2020, Quamar spoke with Mitchel by phone, and he noticed that someone else, later identified as HHA's General Counsel, Keland Lewis, was also on the call. Quamar refused to discuss his request in Lewis's presence.

Quamar alleges that Mitchel and Lewis violated his privacy and discriminated against him. He filed a complaint against them for alleged violations of the Privacy Act and Invasion of Privacy, Discrimination, Aiding and Abetting in Discrimination, Harassment, Intimidation, Retaliation, and Breach of Personal Information. On May 10, 2022, Quamar submitted a second request to HR for a financial hardship withdrawal from his 401(k), explaining that he wanted this request to be kept "confidential." However, when HR emailed Quamar to ask for documents to process his request, Lewis was included in the email thread, despite Quamar's request for confidentiality. Quamar contends that Lewis's inclusion in the email thread was a violation of his request for confidentiality.

Quamar also alleges that he contracted COVID-19 after HHA failed to properly notify him of potential exposure to the virus. On August 18, 2021, HR sent an email to all employees informing them that two individuals in the building tested positive for COVID-19, but Quamar was not contacted by HR, and he later learned that one of the employees who tested positive worked in his department in close quarters with him. Quamar took a leave of absence from work under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) due to his COVID-19 symptoms, which spread to his entire family. Upon returning to work, Quamar reported to HR that a manager created a hostile work environment, but the problem went unresolved. Additionally, Quamar alleges that another manager, Mitchel Sykes, made discriminatory comments about his race and asked him if he was "collecting human dust in a cup." Quamar filed a complaint against Sykes on October 13, 2022. HHA contends that it properly handled Quamar's requests for hardship withdrawals and that it did not discriminate or retaliate against him.

Heidi Husser began working for the New York City Department of Education (DOE) on August 19, 2008, as the Director of Labor Relations in the Division of School Facilities (DSF). Her annual salary started at $80,749 and increased to $83,577 on July 1, 2009, when the DOE raised the salaries of all its employees. Husser's supervisors included John Shea, the DSF's Chief Executive Officer, and John O'Connell, the DSF's Executive Director. 

Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to a sexist culture at DSF, where high-ranking officials, including defendants Shea and O'Connell, made derogatory comments about women, referred to them as "girls," "hot," "doable," and "adorable," and permitted and encouraged sexual innuendo and name-calling. Specifically, Husser claims that Shea and O'Connell made a dozen offensive remarks and incidents from late 2009 through July 2012. Defendant contends that Husser's job is not sufficiently comparable to the other DSF directors, whose higher salaries she complains about, and that her salary was determined pursuant to a gender-neutral plan for managerial compensation.

Husser informally complained about the hostile work environment to the DOE's Executive Director of the Office of Equal Employment Opportunity (OEEO), Mecca Santana, in March or April 2012, and filed a formal complaint on July 5, 2012, alleging sexual harassment, unlawful pay practices, and gender discrimination. The OEEO investigation found that Husser's claims were not substantiated, but criticized Shea for failing to self-report Husser's complaint. The report also noted a "history of inappropriate conduct by all involved parties" and recommended that Husser's salary be reviewed. Following the report, Shea received a two-week suspension. 

Husser claims that the defendants retaliated against her after she complained, by closely monitoring her performance, excluding her from meetings and group email exchanges, and temporarily revoking her privilege to use a DSF car. Defendants contend that they are entitled to judgment on the retaliation claims because Husser cannot demonstrate that she was subjected to any cognizable adverse employment action. Husser also alleges that she was effectively demoted when the DOE appointed Linda Green to the newly created position of Chief Administrative Officer, and had Husser report directly to her rather than to CEO Shea. Defendants argue that the record does not support the proposition that Husser was subjected to a hostile work environment.

Elizabeth Burciaga began working for Channel Prime Alliance, a business unit of Ravago Americas, LLC, in Des Moines, Iowa, as a Customer Service Representative (CSR) in August 2007. Her supervisor was Customer Service Manager Jeremy Howe. Burciaga's responsibilities included contact with sales representatives and customers, receiving and processing orders, scheduling shipments, and fixing customer issues. Throughout her employment, Burciaga used Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave multiple times, including in 2008 after the birth of her oldest son and in 2011 after the birth of her twin children.

Burciaga had several performance-related issues during her employment. Howe began taking notes about Burciaga's employment on May 23, 2011, after she took a longer than normal lunch break without notifying him. He also noted an issue regarding an order that needed to be triggered, which he considered significant but not requiring a corrective action form. In February 2012, Burciaga made a shipping mistake by reshipping an order that had already been shipped, and Howe counseled her to take her time and ensure she entered orders correctly, warning her of the possibility of termination if she continued to make mistakes. 

In July 2012, Burciaga requested FMLA paperwork authorizing intermittent FMLA leave to care for her son, who had a medical condition requiring several medical appointments and a hospital stay. Her request was granted, and she took half days off related to appointments for her son on August 8, 2012; September 5, 2012; and September 6, 2012. However, it is unclear whether Howe was notified of Burciaga's FMLA leave at the time of the requests. Burciaga made a series of mistakes prior to her termination, including errors on September 16, 2012, September 11, 2012, September 18, 2012, and September 27, 2012. Howe met with Stephen Kramer, a controller at Ravago, to discuss the possibility of terminating Burciaga's employment due to her mistakes and poor performance. On September 28, 2012, Burciaga was informed that she was terminated from Ravago because of her mistakes and poor performance, with neither Howe nor Kramer making any reference to her FMLA leave or time missed during the termination process. Plaintiff alleges that she was discharged based on her use of FMLA leave, while Defendant contends that the termination was due to her poor performance and mistakes.

Rebecca Johnson, an African American woman, was employed at the Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities (CHRO) from 2004 to 2008 as an HRO Representative. During her employment, she alleges that she and several other women were subjected to verbal abuse and humiliation by the prior director, Hamisi Ingram, on the basis of gender, which ultimately led to her suspension. Following a series of actions, including a widely publicized hearing before the Connecticut legislature's Committee on Labor and Public Employees in May 2006, Johnson filed a federal court complaint for harassment, discrimination, and retaliation against CHRO and Ingram in 2007. The complaint resulted in a settlement favorable to her with both CHRO and Ingram.

Johnson left CHRO in 2008 to take a management role at Central Connecticut State University. Ten years later, in May and June 2018, she applied for the position of Regional Manager in two different CHRO regional offices but was not invited to interview for either position. Defendants Tanya Hughes, CHRO Executive Director, and Cheryl Sharp, CHRO Deputy Executive Director, both African American women, were involved in the hiring process. Hughes claims she did not participate in reviewing applications or determining which candidates would be interviewed but did review and approve the final selections. Sharp participated in the application review process, completed a checklist review for some candidates, and participated in candidate interviews and the selection memo.

Plaintiff Johnson alleges that she was qualified for the Regional Manager position and that the only reason Defendants could have had not to hire her was either racial discrimination or retaliation. Defendants contend that Johnson was not selected to interview because she lacked sufficient experience, rather than due to racial discrimination, and that neither Defendant could have retaliated against her because they lacked knowledge that Johnson applied for the regional manager positions or that she had engaged in protected activity. Johnson asserts that Hughes was aware of her prior lawsuit against CHRO and Ingram because they had conversations about it, and that the nature of the lawsuit was so publicized that "everyone in the agency knew about the suit." Defendants both claim they were unaware of Johnson's protected activity before the current lawsuit was brought.

In April 2017, Copot, a lawyer, started working at Stewart Title's office in Addison, Illinois, as a claims counsel, reviewing and issuing decisions on title insurance claims. He reported to Charity Makela, who in turn reported to McBee. In June 2018, Makela left the company, and Stewart Title promoted two female attorneys within the claims department. Kelly Rickenbach took over Makela's responsibilities, and Eleanor Sharpe became the managing counsel of Stewart Title's Addison office. 

Plaintiff Copot alleges that in the summer of 2018, Rickenbach informed him of a new company policy requiring employees in the claims department to obtain permission from management before attending continuing education classes, which he claims was not applied to female employees. Defendant Stewart Title contends that this policy was a legitimate business practice. In August 2018, Copot requested Rickenbach's permission to attend a continuing education class, and when she did not reply, he contacted Sharpe, who gave him permission to attend. 

Copot alleges that on August 24, 2018, he sought permission from Rickenbach to take sick days from August 27 to August 29 while he underwent and recovered from surgery, but Rickenbach denied his request and asked him to provide a "valid doctor's note indicating the illness and need to stay home." Copot claims that he had never heard of this policy and that two female employees who had taken lengthy sick leaves were also unaware of it. Defendant Rickenbach contends that the policy was a reasonable requirement for verifying employee absences. Copot also alleges that Rickenbach instructed him to deal with requests from customers that Stewart Title reconsider its claim decisions in a way that differed from the previous practice, and that he was not allowed to work from home, unlike two female claims counsel. Things came to a head in October 2018, when Copot met with Tonya Moseley, who told him that McBee, Rickenbach, and Sharpe had agreed to closely scrutinize his attendance, productivity, and work performance in retaliation for his refusal to provide documentation for his sick leave. On October 30, 2018, McBee and a senior HR director approached Copot's office, accompanied by two armed security guards, and terminated his employment, citing "poor job performance for not following claims handling procedures." 

Prior to his termination, Copot had sent an email to the HR department alleging sex discrimination and an unlawful sick leave policy, and had asked to speak with an HR representative. After his termination, Copot filed a claim for unemployment benefits with the Illinois Department of Employment Security and a complaint alleging violations of the Illinois Employee Sick Leave Act with the Illinois Department of Labor. He also cross-filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the Illinois Department of Human Rights (IDHR), alleging retaliation and discrimination based on sex. The EEOC dismissed his charge and gave him notice of his right to sue, leading to the filing of this lawsuit.

In late 2019 to early 2020, Defendants HCS, a staffing company, and its Vice President of Construction, Robert Burns, hired Plaintiffs Clifford Michel, Guerda Louis, and Ralph Frederic, all of whom identify as Black and Haitian, to work as Module Installers on the Rambler Solar Project in San Angelo, Texas. The project, which covers over 1,700 acres with 733,000 solar panels, was supervised by Foreman Phillip Sirrat. Plaintiffs allege that Sirrat made discriminatory comments on a regular basis, including comments like “these fucking Haitians” and “these people are stupid” in reference to Black, Caribbean, Jamaican, and Haitian employees. They further allege that Sirrat would regularly terminate Black employees and created a hostile work environment.

Around April 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic swept the nation, Defendants shut down the worksite for COVID testing. Plaintiffs allege that, about four days after the test results came back, Defendants called back most white and Hispanic workers while laying off the Haitian, Jamaican, and Black workers. Plaintiffs also allege that an in-house recruiter named Jean Brisseau told Michel via text that the foreman for the Rambler Solar Project was instructed to fire all Caribbean and Black people at all sites. Michel later discovered that Defendants also terminated 50 other Black, Caribbean, Jamaican, and Haitian employees at or around the same time. Plaintiffs allege that 15 Black employees returned to work for Defendants, while the other 35, including Plaintiffs, did not.

Defendants contend that, following the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, HCS implemented various safety requirements for social distancing, wearing masks, and handwashing. They claim that members of the Haitian crew, which included Plaintiffs, were observed violating the quarantine and isolation orders in place, and that the project’s subcontractor, Arraycon, requested removal of the crew. Defendants also offer evidence that the Haitian crew was the only crew seen breaching COVID protocols, and that most positive cases were concentrated within the Haitian installer crew. As a result, HCS removed the crew from the Rambler site on May 12, 2020, at the direction of Arraycon, and immediately worked to get the Haitian workers reassigned to other projects. Plaintiffs contend that Defendants’ stated reason for the terminations—COVID-19 safety violations—was a pretextual basis for race-based discrimination.

Joseph Graham, an employee of Bodine Electric Company, alleges that he was discriminated against by the company due to his race when he was not promoted. Graham filed a two-count complaint in August 1990, with Count I brought under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Count II brought under 42 U.S.C. § 1981. The company, Bodine Electric, argues that Graham does not have a viable Section 1981 claim under the tests enunciated by the United States Supreme Court in Patterson v. McLean Credit Union. Graham contends that the Patterson decision does not apply to his case because it was effectively overruled by the Civil Rights Act of 1991, which was passed on November 21, 1991. 

Graham alleges that he was subjected to racial discrimination by Bodine Electric, which led to his non-promotion. Bodine Electric contends that it did not discriminate against Graham and that its actions were lawful under the applicable laws at the time. The parties disagree on whether the 1991 Act applies to Graham's case, which was pending at the time the Act was passed. Graham claims that the 1991 Act should be applied retroactively, while Bodine Electric argues that it should only be applied prospectively. 

The dispute between Graham and Bodine Electric began when Graham was not promoted, leading him to file his complaint in August 1990. The case has been ongoing since then, with the parties exchanging arguments and evidence. The court must now decide whether the 1991 Act applies to Graham's case, which will determine the outcome of his Section 1981 claim. The legislative history of the 1991 Act and the principles of statutory construction will be crucial in determining the intent of Congress regarding the retroactive application of the Act.

Glenn Duckworth was employed by Mid-State Machine Products as a Gage Control Technician from 1995 until 2002, when his employment was terminated due to a workforce reduction, not his performance. At the time of his termination, Mid-State informed him that he was eligible to be rehired. Between May and July 2005, Mr. Duckworth contacted Mid-State about re-employment but was not hired. Instead, Mid-State hired a 26-year-old applicant for a Gage Control Technician position on July 6, 2005. Mr. Duckworth alleges that this 26-year-old was significantly less qualified for the position than he was.

In April 2008, Mr. Duckworth, then 60 years old, applied to Mid-State for the advertised position of Gage Control Technician. He was interviewed for the position, but claims that Mid-State's managers treated him with hostility and incorrectly told him that his work quality from 1995 to 2002 was poor. A Mid-State manager informed him that the company was looking to hire someone who would be with the company for a long time. Mid-State did not hire Mr. Duckworth for this position and instead hired someone 34 years old, who Mr. Duckworth contends was less qualified than him.

Plaintiff alleges that Mid-State's decision not to hire him in 2005 and 2008 was motivated by age discrimination. Defendant contends that Mr. Duckworth never actually applied for the Gage Control Technician position in 2005 and that there was no open position for a Gage Control Technician in 2005 since Mid-State only posted the position internally. Mid-State also claims that even if Mr. Duckworth made out a prima facie case, he failed to prove that age was the "but-for" cause of Mid-State's decision not to hire him in 2005 and 2008. Mr. Duckworth responds that he has sustained his burden to make out a prima facie case of age discrimination in 2008 and that Mid-State's explanations for its decision are pretexts.

Plaintiff, a former employee of Pro Custom Solar, LLC ("Momentum"), worked at the company's New Jersey call center. Plaintiff alleges that he and other Black employees were regularly subjected to racial hostility and disparate treatment by Defendants, including Momentum's Director of Inside Sales, Jeffrey Anclien, and Manager of Inside Sales, Brian Alper. Plaintiff contends that Anclien and Alper had the authority to control and alter the terms and conditions of all employees who worked at Momentum. According to Plaintiff, the discriminatory treatment included highly offensive and patently racist comments, lower pay than similarly situated white employees, and reprisals.

Plaintiff alleges that he and other Black call center employees were paid less than their white counterparts and were subjected to a hostile work environment. Plaintiff further contends that when he and other Black employees complained about the discriminatory treatment, they faced retaliation from Defendants. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that certain of Plaintiff's proposed amendments to his complaint are futile, implying that they dispute the allegations of discrimination and retaliation.

Prior to filing the lawsuit, Plaintiff worked at Momentum's New Jersey call center, where he allegedly experienced the discriminatory treatment. The events giving rise to the lawsuit occurred during Plaintiff's employment at Momentum, although the exact dates are not specified. Plaintiff filed his initial Complaint on October 22, 2019, and later filed an Amended Complaint on April 2, 2021, adding claims under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Other former employees, including Alissa Winfrey, Ahmed Sunkins, O'Neil Hall, and Basil Oguekwe, have also come forward with similar allegations of discrimination and retaliation against Defendants.

Sandra Mohamed, a plaintiff, worked for the Atlantic County Special Services School District. Plaintiff alleges she was unlawfully discriminated against, harassed, and retaliated against in the workplace because of her race, color, national origin, and/or disabilities, and because of her repeated complaints concerning such conduct. Plaintiff contends that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and was terminated in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination, and the New Jersey Conscientious Employee Protection Act. 

Plaintiff filed a complaint against the School District and Eric Flecken, asserting various claims arising out of the alleged discrimination and retaliation. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the School District being the employer and Mohamed being the employee. The nature of the dispute is centered around the alleged discriminatory and retaliatory actions taken by the School District against Mohamed. 

Defendant School District contends that plaintiff is attempting to use her motion for pro bono counsel to further delay the case. Defendant argues that plaintiff deliberately failed to provide discovery responses by the Court-Ordered deadline and instead chose to file the motion. Defendant also contests plaintiff's basis for her request for counsel, which it argues is unsupported by the record and insufficient to justify granting plaintiff's motion. Plaintiff, on the other hand, alleges that she is unfamiliar with the law and does not have the full ability to present an effective case, and that financial and employment issues have prevented her from pursuing the case or obtaining counsel. Relevant pre-litigation events include plaintiff's repeated complaints concerning the alleged discriminatory conduct, and her subsequent termination. Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff had contacted the Atlantic County Bar Association Lawyer Referral Service in an attempt to find counsel, as advised by the Court.

Alicia Martinez was hired by MSNBC Cable LLC as an associate producer in May 1996, at a salary of $47,000 per annum, after informing the hiring executive, Bob Epstein, that she was pregnant. She took maternity leave in November 1996 and returned to work part-time in March 1997 as a producer in the tape acquisitions group, a higher-level position than her initial role. Martinez decided to breastfeed her son and, with the consent of her supervisor, Pat Walker, pumped breast milk three times a day in an empty edit room at MSNBC's New Jersey studio. However, she became upset when someone tried to enter the room while she was inside on several occasions. Martinez raised concerns about her privacy with MSNBC's human resources officials and rejected suggestions to put a "do not disturb" sign on the door or use alternative sites for pumping.

Plaintiff alleges that Walker became less accommodating of her scheduling concerns, which revolved around her childcare needs, starting in August 1997. Martinez contends that she was told she would have to work weekends and take a pay cut if she moved back to an associate producer position, which she felt would not meet her needs. Defendant contends that Martinez was offered alternative positions and schedules, but she rejected them. Martinez also complains of three occasions on which a male co-worker allegedly made offensive comments regarding her breast pumping. In September 1997, MSNBC notified Martinez that she would be moved to an associate producer position with a fixed schedule, which she felt was not suitable for her needs. Martinez took a medical leave in October and, upon her return, was permitted to take off every Saturday until she resigned on December 12, 1997.

Martinez claims that she experienced difficulties with her schedule and privacy while pumping breast milk at work, and that her complaints to human resources were followed by retaliatory conduct, including verbal harassment and schedule changes. Defendant contends that it provided Martinez with accommodations for her breast pumping needs and that her schedule changes were due to business needs. Martinez filed a charge of discrimination with the EEOC in April 1998, alleging that MSNBC failed to provide her with a safe and private area to breast pump and that she was subjected to retaliatory conduct. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of discrimination and retaliation under the Americans with Disabilities Act and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.

A class of black production-and-maintenance (P & M) workers at the Fairless Works of United States Steel (USS) claim to have been discriminated against by USS and the United Steelworkers of America and its locals (the union). The plaintiffs allege that USS and the union have engaged in discriminatory practices, including transfer, initial assignment, and discipline, which have resulted in unequal treatment of black workers. The plaintiffs contend that the union has failed to bargain away these discriminatory practices and has acquiesced in USS's discriminatory actions. 

The union argues that it cannot be held liable for USS's actions, citing the decision in International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. United States. The plaintiffs, on the other hand, claim that the union's failure to negotiate for non-discriminatory treatment and its acquiescence in USS's discriminatory practices make it liable under Title VII. The plaintiffs point to cases such as Macklin v. Spector Freight Systems and Hairston v. McLean Trucking Co., which have held unions liable for similar actions.

The dispute between the parties began at the Fairless Works of USS, where the plaintiffs are employed. The plaintiffs claim that they have been subjected to discriminatory practices, including being assigned to less desirable jobs and being disciplined more harshly than non-black workers. The union, which represents the plaintiffs, has allegedly failed to address these issues through collective bargaining. The plaintiffs have presented evidence of statistical disparities in treatment between black and non-black workers, which they claim demonstrates a pattern of discrimination. The union has responded with evidence of its own, including testimony from its representatives and documents related to collective bargaining negotiations.

Nayda Echevarria Vazquez was a housekeeping employee at a hotel in Puerto Rico, where she allegedly experienced sexual harassment. Plaintiff Echevarria alleges that she was subjected to sexual harassment while working at the hotel, which was operated by Hyatt Hotels of Puerto Rico, Inc. and Hyatt Vacation Ownership, Inc. Echevarria contends that she filed a timely administrative claim with the EEOC, naming her employer as Hyatt Hacienda del Mar, which is the name under which Defendants do business. Defendants Hyatt Hotels and Hyatt Vacation contend that Echevarria failed to name them in her administrative charge, and therefore, her claims against them should be dismissed. 

Echevarria alleges that she saw references to her employer as Hyatt Hotels of Puerto Rico, Inc., Hyatt Dorado Beach Corp., HR Cerromar Beach, Hyatt Vacation Ownership, Inc., Hyatt Vacation Club, and Cerromar Development Partnership, L.P.S.E. in various documents and stationery. She also alleges that Defendants repeatedly represented themselves as Hyatt Hacienda del Mar to her. Echevarria further alleges that Defendants were notified of the EEOC proceedings at their proper address, albeit through the name Hyatt Hacienda del Mar, and that they made an appearance at the proceedings through counsel Edwin J. Guillot. 

Defendants Hyatt Hotels and Hyatt Vacation, on the other hand, contend that Echevarria's failure to include them in her administrative charge requires that her claims against them be dismissed, as they were not named in the charge and did not participate in the investigation, conciliation, or other administrative proceedings. The parties disagree on whether there is substantial identity between Hyatt Hacienda del Mar and Hyatt Hotels and Hyatt Vacation, with Echevarria arguing that there is substantial identity and Defendants arguing that there is not.

John E. Peet, a Black man, lived at the New Orleans Court apartment complex in Richfield, Minnesota, from January 15, 2011, to February 2, 2013. During his time at the complex, Peet had several conflicts with the management, including Sue Morfitt, the community manager, and Mark Jones, the Chief Manager of Highland Management Group, which operates the complex. Peet alleges that Morfitt and Jones discriminated against him based on his race. 

Plaintiff Peet alleges that he was subjected to harassment by a White tenant, GZ, who lived in an apartment above him, and that Morfitt and Jones failed to address his complaints about the harassment. Peet contends that he complained to Morfitt, the police, and other authorities about GZ's behavior, but that they did not take adequate action to stop the harassment. Defendant Morfitt, on the other hand, contends that she did address Peet's complaints, but that Peet's behavior was also a problem, and that he was often aggressive and confrontational. Morfitt issued Peet several lease violations, including one for his behavior towards GZ and another for refusing to allow a carpenter to enter his apartment to inspect his patio door.

Peet also had conflicts with Morfitt and Jones over issues with his apartment, including cold air coming in through his patio door and windows. Peet alleges that Morfitt and Jones did not adequately address these issues, and that they postponed replacing his windows. Morfitt, however, contends that she did attempt to address Peet's concerns, and that she even offered to mutually terminate his lease, which Peet declined. The conflict between Peet and GZ escalated in August and September 2012, and Morfitt eventually issued Peet a lease violation on September 12, 2012, after Peet allegedly made racial slurs and threatened GZ. Around the same time, the Regional Property Manager, Shari McDonald, decided not to renew Peet's lease when it expired in January 2013, although Peet was not informed of this decision at the time. 

The City Defendants, Debbie Goettel, the former Mayor of Richfield, and Michelle Luna, a former employee of the Richfield Housing and Redevelopment Authority, are also involved in the case. Peet alleges that they failed to address his complaints about the harassment and discrimination he experienced at the New Orleans Court complex. The New Orleans Court Defendants, Morfitt and Jones, contend that they did not discriminate against Peet and that they took reasonable steps to address his complaints. The City Defendants, Goettel and Luna, contend that they did not have any involvement in the management of the complex and that they did not discriminate against Peet.

The White Marsh Institute (WMI) was established in March 1997 by Walter Smith and Neal Berch to provide methadone treatment services to individuals with opiate addiction in the White Marsh area of Baltimore County. Plaintiff alleges that there is a pressing need for additional methadone treatment facilities in the County due to an "escalating heroin problem." WMI located office space for its program at 11450 Pulaski Highway in a small strip shopping center and applied to the Baltimore County Department of Permits and Development Management (Permits Department) for a use permit. Initially, the department issued a permit authorizing the use as an "outpatient counseling center," but later withdrew it when WMI requested that it be amended to identify the approved use as a methadone treatment program.

Defendant contends that the County has a "special policy" regarding methadone facilities, which requires them to undergo a public hearing to determine the category of use and/or to obtain a special exception as a community care center. Defendant asserts that this policy is due to the "unique risks associated with methadone dispensation," including the problem of methadone diversion. In contrast, Defendant admits that non-methadone drug treatment facilities are routinely classified as "medical offices" and permitted to operate as of right in B.R. zones without undergoing a public hearing. WMI alleges that it should have been permitted as of right to use the Pulaski Highway property for its methadone treatment program, as it fits the definitions of both "medical office" and "medical clinic" under the County's zoning regulations.

The Permits Department told WMI that it would have to undergo a public hearing to determine if it qualified as a community care center, and WMI subsequently filed a petition for a special exception under this classification. WMI entered into an agreement with a non-profit organization to "sponsor" its methadone treatment program in order to satisfy the requirements for a "community care center." A mandatory hearing on WMI's special exception petition was scheduled, but was postponed at the request of citizens who opposed WMI's plans to operate a methadone clinic at the Pulaski Highway location. Plaintiff alleges that a "firestorm of opposition erupted" from local residents, civic organizations, and politicians when WMI's plans became known, and that this opposition was fueled by discriminatory attitudes towards individuals with disabilities, including those with opiate addiction.

From March 2006 to January 2010, Georgetown University Hospital employed Patricia Wheeler as a registered nurse in the "4 East" department. Wheeler's responsibilities included providing direct patient care and communicating patient information to the medical team, patients, and their families. The hospital has various rules and policies governing patient treatment and information sharing. Wheeler was supervised by Angela Hollandsworth starting in March 2007, and the two often had disagreements. Hollandsworth gave Wheeler formal warnings regarding her work performance on at least two occasions prior to December 27, 2009, including incidents where Wheeler allegedly withheld medication, failed to change a patient's IV dressing, and missed work.

On December 27, 2009, Wheeler was floated to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) due to staffing needs. During her shift, four other nurses expressed concerns about Wheeler's treatment of her patients, including allegations that she had administered the wrong medication, neglected to give a patient insulin, failed to record vital signs, and left a patient unattended and soiled. These incidents were reported to Hollandsworth, who suspended Wheeler pending an investigation. Hollandsworth interviewed the nurses who reported the incidents and asked Wheeler to provide a written explanation. After reviewing the information, Hollandsworth and the hospital's Human Resources Department determined that Wheeler's actions warranted termination.

Plaintiff alleges that she was fired due to racial discrimination, claiming that white nurses who engaged in similar misconduct were not fired or reprimanded. Defendant contends that Wheeler's termination was based on her performance issues, including the incidents on December 27, 2009, and her history of disciplinary problems. Wheeler filed a complaint with the EEOC on January 7, 2010, and later filed formal charges with the EEOC and D.C. Office of Human Rights, leading to this litigation. Wheeler claims that white nurses, such as C.S., K.M., W.L., and A.A., engaged in comparable misconduct without facing disciplinary action, and that two nurses, B.D. and C.R., were not fired after their actions resulted in a patient's death.

Jerry Painadath was employed as a "clinical nurse 2" at Philadelphia Post-Acute Partners, LLC, doing business as Good Shepherd Penn Partners (GSPP). During his employment, Painadath reported several patient safety-related incidents, including finding a full vial of Naropin near a patient's bedside table, witnessing a GSPP employee use "excessive force" on a patient, and observing a "neglect situation" involving an older, African American patient. He reported the neglect to a clinical coordinator, "Mrs. Susan," who allegedly told him she would "secure [his] job" if he would "lie down" for her. Despite this, Painadath claims he was suspended "in retaliation" for reporting the neglect. He also gave an oral report of the neglect to the local area of aging in November 2021.

Painadath alleges that after reporting these incidents, GSPP employees became increasingly hostile toward him, and he suffered from emotional stress, was "assaulted and called names" by coworkers, and was "left with notice" for reporting the alleged bad behavior by a coworker. His medical coverage was "revoked without warning" a couple of weeks after his suspension. Painadath filed a complaint pursuant to the Affordable Care Act (ACA) with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) on December 5, 2021, and was fired nine days later, on December 14, 2021. Plaintiff alleges that GSPP violated the Pennsylvania Older Adults Protective Services Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Affordable Care Act.

GSPP contends that Painadath's reports and complaints were not protected activity and that his suspension and termination were not retaliatory. GSPP also argues that Painadath's claims under Title VII are time-barred and that he has not alleged sufficient facts to establish a hostile work environment or disparate treatment based on his sex or religion. Painadath, on the other hand, alleges that GSPP disregarded his patient safety submissions because he is a Catholic male, whereas it "acted swiftly and responsibly" to submissions by females and non-Catholics. He claims that he was discriminated against and retaliated against for reporting patient safety incidents and for his protected activity under the ACA.

Carlos D. Robles, the plaintiff, was diagnosed with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) in 1993 or 1994 and began taking Atripla to treat his condition, which caused side effects including mood swings. In 1996, Robles was hired by Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center (the Center) as a patient specialist and coder in the hospital's OB-GYN department, and he informed his supervisors of his HIV diagnosis. He was later promoted to a position in the pediatrics unit, first as a patient accounts representative and then as a patient services specialist (PSS), where his responsibilities included scheduling appointments, preparing paperwork, and maintaining records.

Plaintiff alleges that he experienced difficulties due to his HIV diagnosis and the side effects of Atripla, and he requested multiple leaves of absence under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA), which were granted. However, Defendant contends that these requests were not associated with his HIV diagnosis. Robles also made two unwritten requests to a supervisor for a reasonable accommodation, specifically a transfer to an operator position in the pediatrics unit's call center, but these requests were not granted. Defendant asserts that no alternative accommodations were proposed by Robles or his supervisor.

During his employment as a PSS, Robles was disciplined on multiple occasions, including a disciplinary counseling in 2011 for turning away a patient without consulting with the clinic facilitator, a Letter of Disciplinary Reprimand in 2011 for insubordination and failing to register a patient, and a Letter of Final Warning in 2011 for refusing service to patients and being insubordinate to supervisors. He was also informally counseled in 2013 for unacceptable behavior towards a coworker and received another Letter of Final Warning in 2013 for incidents involving a newborn patient and a coworker. The final incident occurred in 2013, when Robles told a parent that the Center would not see her children due to their primary physician's departure, and he was subsequently terminated on September 24, 2013. Plaintiff alleges that his termination was due to his disability, while Defendant contends that it was due to his misconduct and poor performance.

In late 2019 to early 2020, Defendants HCS, a staffing company, and its Vice President of Construction, Robert Burns, hired Plaintiffs Clifford Michel, Guerda Louis, and Ralph Frederic, all of whom identify as Black and Haitian, to work as Module Installers on the Rambler Solar Project in San Angelo, Texas. The project, which covers over 1,700 acres with 733,000 solar panels, was supervised by Foreman Phillip Sirrat. Plaintiffs allege that Sirrat made discriminatory comments on a regular basis, including comments like “these fucking Haitians” and “these people are stupid” in reference to Black, Caribbean, Jamaican, and Haitian employees. They further allege that Sirrat would regularly terminate Black employees and created a hostile work environment.

Around April 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic swept the nation, Defendants shut down the worksite for COVID testing. Plaintiffs allege that, about four days after the test results came back, Defendants called back most white and Hispanic workers while laying off the Haitian, Jamaican, and Black workers. Plaintiffs also allege that an in-house recruiter named Jean Brisseau told Michel via text that the foreman for the Rambler Solar Project was instructed to fire all Caribbean and Black people at all sites. Michel later discovered that Defendants also terminated 50 other Black, Caribbean, Jamaican, and Haitian employees at or around the same time. Plaintiffs allege that 15 Black employees returned to work for Defendants, while the other 35, including Plaintiffs, did not.

Defendants contend that, following the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, HCS implemented various safety requirements for social distancing, wearing masks, and handwashing. They claim that members of the Haitian crew, which included Plaintiffs, were observed violating the quarantine and isolation orders in place, and that the project’s subcontractor, Arraycon, requested removal of the crew. Defendants also offer evidence that the Haitian crew was the only crew seen breaching COVID protocols, and that most positive cases were concentrated within the Haitian installer crew. As a result, HCS removed the crew from the Rambler site on May 12, 2020, at the direction of Arraycon, and immediately worked to get the Haitian workers reassigned to other projects. Plaintiffs contend that Defendants’ stated reason for the terminations—COVID-19 safety violations—was a pretextual basis for race-based discrimination.

St. Luke's Methodist Hospital, a hospital-based skilled nursing facility (HB-SNF) in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, provided atypical services to Medicare patients in 1992. Plaintiff alleges that its costs for these services exceeded the applicable cost limits, and it is entitled to reimbursement for these costs under 42 C.F.R. § 413.30. Defendant contends that St. Luke's is not eligible for reimbursement because its costs did not exceed 112% of the peer group mean for HB-SNFs, as required by the Provider Reimbursement Manual (PRM) § 2534.5. 

Prior to 1992, St. Luke's had been granted exceptions to the cost limits for providing atypical services, but the Secretary of Health and Human Services had reinterpreted the regulation in PRM § 2534.5, effectively raising the threshold for exception eligibility. St. Luke's alleges that this reinterpretation is arbitrary, capricious, and not in accordance with law. The parties agree that the relevant facts are undisputed, and the dispute centers on the validity of PRM § 2534.5. 

The Medicare program reimburses skilled nursing facilities for the "reasonable cost" of covered services, and 42 C.F.R. § 413.30 provides for exceptions to the cost limits for facilities that provide atypical services. The regulation requires that the services be necessary for the special needs of the patients and be furnished efficiently. The Secretary had previously granted exceptions to St. Luke's based on its actual costs exceeding the routine cost limit (RCL), but the new interpretation in PRM § 2534.5 requires that the costs exceed 112% of the peer group mean. St. Luke's contends that its costs for 1992 exceeded the RCL but not the new threshold, and it is seeking reimbursement for the difference. Defendant argues that the new interpretation is a valid exercise of the Secretary's discretion and that St. Luke's does not meet the new criteria for exception eligibility.

Tom and Debbie Reynolds, an interracial couple, own a property in Mueller Ranch, an unincorporated subdivision in El Paso County, Colorado. In August 1998, they became the record owners of the site and began making plans to build a home on the property in October 1998. The Reynolds submitted four different sets of architectural plans to the Architectural Committee (AC) for approval between January 2000 and November 2000, all of which were rejected. The Reynolds claim that the rejections were not due to any legitimate problems with the plans, but because Tom Reynolds is African American. 

Plaintiff Debbie Reynolds was appointed a member of the AC and elected Secretary of the Homeowners Association (HOA) on October 20, 1998. The parties dispute the actual process of architectural plan approval as practiced by the AC. During Debbie Reynolds' tenure on the AC, no architectural plans for homes were submitted apart from those submitted by her husband. However, Defendant Mr. Witte submitted plans for his home just before Debbie Reynolds was appointed to the AC, and his home was built between October 1998 and February 1999. In August 1999, Defendant Phred Jahner stopped by the Reynolds' home to have plans for a loafing shed approved, which was done informally. The Reynolds attempted to follow this same informal process in seeking approval for their house plans.
