The Reynolds allege that they were subjected to special surveillance, had property stolen from their lot, caught Defendant Phred Jahner on their property, and some of their property was vandalized after they sought approval of their building plans. They reported these incidents to the police. Plaintiff alleges that the AC's rejection of their plans and the incidents of vandalism and surveillance were motivated by discriminatory intent, specifically because Tom Reynolds is African American. Defendants contend that the rejections were due to the inadequacy of the plans and that they treated the Reynolds fairly and in accordance with the covenants and procedures of the HOA. The Defendants also point out that other homeowners in Mueller Ranch submitted plans for structures other than houses, which were approved, while the Reynolds' plans for similar structures were rejected due to nonconformance with the covenants and submission of plans not in accordance with procedure.

Satheesh Tummala, a 44-year-old man of Indian national origin, was employed as an IT Specialist at the U.S. Army Armament Research, Development & Engineering Center (ARDEC) from August 25, 2014, to April 24, 2015. He was supervised by Brian Coombs, Scott Miller, and George Albinson. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, his supervisors and colleagues made comments about his age on several occasions. He also claims that he was given a heavier workload compared to other IT specialists between September 2014 and April 2015.

Plaintiff alleges that he experienced several incidents of harassment and retaliation, including having his login credentials changed without his knowledge, being introduced to the team with false information, and being blamed for delayed tasks. He reported his supervisor, Coombs, for allegedly misusing government time and resources, but was told that these were ethical issues and that he should not discuss them further. Plaintiff also alleges that his colleague, Chou, intentionally misguided him on tasks, yelled at him in front of the team, and asked him to leave a meeting. Additionally, Plaintiff claims that he was denied the opportunity to study for a professional exam during work hours and was ultimately terminated on April 23, 2015, for refusing to complete an assigned task and questioning his workload.

Defendant contends that Plaintiff was terminated for legitimate reasons, including his refusal to complete an assigned task and his failure to be a cooperative team player. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of employment discrimination based on age and national origin. Prior to his termination, Plaintiff had filed a complaint with the EEO office on June 24, 2015, which was later appealed to the Office of Federal Operations (OFO). The OFO issued a decision denying the appeal on March 31, 2022. Relevant pre-litigation events include the incidents of alleged harassment and retaliation, as well as the communications and meetings between Plaintiff and his supervisors and colleagues.

Richard Pearson, an inmate, was housed at the State Correctional Institution at Graterford on three separate occasions, in 1994, 1995, and 1996. In March 1994, while imprisoned at Graterford in general population, he was stabbed six times by several inmates in a hallway corridor and hospitalized as a result of his injuries. The Graterford Program Review Committee subsequently determined that he should be removed from, and never returned to, the general population at Graterford due to the danger of another attack on his life. 

In August or September 1994, Pearson was transferred to the State Correctional Institution at Dallas and subsequently paroled. However, in February 1995, he was arrested for a parole violation and housed at Graterford for approximately 2-3 weeks without incident before being transferred to the State Correctional Institution Camp Hill for classification. At Camp Hill, Pearson signed two Acknowledgment of Orientation forms indicating he did not need separation from any named inmates, as he did not know the names of the inmates from whom he needed to be separated and believed his enemies were housed at Graterford.

On February 8, 1996, Pearson was moved from Dallas to Graterford for a parole board hearing and placed in the general population on B-Block, where Defendant Murray was the Unit Manager. Pearson told Murray about the 1994 assault at Graterford, and Murray assured him he would be double-locked in his cell until he left Graterford. However, after the parole board hearing on February 9, 1996, Pearson discovered his cell was no longer double-locked, and he again expressed his concerns to Murray, requesting to be returned to Dallas or double-locked in his cell or placed in administrative custody. Murray allegedly responded that Pearson had been cleared for admittance into the general population and did not need administrative custody.

On February 21, 1996, Pearson was stabbed in the prison law library by three unknown inmates, resulting in three puncture wounds. Following the incident, he was treated and then placed in administrative custody. After his release from medical hold, Pearson was returned to Dallas. Plaintiff alleges that the Graterford officials, including Superintendent Donald Vaughn, Deputy Superintendents William Widner and Thomas Stachelek, and Unit Manager John Murray, failed to protect him against the attack, violating his Eighth Amendment rights by housing him in the general population despite knowing the danger he faced.

Defendant Vaughn and Murray contend that Pearson failed to exhaust his available administrative remedies as required by the Prison Litigation Reform Act. They argue that Pearson's claims should be dismissed due to this failure. Pearson, however, claims that he did file a grievance on February 9, 1996, asking to be removed from general population and placed in administrative custody, and that the grievance coordinator, Mary Ann Williams, responded on February 27, 1996, stating his custody level was not addressable under the grievance process. Pearson argues that this response indicates he substantially complied with the administrative remedy scheme, as he was told his grievance regarding custody was not addressable, similar to a case where an inmate was told a grievance was closed and did not have the right to appeal. 

Pearson also filed another grievance on March 4, 1996, requesting to be returned to Dallas due to safety concerns, but this was denied, with Williams stating he would remain at Graterford until his medical hold was lifted. Pearson did not appeal this decision. The defendants argue that Pearson's failure to exhaust his administrative remedies, including not filing to final review a grievance appeal claiming he should have been placed in administrative custody or transferred, mandates dismissal of the action. Pearson, however, maintains that he has substantially complied with the grievance procedure, having followed the instructions given by Williams to speak to his counselor about his custody concerns.

On July 5, 2016, plaintiff was hired by defendant as a social worker in the foster care unit at New Hanover County Department of Social Services (NHCDSS). Plaintiff had been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), which substantially limited his ability to concentrate, think, interact with others, work, and sleep. As a social worker, one of plaintiff's primary tasks was to reunify families. However, unlike his previous employer, plaintiff's position with defendant required him to work solely during business hours in a cubical setting amongst other social workers, which he found distracting and difficult to perform his duties, including timely completion of necessary paperwork.

Plaintiff alleges that he attempted to alleviate some of the distraction of the work setting by working partially from home, but was advised that working from home was against company policy. However, plaintiff later learned that defendant allowed other employees to work from home. On August 29, 2016, plaintiff emailed Mark Francolini, defendant's chief human resources officer, informing him of his disability and requesting an accommodation. Defendant contends that it provided accommodations for plaintiff's ADHD, including moving him to a different office shared with another coworker and issuing a noise-cancelling headset on October 18, 2016. 

Plaintiff alleges that these accommodations were ineffective, as the office was small and the headset did not fit properly, and that he informed defendant of this but received no response. Plaintiff had also suggested being transferred to an after-hours position in child protective services as an accommodation, but defendant advised that the position required a master's degree in social work, which plaintiff did not have, and refused to waive the education requirement. Defendant contends that plaintiff was terminated on December 6, 2016, due to performance deficiencies addressed during prior feedback sessions with his supervisors.

Bilan Nur, a Muslim woman, immigrated to the United States from Somalia in 1998. In November 1999, she was hired by Alamo as a rental agent at a location on East Washington Street in Phoenix, Arizona. Her duties included renting cars to customers, accepting payment, and answering the telephone, all of which required interaction with clients. Until the events leading to her termination, Ms. Nur's job performance was "fine." Alamo had a "Dress Smart Policy" in place, which aimed to promote a favorable first impression with customers and prohibited employees from wearing certain clothing and accessories, such as more than one earring, open-toe shoes, and half-grown beards. The policy did not explicitly prohibit the wearing of head coverings, but Alamo contends that it prohibited any "garment or item of outer clothing not specifically mentioned in the policy."

In November 2001, during the Muslim holiday of Ramadan, Ms. Nur requested permission from Alamo's City Manager, Victor Bellavia, to wear a head covering at work. Bellavia contacted Alamo's Human Resource Manager, Heather Phillips, who instructed him that Ms. Nur could wear a head covering in the back of the office but would need to remove it while at the rental counter. Alamo did not excuse Ms. Nur from working at the rental counter during Ramadan. On December 1, 2001, Ms. Nur was given a "Counselling Review" for wearing a veil over her hair, and she was told to clock out and discuss the issue with the City Manager. The next day, she received another Counselling Review, was suspended, and was advised to discuss the issue with the City Manager. On December 3, 2001, Ms. Nur received another counselling review, was suspended pending investigation, and was told to return on December 6, 2001, to meet with the City Manager. On December 6, 2001, Alamo terminated Ms. Nur's employment for violating company rules, and the termination form indicated that she was not eligible for re-hire.

Plaintiff alleges that Alamo discriminated against Ms. Nur based on her religion by not accommodating her request to wear a head covering during Ramadan. Alamo contends that it did not discriminate against Ms. Nur and that her religious beliefs did not conflict with her job requirements. Alamo also points to evidence that during Ramadan in 2000, Ms. Nur was asked to remove her head covering and complied without asserting a religious need to object, which Alamo argues raises questions about the sincerity of Ms. Nur's religious beliefs in 2001. The EEOC filed a complaint on September 27, 2002, on behalf of Ms. Nur, asserting a claim of religious discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The matter was stayed due to Alamo's bankruptcy filing but was later lifted, and the EEOC filed a motion for partial summary judgment regarding liability on its religious discrimination claim.

Kishna Brown, an employee of the United States Postal Service, alleges she was subject to discrimination and harassment at her workplace. Plaintiff alleges that she suffered discriminatory and harassing treatment, but the specific details of these incidents are not provided. Defendant Amy Puhalski, presumably a representative or employee of the United States Postal Service, was initially named as a defendant in the lawsuit. The United States Postal Service is also a defendant in the case. 

Plaintiff Brown filed her complaint without the assistance of counsel and was granted leave to proceed without prepayment of the filing fee. The lawsuit was referred to a Magistrate Judge, who issued a report recommending that the court grant Defendant Puhalski's motion to dismiss. Although Plaintiff Brown was granted an extension of time to respond to the motion, she did not file any response. The remaining defendants, presumably including the United States Postal Service, later filed a motion to dismiss, to which Plaintiff Brown also did not respond initially. However, after the Magistrate Judge issued a second report recommending the court grant the motion to dismiss, Plaintiff Brown filed objections.

The Magistrate Judge concluded that Plaintiff Brown had not named the correct defendant in the lawsuit, as Title VII requires employees of the United States Postal Service to sue the head of the United States Postal Service, specifically Postmaster General Louis DeJoy. Plaintiff Brown's objections to the report and recommendation did not address this issue, instead outlining and summarizing the discrimination and harassment she allegedly suffered, and attaching letters from third parties attesting to these incidents. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the United States Postal Service being the employer and Kishna Brown being the employee. The nature of the dispute is a claim of discrimination and harassment under Title VII. Defendant contends that the correct defendant was not named in the lawsuit, while Plaintiff alleges that she was subject to discriminatory and harassing treatment. Relevant pre-litigation events include the alleged incidents of discrimination and harassment, as well as any internal complaints or reports made by Plaintiff Brown to the United States Postal Service.

The city of Hampton has a councilmanic electoral system where seven members, including the mayor, are elected at large. Plaintiffs, who are minority voters, claim that this system dilutes their voting power and that the city maintains it with the purpose of discriminating against black voters. They seek a new electoral plan that utilizes a ward system. In 1994, the city appointed a Charter Review Commission to recommend a redistricting plan. The commission recommended a 6-2-1 plan, which was rejected by the city council in favor of a 2-2-3 plan. The city council adopted this plan in September 1995, but it requires amendment of the city charter and preclearance by the Department of Justice, which was declined in November 1995. 

Plaintiffs allege that the 2-2-3 plan was adopted to protect incumbents, as it allows them to run unopposed by other incumbents. Defendants contend that the plan is lawful and that the city council acted in good faith. The city council members claim that their personal notes and files are protected by testimonial legislative privilege, which Plaintiffs dispute. Plaintiffs and Defendants have engaged in discovery, with Plaintiffs requesting production of documents, including the council members' personal notes and files. Defendants have refused to produce these documents, citing the testimonial legislative privilege. The parties have attempted to settle this dispute but were unsuccessful.

Plaintiffs claim that the city's electoral system has been in place for approximately 14 years and that the city council's actions are motivated by a desire to discriminate against minority voters. Defendants contend that the city council's actions are lawful and that the electoral system is fair. The dispute centers on the city council's motivations and the lawfulness of the electoral system, with Plaintiffs seeking to prove that the city council intentionally discriminated against minority voters. The city council's decision to adopt the 2-2-3 plan and the Department of Justice's declination of preclearance are key events in the dispute. The parties' contentions regarding the testimonial legislative privilege and the discoverability of the council members' personal notes and files are also central to the case.

Plaintiff, a former employee of Pro Custom Solar, LLC ("Momentum"), worked at the company's New Jersey call center. Plaintiff alleges that he and other Black employees were regularly subjected to racial hostility and disparate treatment by Defendants, including Momentum's Director of Inside Sales, Jeffrey Anclien, and Manager of Inside Sales, Brian Alper. Plaintiff contends that Anclien and Alper had the authority to control and alter the terms and conditions of all employees who worked at Momentum. According to Plaintiff, the discriminatory treatment included highly offensive and patently racist comments, lower pay than similarly situated white employees, and reprisals.

Plaintiff alleges that he and other Black call center employees were paid less than their white counterparts and were subjected to a hostile work environment. Plaintiff further contends that when he and other Black employees complained about the discriminatory treatment, they faced retaliation from Defendants. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that certain of Plaintiff's proposed amendments to his complaint are futile, implying that they dispute the allegations of discrimination and retaliation.

Prior to filing the lawsuit, Plaintiff worked at Momentum's New Jersey call center, where he allegedly experienced the discriminatory treatment. The events giving rise to the lawsuit occurred during Plaintiff's employment at Momentum, although the exact dates are not specified. Plaintiff filed his initial Complaint on October 22, 2019, and later filed an Amended Complaint on April 2, 2021, adding claims under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Other former employees, including Alissa Winfrey, Ahmed Sunkins, O'Neil Hall, and Basil Oguekwe, have also come forward with similar allegations of discrimination and retaliation against Defendants.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has required employers with 100 or more employees to file the Employer Information Report EEO-1 since 1966. The EEO-1 report collects data on the number of individuals employed by job category, sex, race, and ethnicity. In 2010, the EEOC began exploring ways to improve enforcement of federal laws prohibiting pay discrimination, including collecting pay data from employers. The EEOC commissioned a study by the National Academy of Sciences (NAS), which recommended collecting pay data through a survey such as the EEO-1. The EEOC also conducted a pilot study to identify the most efficient means to collect pay data.

In 2016, the EEOC published a Federal Register notice proposing a revised EEO-1 data collection, which included a new component (Component 2) to collect data on employees' W-2 earnings and hours worked. The EEOC estimated that the new pay data collection would increase the reporting time per filer by 3.4 hours. After a public comment period, the EEOC published a second Federal Register notice seeking a three-year approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for the revised EEO-1 data collection. OMB approved the proposed collection on September 29, 2016, and issued an OMB control number for the revised EEO-1.

Plaintiff alleges that OMB's subsequent decision to review and stay Component 2 of the EEO-1 report was improper. Defendant contends that the decision was made in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) and was based on a determination that the relevant circumstances related to the collection had changed and that the burden estimates provided by the EEOC were materially in error. Defendant also contends that the EEOC's data file specifications for submitting EEO-1 data were not contained in the Federal Register notices and were not outlined in the supporting statement for the collection of information, and that the public did not have an opportunity to provide comment on the method of data submission. The parties dispute the practical utility and burden of the revised EEO-1 data collection, as well as the adequacy of the EEOC's efforts to address privacy and confidentiality issues.

From June 2007 to July 2007, plaintiff, a 53-year-old African American male, applied for several jobs at NASA, including a Management and Program Analyst position, two General Engineer positions, and a Program Analyst position. To complete his applications, plaintiff submitted a resume highlighting his relevant experience for each position. The vacancies required successful applicants to have high-level scientific and managerial skills, as well as "one year of specialized experience equivalent to the next lower grade." 

Plaintiff alleges that his unsuccessful attempts at employment are a result of "the systematic devaluation of [his] credentials by RESUMIX," NASA's automated hiring system, and that the RESUMIX selection process is discriminatory, denying him employment on the basis of his race and age. Defendant contends that plaintiff's applications were rejected because he was not highly qualified for any of the positions. According to defendant, RESUMIX "does not take race, gender, or age into consideration when analyzing applicant resumes and generating a score for resumes."

Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff filed a formal complaint of discrimination with NASA on December 27, 2007, and later requested a hearing before an Administrative Judge of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on June 4, 2008. After engaging in discovery and receiving no decision from the EEOC Administrative Judge, plaintiff withdrew his hearing request and asked NASA to issue a Final Agency Decision (FAD) on January 4, 2010. NASA issued its FAD on August 10, 2010, finding that plaintiff failed to establish that management's reasons for not hiring him were pretextual or that he was discriminated against on the bases of his race or age. Plaintiff received the FAD on August 16, 2010, and was advised of his right to appeal or file a civil action within 90 days.

Kelly Migdon was employed by 171 Holdings, LLC, d/b/a 171 Junction Roadhouse, and was promoted to Assistant General Manager (AGM) on October 19, 2015, with an annual salary rate of $30,000.00. Plaintiff alleges that the male AGM she replaced, Chance Hebert, was paid an annual salary rate of $40,000.00. Migdon was terminated on November 27, 2015. The 171 Junction Roadhouse permanently closed on or about November 2016. 

Plaintiff alleges that she was paid less than her male counterpart, Hebert, and that her termination was retaliatory. Defendant contends that the pay difference was not based on sex and that the termination was lawful. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of sex-based pay discrimination and retaliation under the Equal Pay Act (EPA). 

Prior to her termination, Migdon earned $576.92 per week, whereas Hebert earned $769.23 per week, a weekly difference of $192.21. Migdon calculates her back pay damages based on this difference. The parties engaged in pre-litigation communications and negotiations, but the details of these interactions are not specified. Migdon filed this lawsuit against 171 Holdings, alleging violations of the EPA, and the court has considered her claims. Relevant pre-litigation events include Migdon's promotion, her termination, and the closure of the 171 Junction Roadhouse. The parties have exchanged documents and communications, including filings and motions in this lawsuit. Migdon's counsel has submitted a detailed summation of the hours expended by each attorney, paralegal, and law clerk, with the commensurate rate of pay, in support of her claim for attorney fees.

The plaintiff, a former USPTO employee, claims that defendants, also USPTO employees, wrongfully terminated her and interfered with her ability to receive fair representation from her union and the USPTO's Office of Equal Employment Opportunity and Diversity (OEEOD). Plaintiff alleges that defendants doctored or falsified documents concerning her extended, unexcused absence from work between April and May 2014, which ultimately resulted in her termination. Defendants contend that they are not proper defendants in this action, as they were acting in their official capacities with respect to plaintiff's claims, and that the proper defendant would be the agency head or the United States.

The events leading up to the lawsuit began with plaintiff's extended absence from work, which was deemed unexcused. Plaintiff believes that defendants falsified documents related to her absence, which led to her termination. Prior to filing this lawsuit, plaintiff brought a separate suit against the USPTO, seeking to hold the agency responsible for its employees' alleged wrongful conduct. That case, known as Evans v. U.S. Patent & Trademark Office (Evans I), was dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

Plaintiff then filed this action, and defendants initially moved to dismiss on a theory of claim preclusion, which was denied by the court. Defendants have since moved for summary judgment, arguing that they are not proper defendants and that the court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to pursue her administrative remedies prior to filing suit. Plaintiff has responded with factual arguments regarding defendants' conduct, but has not addressed the merits of defendants' legal arguments. The parties' dispute centers on the circumstances surrounding plaintiff's termination and the alleged falsification of documents, as well as the proper defendants and the court's jurisdiction to hear the case.

Keith Wilhelm, a locomotive engineer, has worked for CSX Transportation, Inc. (CSX) since 1979 and is currently based at the Walbridge, Ohio terminal. In May 1997, Wilhelm was diagnosed with severe asthma. CSX had a policy prohibiting smoking in all buildings at the Walbridge terminal, except for certain designated areas, effective May 15, 1996. This policy was later extended to a full ban on smoking in all buildings in February 1998 and in all locomotive cabs in January 1999. Wilhelm alleges that despite these policies, CSX has failed to enforce the no-smoking policy at the Walbridge terminal, in locomotive cabs, and in company-controlled vehicles since February 1998. 

Wilhelm claims that as a result of this failure, he is subjected to second-hand smoke in the workplace daily. He alleges that on two occasions, November 29, 1998, and August 19, 1999, heavy second-hand cigarette smoke at work caused asthma attacks that required emergency medical care. Wilhelm had informed CSX about his exposure to second-hand smoke on several occasions and demanded that the company enforce its no-smoking policy. He also submitted written incident reports detailing unauthorized smoking at the Walbridge terminal. Wilhelm's physician notified CSX that his workplace should be smoke-free to control his asthma.

Plaintiff Wilhelm alleges that CSX's failure to enforce its no-smoking policy breached its duty to provide a reasonably safe work environment, violating the Federal Employer's Liability Act (FELA). Wilhelm also contends that CSX's failure to enforce the policy constitutes handicap discrimination under Ohio Revised Code § 4112.02, as he believes the company's actions were taken because of his handicap. Defendant CSX argues that it did not discriminate against Wilhelm on the basis of his handicap and that any failure to enforce the smoking ban was not done because of Wilhelm's special sensitivity to cigarette smoke. CSX also argues that co-worker and managerial ostracism of Wilhelm is not an adverse employment action. The parties' dispute centers on whether CSX's actions or lack thereof regarding its no-smoking policy and treatment of Wilhelm constitute a breach of its duties under FELA and Ohio law.

In September 1981, individual plaintiffs filed charges with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) alleging that the State of Washington discriminated against women employed in state service by establishing and maintaining lower wage rates or salaries for predominantly female job classifications compared to predominantly male job classifications that required equal or less skill, effort, and responsibility. The EEOC took no action on these charges. On April 31, 1982, the U.S. Department of Justice issued Notices of Right to Sue to the plaintiffs. 

The American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) and the Washington Federation of State Employees (WFSE) unions, on behalf of approximately 15,500 workers in jobs held primarily by females, filed a complaint against the State of Washington on July 20, 1982. The plaintiffs, who are male and female employees of the State of Washington, allege that the state's compensation system discriminates against them based on sex. The plaintiffs contend that the state has and continues to discriminate against women in compensation by paying lower wages or salaries for predominantly female job classifications compared to predominantly male job classifications that require equal or less skill, effort, and responsibility. 

The State of Washington, the defendant, argues that the plaintiffs' claims are without merit and that the state's compensation system is fair and non-discriminatory. The defendant also contends that the plaintiffs' claims are barred by the Eleventh Amendment and that the state is not liable for damages under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The plaintiffs and the defendant have engaged in pretrial conferences and have submitted proposed pretrial orders, but they have been unable to agree on the issues in the case. The case has been bifurcated into two phases: liability and remedy. The liability phase was tried to the court, and the court has heard oral arguments from both parties. The plaintiffs seek a declaratory judgment and money damages, as well as injunctive relief to provide enforcement of a non-discriminatory compensation system.

Joseph Laguana, a part-time Customer Service Representative for United Airlines, Inc., has asthma, which he has had since he was around ten years old. Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020, Laguana had not taken any extended periods of medical leave of absence, and his asthma had not interfered with his ability to perform his work duties. Laguana's employment was subject to a collective bargaining agreement between United and his union, the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers. 

In April 2020, Laguana requested to work remotely, questioned the number of employees at work, and requested to move the location of an operational briefing due to concerns about social distancing. He also asked his doctor, Dr. Scott Wesley Hughes, for a diagnosis of asthma so that he could submit FMLA paperwork, stating that he wanted to utilize his earned hours to excuse himself from work and get paid. Laguana claimed he was trying to avoid contracting COVID-19, as he was not experiencing asthma or COVID-19 conditions at the time. He later emailed United's Employee Advocacy Director, Rahman Henderson, regarding the lack of communication about his request to work remotely and his concerns about retaliation.

In May 2020, Laguana went on a two-and-a-half-year medical leave of absence, which continued until his employment with United ended in November 2022. During this time, United requested additional medical documentation to support his leave, and Laguana expressed concerns about putting himself and his family at risk by going to work due to the continued travel of passengers from COVID-19 hotspots. United became aware of a video depicting Laguana at a bar on June 19, 2020, without a mask and holding an alcoholic beverage, which they believed was inconsistent with his taking of medical leave. This led to an investigation, and Laguana's supervisor, Ellie Sandlin, concluded that he had abused sick leave and was uncooperative during the investigation, violating company policies. 

Plaintiff Laguana alleges that he suffered disability discrimination and was subjected to a hostile work environment, including homophobic and insulting comments. Defendant United contends that Laguana abused sick leave and was uncooperative during the investigation, and that his termination was warranted due to violations of company policies. Laguana claims that his asthma and concerns about COVID-19 led to his requests for accommodations, while United argues that his behavior was inconsistent with his claims of disability and medical leave.

Anthony Sollazzo, a security guard, worked at a residential community in Bossier City, Louisiana, for Allied Universal. Sollazzo alleges that his coworker, Deborah Sanders, discriminated against him because of his Muslim faith. He claims that in late December 2020, Sanders asked him about his faith and followed him to his car, saying "Jesus is God and every knee shall bow." Sollazzo also alleges that on August 18, 2021, Sanders told him that Islam is "a stupid religion." He reported these incidents to management, who advised him to avoid Sanders.

Sollazzo also alleges that Allied Universal promotes a hostile work environment, citing several incidents. He claims that a resident took photographs of his car because the resident had previously observed guards sleeping during their shifts. Sollazzo also alleges that vehicles would "prowl" the guard shack to see if he was asleep and that a resident beeped his horn repeatedly to annoy him while he used the restroom. He further alleges that a coworker filed a complaint against him for applying bug spray near the guard station. Sollazzo claims that he reported these incidents to management but does not indicate whether anyone at Allied Universal followed up with him.

Sollazzo also brings a retaliation claim against Allied Universal, alleging that an unnamed manager retaliated against him for sharing his phone number with Marion Charles to discuss the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the hostile work environment at Allied Universal. Sollazzo claims that he was told he could be transferred or terminated for possessing a taser, a conversation that took place after he was questioned about his interactions with Charles. On August 19, 2021, Allied Universal informed Sollazzo that he was being transferred to another site, which Sollazzo alleges was in retaliation for his actions. Defendant Allied Universal contends that Sollazzo failed to exhaust his administrative remedies with the EEOC before filing suit in federal court, and that his complaint does not allege that he has a viable Title VII claim.

John Foreman and Gary Runge worked for Five Star Food Service, Inc., a Delaware corporation with a principal place of business in Chattanooga, Tennessee, which provides vending, coffee service, and food services. Foreman was hired as a vending route driver on September 6, 2011, and later transferred to an Avanti Markets merchandiser position. He worked in these roles until his discharge on November 8, 2011. Foreman alleges that he worked more than 40 hours per week as a vending route driver and was not paid overtime compensation. He also claims that, as a merchandiser, he was required to work "off the clock" without recording certain overtime hours. 

Five Star contends that Foreman's employment falls within the Motor Carrier Act exemption from the Fair Labor Standards Act's (FLSA) overtime requirements. The company argues that Foreman's activities as a vending route driver and merchandiser were part of a continuous movement in interstate commerce, as the products he transported were originally manufactured and packaged outside of Tennessee. Five Star purchases these products from Vistar of Tennessee, which distributes them to Five Star's Nashville warehouse. From there, Foreman and other drivers would transport the products to locations within Middle Tennessee. 

The parties dispute whether Foreman was able to record all of his overtime hours, with Foreman testifying that his supervisor, McDaniel, required him to work "off the clock" without recording certain hours, while McDaniel denies this allegation. Foreman also claims that he was terminated in retaliation for intending to comply with a lawful trial subpoena, in violation of Tennessee law. The relationship between Five Star and its employees, including Foreman and Runge, is that of employer and employee, with the company providing vending and food services to clients in Middle Tennessee. Relevant pre-litigation events include Foreman's employment and termination, as well as his interactions with McDaniel and other Five Star employees.

Rita Novak, a Supply Sergeant with the 323rd Chemical Company based in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, was hired by Dakota Industries, Inc. on March 28, 1989. At the time of her hiring, Novak informed Dakota Industries that she was in the Army Reserve. On November 17, 1990, Novak was ordered to active duty in support of Desert Shield and was released from active duty on May 14, 1991. She returned to work at Dakota Industries on June 3, 1991. During her employment, Novak was promoted to various positions, including Office Manager, Personnel Manager, and Production Control Manager, with corresponding raises in pay.

Plaintiff alleges that she was treated unfairly by her employer, Dakota Industries, and its President, Donald P. Mackintosh, upon her return from active duty. Novak contends that she was not given the raise she had been promised before leaving for Desert Storm and that her duties and responsibilities were changed. Defendant Mackintosh, on the other hand, contends that Novak's behavior and performance changed after her return from Desert Storm, and that she was insubordinate and violated company rules. Mackintosh also claims that Novak's position was eliminated as part of a reduction in force at Dakota Industries.

The relationship between Novak and Mackintosh became increasingly strained after Novak's return from Desert Storm. Novak alleges that Mackintosh was resistant to her attempts to balance her work and military obligations, and that he interfered with her ability to perform her job duties. In January 1992, Novak was scheduled to attend a trade show in Denver, Colorado, and also had a dental appointment and upcoming active duty training. The events surrounding these appointments and her subsequent termination are disputed by the parties. Novak alleges that she was terminated in violation of the Veterans' Reemployment Rights Act, while Mackintosh contends that she abandoned her job and was insubordinate. Prior to her termination, Novak had missed a total of 36 days of work due to her military obligations, excluding her time on active duty for Desert Storm. Novak had also received several promotions and raises during her employment, with her salary increasing to $7.00 per hour before she left for Desert Storm. However, upon her return, she was paid at the $6.50 rate. The company's payroll journal indicates that management employees received two $0.50 per hour raises while Novak was on active duty, but Novak did not receive these raises. The parties' contentions regarding the circumstances of Novak's termination, including the reasons for her discharge and the events leading up to it, are in dispute.

The plaintiff, whose name is not specified, alleges that they were subjected to a substantial demotion and constructive discharge by their employer, the defendants, due to their race. The plaintiff contends that these actions were taken in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1981, which prohibits racial discrimination in the making and enforcement of contracts. The defendants, on the other hand, argue that the plaintiff's claims are not viable under § 1981 in light of the Supreme Court's decision in Patterson v. McLean Credit Union, which they interpret as limiting the scope of the statute to conduct related to the initial formation of a contract.

The plaintiff alleges that they were demoted and ultimately forced to leave their job due to discriminatory actions by the defendants. The plaintiff contends that these actions were taken because of their race and that they were treated differently than similarly situated employees of other races. The defendants, however, contend that the plaintiff's claims are based on post-formation conduct, which they argue is not actionable under § 1981. The defendants also argue that the plaintiff's claims are barred by the Supreme Court's decision in Patterson, which they interpret as holding that § 1981 does not provide a cause of action for discriminatory discharge or demotion claims.

Prior to the lawsuit, the plaintiff and the defendants were engaged in an employment relationship, the details of which are not specified. The plaintiff alleges that the defendants' discriminatory actions created a hostile work environment and ultimately led to their constructive discharge. The defendants, on the other hand, contend that the plaintiff's claims are without merit and that they are entitled to dismissal of the lawsuit. The parties' dispute centers on the interpretation of § 1981 and whether it provides a cause of action for the plaintiff's claims of substantial demotion and constructive discharge.

Sarita Wilson worked at the Mid-Hudson Forensic Psychiatric Center (MHFPC) for over seventeen years, starting as a Security Hospital Treatment Assistant in April 2005 and becoming a Rehabilitation Assistant in 2017. In her role as a Rehabilitation Assistant, she led and planned group rehabilitation activities and developed group protocols and curriculum with patients. On October 6, 2021, the New York State Office of Mental Health (OMH) issued an emergency regulation requiring all staff working in psychiatric hospitals to receive at least one dose of the COVID-19 vaccine by November 1, 2021. The regulation, known as the OMH Mandate, defined "staff" to include all persons employed or affiliated with a hospital, whether paid or unpaid.

Plaintiff alleges that she submitted an application to the Human Resources Department at MHFPC on October 25, 2021, requesting a religious exemption from the vaccine requirement, stating that her religious beliefs prevented her from consenting to a vaccine. Defendant contends that Plaintiff's job required her to be directly involved in an inpatient area and that she had not identified any alternate accommodation besides an outright exemption, which would constitute an undue hardship. Plaintiff claims that she was willing to wear a mask and comply with other protocols, but refused to be vaccinated. Defendants informed her that her request was denied and warned her that she would be suspended without pay if she failed to get vaccinated by November 17, 2021. On November 18, 2021, Plaintiff received a Notice of Discipline informing her that she was suspended without pay. After a union arbitration hearing on July 13, 2022, during which she reiterated her willingness to wear a mask but not receive the vaccine, Plaintiff was officially terminated.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with MHFPC and OMH being the employers and Plaintiff being the employee. The nature of the dispute is a claim of religious discrimination, with Plaintiff alleging that her religious exemption request was improperly denied and that she was suspended and terminated as a result. Relevant pre-litigation events include the issuance of the OMH Mandate, Plaintiff's request for a religious exemption, and the subsequent denial of that request and her suspension and termination. Relevant documents include the OMH Mandate, Plaintiff's request for a religious exemption, and the notices of discipline and termination. Relevant employment and workplace facts include Plaintiff's role as a Rehabilitation Assistant, the requirements of her job, and the protocols in place at MHFPC.

Nicholas Recchia was a 55-year-old warehouse supervisor at Kellogg Company's facility in Blue Anchor, New Jersey, where he had worked since 1981. In 2008, Recchia began drinking excessively due to concerns about his son's substance abuse problems, and in March 2009, he checked into an inpatient rehabilitation center to treat his alcohol dependency. After his discharge from the treatment center in June 2009, Recchia was diagnosed with kidney cancer and underwent surgery and treatment from June to August 2009. During this period, Recchia was on an approved leave of absence from work.

While Recchia was on leave, Kellogg was undergoing a restructuring program called K-Lean, which involved creating new job descriptions and assessing the workforce to determine which employees were most qualified for the new jobs. An outside consultant, Celerant, assisted Kellogg in creating the new job descriptions and facility-wide organizational charts. Recchia was assessed for three positions: Operations Services Manager, Operations Supervisor, and Operations Supervisor — Logistics. However, he was disqualified from the first two positions due to low scores and, although he qualified for the third position, another employee, Juan Ferriero, received a higher score and was selected for the job. As a result, Recchia was deemed "without a position" and, upon his return to work on September 1, 2009, he was terminated due to his low score for the available Operations Supervisor positions.

Plaintiff Recchia alleges that his termination was discriminatory, while Defendant Kellogg contends that the termination was a result of the K-Lean assessment process. Recchia received a written Employee Separation Packet, which included a benefits summary, a Severance Plan, and a Separation Agreement and General Release. The packet explained the various benefits for which Recchia was eligible, including continuation of health insurance pursuant to COBRA. However, Recchia's receipt of severance pay and benefits was contingent upon him signing the Release and waiving any possible claims against Kellogg. Recchia consulted with an attorney, Jacqueline Vigilante, regarding the Severance Plan and the Release, and on October 6, 2009, Ms. Vigilante sent a letter to Kellogg indicating that she believed there was "potential liability for Kellogg's" and requesting a revised severance package. On October 9, 2009, Kellogg terminated Recchia's severance pay and benefits, and Recchia did not become aware of this until October 28, 2009, when his son's insurance coverage was denied. Recchia eventually signed the Release on November 9, 2009, after which Kellogg reinstated his severance payments and benefits. Recchia filed his Complaint on September 24, 2010, bringing six counts against Kellogg, including fraud and duress with respect to the Release, age and disability discrimination, and unlawful interference in violation of ERISA.

In the state of North Dakota, a controversy arose regarding public rights-of-way along section lines within the Dakota Prairie Grasslands, which are managed by the United States Forest Service. The State of North Dakota and several counties, including Billings County, Golden Valley County, McKenzie County, and Slope County, claim that all section lines in North Dakota, including those within the Dakota Prairie Grasslands, are subject to right-of-way for travel by the public. Plaintiff North Dakota alleges that its claim arises from Forest Service decisions in 2001 and 2002, in which the Forest Service rejected and no longer intended to recognize the state's valid and existing right to section line easements in the National Grasslands. The Forest Service issued a Record of Decision in 2001, prohibiting off-highway motor vehicle travel in the Little Missouri National Grassland, and later issued an order closing non-system roads or trails to motorized travel.

The Plaintiffs, including North Dakota and the counties, contend that their quiet title claims are timely filed and that the Court has jurisdiction over the matter. They argue that the public's right to travel along section lines arises from North Dakota's acceptance of the grant for construction of public highways offered by federal statute, known as R.S. 2477. The United States, on the other hand, argues that the Plaintiffs' claims are untimely under the Quiet Title Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2409a, because both North Dakota and the counties had sufficient notice of the United States' position that North Dakota had not accepted the R.S. 2477 grant to create rights-of-way for public travel along the section lines. The controversy has been amplified by recent oil and gas development on lands owned by North Dakota, with the State owning both the subsurface and surface estate, and lessees seeking to access these lands by way of section lines.

The Plaintiffs allege that the United States has unlawfully interfered with section line easements in the Little Missouri National Grassland, Sheyenne National Grassland, and Cedar River National Grassland by failing to recognize the state's valid and existing rights in the easement over the 33 feet of federal land abutting section lines in the Dakota Prairie Grasslands. The Plaintiffs also claim that the United States has refused to abide by the reservation and exception in the conveyances by which it reacquired title. The United States' refusal to recognize section line right-of-way has led to consequences, including the burden of building access roads falling entirely on state school lands and the state incurring the responsibility for overseeing road reclamations when the purposes for which the roads were built terminate. The Plaintiffs seek to quiet title to the public's right-of-way along section lines within the lands managed by the Forest Service.

Z.R. was born on September 1, 2015, to Ms. Harris-Reese and Sgt. Reese. During his first year of life, Z.R. was diagnosed with sickle cell disease and reactive airway disease, which would later be considered asthma. He experienced a series of ear infections, upper respiratory infections, and a sickle cell pain crisis, requiring emergency room visits or treatment at several hospitals. Z.R.'s pediatrician referred him to the WRNMMC Otolaryngology Clinic for an evaluation of the suitability of BMTT surgery to implant ear tubes and prevent future ear infections.

On June 22, 2016, Dr. Brietzke evaluated Z.R. at WRNMMC and recommended that Z.R. receive a BMTT procedure to address the recurrent ear infections, as well as an adenoidectomy to address reported snoring and mouth-breathing issues. Dr. Brietzke considered both procedures to be elective, meaning they were medically optional, and that the conditions could still be treated with medication if the parents opted against the surgery. Based on Dr. Brietzke's recommendation, Z.R.'s recurring ear infections, and the fact that Z.R.'s older brother had previously undergone a BMTT procedure without issue, Z.R.'s parents decided to proceed with the surgery. The surgery was scheduled for September 13, 2016, shortly after Z.R.'s first birthday.

In the week leading up to the surgery, Dr. Brietzke and the surgical staff discussed Z.R.'s case, and Dr. Brietzke called Z.R.'s hematologist, Dr. Kip Hartman, to ask for input on managing the risks of surgery due to Z.R.'s sickle cell disease. Dr. Hartman recommended that Z.R. be admitted to the hospital following surgery but did not advise pre-admission. Dr. Gerbstadt, the anesthesiologist, expressed concerns about the difficulty and risk of the case, classifying Z.R. as a high-risk patient due to his sickle cell disease, history of pneumonia and wheezing, and prior hospital visits. Dr. Gerbstadt discussed Z.R.'s case with Dr. Willett, and they planned to have albuterol ready during the surgery to control Z.R.'s breathing and vital signs. On the morning of the surgery, Dr. Brietzke and Dr. Townes met with Sgt. Reese and gave a standard description of the risks of the BMTT and adenoidectomy surgeries, but did not inform Z.R.'s parents that Z.R. was at heightened risk for injury or death from complications arising from anesthesia due to his sickle cell disease and reactive airway disease. Dr. Willett reviewed a standard form containing general risks of anesthesia with Z.R.'s parents, but did not reference any heightened risk for patients with sickle cell disease or reactive airway disease. Dr. Gerbstadt later reviewed Z.R.'s medical history with Ms. Harris-Reese and stated that Z.R. was at high risk for complications from anesthesia due to his preexisting conditions. Despite these concerns, the surgery proceeded, and Z.R. was taken into the operating room.

Tammy Ward, an Alabama resident, met with a W & H Voortman, Ltd. employee in Alabama, who encouraged her to apply for a job as the company's products distributor in middle and southern Alabama. Ward alleges that she was offered the job and accepted it, but was either fired or never officially hired because of her sex. W & H Voortman, Ltd. is a foreign corporation with its principal place of business in Burlington, Ontario, Canada. Plaintiff alleges that the company's actions constituted sex discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Defendant contends that it is not subject to suit under Title VII because it is a foreign corporation. Ward admits that W & H Voortman is a foreign corporation, but argues that the company's actions in the United States, specifically in Alabama, are subject to Title VII. The parties' relationship began when Ward was encouraged to apply for the job, and the nature of the dispute centers on whether W & H Voortman's alleged discriminatory actions are covered under Title VII. Prior to the lawsuit, there were communications and a meeting between Ward and the W & H Voortman employee in Alabama, which led to Ward's job application and alleged subsequent discrimination.

The plaintiff, a Black male, was hired by the Vance County Sheriff's Office as a patrol deputy on June 5, 2017. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, the Vance County Sheriff's Office discriminated against Black deputies, including himself, by not providing them with the same privileges as White deputies. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Black deputies were not provided with protective gear, were issued fewer new uniforms, received unsafe patrol vehicles, and were not given adequate training, whereas White deputies were afforded these benefits. Plaintiff contends that he personally experienced these forms of disparate treatment, including not being issued a laptop, having to use a patrol vehicle in need of repair, and not being provided opportunities for additional training.

Plaintiff alleges that he was also subjected to a hostile work environment, including being openly harassed and called gay. He further alleges that he was retaliated against for failing to discriminate in his policing and that his lieutenant created a paper trail to support a false narrative that plaintiff was insubordinate. In June 2018, plaintiff filed two internal written discrimination complaints against his lieutenant, alleging a hostile work environment based on race and gender discrimination. Plaintiff contends that Sheriff White ordered him to drop the discrimination complaints or face termination. Plaintiff then filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in August 2018, asserting race and gender discrimination and later retaliatory discharge.

The events leading to plaintiff's termination began on October 21, 2018, when he was serving warrants on an individual who allegedly refused multiple orders and became combative and physically aggressive. Plaintiff performed a takedown of the subject, and the subject's arm may have been broken in the process. The subject subsequently complained that plaintiff assaulted and harassed her. Plaintiff's supervisors determined that he had used excessive force, and on October 24, 2018, plaintiff was informed that his services were no longer needed. Defendant contends that plaintiff's termination was due to his use of excessive force, while plaintiff alleges that his termination was retaliatory and motivated by his prior discrimination complaints. Plaintiff also alleges that since his termination, the Vance County Sheriff's Office has made remarks that deputies who file complaints end up like him, and that he has been unable to gain employment in law enforcement due to the Vance County Sheriff's Office's characterization of his employment and termination.

Heidi Husser began working for the New York City Department of Education (DOE) on August 19, 2008, as the Director of Labor Relations in the Division of School Facilities (DSF). Her annual salary started at $80,749 and increased to $83,577 on July 1, 2009, when the DOE raised the salaries of all its employees. Husser's supervisors included John Shea, the DSF's Chief Executive Officer, and John O'Connell, the DSF's Executive Director. 

Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to a sexist culture at DSF, where high-ranking officials, including defendants Shea and O'Connell, made derogatory comments about women, referred to them as "girls," "hot," "doable," and "adorable," and permitted and encouraged sexual innuendo and name-calling. Specifically, Husser claims that Shea and O'Connell made a dozen offensive remarks and incidents from late 2009 through July 2012. Defendant contends that Husser's job is not sufficiently comparable to the other DSF directors, whose higher salaries she complains about, and that her salary was determined pursuant to a gender-neutral plan for managerial compensation.

Husser informally complained about the hostile work environment to the DOE's Executive Director of the Office of Equal Employment Opportunity (OEEO), Mecca Santana, in March or April 2012, and filed a formal complaint on July 5, 2012, alleging sexual harassment, unlawful pay practices, and gender discrimination. The OEEO investigation found that Husser's claims were not substantiated, but criticized Shea for failing to self-report Husser's complaint. The report also noted a "history of inappropriate conduct by all involved parties" and recommended that Husser's salary be reviewed. Following the report, Shea received a two-week suspension. 

Husser claims that the defendants retaliated against her after she complained, by closely monitoring her performance, excluding her from meetings and group email exchanges, and temporarily revoking her privilege to use a DSF car. Defendants contend that they are entitled to judgment on the retaliation claims because Husser cannot demonstrate that she was subjected to any cognizable adverse employment action. Husser also alleges that she was effectively demoted when the DOE appointed Linda Green to the newly created position of Chief Administrative Officer, and had Husser report directly to her rather than to CEO Shea. Defendants argue that the record does not support the proposition that Husser was subjected to a hostile work environment.

In April 2017, Copot, a lawyer, started working at Stewart Title's office in Addison, Illinois, as a claims counsel, reviewing and issuing decisions on title insurance claims. He reported to Charity Makela, who in turn reported to McBee. In June 2018, Makela left the company, and Stewart Title promoted two female attorneys within the claims department. Kelly Rickenbach took over Makela's responsibilities, and Eleanor Sharpe became the managing counsel of Stewart Title's Addison office. 

Plaintiff Copot alleges that in the summer of 2018, Rickenbach informed him of a new company policy requiring employees in the claims department to obtain permission from management before attending continuing education classes, which he claims was not applied to female employees. Defendant Stewart Title contends that this policy was a legitimate business practice. In August 2018, Copot requested Rickenbach's permission to attend a continuing education class, and when she did not reply, he contacted Sharpe, who gave him permission to attend. 

Copot alleges that on August 24, 2018, he sought permission from Rickenbach to take sick days from August 27 to August 29 while he underwent and recovered from surgery, but Rickenbach denied his request and asked him to provide a "valid doctor's note indicating the illness and need to stay home." Copot claims that he had never heard of this policy and that two female employees who had taken lengthy sick leaves were also unaware of it. Defendant Rickenbach contends that the policy was a reasonable requirement for verifying employee absences. Copot also alleges that Rickenbach instructed him to deal with requests from customers that Stewart Title reconsider its claim decisions in a way that differed from the previous practice, and that he was not allowed to work from home, unlike two female claims counsel. Things came to a head in October 2018, when Copot met with Tonya Moseley, who told him that McBee, Rickenbach, and Sharpe had agreed to closely scrutinize his attendance, productivity, and work performance in retaliation for his refusal to provide documentation for his sick leave. On October 30, 2018, McBee and a senior HR director approached Copot's office, accompanied by two armed security guards, and terminated his employment, citing "poor job performance for not following claims handling procedures." 

Prior to his termination, Copot had sent an email to the HR department alleging sex discrimination and an unlawful sick leave policy, and had asked to speak with an HR representative. After his termination, Copot filed a claim for unemployment benefits with the Illinois Department of Employment Security and a complaint alleging violations of the Illinois Employee Sick Leave Act with the Illinois Department of Labor. He also cross-filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the Illinois Department of Human Rights (IDHR), alleging retaliation and discrimination based on sex. The EEOC dismissed his charge and gave him notice of his right to sue, leading to the filing of this lawsuit.

Vera Brown-Morrison, a black woman who practices Pentecostalism, began working for Vinfen as a Community Integration Coordinator on February 14, 2011. In November 2013, Katherine Sharby was hired as Brown-Morrison's team leader. Plaintiff alleges that Sharby targeted non-white team members by constantly switching their work assignments and clients, and delegating licensed caseloads to unlicensed practitioners. Brown-Morrison also alleges that from December 2013 to May 2014, Sharby organized mandatory trainings during lunch, which made Brown-Morrison uncomfortable because she and three other co-workers were fasting for 30-40 days around the Easter holiday due to their Pentecostal faith.

Plaintiff alleges that she expressed her concerns to Abbott in an email on October 6, 2014, stating that Sharby was giving her work assignments that required a license, and that she felt uncomfortable doing these duties as she was not qualified. Brown-Morrison also mentioned Sharby's unprofessional behavior towards her because of her race, but claims she never received a response from Abbott. Defendant Sharby contends that she was simply managing her team and making assignments based on job requirements. In November 2014, Brown-Morrison alleges that Sharby reprimanded her and other employees who were fasting for religious reasons for not attending a potluck prior to a training.

Brown-Morrison claims that she attempted to transfer to other positions or teams but was unsuccessful. On February 12, 2015, she received a Corrective Action form, which she alleges was fabricated by Sharby to accuse her of failing 25% of the time. Plaintiff contends that the Corrective Action form was issued in retaliation for her complaint to Abbott. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Vinfen being the employer, and Sharby being Brown-Morrison's team leader. The nature of the dispute is one of alleged racial discrimination, retaliation, and violation of labor laws. Relevant pre-litigation events include Brown-Morrison's email to Abbott, the mandatory trainings during lunch, and the issuance of the Corrective Action form.

Conrad S. Caruso began working at Peat Marwick's New York office in May 1969 as a senior consultant in the Management Consulting Department. He was promoted to manager in 1970 and to partner in 1980. As a partner, Caruso's duties and responsibilities changed little, and he was required to submit time sheets every two weeks showing the number of hours he had worked for various accounts. He received a base salary and additional compensation derived from firm profits, determined by the number of "units" assigned to him. Caruso held no more than 350 units, whereas most partners in management positions held at least 1,500 units. 

Plaintiff Caruso alleges that in December 1985, when he was 50 years old, the Partner in Charge of Peat Marwick's New York office asked him to resign from the firm. Defendant Peat Marwick contends that Caruso was asked to resign because he did not bring a sufficient number of new clients to the firm. Caruso agreed to resign and left Peat Marwick by December 31, 1985. After his resignation, he received occasional work as an independent consultant for the firm until Peat Marwick discontinued his employment as an outside consultant on May 9, 1986. 

Caruso alleges that Peat Marwick's decision to ask for his resignation constituted unlawful age discrimination and that the firm unlawfully discontinued his outside consulting work in retaliation for his age discrimination action. Defendant Peat Marwick argues that as a partner, Caruso is not an "employee" under the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) and therefore cannot bring an age discrimination action against the firm. Caruso, on the other hand, contends that despite his title as a partner, his duties and responsibilities were more akin to those of a typical salaried worker, with little role in corporate decision-making, and thus he should be considered an employee under the ADEA.

Javier Mayorga, a Nicaraguan immigrant, moved to the United States at age twenty-five to avoid political turmoil. He worked in heating and air conditioning services for nearly nine years at Permanent Solutions Industries before leaving his job to attend Stratford University, where he earned an associate’s degree in "Network." Mayorga then worked for various companies, including Maytag, TK Services, Inc., and Advanced Power Control, before joining the Architect of the Capitol (AOC) in late 2007 as an Electronic Industrial Controls Mechanic at the Wage Grade (WG) 12 level.

Mayorga's job at AOC involved working on and maintaining the building's network operations and building automation system (BAS) at the Capitol Visitor Center. In 2014, Mayorga responded to a vacancy announcement for an Electronics Technician in the Energy Management Control Systems (EMCS) Branch of the Planning and Project Management Office within AOC. The vacancy announcement listed multiple openings at the GS-10 and GS-11 salary levels. Mayorga alleges that he was qualified for the position, having experience with BAS, automated logic controls, network, and HVAC. 

The plaintiff alleges that the selection process was flawed, claiming that the selection panel, which included Scott Bieber, Clifford Wallace, and Terry Watson, did not include an impartial member from a department outside the vacancy. Mayorga also claims that Bieber, who supervised the EMCS Branch, had a history of preferring white employees who spoke without a foreign accent and had specifically displayed a distaste for Mayorga's Hispanic origin. Mayorga contends that he was treated unfairly during the interview process, with the interviewers not looking at him when he spoke and not asking him follow-up questions. The plaintiff further alleges that Bieber and Wallace had previously discriminated against him, with Bieber mocking and interrupting him in meetings, telling him to speak better English, and laughing at him. Mayorga claims that he was passed over for promotion three times and that an HVAC technician at AOC warned him that Wallace and Bieber did not like him. Mayorga's coworker, Hector Molina, allegedly heard other employees making derogatory comments about Mayorga's Hispanic origin. Defendant contends that the selection process was fair and that Mayorga was not selected due to his lack of experience with certain systems and equipment. Defendant also disputes Mayorga's allegations of discriminatory treatment, contending that Bieber and Wallace treated him fairly and that the selection panel's decision was based on the candidates' qualifications and experience.

Nicole Sanders filled out an online application to become an HPD Metropolitan Police Recruit on September 10, 2018. She passed a written test on October 13, 2018, and met the objective requirements for the position, including having a high school diploma and driver's license. On January 19, 2019, Sanders completed a personal history statement (PHS) as part of the application process, which instructed her to disclose any criminal acts, including "undetected acts" - acts committed but for which she was not caught. The PHS emphasized the importance of transparency and comprehensiveness, warning that failure to disclose undetected acts or providing false information would result in disqualification.

Sanders alleges that during a pre-polygraph interview on May 2, 2019, with now-retired HPD Detective Mitchell Chung, she was sexually harassed. She claims that Chung made inappropriate comments, including telling her he understood why she was divorced three times because she was beautiful, asking if she liked Hawaiian guys, and asking if she had ever cheated on her husband. Sanders also alleges that Chung accused her of being a prostitute because she revealed that her husband had sex trafficked her to his peers in Turkmenistan. During the interview, Sanders disclosed three undetected acts for the first time: physical altercations as a school-age child in Turkmenistan, taking $15 from her then-husband's pocket without his knowledge in 2004, and sending $3,000 to her mother in Turkmenistan in 2008 to facilitate her son's escape from her abusive ex-husband.

The HPD Background Section later informed Sanders that her admittance as a recruit was denied due to disclosures, omissions, and/or inconsistencies found during the background investigation. The selection committee determined that she was not suitable for the position at the time. Sanders disputes the reason for the denial, claiming that she did not intentionally omit material information from her application. She also disputes the characterization of the events she disclosed, claiming that they were coerced and/or dictated by Chung. The parties' relationship is that of a job applicant and a potential employer, with Sanders seeking to become a police officer and HPD evaluating her suitability for the position. The nature of the dispute is Sanders' allegations of sexual harassment and coercion during the application process, as well as the denial of her application due to alleged omissions and inconsistencies.

The plaintiff was employed in the Department of the Treasury's Global High Wealth division from June 21, 2010, until she was terminated on May 10, 2011. Prior to her termination, she received a "Notice of Proposed Termination" that stated her termination was due to her alleged misrepresentation of her employment history, specifically regarding her work with Ashbourne & Company, her sole proprietorship, and her resignation from another employer. Plaintiff alleges that these reasons were pretextual and that her termination and other adverse employment actions were the result of race and gender discrimination.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the Department of the Treasury being the plaintiff's former employer. The nature of the dispute is a claim of employment discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that she was discriminated against based on her race and gender, while the defendants contend that her termination was due to her misrepresentation of her employment history. The plaintiff had initiated administrative proceedings regarding her termination, alleging "harassment and/or disparate treatment due to her race (African American) and/or sex (female)" under Title VII. The Department of the Treasury issued a Final Agency Decision concluding that there was no discrimination or harassment.

The plaintiff had also filed three lawsuits in the United States District Court for the District of Maryland against the Treasury Department and her former supervisors, alleging violations of various federal laws, including 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Equal Pay Act, and the Privacy Act of 1974. These cases were consolidated and transferred to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia. The plaintiff filed an amended complaint, which was brought against the same parties as the complaint in this action, alleging violations of 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Privacy Act. The plaintiff also pursued an appeal to the EEOC, which was later dismissed due to the pending civil case. Defendant contends that the reasons for the plaintiff's termination were legitimate and not pretextual.

David Cruz Carrillo, a Seventh Day Adventist, was hired as a temporary employee by the Autoridad de Acueductos y Acantarillados (AAA) of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico in 1986. At the time of his application, Cruz did not mention his affiliation with the Seventh Day Adventist Church or its doctrine prohibiting union membership. However, his application did indicate that he attended Seventh Day Adventist schools and graduated from a Seventh Day Adventist college. In 1988, Cruz became a permanent employee of AAA, and as part of his employment contract, he was informed of his obligation to join the Union Independiente de la Autoridad de Acueductos y Acantarillados (UIA) and pay union dues due to the "union shop" clause in the Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) between AAA and UIA.

Plaintiff alleges that his religious beliefs forbid him from joining the UIA, and he refused to do so, citing his adherence to the Seventh Day Adventist Church's doctrine. UIA, on the other hand, contends that Cruz must be a member of the union, despite offering to exempt him from Saturday meetings, public strikes or picketing, and allowing him to paraphrase the union's loyalty oath and transfer his dues to a nonprofit organization. UIA maintains that Cruz's refusal to join the union is not justified, as other Seventh Day Adventists have joined the union. Cruz, however, insists that his religious beliefs are sincere and that he cannot compromise on the issue of union membership.

The dispute between Cruz and UIA began in 1991, when UIA commenced disciplinary proceedings against Cruz for his refusal to join the union. Cruz appealed the resolution to the UIA's Executive Central Committee, which ultimately resolved to apply disciplinary measures against him. In 1992, Cruz filed a grievance with the Grievance Committee of AAA, protesting the UIA's decision requiring him to join the union to keep his job. The decision on his grievance went against him, and in October 1993, AAA discharged Cruz for his refusal to join UIA. Two weeks later, Cruz filed a complaint under Title VII with the FEPA and the EEOC, alleging discrimination in his employment due to his religious beliefs.

Tameka Turner began working as a Truck Driver II for the City of Dallas on May 24, 2021. Approximately six weeks into her job, she got into a verbal altercation with a co-worker named Charles, who allegedly threatened her, saying he would have her reassigned to Lalo's group. The next day, Turner's supervisor, Nino, reassigned her to Lalo's group, which Turner felt was retaliation. On her first day with the new team, Turner received contradictory instructions, resulting in Lalo yelling at her and sending her to Nino. Nino instructed Turner to return to work, but when she did, her crew had already left. Nino told Turner she could go home but would not get paid for the day. Turner decided to go home, but Nino reported her to human resources for walking off the job. Human resources warned Turner that she could be terminated for walking off the job and told her that being the only female on an all-male job would cause her to get the short end of the stick.

Plaintiff Tameka Turner alleges that Charles called her derogatory names and told her he would make her lose her job about a month after the initial altercation. Turner made a complaint against Charles with ethics and human resources. After the complaint, Turner alleges she faced harassment from Charles nearly daily, in the form of sexist and hostile threats, creating a hostile work environment. Turner also alleges that she suffered retaliation for her complaints when the City terminated her employment after her probationary period was over on November 16, 2021. Turner contends that the City disciplines men less harshly than women, citing an incident where she and a male co-worker were involved in separate car accidents, and while her wreck was minor, she was investigated, but the man was not.

Defendant City of Dallas contends that it did not discriminate against Turner based on her race or gender. The City's motion to dismiss argues that Turner failed to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. Turner alleges that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and retaliation, but the City contends that her allegations are insufficient to support these claims. The City also argues that Turner was treated fairly and that her termination was not based on her protected status. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of employment discrimination and retaliation under Title VII. Relevant pre-litigation events include Turner's complaints to human resources and ethics, as well as her interactions with her supervisors and co-workers.

President Joseph R. Biden nominated Harris to be a member of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) in January 2022. The Senate confirmed her on May 25, 2022, and she was sworn in on June 1, 2022. Her term expires on March 1, 2028. The Senate later confirmed Harris as Chairman, and she was sworn in as Chairman on March 14, 2024. Harris has been efficient and effective in her role at the MSPB, and when the MSPB's quorum was restored in March 2022, the agency had a backlog of approximately 3,800 cases that had accrued since 2017. By January 2025, however, the MSPB had cleared nearly 99 percent of its backlog. From June 1, 2022, to February 10, 2025, Harris participated in nearly 4,500 decisions.

Plaintiff Harris alleges that on February 10, 2025, she received an email from Trent Morse, Deputy Assistant to the President and the Deputy Director of the White House Presidential Personnel Office, stating that her position on the Merit Systems Protection Board was terminated, effective immediately, on behalf of President Donald J.
