Trump. Defendants do not dispute that Harris received this email, but they contend that the President has the authority to remove her from her position. Plaintiff alleges that her firing was ultra vires, unconstitutional, and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Harris serving as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, an independent agency responsible for protecting the merit system principles and adjudicating conflicts between federal workers and their employing agencies. The nature of the dispute is Harris's termination from her position, which she claims was unlawful, and the Defendants' contention that the President has the authority to remove her. Relevant pre-litigation events include Harris's nomination, confirmation, and swearing-in as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, as well as her participation in nearly 4,500 decisions during her tenure. The email from Trent Morse to Harris on February 10, 2025, is also a relevant pre-litigation event.

Beverly Lane Dexter, a 43-year-old Licensed Physical Therapist Assistant (LPTA), was hired by Amedisys Home Health, Inc. of Alabama in January 2009. She worked at the Fayette, Alabama branch, where she provided physical therapy to patients at their homes. During her employment, Dexter frequently rescheduled her patient visits, which sometimes included moving visits to weekends, for which LPTAs received a 15% premium. 

Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and retaliation based on her age. She contends that Amy Moye, the Business Office Scheduler, made age-related comments, saying "it may be hard, but I can teach an old dog new tricks" when Dexter attempted to change her schedule. Plaintiff also alleges that Traci Ferguson, the Director of Operations, and Moye occasionally said the office needed "new blood" during employee conferences, which Plaintiff believes referred to her age. Dexter claims that Jeff Boyles, the Rehabilitation Specialty Director, failed to act when she informed him of these comments. 

Dexter also contends that she was unfairly treated and disciplined, including being issued two written warnings by Ferguson for rescheduling patient visits and failing to follow office policies. She claims that the warnings and the implementation of an "Action Plan" for her to improve her performance were discriminatory and based on her age. Amedisys, on the other hand, contends that Dexter's performance issues and discipline were legitimate and not based on her age. The company argues that the "new blood" comment was innocuous and referred to new patients and employees, not age. Amedisys also points out that Dexter was aware of the company's policies and procedures, including the "Zero Missed Visit" policy, and failed to follow them, leading to her discipline and eventual resignation.

John E. Carpenter, an African-American, worked for Southwestern Bell Telephone Company in its Kansas facility. Several of his co-workers made whistling noises throughout the workday, which annoyed and offended Carpenter. He repeatedly complained about the whistling to his supervisor, Joseph Arri. Arri took steps to reduce the whistling, including distributing an office memo and asking the whistling employees to whistle less frequently, but did not expressly prohibit whistling in the office. On September 4, 2008, Carpenter was sent home after complaining of the noise, and he reported four coworkers for racial harassment to the Equal Employment Opportunity hotline. 

Carpenter alleges that the whistling was a disruption by non-black fellow employees "clearly directed at and designed to aggravate, obstruct, and undermine" him. He also points to one comment as evidence of a hostile work environment: about six years ago, a co-worker said, "This is the dark side in more ways than one," while passing his cubicle. Carpenter contends that the whistling was a form of racial harassment and that it substantially obstructed him in the performance of his duties. 

Defendant Southwestern Bell and Arri contend that the whistling was not discriminatory and that Carpenter was the only person in the office who was offended by it. They argue that the other employees, including non-white ones, did not complain about the whistling, and that the whistling occurred regardless of whether Carpenter was present. They also contend that the single, isolated comment made by a co-worker was not sufficient to establish a hostile work environment, and that Carpenter has not shown that the whistling was racially-motivated.

Robert Nicholson, Jr. has been employed by Petco Animal Supplies Stores, Inc. since April 2006. At the time of the events in question, Nicholson was a District Leader, overseeing 12 to 25 Petco stores in Maryland and Pennsylvania. In January 2016, Alan McVey, who is approximately 12 years Nicholson's junior, was promoted to Vice President of Regional Operations, becoming Nicholson's immediate supervisor. Nicholson alleges that McVey made a series of discriminatory comments regarding his age, including referring to him as the "senior" or "elder" District Leader, an "elder statesman," and making a joke about an "old dog" that Nicholson claims was directed at him.

Plaintiff Nicholson alleges that these comments created a hostile work environment and that McVey's behavior towards him changed after Nicholson reported the "old dog" comment to Human Resources Business Partner Wayne Barnett. Nicholson claims that McVey began to treat him differently, ignoring his phone calls and emails, and that their relationship turned "icy." Nicholson also contends that McVey performed retaliatory, unannounced store visits in his district, targeting stores that Nicholson had previously identified as "problem" locations. Defendant Petco contends that McVey's actions were legitimate business decisions, aimed at improving store performance, and that Nicholson was treated fairly and without discrimination.

In the summer of 2016, Regional Pet Services Director Ronee Wyatt made several unannounced visits to stores in Nicholson's district, reporting back to McVey that some stores were in poor condition. McVey then performed his own unannounced visits, identifying four stores that needed immediate attention. Nicholson was asked to create an action plan to address these issues, which he submitted on October 7, 2016. However, on October 10, 2016, McVey issued Nicholson a formal warning, citing his lack of urgency in addressing the problems, and suggested that Nicholson step down to a Store Leader position, which would result in an eight percent salary reduction. The parties dispute the nature of this offer, with Petco claiming it was a voluntary choice and Nicholson asserting it was an ultimatum. Nicholson attempted to contact Petco's Senior Employee Relations Specialist, Kristine Kaswell, about the warning and the step-down offer, but she did not return his calls.

Thomas McKeithan worked for the Government Printing Office (GPO) for over 42 years, developing a strong work record and reputation. Plaintiff McKeithan alleges that his supervisor, Randy Wilson, engaged in sexually harassing behavior towards women in the workplace, which McKeithan reported to Wilson and then to Wilson's supervisor, Alphonzo Woods. McKeithan claims that after he made these complaints, Wilson retaliated against him by falsely accusing him of unprofessional conduct, resulting in McKeithan's first disciplinary action in his career. McKeithan also alleges that Wilson made threatening comments about his personal life and restricted his access to certain areas of the office.

Defendant William Boarman, as Public Printer of the GPO, is being sued in his official capacity. Plaintiff McKeithan contends that he was subjected to a hostile work environment and discriminatory treatment based on his age, sex, and religion. McKeithan filed a formal complaint with the Office of Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) in April 2010, alleging discrimination on the basis of sex, age, and religion, but did not formally claim retaliation. The EEO accepted his complaint for processing, but only identified his age-related discrimination claim as the accepted issue for investigation. McKeithan signed an affidavit stating that he believed he was discriminated against based on his age.

McKeithan had previously spoken with a counselor in the EEO in February 2010 and filed his formal complaint on April 1, 2010. The EEO warned McKeithan that if he failed to contact the investigator to specify why he believed his claims had not been correctly identified, it would be concluded that he agreed with the identified claims. McKeithan did not challenge the EEO's letter and did not attempt to amend or alter the decision to only investigate his age-related discrimination claim. McKeithan eventually retired from the GPO and filed suit against Boarman on January 13, 2011, alleging violations of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967. Defendant Boarman has moved to dismiss McKeithan's claims, arguing that McKeithan failed to exhaust his administrative remedies with respect to his gender and religious discrimination claims and his retaliation claim.

Patricia Holmes, an employee of the Marion County Office of Family and Children, holds a sincere religious belief that conflicts with a requirement of her employment. Plaintiff alleges that she informed the State of this conflict, but the State failed to make a reasonable accommodation for her religious practice. Holmes contends that the State's failure to accommodate her religious belief constitutes religious discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The State, on the other hand, claims that it cannot be sued under Title VII for failure to accommodate an employee's religious beliefs due to the Eleventh Amendment, which provides immunity to non-consenting states from suits by private individuals in federal court. Defendant contends that Congress did not have the authority under the Fourteenth Amendment to abrogate the States' immunity in this context. The United States has intervened in the case, arguing that Title VII's requirement of reasonable accommodation for religious beliefs is a valid exercise of Congressional authority under Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment. Prior to filing her complaint, Holmes worked for the State, and her religious beliefs allegedly conflicted with a requirement of her employment, leading to a dispute over the State's obligation to accommodate her religious practice. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the State being the employer and Holmes being the employee. The nature of the dispute is a claim of religious discrimination under Title VII, with the State challenging the applicability of the statute to its employment practices due to the Eleventh Amendment. Relevant pre-litigation events include Holmes' notification to the State of her religious conflict and the State's alleged failure to accommodate her religious beliefs.

Plaintiff, an African American man, began working for Costco as a bakery employee in December 2014. In 2020, he applied for a loss prevention position, but was informed by Costco that he did not qualify. However, Plaintiff alleges that Costco later filled the role with a less qualified white employee. In March 2021, Plaintiff applied for Bakery Supervisor and Bakery Manager positions, but did not receive either position, despite having over 40 years of bakery experience and being 59 years old at the time. Plaintiff contends that the positions were given to less qualified employees, including a white employee under the age of 40 with no bakery experience.

Plaintiff alleges that in April 2021, his supervisor, Stefan Mannsbart, gave him a counseling notice, stating that he was being disciplined for discouraging employees from cooperating with management. However, Plaintiff claims that the reports leading to the counseling notice were false and that Mannsbart refused to investigate the matter thoroughly or listen to his side of the story. Later that month, Costco moved Plaintiff out of his baker position and gave him a permanent counseling notice, which Plaintiff alleges was retaliatory. Plaintiff was then demoted to a cashier assistant position. Plaintiff also alleges that an assistant warehouse manager constantly told him that he should retire.

Plaintiff had previously reported race discrimination to Mannsbart in 2015, after being demoted from a bakery manager position for storing out-of-date products, while a white bakery manager received no discipline for a similar infraction. Plaintiff filed discrimination charges with the EEOC in 2015 and again in July 2021, alleging race and age discrimination, as well as retaliation. The EEOC issued a right to sue letter in October 2021. Plaintiff alleges that Costco's actions, including the denial of promotions and demotion, were discriminatory and retaliatory, and that he was treated unfairly compared to his white counterparts. Defendant contends that Plaintiff did not qualify for the positions he applied for and that the counseling notices and demotion were legitimate employment actions.

Dreiband, an IT specialist of Iranian national origin with a disability, was hired by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in 1989 and worked for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) since 2003. Between 1998 and 1999, she worked on the same team as Nancy Luc, another IT specialist, and filed an EEO complaint against Luc for harassment, which led to her reassignment. Although they no longer worked together, they continued to work in the same office building. On February 7, 2014, the two women were involved in a physical altercation at a gym, resulting in Dreiband being bitten by Luc, and both were arrested. 

Plaintiff alleges that following the incident, Luc told coworkers and supervisors that Dreiband had initiated the fight, and despite complaining to management, no action was taken. Defendant contends that Dreiband was involved in the altercation and was subsequently suspended for five days without pay for conduct unbecoming a federal employee. Dreiband responded to the proposed suspension, stating she was the innocent victim of a malicious attack. In May 2014, Dreiband received a mid-year performance evaluation, which rated her as "fully satisfactory" in several areas but noted she had "much room for improvement" in teamwork, citing the altercation and counseling regarding management policy.

Dreiband contacted an EEO Counselor regarding her suspension and treatment after the gym altercation in October 2014 and later filed a formal complaint with ICE's Office of Diversity and Civil Rights (ODCR) in January 2015, alleging discrimination and a hostile work environment based on national origin, religion, age, disability, and reprisal. The complaint cited the physical attack, false statements made by Luc during the investigation, an unfavorable mid-year review, and her suspension. Dreiband received a Report of Investigation (ROI) and the final agency decision from ODCR in August 2015. She filed suit in May 2017, alleging national-origin discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation under Title VII, as well as disability discrimination, retaliation, and hostile-work environment under the Rehabilitation Act.

DaBin Ki, an Asian-American woman, has been an employee of the United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) since September 28, 2008. From 2016 to 2018, she served on a detail to the PRA Operations and Human Factors Branch (APHB) within the Division of Risk Assessment (DRA), NRR. During this time, her supervisor was Sunil Weerakkody, a Sinhalese male, and later Christopher J. Fong, a "Caucasian/Asian" male. Plaintiff alleges that a fellow employee, Jeff Circle, subjected her to incidents of unlawful harassment based on her race, including mocking Asian accents, making fun of Asian-Americans during branch meetings, and ridiculing their stature.

Plaintiff contends that she witnessed and was subject to Mr. Circle's "persistent belittling mockery of his Asian colleagues" throughout her two-year detail. She alleges that Mr. Circle frequently referred to the way "they" talk, referring to NRC employees with Asian accents, and made jokes about Asian-Americans who were late to meetings. Plaintiff also claims that Mr. Circle mocked Asian-American colleagues during individual, private meetings. Additionally, she alleges that during a fire drill, Mr. Circle berated her in an intimidating and threatening manner. Plaintiff informed her supervisors at NRC multiple times about Mr. Circle's conduct, but they failed to take any corrective action. She reported the incidents to Mr. Weerakkody, who told her to "just forget about it" and "let it go."

Plaintiff also described Mr. Circle's behavior to other branch members, including two Asian-American branch members, Mr. Donald Chung and Mr. Ching Ng. Other branch members, including Mr. Jerrod Demers and Mr. Antonios Zoulis, witnessed Mr. Circle's conduct and confirmed that he made derogatory comments about Asian-Americans. Before her detail ended in September 2018, Plaintiff obtained counseling from the union and brought her concerns to NRC's EEO office and the Office of the Chief Human Capital Officer (OCHCO). In October 2018, Plaintiff had her final performance appraisal with Mr. Fong, during which she discussed her claims against Mr. Circle and her actions with the union and OCHCO. Despite her complaints, Plaintiff alleges that the NRC had not taken any preventative or corrective action as of the time of her final performance appraisal. The OCHCO later concluded an inquiry into Plaintiff's allegations and found that Mr. Circle's conduct violated the NRC's Anti-Harassment Policy. However, the NRC issued a final agency decision stating that Plaintiff was "not subjected to unlawful discrimination or harassment based on race" and "no relief [was] warranted."

Eight states and three private healthcare providers, including Franciscan Alliance, Inc., Specialty Physicians of Illinois, LLC, and the Christian Medical & Dental Society, have sued the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and HHS Secretary Sylvia Burwell. The plaintiffs challenge a new rule issued by HHS, entitled Nondiscrimination in Health Programs & Activities, which implements Section 1557 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA). The rule prohibits discrimination by any health program or activity receiving federal financial assistance on the grounds prohibited under four federal nondiscrimination statutes, including Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972. 

Plaintiffs allege that the rule's interpretation of discrimination "on the basis of sex" under Title IX as encompassing "gender identity" and "termination of pregnancy" will require them to perform and provide insurance coverage for gender transitions and abortions, regardless of their contrary religious beliefs or medical judgment. They contend that the rule's definition of sex does not apply to them because the text of Section 1557 incorporates the religious and abortion exemptions of Title IX, and the rule's failure to incorporate those exemptions renders it contrary to law. 

Defendants claim that the rule does not mandate any particular procedure, but rather requires only that covered entities provide nondiscriminatory health services and health insurance in a nondiscriminatory manner. They argue that the rule does not require the performance or insurance coverage of any procedure, but merely prohibits policies from "operating in a discriminatory manner, both in design and implementation." The plaintiffs, including Franciscan and the Christian Medical & Dental Society, are covered entities under the rule because they receive federal financial assistance and provide employee health insurance. They fear that the rule will require them to perform and provide insurance coverage for abortion- and transition-related procedures, which they believe would violate their religious freedom and medical judgment.

Plaintiff, a Negro employee at Crown Zellerbach's Bogalusa box plant, filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) alleging that the company had engaged in unlawful employment practices, including racial discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that he was denied promotion from "take-off man" to "slitter man" due to his race. He also alleges that the company has a policy of segregating jobs by race, with certain jobs being reserved for white employees, and that the company's testing procedures for promotions are designed to discriminate against Negroes. Plaintiff further alleges that the company's locker facilities are segregated by race.

Defendant Crown Zellerbach contends that it has a policy against racial discrimination in employment and that plaintiff's allegations are unfounded. Defendant argues that each member of the proposed class of Negro employees has unique circumstances, such as seniority and job position, that would require individualized consideration, and that a class action is therefore improper. Defendant also claims that it has taken an affirmative stand against racial discrimination in employment.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with plaintiff being a Negro employee at Crown Zellerbach's Bogalusa box plant. The nature of the dispute is a claim of racial discrimination in employment, with plaintiff alleging that the company has engaged in unlawful employment practices that affect not only him but also other Negro employees. Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff exhausted his administrative remedies by filing a charge with the EEOC, which attempted to conciliate the matter but was unsuccessful. The EEOC's conciliation efforts were directed at eliminating the company's allegedly discriminatory policies, rather than just addressing plaintiff's individual grievance. Plaintiff now seeks to represent a class of Negro employees at the Bogalusa box plant in a lawsuit against Crown Zellerbach, alleging that the company's policies and practices have a discriminatory impact on all Negro employees.

Alma, a 36-year-old Hispanic man, has been a police officer with the Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) since August 2002. Between 2006 and 2007, Alma alleges that he was the victim of sexual harassment and retaliation at the hands of his female first line supervisor. In response, Alma filed a federal lawsuit claiming sex discrimination and reprisal, which settled in mid-2010 with the help of the court's alternative resolution program. 

Following the settlement, the MPD proposed a 25-day suspension, which Alma appealed to the Chief of Police. The Chief offered Alma the opportunity to transfer to a different unit with no discipline on his record, which Alma accepted. However, days later, Alma was proposed for another suspension (15 days) on what he alleges were pretextual grounds. After his internal appeal failed, Alma served the suspension in 2011. On October 18, 2011, Alma was allegedly threatened with discipline for his facial hair, despite explaining that he was wearing a beard for religious purposes. His supervisor told him that he needed to get a religious waiver, although the complaint alleges that other coworkers and supervisors were permitted to wear beards without a waiver. Alma ultimately requested and received a waiver from the Chief of Police.

Plaintiff alleges that these actions were retaliatory, while Defendant contends that there are insufficient facts to support any cause of action under Section 1981. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the MPD being Alma's workplace. The nature of the dispute is a claim of retaliation, with Alma alleging that the MPD took adverse actions against him after he filed a complaint of sexual harassment. Relevant pre-litigation events include the settlement of Alma's prior lawsuit, the proposed suspensions, and the incident regarding Alma's facial hair. The complaint was filed on February 27, 2015, and Defendant filed a motion to dismiss on May 27, 2015.

Kandra Amboh, a middle-aged Native American woman, was hired as a part-time produce clerk at Smith's Food and Drug, a subsidiary of Kroger, in Vernal, Utah, in August 2021. Shortly after starting, a fellow clerk pretended to be her manager and began bossing her around, prompting Ms. Amboh to complain to her supervisor and submit a written complaint to the store's HR specialist. However, HR did not address the problem to her satisfaction. A couple of weeks later, her hours at the store were decreased and given to a young Caucasian male, leading Ms. Amboh to suspect unlawful discrimination. Despite her demands for more hours, her higher-ups turned her away. After several physically violent incidents with coworkers, Ms. Amboh resigned in April 2022, feeling unsafe at the store.

Plaintiff alleges that she was discriminated against based on her race, sex, and age, and that her employer's actions created a hostile work environment. Defendant contends that it did not discriminate against Ms. Amboh and that her hours were decreased due to legitimate business reasons. Before resigning, Ms. Amboh filed a charge of discrimination with the Utah Labor Commission's Anti-Discrimination and Labor Division (UALD) and the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in February 2022. The UALD dismissed her charge, finding no reasonable cause to believe that Kroger or its employees had discriminated against her. Ms. Amboh then requested de novo review of the UALD decision, but failed to timely file her petitioner's statement, resulting in the dismissal of her claims with prejudice.

The EEOC adopted the ALJ's findings and issued Ms. Amboh a notice of her right to sue on October 3, 2023, specifying that she had 90 days to file a lawsuit. Plaintiff alleges that she received the right-to-sue letter on October 18, 2023. Defendant contends that Ms. Amboh's lawsuit, filed on January 11, 2024, is time-barred because it was filed more than 90 days after the EEOC issued the right-to-sue letter. The parties' dispute centers on the timeliness of the lawsuit and the preclusive effect of the ALJ's dismissal of Ms. Amboh's claims.

Cloutier, a pilot, was employed by GoJet Airlines. He had diabetes mellitus, a serious health condition. Cloutier alleges that he needed to take leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) due to his condition. GoJet was aware of Cloutier's need for leave. Plaintiff alleges that GoJet interfered with his right to take FMLA leave, while Defendant contends that it did not. The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding Cloutier's termination from GoJet. 

Cloutier contends that he was terminated because he had requested or taken FMLA leave, while GoJet claims that the termination was for other reasons. The parties also dispute the amount of back pay Cloutier is entitled to, with GoJet proposing to calculate it using the minimum amount of flight hours per month guaranteed under the collective bargaining agreement, and Cloutier arguing that he would have worked more hours in overtime. Additionally, GoJet claims that Cloutier unreasonably failed to mitigate damages by turning down a job offer from Republic Airways, which required him to sign a promissory note agreeing to pay the airline $25,000 if he left the company before completing two years of work.

In April 2017, GoJet made Cloutier an offer of reinstatement, which he did not accept. The offer stated that Cloutier would return to his position as a Captain with the same responsibilities and seniority, and that he would not be required to discontinue or dismiss his grievance and complaint against GoJet. However, Cloutier alleges that the offer was not unconditional, as it required him to complete a weeks-long training program before returning to work. GoJet contends that Cloutier's non-acceptance of the offer was unreasonable and that he is not entitled to recover back pay or front pay after the date of the offer. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is Cloutier's allegations of FMLA interference and retaliation against GoJet.

In 2014, Plaintiff was diagnosed with hypertension and has been on blood pressure medication since then. His hypertension substantially limits the functioning of his circulatory system, and without medication, he can suffer vision loss, heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, and other conditions. On October 16, 2019, Defendant hired Plaintiff as a mental health technician to work on a campus with approximately fifty separate houses, each with eight to ten residents. 

In April 2020, during the pandemic, Defendant provided no guidance to mental health technicians like Plaintiff on how to handle or interact with residents to protect them and the employees, despite multiple residents contracting COVID. Defendant provided the same non-95 paper masks and face shields as before the pandemic, but no other personal protective equipment or special training on handling COVID patients. Around late April 2020, Plaintiff spent three days in the hospital after contracting COVID and was ordered off work by his doctor between April 26 and June 14, 2020, due to pneumonia, tachycardia, uncontrolled blood pressure, and renal insufficiency.

Plaintiff alleges that he could have been given a reassignment to a vacant position that would not have presented an undue burden to Defendant, noting that other mental health technicians had been previously reassigned to full-time positions involving food preparation and delivery. Plaintiff contends that he submitted a request for accommodation on June 9, 2020, to be given a modified or alternative work assignment with limited contact with residents, but his request was denied, and Defendant did not engage in an interactive process to determine whether an alternative accommodation could have been provided. Defendant contends that it did not violate the ADA, but the specific contentions of Defendant regarding the accommodation request and the interactive process are not stated in the complaint. Plaintiff claims that he is a qualified individual with a disability who could perform the essential functions of his job with an accommodation and that a reasonable accommodation in his case would not create undue hardship for his employer. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant's actions resulted in his extended leave of absence and eventual termination on August 4, 2020.

Alicia Martinez was hired by MSNBC Cable LLC as an associate producer in May 1996, at a salary of $47,000 per annum, after informing the hiring executive, Bob Epstein, that she was pregnant. She took maternity leave in November 1996 and returned to work part-time in March 1997 as a producer in the tape acquisitions group, a higher-level position than her initial role. Martinez decided to breastfeed her son and, with the consent of her supervisor, Pat Walker, pumped breast milk three times a day in an empty edit room at MSNBC's New Jersey studio. However, she became upset when someone tried to enter the room while she was inside on several occasions. Martinez raised concerns about her privacy with MSNBC's human resources officials and rejected suggestions to put a "do not disturb" sign on the door or use alternative sites for pumping.

Plaintiff alleges that Walker became less accommodating of her scheduling concerns, which revolved around her childcare needs, starting in August 1997. Martinez contends that she was told she would have to work weekends and take a pay cut if she moved back to an associate producer position, which she felt would not meet her needs. Defendant contends that Martinez was offered alternative positions and schedules, but she rejected them. Martinez also complains of three occasions on which a male co-worker allegedly made offensive comments regarding her breast pumping. In September 1997, MSNBC notified Martinez that she would be moved to an associate producer position with a fixed schedule, which she felt was not suitable for her needs. Martinez took a medical leave in October and, upon her return, was permitted to take off every Saturday until she resigned on December 12, 1997.

Martinez claims that she experienced difficulties with her schedule and privacy while pumping breast milk at work, and that her complaints to human resources were followed by retaliatory conduct, including verbal harassment and schedule changes. Defendant contends that it provided Martinez with accommodations for her breast pumping needs and that her schedule changes were due to business needs. Martinez filed a charge of discrimination with the EEOC in April 1998, alleging that MSNBC failed to provide her with a safe and private area to breast pump and that she was subjected to retaliatory conduct. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of discrimination and retaliation under the Americans with Disabilities Act and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.

Rhonda Kriss was a sales representative at Sprint Communications Company, hired in 1988 as a Major Account Representative in the Business Market Group (BMG). She had over six years of experience in the telecommunications industry and consistently exceeded her sales quotas, ranking high in the Minneapolis office and the entire West Division. Kriss was recognized for her performance through various awards and incentives, including the President's Club and incentive trips. However, her manager, Scott Miller, was found to be less supportive of her compared to male representatives, and the support staff resources were unequally distributed. Miller had a poor record of retaining women sales representatives, and his behavior contributed to a male-dominated atmosphere in the workplace.

Plaintiff alleges that in September 1990, Sprint decided not to transfer her to the New Business Management Group (New BMG), and she claims this decision was based on her gender. Defendant Sprint contends that the decision was based on legitimate business reasons. Kriss had applied for a position in the New BMG, but was not selected. The New BMG was a new organization within Sprint, and the selection process for positions in this group was competitive. Kriss claims that she was qualified for a position in the New BMG and that her skills and experience were comparable to those of the representatives who were eventually chosen for the transfer.

In the months leading up to the decision, Kriss was working on a major sales proposal for The Roach Organization (TRO) account, which was a demanding customer that requested pricing and technical information on various long distance systems. Kriss had been involved in sales proposals for TRO's long distance business, along with representatives from other major long distance carriers. On February 15, 1990, Kriss approached the sales support staff in the National Accounts Division with a Virtual Private Network (VPN) order for TRO, but the order was not completed due to missing information and signatures. Kriss had not disclosed that TRO was placing similar orders with two other carriers, and the National Accounts staff had worked late to process the order, only to find out that it was not a priority. This incident was cited as one of the reasons for Kriss not being selected for the New BMG, but Kriss claims that it was not a significant factor and that her overall performance and qualifications made her a strong candidate for the transfer.

In December 1980, the Administrative Committees of the Phase II Corporation Restated Profit Sharing Plan and the California Etching Corporation Restated Profit Sharing Plan decided to invest in a residential real estate development project, with each plan initially investing $100,000 and later adding another $30,000. Plaintiffs, who were participants in at least one of the plans and members of one or both of the plans' Administrative Committees, allege that this investment was made on the advice of defendants Khateeb Lateef and Lateef Management Associates. As part of the real estate deal, defendant Sumitomo Bank, the trustee for the plans, and defendant Roy Sherman, the escrow holder, executed escrow instructions, which provided that Sherman would deliver to Sumitomo a recorded deed of trust securing promissory notes that the plans had received in return for their investment. However, neither Sherman nor Sumitomo recorded the trust deed.

Plaintiffs allege that the failure to record the trust deed resulted in the plans being unsecured, leading to a total loss when the entity in which the plans had invested filed for reorganization under the Bankruptcy Act on June 4, 1984. The United States Department of Labor (DOL) later concluded an investigation of these events and determined that plan fiduciaries had violated their duties under ERISA in their initial participation and subsequent handling of the real estate investment. The DOL ordered restoration of the funds lost as a result of the breach of duty, which plaintiffs complied with through a combination of actual deposits to the plans and forfeitures of their own individual plan accounts. Plaintiffs contend that defendants are at least equally culpable for the loss and seek recovery for themselves and for the plans.

Defendants contend that the plans were fully compensated for the losses suffered as a result of the real estate debacle. Plaintiffs respond that the plan was compensated only to the extent funds were actually deposited, thus creating a shortfall equal to the forfeitures. The parties dispute the effect of the reimbursement arrangement on the plans' assets and liabilities, with plaintiffs arguing that the forfeitures did not replenish plan assets and defendants arguing that the forfeitures reduced plan liabilities. Plaintiffs also assert that defendants breached their fiduciary duties under ERISA and seek recovery for the amounts forfeited pursuant to the DOL order, as well as contribution from defendants for amounts actually deposited to the plans. Defendants argue that ERISA does not authorize an action for contribution on behalf of individual plaintiffs.

The Joint Apprenticeship Committee (JAC) had a requirement that applicants for its programs must have a high school diploma and, until 1985, be no older than 22 years old. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) alleges that these requirements had a discriminatory impact on blacks and women. The EEOC contends that the high school diploma requirement disproportionately affected blacks, as a lower percentage of black applicants met this requirement compared to white applicants. Plaintiff alleges that the difference in the percentage of blacks and whites who met the educational requirement is statistically significant. The EEOC also claims that the age maximum had a disparate impact on women, as a significantly greater percentage of female applicants were over the age of 22 and thus deemed ineligible.

The JAC and the EEOC have different contentions regarding the statistical analysis of the impact of these requirements. The JAC contends that the EEOC's statistical analysis is flawed, while the EEOC argues that its analysis demonstrates a statistically significant disparity. The EEOC points to the fact that the percentage of blacks among total applicants to the programs was significantly lower than the percentage of blacks in the pool of potential applicants. The JAC, on the other hand, suggests alternative methods of statistical analysis, such as using a pass ratio rather than a fail ratio, which it claims would show no disparity.

The EEOC and the JAC also disagree on the causal link between the challenged practices and the statistical disparities. The EEOC alleges that the educational requirement and age maximum had a chilling effect on potential black and women applicants, which caused the statistical disparities. The EEOC points to JAC advertisements that expressly stated the age, educational, and other requirements, which it claims deterred potential applicants. The JAC, however, argues that the EEOC has not produced evidence of a single otherwise qualified individual who was deterred by the advertisements from applying to a program. The parties have submitted various affidavits and expert analyses in support of their positions, including those from experts such as Gardenier and Valinsky. The JAC has also submitted business justification affidavits, which the EEOC argues are unpersuasive and lack supporting evidence.

Manuel Guevara worked as a bell stand attendant at The Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Los Angeles, California, from approximately June 4, 2012, to March 5, 2021. Plaintiff Guevara alleges that, beginning in May 2020, Ritz-Carlton incorrectly regarded him as disabled with a contagious disease and impaired immune and respiratory systems. Guevara further alleges that, as a result, Ritz-Carlton imposed unwanted "accommodations" on him, including requiring him to wear a mask and submit to temperature checks, which were allegedly implemented to mitigate his perceived disability.

Guevara contends that these accommodations were actually Ritz-Carlton's policies for preventing the spread of COVID-19, which applied to all employees. He submits documents that state these policies required all employees to participate in temperature checks and wear facemasks while at work. Guevara alleges that by requiring him to comply with these COVID-19 policies and procedures, Ritz-Carlton imposed unwanted and discriminatory accommodations on him. When Guevara objected to these "accommodations," he claims that Ritz-Carlton retaliated against him, ultimately terminating his employment.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Ritz-Carlton being Guevara's employer during the relevant time period. The nature of the dispute is a claim of disability discrimination and retaliation under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Defendant Ritz-Carlton contends that its policies were intended to prevent the spread of COVID-19 and applied to all employees, not just Guevara. The pre-litigation events include Guevara's employment with Ritz-Carlton, the implementation of COVID-19 policies, and Guevara's objections to these policies, which ultimately led to his termination. Relevant documents and communications include the policies and procedures implemented by Ritz-Carlton, as well as Guevara's complaints and objections to these policies.

In 1976, the plaintiff, who is not named, filed a civil rights action against his employers, alleging racial discrimination in his firing. The plaintiff's attorney at the time, Helen Cutner, filed the complaint, basing the claim solely upon Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Cutner conducted discovery, responded to a defense motion for summary judgment, and completed most other pretrial matters before withdrawing from the case in June 1978. The plaintiff's representation was then taken over by Michael K. Simon, of the Philadelphia law firm Sidkoff, Pincus, Greenberg and Green. 

Plaintiff alleges that he was improperly discharged by his employers due to racial discrimination. Defendants contend that the plaintiff's evidence failed to establish a Title VII jurisdictional requirement that the defendant employer must have had "fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year." During the trial, Simon moved to amend the complaint to assert a claim under section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act, which was permitted by the court. 

Prior to the lawsuit, the plaintiff was employed by the defendants, but the exact nature and duration of his employment are not specified. The plaintiff's attorneys, Cutner and Simon, spent a significant amount of time working on the case, including conducting discovery, responding to motions, and preparing for trial. The plaintiff's attorneys now seek attorneys' fees for their work on the case, citing the time and labor required, the skill needed to present the case, and the customary fee for similar work. The defendants have not explicitly contested the amount of time spent by the plaintiff's attorneys, but have raised questions about the reasonableness of the hours claimed and the hourly rates sought.

Ms. Jordan, a woman of African ancestry, was employed by Varicosity, a medical clinic, as a front desk attendant from March 2018 to June 2023. Plaintiff alleges that her starting salary was lower than that of a white colleague with no medical background, despite her having over ten years of experience in the medical field. Over time, Ms. Jordan's responsibilities expanded to include billing, scheduling, and handling referrals, but she contends that her salary was not increased, nor was she paid overtime wages or given a title change. 

Plaintiff alleges that she was also asked to clean the office space for two hours after work at an hourly rate of $37.50 and was required to travel and work additional hours to clean a new, larger clinic in Montgomery. In January 2023, Varicosity hired Amanda Gilmore as its Human Resources Manager, and Ms. Jordan states that Gilmore or another manager installed call recording software on her computer without notice or consent. Plaintiff contends that this software was only installed on her computer and that of another black employee, while white employees did not have the software. Ms. Jordan also alleges that Gilmore closely scrutinized her work and accused her of staying late without permission, despite never being advised that she needed permission to work over 40 hours.

Defendant Varicosity denies all material allegations. In June 2023, after Ms. Jordan expressed concerns about discrimination in an email chain with Gilmore and requested a meeting with the clinic's owner, she was called to a meeting with the Chief Operating Officer and Gilmore, where she was fired. Plaintiff alleges that she was not provided with any evidence of poor performance or disciplinary reasons for her termination and was told that the owner wanted to "go another route." Ms. Jordan contends that her position was filled by a younger white person and that every person hired to fill the role since her termination has been white. Relevant pre-litigation events include the email chain between Ms. Jordan and Gilmore, as well as the meeting where Ms. Jordan was fired.

The plaintiff, a former employee of Health Insurance Plan of New York (HIP), alleges that she was subjected to age and sex discrimination by HIP and her supervisors. She was employed by HIP from February 11, 1985, until April 17, 1987, when she took sick leave status due to a nervous breakdown, which she claims was caused by the alleged harassment and discrimination. The plaintiff contends that she was paid differently than her male colleagues, including defendant Pellegrino, who was the head of the department in which she worked, and an unnamed consultant who allegedly performed her job after she left. 

Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to physical assault and verbal harassment by her co-employees, and that HIP was responsible for these actions. She also claims that HIP's Vice President for Human Resources, Fred Blickman, sent her a letter that was part of the alleged harassment. The plaintiff further alleges that she was defamed by HIP and seeks to apply the self-publication rule, which is not currently recognized in New York law. 

Defendant HIP contends that the plaintiff's claims are without merit and that the proposed amended complaint fails to assert a claim under the Equal Pay Act. HIP argues that the plaintiff's job was not equal in responsibility to that of Pellegrino, and that there is no allegation that the consultant performed a job of equal skill, effort, or responsibility as the plaintiff. HIP also objects to the plaintiff's claims of intentional infliction of emotional distress and defamation, arguing that the plaintiff has not alleged extreme and outrageous conduct by HIP, and that the self-publication rule is not recognized in New York law.

April Brown, the Plaintiff, was an employee of Mecklenburg County. Plaintiff alleges that she has a disability and requested reasonable accommodations from her employer. Defendant Lisa Burns, Senior Human Resources Manager for Mecklenburg County, was responsible for handling Plaintiff's accommodation request. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant Burns refused to make reasonable accommodations in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Plaintiff also contends that she suffered retaliation as a result of her request for accommodations. 

Plaintiff and Defendant Burns' interactions occurred while Plaintiff was employed by Mecklenburg County, with Defendant Burns acting in her capacity as Senior Human Resources Manager. The parties' relationship is that of employee and human resources representative, with the nature of the dispute centering on the alleged failure to provide reasonable accommodations and retaliation. Plaintiff alleges that she was entitled to accommodations under the ADA and that Defendant Burns' refusal to provide them was unlawful. Defendant contends that the accommodations requested by Plaintiff were not reasonable or necessary.

Prior to filing the lawsuit, Plaintiff made requests for accommodations to Defendant Burns, which Defendant allegedly denied. The specific requests made by Plaintiff and the reasons for Defendant's denial are disputed. Plaintiff also alleges that she experienced retaliation after making her requests, which Defendant contends did not occur. The events giving rise to the lawsuit took place while Plaintiff was employed by Mecklenburg County, and the lawsuit was filed on September 17, 2021, naming Defendant Burns as the sole Defendant.

Andrea Banks-McClure was employed as a registered nurse (RN) by the University of Chicago Medical Center from August 21, 2023, until she claims she was constructively discharged on September 13, 2024. Plaintiff alleges that she experienced race and disability discrimination and retaliation during her employment, which ultimately led to her constructive discharge. Defendant University of Chicago Medical Center contends that it did not discriminate or retaliate against Plaintiff. On September 27, 2024, Banks-McClure filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), alleging violations of Title VII and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The EEOC issued a Notice of Right to Sue (NRTS) to Banks-McClure on October 9, 2024. 

Banks-McClure received the NRTS and subsequently filed a complaint with the court on January 8, 2025, which is 91 days after receiving the notice. The University of Chicago Medical Center notes that its correct name is "University of Chicago Medical Center," not "University of Chicago Hospital" as stated in the complaint. Plaintiff alleges that the events leading to her constructive discharge occurred while she was working at the University of Chicago Medical Center, but the specific details of these events are disputed. 

The parties' relationship is that of employer and former employee, with the University of Chicago Medical Center being the employer and Banks-McClure being the former employee. The nature of the dispute is Banks-McClure's allegations of discrimination, retaliation, and constructive discharge, which the University of Chicago Medical Center denies. The pre-litigation events include Banks-McClure's employment, her filing of the EEOC charge, and the issuance of the NRTS. Relevant documents include the EEOC charge, the NRTS, and the complaint filed with the court. Communications between the parties prior to the lawsuit are not specified, but it is clear that Banks-McClure made allegations of discrimination and retaliation to the EEOC, which led to the issuance of the NRTS and ultimately the filing of the complaint.

The plaintiff, a man of African, Hispanic, and Native American ancestry born in 1951, has had a long career in the federal government, including positions with the Army, the U.S. Air Force, and the International Boundary & Water Commission. He served on active duty with the U.S. Coast Guard Judge Advocate General ("JAG") Corp from 1989 through 1993 and as a reservist with the U.S. Air Force and Air National Guard from 1993 through 2000. The plaintiff alleges that he applied for at least 16 vacancies with the 411 Contracting Support Brigade (CSB) since 2012 without being interviewed or selected. Two of these applications, both for a contract specialist position with the 411 Contract Support Brigade based in Daegu, South Korea, are relevant to this litigation.

The selection process for the contract specialist position involved three stages: application review, résumé rating, and interviews. The plaintiff first applied for the position in response to a vacancy announcement in December 2016, but his application was not initially referred for review. A government hiring freeze was announced in January 2017, and the hiring process stopped. The plaintiff filed an EEO complaint on January 23, 2017, based on the defendant's failure to refer his application for review. A new vacancy announcement was issued in June 2017, and the plaintiff submitted another application, which was referred to the résumé rating panel. The panel consisted of three reviewers who gave numerical ratings to each résumé based on five criteria: Education, Leadership Training, Contract Specialist Experience, Contracting Officer Experience, and Awards.

Plaintiff alleges that he was subjected to discrimination based on his race, age, and prior EEO activity when he was not selected for the contract specialist position. He contends that the résumé rating panel inconsistently applied the scoring criteria, particularly with regard to his Contract Specialist Experience. The plaintiff had served as a contract specialist from 1986 to 1995, but this experience was outside the 15-year window considered by the panel. However, he had also worked as a contracts attorney from 2006 to 2008, which was within the 15-year window. The plaintiff's final résumé score was 50, which was lower than the scores of the top-rated applicants who were referred for an interview. Defendant contends that the selection process was fair and that the plaintiff was not selected due to his lower résumé score and the high qualifications of the other applicants. The plaintiff filed an EEO complaint on April 12, 2018, after learning that another candidate, Daniel Shin, was selected for the position. The Army issued a Final Agency Decision on the plaintiff's EEO complaint, finding that he was not subjected to discrimination. The plaintiff then filed a lawsuit in the United States District Court, alleging racial discrimination, age discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation.

Collins, an African-American man, was employed by CB&I as a pipefitter in Sulphur, Louisiana. Plaintiff alleges that he was fired by CB&I in June 2017 due to his race. He filed a charge of discrimination with the United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), which closed the investigation and issued a notice of right to sue on November 5, 2018, giving Collins 90 days to pursue his claim in state or federal court. Collins then filed a pro se complaint against CB&I on February 5, 2019, alleging violations of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. His application to proceed in forma pauperis was approved on February 19, 2019.

CB&I contends that service of the complaint was improper because the person served, Kelvin Burns, was not the company's registered agent and because a copy of the complaint was not attached to the summons. Collins admits that service upon Burns was improper and does not contest the allegation that he failed to attach a copy of the complaint to the summons. Collins's counsel enrolled on his behalf on April 15, 2019, and made the deficient first attempt at service a week later. A second attempt at service was made on May 30, 2019, through agent Ashley Minvielle.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and former employee, with Collins alleging that he was discriminated against by CB&I due to his race. The nature of the dispute is a claim of racial discrimination under Title VII. Relevant pre-litigation events include Collins's employment and termination by CB&I, his filing of a charge with the EEOC, and the EEOC's issuance of a notice of right to sue. Relevant documents include the complaint, the EEOC charge, and the notice of right to sue. Communications between the parties include the service of the complaint and the filing of the motion to dismiss. Employment and workplace facts include Collins's position as a pipefitter and his termination by CB&I.

In August 2017, Plaintiff A.S. entered the Ocean County Fire and First Aid Training Center to become a member of the Seaside Heights Fire Department. John Syers, an instructor at the Training Center, made a comment to Plaintiff with sexual implications during a class on ropes and knots in firefighting. Plaintiff interpreted this comment as a sexual reference and confided in another student about the incident, feeling uncomfortable. Despite this, Plaintiff completed her requisite hours at the Training Center in April 2018 and became an active firefighter with the Seaside Heights Fire Department.

Plaintiff alleges that she and Syers had a brief romantic encounter in April 2018, followed by "on again/off again conversations" until September 2018. On September 26, 2018, Syers allegedly raped, tortured, and sexually abused Plaintiff. At the time, Syers was an instructor at the Fire Academy and Training Center. Plaintiff contends that after reporting the incident, she was told by a government attorney not to return to the Training Center and was reprimanded by employees and instructors. 

The Ocean County Defendants, including the Ocean County Fire Academy, the Training Center, and the Ocean County Board of Chosen Freeholders, are accused of failing to investigate Syers, discipline him, train and supervise employees, and protect Plaintiff from sexual assault and harassment. Plaintiff claims that the Fire Academy and Training Center maintained unconstitutional customs or policies, including failing to investigate evidence of misconduct and inadequately training employees. The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding the events, with Plaintiff alleging that she was dissuaded from filing a complaint due to the reprehensible treatment she received after reporting the rape and torture. The Ocean County Defendants argue that Plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies required before filing a Title VII claim.

A.T., a minor, was a student at Cleveland Middle School (CMS) where she allegedly experienced extreme student-on-student sexual harassment, sexual assault, sexual battery, and bullying. Plaintiffs, A.T. and her parents, B.G. and J.G., claim that the defendants, CMS and the Cleveland City Schools Board of Education (CCSBE), were deliberately indifferent to these incidents. The plaintiffs allege that the defendants' actions, or lack thereof, subjected A.T. to further harassment, embarrassment, and trauma, including an assembly where the subject of sexual harassment was explicitly discussed in relation to lawsuits.

Plaintiff A.T. alleges that she was subjected to sexual harassment, assault, and bullying while at CMS, and that the school administration was aware of these incidents but failed to take adequate action to prevent them. Plaintiff's mother and step-father, B.G. and J.G., also bring claims against the defendants for violations of Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, as well as under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Tennessee Governmental Tort Liability Act (GTLA). The defendants contend that they took reasonable steps to address the incidents and that the plaintiffs' claims are without merit.

Prior to the lawsuit, the plaintiffs and defendants engaged in discovery, during which the plaintiffs failed to disclose a potential witness, G.H., who was a classmate of A.T.'s and allegedly witnessed an assembly where sexual harassment was discussed. The defendants argue that the plaintiffs' failure to disclose G.H. as a witness was a violation of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(a)(1)(A)(i), which requires parties to disclose individuals who may have discoverable information. The plaintiffs claim that they were unaware of the necessity of calling G.H. as a witness until after the defendants' summary judgment motion was filed, and that they did not have the opportunity to disclose G.H. prior to filing their response brief. The defendants also note that the plaintiffs' response brief was filed untimely, 20 days after the deadline had expired, and that the plaintiffs did not seek an extension of time to file their response prior to the deadline's expiration.

On June 21, 2009, the plaintiff, a middle-aged white woman, was hired as a Senior Case Technician (SCT) in the Social Security Administration's (SSA) Office of Disability Adjudication and Review (ODAR) in Washington, D.C. for a two-year trial period. As an SCT, she assisted in the administrative adjudication of appeals brought by individuals denied Social Security and Social Security Insurance benefits. In addition to her regular SCT work, she performed clerical and technical tasks as a personal clerk to an administrative law judge and frequently filled in as the receptionist at the front desk of ODAR.

Three months after commencing her job, an African American male co-worker physically assaulted her, prompting her to file an informal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint. The co-worker claimed that the plaintiff attacked him. The plaintiff's supervisor, Hariette Hindie, responded to the incident by interrogating the plaintiff in a Weingarten session. When an SSA EEO official told the plaintiff that formal EEO complaints must be filed against "management," the plaintiff decided not to pursue a formal complaint for fear of losing her job. Plaintiff alleges that she did not take any formal action because she feared losing her job, while Defendant contends that the plaintiff had the opportunity to file a formal complaint but chose not to.

The plaintiff earned a promotion to a General Schedule (GS) level seven from a GS level six in June 2010, which was supported by Hindie and based on the plaintiff's job performance during the first year of her probationary period. However, in the following months, Hindie began scrutinizing the plaintiff's work more closely, and in September, she gave the plaintiff a counseling memorandum that identified specific problems with her recent job performance. The plaintiff responded by defending her performance in a rebuttal memorandum. On November 22, 2010, Hindie recommended the plaintiff's termination on the basis of poor work performance during the second year of the plaintiff's probationary period. Plaintiff alleges that Hindie's actions were retaliatory, while Defendant contends that the termination was based on the plaintiff's poor work performance. The plaintiff resigned effective January 5, 2011, to avoid embarrassment, increase her chances of obtaining future employment, and leave a work environment that caused her stress-related illnesses. Following her resignation, the plaintiff filed a formal EEO complaint against SSA management, alleging retaliation and coerced resignation.

Dawn M. Churney was employed as a probationary police officer in Downers Grove, Illinois, until she was fired on April 1, 1994. On May 4, 1994, she filed a sex discrimination charge with the Illinois Department of Human Rights against her former employer. Two years later, in August 1996, Churney was working part-time as part of a security detail at the Downers Grove Eagle Foods, alongside other off-duty police officers from Downers Grove. She was also working regular hours as a police officer for the Village of Somonauk, where she had been employed since October 1994. 

Plaintiff alleges that Andy Eliakis, the Eagle loss prevention director, had conversations with Downers Grove Police Chief George Graves, Deputy Chief Wiemer, and other Downers Grove Police Department employees, after which Eliakis fired Churney from the security detail. Churney claims she was told by Eliakis that Chief Graves had said she was not supposed to be working on the detail and had no authority to initiate arrests. Defendant Downers Grove contends that it provided only truthful information to Eagle and denies that Chief Graves or anyone else told Eliakis that Churney had no power to make an arrest. 

Churney asserts that she had the same arrest powers as any citizen in Downers Grove, and that Chief Graves's statement was false. She also claims that Chief Graves has provided negative information to other employers, including the Yorkville and Somonauk police departments, and has lied in various matters connected with this case. Downers Grove argues that the information it provided was true, and that Churney did not have "full" arrest powers as an off-duty officer. The parties dispute whether Downers Grove took adverse employment action against Churney, but agree that post-termination acts of retaliation with a nexus to employment are actionable under Title VII. Churney had been fired from the security detail at Eagle, and she claims this was a result of retaliation by Downers Grove for her filing the sex discrimination charge two years earlier.

The plaintiff, a former employee of the Davidson County Criminal Court Clerk's Office, alleges that she was subjected to sexual advances and acts of sexual harassment by defendant Ernie Moore, and that defendant Joe Torrence failed to take any action to halt Moore's alleged conduct. The plaintiff contends that as a result of the alleged harassment and adverse actions taken against her, she suffered severe economic, physical, and emotional damages, including the loss of her regular employment and the monetary compensation and benefits provided by that employment. Plaintiff alleges that she was forced to resign from her position on December 18, 1984, due to the unbearable working conditions created by the defendants' actions. 

Defendants Ernie Moore and Joe Torrence contend that the plaintiff voluntarily resigned her position, making recovery for monetary damages for lost wages inappropriate. They base their position on the plaintiff's deposition testimony. The defendants argue that the plaintiff's resignation was not a result of any actions taken by them, but rather a personal decision made by the plaintiff. The plaintiff, on the other hand, alleges that her resignation was a direct result of the sexual harassment and hostile work environment created by the defendants, and that she was constructively discharged.

The plaintiff and defendants were employed at the Davidson County Criminal Court Clerk's Office, where the alleged incidents of sexual harassment occurred. The plaintiff's Second Amended Complaint, filed on July 3, 1986, relates back to the date the civil action was commenced on December 19, 1985. The complaint names Ernie Moore, Joe Torrence, and the Metropolitan Government of Nashville, Davidson County as defendants. The plaintiff's allegations of sexual harassment and the defendants' responses are the central issues in the dispute, with the plaintiff seeking damages for the harm she claims to have suffered. Relevant pre-litigation events include the plaintiff's employment at the Davidson County Criminal Court Clerk's Office, the alleged incidents of sexual harassment, and the plaintiff's subsequent resignation.

Rothman began working for Complete in or around 2005 as a salesman and eventually became one of two Directors of Government Sales. The other Director, Wunk, performed similar work but earned a lower commission percentage. Rothman alleges that Mankosa, part of the group that purchased Complete, repeatedly mistreated and complained to him about Wunk, who is a gay woman. Rothman claims he complained to Mankosa about the perceived discriminatory behavior towards Wunk and told him that his treatment of her was wrong.

Rothman alleges that his support for Wunk came to a head in 2020 when he cooperated in Wunk's Title VII case against Complete, including providing recordings of conversations between him and Mankosa. Rothman claims that after his participation in the case became known to the defendants through the discovery process, he faced several decreases in his compensation package and was repeatedly underpaid his commissions. Two weeks after Wunk's lawsuit against Complete was settled, Rothman was terminated from his employment by Mankosa. Rothman alleges that his termination was motivated by his complaints regarding the discriminatory treatment of Wunk and his own commission underpayments.

Complete had a written contract with Arch Insurance to provide liability insurance for the period covering December 5, 2021, to December 5, 2022. The insurance policy required Arch Insurance to defend and indemnify Complete against suits seeking damages for allegations of discrimination and wrongful termination of employment. After Rothman initiated a lawsuit against Complete, alleging violations of Title VII, the New York Labor Law, and the New York State Human Rights Law, Complete demanded that Arch Insurance defend and indemnify them pursuant to the insurance policy, claiming that Rothman's termination and lawsuit fell within the policy period.

Chandler, a former employee of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), worked at the agency from February 25, 1977, until her retirement on August 30, 2007. During her time at the FDIC, she filed ten Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) administrative complaints and two civil actions against the agency. After her retirement, in 2009, Mir, Mitchel & Company (MMIC), a contractor that works with the FDIC, contacted her about a potential position. Chandler applied and was hired, but despite her repeated requests, she never received a work assignment from MMIC between 2009 and 2013. MMIC allegedly told her there was no work available for her.

In 2015, another FDIC contractor, the SolomonEdwards Group (SEG), offered Chandler a position as an investigative technician on a contract with the FDIC. She accepted and was assigned to work on the closing of the Doral Bank in San Juan, Puerto Rico. However, on March 23, 2015, her supervisor, Doug Thorpe, allegedly told her that he had been ordered to terminate her employment, claiming the order came from the FDIC, not SEG management. Chandler alleges that she was never assigned another project with SEG after her termination. Plaintiff alleges that the FDIC retaliated against her by "poisoning her prospects of working on its contracts" due to her successful litigation of prior EEO complaints during her time as an FDIC employee.

Chandler contends that she was retaliated against by the FDIC, while the FDIC's actions, as described by Chandler, suggest that the agency took no action to assign her work or interfere with her employment opportunities with its contractors. The FDIC's relationship with its contractors, including MMIC and SEG, is also relevant to the dispute. Chandler's EEO complaints and civil actions against the FDIC during her employment, as well as her subsequent attempts to work with FDIC contractors, are central to her allegations of retaliation. The parties' contentions regarding the events surrounding Chandler's employment with MMIC and SEG, as well as the FDIC's alleged involvement in her termination, are in dispute.

Darick Easterling, an employee of the County of Delaware, alleged that his employer discriminated against him on the basis of his disability, failed to accommodate his disability, and retaliated against him in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act (PHRA). Plaintiff also claimed that the County interfered with his ability to exercise his rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA), discriminated against him for exercising those rights, and retaliated against him. Easterling worked for the County, and the parties' relationship was that of employer and employee. 

Plaintiff alleges that the County's actions were unlawful and caused him harm, while Defendant contends that its actions were lawful and that Easterling's claims are without merit. The parties engaged in various pre-litigation interactions, including Easterling's requests for accommodation and the County's responses. Easterling's attorneys, Edward Sweeney and M. Frances Ryan, worked on his case, expending hours on various tasks, including drafting memoranda and litigating motions. The County argues that some of these hours were unnecessary, particularly those spent on Easterling's unsuccessful FMLA and retaliation claims.

The parties disagree on the reasonableness of the hours expended by Easterling's counsel and the hourly rates they should be paid. Easterling's counsel submitted evidence of their work, including hours spent and rates charged, while the County argues that these hours and rates are excessive. The County specifically contends that hours spent on the FMLA claims and retaliation claims should be deducted from the total hours, as these claims were ultimately unsuccessful. Easterling's counsel, on the other hand, argues that their rates and hours are reasonable, citing their experience and the prevailing market rates in Philadelphia.

Michael R. Gerd was employed by United Parcel Service, Inc. (UPS) on September 22, 1985, and was promoted to part-time supervisor in 1989. Plaintiff alleges that beginning in October 1993, he was subjected to unwelcome sexual and abusive conduct by his male coworkers and supervisors, including John Wish, Brad Ansel, and Lyle Dutton. Gerd contends that this conduct was directed at him because of his gender. The alleged incidents included Wish making suggestive comments about Gerd's phone numbers, Ansel rubbing his hands on Gerd's thighs and making lewd comments, and Dutton grabbing and squeezing Gerd's buttocks. 

Gerd alleges that he tried to report these incidents to Steven Nord, UPS's human resources manager, but Nord never returned his calls. When Gerd finally spoke with Nord on November 18, 1993, Nord told him to "stick it out" until peak season was over and promised to get him an interview with a different department. However, Gerd claims that the abusive conduct continued, and when he met with Tom Vale, manager of customer services, to discuss a transfer, Vale made light of the situation and told Gerd that he should get his supervisors to recommend him. Gerd replied that he had been subjected to abusive behavior by his coworkers, some of whom were his supervisors, and Vale responded that such behavior was essentially acceptable because UPS was founded as a trucking company.

Gerd filed sex discrimination charges with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on February 9, 1994, and later filed charges of retaliation. Defendant contends that the conduct alleged by Gerd was mere "locker room" activity and not subject to Title VII protection. Gerd alleges that after he filed the EEOC charges, Dutton confronted him and threatened to "drop" him or put him in a job he would dislike if he did not recant his statements. Gerd terminated his employment with UPS on June 30, 1994. UPS argues that it did not breach any contractual obligations to Gerd, while Gerd claims that UPS created express and implied contractual conditions and guarantees of employment that included a safe working environment, which UPS breached by failing to transfer him and permitting the abusive conduct to continue.

Kim Patrick Johnson, a resident of Margate, Florida, worked for Bennett Auto Supply, Inc., a Florida corporation, for approximately 27 years until his termination on January 24, 2017. Johnson initially worked in a counter sales position, taking orders, helping clients, and managing accounts, for 22 years, with the first 12 years at the Oakland Park store and the next 10 years at the Plantation store under manager Mario Acosta. Johnson's work was satisfactory, and in 2012, he was the second-highest sales writer at the Plantation store. 

Plaintiff alleges that he suffered from rheumatoid arthritis for several years, which worsened significantly in 2012, limiting his ability to stand or sit for long periods or lift heavy weights. Johnson requested a stool from Acosta to accommodate his disability, providing a doctor's letter confirming his condition, and Acosta provided the stool. However, Defendant then took away Johnson's two 15-minute breaks given to other employees, citing the stool as sufficient accommodation. Over the next 21 months, Defendant transferred Johnson four times to three different stores, with employees encouraging him to resign each time. In 2014, Acosta and Anita Smith, who oversaw Human Resources, notified Johnson of mistakes using the new MAM system, despite his lack of proper training, and demoted him to a cashier position, then later to a warehouse driver position, which Johnson struggled with due to his arthritis. 

Plaintiff alleges that Defendant created a hostile work environment by altering his employment terms due to his disability and that his termination was a pretext for unlawful discrimination. Defendant contends that Johnson's claim should be dismissed because the EEOC issued a notice of right to sue before the 180-day administrative period expired. Johnson filed a charge with the EEOC on April 28, 2017, and received a Notice of Right to Sue on September 28, 2017, before filing his Amended Complaint on April 6, 2018, alleging one count of unlawful disability discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Defendant argues that Johnson does not state a cause of action under the ADA, but Johnson maintains that he has a disability, is a qualified individual, and was discriminated against because of his disability.

James McLean began working as a supervisor for Delhaize America Distribution, LLC in February 2016, overseeing food product shipping and receiving crews at one of Delhaize's distribution centers. McLean reported to Dan Thyng, a manager, who in turn reported to Bruce Southwick, the general manager of the distribution center. The associates in McLean's crews were unionized, and McLean, Thyng, and Southwick managed day-to-day operations but were not involved in the approval process for associates' Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave requests.

In December 2016, the Associate Service Center and Leave Administration Department (ASC) approved a request for intermittent FMLA leave made by one of McLean's associates, BG, allowing him to take leave two times per year for up to three days each time to care for his son. BG submitted a schedule change request form to McLean in December 2016, seeking to amend his start time to 3:30 p.m., which McLean approved without further investigation. Plaintiff alleges that McLean had authority to modify associate schedules and that he accepted BG's explanation for the schedule change without questioning it. Defendant contends that McLean should have consulted with Thyng or the ASC before approving the schedule change.

In February 2017, Southwick met with BG to discuss concerns about his poor attendance record, and BG informed Southwick about his son's health and his request for expanded FMLA leave.
