Southwick chose not to punish BG and instructed him to continue working through the FMLA process. Around the same time, McLean received a report of an offensive ethnic slur from one of his associates, which he relayed to Thyng, who assured McLean that he would take care of it. However, Thyng spoke with the supervisor who made the slur, JB, and did not report the allegation to anyone else, despite Delhaize policy requiring managers to inform an Associate Relations representative of such complaints.

In March 2017, the ASC approved BG's new FMLA request, granting him four days of intermittent leave per month. Thyng met with McLean to discuss BG's schedule issues, and McLean approved another schedule change request from BG, seeking a start time of 4:30 p.m. Thyng disapproved the new schedule change, and McLean was instructed to tell BG that he needed to be at work by 3:30. McLean alleges that he told BG about the disapproval, while Defendant contends that McLean did not follow Thyng's instructions and instead asked another supervisor, Salamone, to approve the schedule change without informing her of the disapproval.

The parties dispute the events of the March 8 meeting between McLean, Salamone, and BG, with McLean claiming that he showed Salamone the disapproved schedule change form and Salamone denying this. The next day, Salamone met with Thyng and Shaw, and later prepared a written statement about the meeting, which she claimed was inconsistent with McLean's account. Southwick and Thyng met with McLean on March 10, accusing him of lying about telling BG that his schedule change request was denied. McLean was suspended pending further investigation, and Southwick ultimately decided to terminate him, citing insubordination. McLean filed two internal company appeals, which Delhaize denied.

The United States government, as trustee of the Individual Indian Money (IIM) trust, has been responsible for managing the trust since its establishment in the late 19th century. The trust was created as a result of the government's policy of relocating tribal communities from their homelands to remote locations, and the subsequent allotment of Indian land to individual Indians, with the "surplus" lands being opened to non-Indian settlement. The government has been holding the allotted land in trust for the individual Indians, and has been responsible for managing the income generated from the land, such as oil and gas royalties, timber sales, and lease payments. 

Plaintiff Eloise Pepion Cobell, on behalf of herself and over 300,000 other IIM trust beneficiaries, alleges that the government has mismanaged the trust, failing to provide accurate accounting of the trust funds, and has lost or destroyed records of the trust assets. The plaintiffs contend that the government's mismanagement has resulted in the loss of millions of dollars in trust funds, and has denied them their rightful inheritance. The government, on the other hand, contends that it has taken steps to reform the trust management system, including the passage of the Indian Trust Fund Management Reform Act of 1994, and the development of a strategic plan to improve the management of the trust. 

The plaintiffs and the government have a long and complex history, with the government having imposed the trust on the Indian people, and the plaintiffs having been born and raised with the assurance that their trustee, the United States, was acting properly with their money. The plaintiffs have been seeking an accurate accounting of the trust funds, and have been denied this information by the government. The government has been writing checks on an account that it cannot balance or reconcile, and has been unable to provide an accounting of the plaintiffs' money. The plaintiffs have brought this lawsuit to force the government to abide by its duty to render an accurate accounting of the money currently held within the IIM trust. Relevant pre-litigation events include the government's admission that it cannot render an accurate accounting to the beneficiaries, and the plaintiffs' attempts to obtain this information through other means. The case concerns the issue of whether the government is in breach of any trust duties owed to the plaintiffs, and whether the plaintiffs should be afforded some prospective relief to prevent further injury of their legal rights.

Rick Gomez, an African-American male, was employed by the Metropolitan District (the "District") from October 2001 to October 7, 2011. Initially, he held the position of Affirmative Action Officer, later changed to Diversity Officer, reporting directly to the District's CEO, Charles Sheehan. Gomez was responsible for reviewing hires and promotions for racial neutrality and conducting investigations of employee complaints. In 2006, Gomez had a conflict with management over the District's affirmative action plan and felt isolated and excluded from hiring and promotional decisions. He was involuntarily transferred to the Program Management Unit ("PMU") as the Diversity Officer, reporting to Michael Jefferson, Diversity Manager for PMU.

Gomez alleges that during his final two years of employment, he was targeted and subjected to harassment and disparate treatment by District management on account of his race. In January 2010, Gomez was suspended for two days after an altercation with a coworker, Mark Bednarz, over a work-issued laptop. Gomez believed he was the victim of an assault and filed internal complaints, while Bednarz received a one-day suspension. In June 2010, Gomez filed a complaint with the Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities ("CHRO"), alleging race-based disparate treatment. He filed amended complaints in December 2010 and March 2011, alleging exclusion from hiring decisions and denial of a promotion due to his race. Gomez also filed an internal complaint in March 2011, alleging hostile and retaliatory treatment from his supervisor, Jefferson.

The District contends that community groups had begun to distrust the District's contractor diversity statistics, which were collected by Gomez, and that personnel were concerned about the reliability of the data. The District hired an outside consultant, Lilian Ruiz, to provide an independent audit of Gomez's work, and eventually, she assumed his responsibilities. Gomez's job responsibilities were curtailed, and he was notified of his termination on October 7, 2011, due to a reduction in force caused by the loss of a $2.1 million annual contract. The District selected positions for elimination, including Gomez's, based on their potential to recoup the lost funds without impacting the District's core mission. Gomez alleges that his termination was based on discriminatory animus and retaliation for his previous complaints. Plaintiff alleges that he was terminated and subsequently not hired for a different position at the District due to discrimination on the basis of race and as a result of retaliation for complaints that he filed opposing discrimination. Defendant contends that the termination was due to a legitimate reduction in force caused by the loss of a major contract.

Barbara Weeks was a Tax Examiner in the Enforcement Office at the State of Maine's Bureau of Taxation. She filed sex and age discrimination complaints with the Maine Human Rights Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Plaintiff alleges that she was illegally retaliated against for filing these complaints. The individually named defendants are Stephen Murray, Director of the Bureau's Enforcement Division, and Elizabeth Dodge, Acting Director of the Enforcement Division. Plaintiff names the State of Maine and these two superiors as Defendants. 

Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to retaliation after filing her discrimination complaints. Defendants contend that they do not qualify as "employers" under the acts pursuant to which Plaintiff's claims arise, and thus cannot be held personally liable. Specifically, Defendants argue that the case law interpreting Title VII exempts supervisory agents of employers from personal liability, while Plaintiff responds that the plain language of the statute clearly contemplates such personal liability. 

The parties disagree on the interpretation of the relevant statutes, including Title VII, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA), and the Maine Human Rights Act (MHRA). Plaintiff contends that supervisory employees can be liable under these statutes, while Defendants argue that they are not liable. The dispute centers on whether the individual Defendants, as supervisory employees, can be held personally liable for the alleged retaliation. Relevant pre-litigation events include Plaintiff's filing of discrimination complaints and the subsequent alleged retaliation. The case is scheduled to go to trial, and the individual Defendants have moved for dismissal under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.

Neil Taylor began working as a mechanic for Arlington Transit Mix, Inc. in June 1985. At the time of his hiring, he informed the plant manager, Kenneth Abraham Sr., that he would need to leave work early on Wednesdays to attend church services, which he believed were mandated by the Bible. Taylor was allowed to leave early on Wednesdays for approximately two years, from June 1985 until July 8, 1987. During this time, Taylor and the other three mechanics, Dana Justice, Charles Belcher, and Lee Roy Cox, worked the same hours and often stayed late to complete repairs on the company's trucks.

The company, which owns about 15 trucks, including large cement mixers, requires four full-time mechanics to inspect and repair the trucks when they return to the garage at the end of the day. In the spring of 1987, Arlington's management became concerned about the amount of overtime paid to the mechanics and decided to stagger their hours to maximize straight-time coverage. As part of this change, Belcher was appointed working foreman of the mechanics and was tasked with implementing a new schedule. The schedule change resulted in two mechanics starting at 6:00 a.m. and two starting at 9:00 or 10:00 a.m. Taylor, who had previously been allowed to leave early on Wednesdays, was assigned to the later shift.

Plaintiff alleges that Taylor's discharge on July 9, 1987, was due to his refusal to work late on Wednesday, July 8, 1987, in order to attend church services. Defendant contends that Taylor was discharged because he left work without permission, despite being told that his presence was needed to complete repairs on the trucks. Defendant also claims that it had accommodated Taylor's religious beliefs for two years, but was unable to do so on July 8, 1987, without incurring undue hardship. Prior to his discharge, Taylor had been involved in an incident in which he removed and destroyed a Playboy magazine centerfold and other similar photographs that had been posted in the garage by mechanic Cox, which had led to a reprimand from Abraham. Taylor had also been allowed to post notice of a Bible study group meeting in the garage area and distribute religious literature to his fellow employees.

Global Horizons, Inc. supplied workers, including those of Asian race and/or Thai national origin, to farms owned and operated by other entities in Hawaii. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) alleges that since 2003, Global Horizons engaged in a pattern or practice of discriminatory employment practices, including harassment and hostile work environment, against these workers. The EEOC contends that Global Horizons' supervisors, such as Sam Wongsesanit, Shane Germann, and Joseph Knoller, physically and verbally abused some of the workers, and that these supervisors had immediate authority over the workers. 

The EEOC alleges that the physical abuse included incidents such as Wongsesanit breaking a worker's sunglasses, grabbing a worker by the throat, and punching a worker in the face. The EEOC also alleges that the verbal harassment included threats of physical abuse, deportation, and arrest. The EEOC further contends that Global Horizons' supervisors routinely restricted the workers' movements, imposed curfews, and denied them required food, housing, and transportation, worsening the hostile work environment. 

Global Horizons did not respond to the EEOC's requests for admissions, which included allegations of these incidents of physical and verbal abuse. The EEOC argues that, pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 36(a)(3), these allegations are deemed admitted as a matter of law. The EEOC seeks to establish that Global Horizons' actions constituted a pattern or practice of discriminatory treatment, including hostile work environment, disparate treatment, and retaliation, in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The plaintiff was employed by the defendant from 2014 until her termination on December 1, 2021, working as a Medical Technologist I at Methodist North Hospital. Her role involved working in the laboratory testing patient specimens with no direct interaction with patients. The defendant implemented a policy requiring all employees to be fully vaccinated against COVID-19 by October 31, 2021. Plaintiff alleges she sought a religious exemption from the vaccine requirement, requesting to wear a non-fitted surgical mask, continue social distancing, and be exempt from COVID-19 testing, citing her religious beliefs that require her to "decline all attempts to access, influence and/or otherwise alter any and all of my God-given biological material and/or biological systems."

Plaintiff contends that her religious beliefs, which she described as being based on "1 Corinthians 3:16-17 & 6:19-20" and considering herself a "Temple of the Holy Spirit," prohibited her from undergoing COVID-19 testing, which she viewed as an invasive medical procedure. Defendant, on the other hand, responded to Plaintiff's exemption request by granting an exemption with alternative conditions: a respirator mask, weekly COVID-19 testing, and social distancing. Plaintiff alleges she objected to these conditions, particularly the testing requirement, as violating her religious beliefs.

The parties' dispute centers on the defendant's vaccination policy, the plaintiff's request for a religious exemption, and the conditions imposed by the defendant in response to that request. Plaintiff alleges that when she refused to comply with the conditions, specifically the weekly COVID-19 testing, the defendant terminated her employment. Defendant's actions and the plaintiff's termination are the focal points of the dispute, with each side having different contentions regarding the legitimacy of the exemption request, the reasonableness of the alternative conditions, and the lawfulness of the termination.

Larry Wayne Nash began working as a project superintendent for D.S. Nash Construction Company in 1976. In 1991, he suffered a serious back injury in a car accident while on the job, but continued to work despite his injury. Nash had back surgery in 1994 and again in 1995, returning to work after each surgery. In February 1996, his primary treating physician completed a disability form outlining physical activity restrictions due to his back injury and surgeries. Nash provided this form to his employer but continued working as a project superintendent.

Plaintiff Larry Wayne Nash alleges that on January 29, 1998, company president Gray Nash told him the company could no longer accommodate his disability. When Nash refused to resign, the company sent his job description to his doctor, who reaffirmed Nash's physical limitations. The company then terminated Nash's employment. Defendant D.S. Nash Construction Company contends that it could no longer accommodate Nash due to his physical limitations and the requirements of his job.

Nash filed an EEOC complaint on May 18, 1998, alleging ADA violations. He completed an EEOC Form 5, which included a sworn affidavit detailing his discrimination claim. Although Nash did not check a box on the form indicating he wanted the charge filed with both the EEOC and the state agency, the EEOC forwarded his claim to the Virginia Council on Human Rights (VCHR) pursuant to a worksharing agreement. The VCHR acknowledged receipt of Nash's charge and indicated it would not initially investigate. The EEOC subsequently issued Nash a notice of right to sue. Nash Construction now argues that the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over Nash's claim due to his failure to check the box on the EEOC form and his failure to specifically allege a violation of state law.

Dr. Charles K. Gatebe, an African American man, has worked as a research scientist with NASA for many years, initially through a cooperative agreement with the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, and later with the Universities Space Research Association (USRA). Since 2009, Dr. Gatebe has applied for at least ten NASA positions, including two at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, but has been rejected each time. 

Dr. Gatebe alleges that his race motivated the non-selection for the two positions in question: the Research Physical Scientist position in the Climate and Radiation Laboratory and the Research Physical Scientist position in the Hydrological Sciences Laboratory. He also claims that NASA refused to hire him for the Hydrological Sciences Laboratory position in retaliation for his complaints of racial discrimination in the workplace. Plaintiff alleges that he was qualified for both positions and that the selection processes were flawed. 

Defendant NASA contends that the selection processes for both positions were fair and based on the applicants' qualifications. For the Climate and Radiation position, NASA's selecting official, Dr. Lazaros Oreopoulos, chose Dr. Daniel Feldman, citing his expertise in radiative transfer codes and his potential for excellence. Dr. Oreopoulos claims that Dr. Gatebe's experience was less relevant to the position. For the Hydrological Sciences position, the selecting official, Dr. Matthew Rodell, led a diverse hiring committee that conducted interviews and selected a candidate based on their expertise in remote sensing of snow water equivalent and snow depth. NASA contends that Dr. Gatebe was not selected because he was not the most qualified candidate for the position. Relevant pre-litigation events include Dr. Gatebe's applications, interviews, and communications with NASA officials, as well as the creation of vacancy announcements, the implementation of screening processes, and the selection of hiring committees.

Jo Anne Pepitone has worked for the Township of Lower Merion for several years in various roles. Plaintiff alleges that numerous sexually charged rumors have been circulating throughout the police department, contributing to a sexually hostile and gender discriminatory hostile work environment, which Defendants have condoned or ignored. Pepitone contends that she spoke with multiple police department supervisors about the ongoing rumors about her, and they told her "that is how this place works." 

The Lower Merion Police Department (LMPD) conducted an investigation into whether Pepitone was having an inappropriate relationship with another officer. Shortly thereafter, LMPD transferred Pepitone to a less senior and less prestigious platoon, despite telling her that she had done nothing wrong and there were no policy violations. In contrast, Pepitone alleges that LMPD did not discipline a male officer for having a relationship with a female subordinate. Pepitone suggests that her reassignment was punitive, as platoon assignments are typically changed due to performance deficiencies.

On April 3, 2018, Pepitone emailed a sexual harassment, discrimination, and retaliation complaint to Michael J. McGrath, the police department superintendent, and others. She met with an investigator to discuss her complaint on April 17, 2018. After submitting and discussing her complaint, Pepitone received her first negative evaluation in her 10 years at LMPD on April 23, 2018. Pepitone then filed a sexual harassment and retaliation complaint with the EEOC, which LMPD was aware of by June 2018. The Township and LMPD investigated the claims underlying her complaint, and during a meeting to review the results, McGrath told Pepitone that she was being placed on a performance improvement plan.

Albert Buonanno was employed by AT&T Broadband, LLC from January 10, 1999, to February 1, 2001, initially as a cable dispatcher and later as a quota specialist. He was a Christian who believed in living his life according to the Bible's literal language. In January 2001, AT&T introduced a new "Employee Handbook" that included a section on diversity, which stated that each person at AT&T was responsible for recognizing, respecting, and valuing the differences among all employees. Buonanno questioned the meaning of this language, believing that it would require him to "value" behaviors or beliefs that were repudiated by Scripture, which would compromise his own religious beliefs.

Plaintiff alleges that he could not comply with the challenged language without denying his faith, and therefore, he could not sign the Certificate of Understanding, which was required by AT&T's Certification Policy. Defendant contends that the Diversity Policy was essential to its business development and that permitting an employee to certify anything other than full agreement with all of the language in the Handbook would destroy its competitive advantage. Buonanno's supervisor, Jonathan Dunn, suggested that he seek clarification on the language, and Buonanno wrote a letter to his Human Resources Manager, Susan Batliner, explaining his concerns. 

Buonanno met with Batliner and Dunn to discuss his concerns, but Batliner refused to clarify the meaning of the challenged language, stating that it was not a "philosophical debate." Buonanno reiterated that he supported the Diversity Philosophy but could not disavow his religious beliefs by endorsing behavior or beliefs he considered sinful. Batliner terminated his employment due to his refusal to sign the Certificate, stating that it was a requirement for continued employment. AT&T maintains that its Diversity Philosophy is essential to its business development, and that all employees must agree to it in order to work for the company. Buonanno contends that he was willing to comply with the principles underlying the Diversity Philosophy but could not sign the Certificate due to the ambiguous language.

Davoud Allen Eghbali, a naturalized citizen of the United States originally from Iran, worked as a nuclear criticality safety specialist at the Savannah River Site (SRS) from 1989 to 2010. From 1997 to September 2009, he worked for Washington Safety Management Solution, LLC (WSMS), a contractor for SRS, in a job that did not require a security clearance. In September 2009, Eghbali was indicted, and as a result, SRS personnel instructed WSMS to deny him access to the site pending the outcome of his indictment. Although the indictment was later dismissed, SRS continued to deny him access. Consequently, WSMS terminated his employment in February 2010. During his suspension from WSMS in January 2010, Eghbali was offered an interview for a position with Savannah River Nuclear Solutions, LLC (SRNS), another SRS contractor, but he was unable to attend the interview due to SRS's denial of access. 

Plaintiff alleges that the basis for SRS's denial of access was "mere speculation, prejudice, and the unfavorable political climate between the United States and Iran," amounting to national origin discrimination. He claims this discrimination led to the loss of his employment with WSMS and the loss of an employment opportunity with SRNS. Defendant contends that Eghbali was not an employee of the Department of Energy at the Savannah River National Lab but rather worked for contractors (WSMS and potentially SRNS), and thus, the employment relationship required for a Title VII claim against the federal government does not exist. 

Relevant pre-litigation events include Eghbali's work history at SRS, his indictment and subsequent denial of access to the site, the termination of his employment by WSMS, and the missed job opportunity with SRNS. Communications and documents relevant to the case include the instructions from SRS to WSMS to deny Eghbali access, the indictment and its dismissal, and the job offer from SRNS. The relationship between the parties is that of an employer (or in this case, a governmental agency overseeing contractors) and an employee/contractor, with the dispute centering on alleged national origin discrimination in the denial of access to the SRS site and the consequent loss of employment and employment opportunities.

Dan Williams has been a school social worker employed by the Board of Education of the City of Chicago (the "Board") since September 2008. He works in the Chicago Public Schools ("CPS") system, which has over 600 elementary and high schools with varying start and dismissal times. As a CPS social worker, Williams's primary job functions include assisting students, providing crisis intervention services, and developing Individualized Education Plans ("IEPs"). Williams suffers from depression, anxiety, and chronic sinusitis, which affect his ability to sleep, concentrate, and perform tasks. He requires a reasonably quiet workspace with adequate resources and a consistent work schedule to manage his conditions.

Plaintiff Williams alleges that he submitted an accommodation request on October 9, 2014, seeking consistent start and end times of 7:45 a.m. and 2:45 p.m. every day due to his health conditions. Defendant Board contends that Williams's healthcare provider did not provide enough information to support this request, and the Board denied it on November 14, 2014. Williams submitted two more accommodation requests, on May 7, 2015, and September 7, 2015, seeking various accommodations, including a consistent start time, reduced caseload, assignment to a single school, and a private office with specific equipment. The Board denied or partially denied these requests, citing reasons such as the lack of vacancies at 7:45 a.m.-start schools, the need for social workers to support all students in a school building, and the fact that some requests were unrelated to Williams's disability.

Williams's performance evaluations and disciplinary history are also relevant to the dispute. The Board uses the "REACH" tool to evaluate CPS teachers and social workers, and Williams received a "developing" rating for the 2013-2014 school year, which led to his placement on a professional development plan. During the 2014-2015 school year, Williams was placed on a Performance Improvement Plan ("PIP") due to complaints about his behavior at one of his assigned schools, Prescott. Williams disputes the effectiveness of the REACH tool in evaluating social workers, but the Board contends that it is a valid evaluation method. The parties' contentions regarding Williams's accommodation requests, performance evaluations, and disciplinary history are central to the dispute, with Williams alleging that the Board failed to provide reasonable accommodations and the Board contending that it made efforts to assist Williams while also considering the needs of the schools and students.

Rola Hamandi, a citizen and national of both France and Lebanon, has lived in the United States since 1990 and has been a legal permanent resident since October 2, 2001. She filed an application for naturalization (form N-400) with the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) on July 31, 2006. In May and July 2007, Hamandi contacted USCIS by telephone about the status of her application, but was given no information. On August 16, 2007, she visited the USCIS Miami District Office in person and was told that her application was delayed because the required FBI name check had not yet been completed. The office followed up with a letter dated September 15, 2007, stating that her case was not yet ready for decision due to the ongoing background investigation.

Hamandi alleges that USCIS failed to schedule her for the requisite interview and test of her language abilities and knowledge of U.S. history and culture. Plaintiff contends that the defendants, including the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, the Director of USCIS, and the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have a nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate her application within a reasonable time. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that they have no clear nondiscretionary duty to complete the adjudication of Hamandi's application prior to the receipt of her name check results and completion of her interview. They also claim that no statute or regulation gives USCIS a nondiscretionary duty to request expedited background checks or imposes any limitations on the FBI's discretion regarding the timetable for conducting name checks.

The FBI performs criminal background checks, including the FBI "name check," with respect to applicants for U.S. citizenship. Hamandi's application has been delayed due to the pending name check. The USCIS has a mandatory, nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate naturalization applications, which includes conducting a background investigation and examination of the applicant. The FBI, however, has no adjudicative responsibilities with respect to naturalization applications, and no statute or regulation cited by Hamandi expressly creates a mandatory duty owed by the FBI to individual naturalization applicants to process background and name checks. Hamandi filed this action seeking to compel defendants to process her naturalization application, which has been pending for over a year.

Irina Frederick was a student in a summer 1997 class at Simpson College, where she was taught by Professor Steven Rose. Plaintiff alleges that Professor Rose made comments about sexual activity and engaged in inappropriate conduct directed at her, both in and out of the classroom. These interactions continued beyond the completion of the class and related practicum. On February 24, 1998, Frederick wrote a letter to Bruce Haddox, assistant dean of student affairs, complaining about Professor Rose's behavior. This letter was referred to Mimi Bartley, human resource director for Simpson College, for investigation. An investigation occurred in March 1998, and a report was issued on April 2, 1998. 

Frederick contends that Simpson College failed to properly address her complaints and that the college's response was inadequate. Defendant Simpson College, on the other hand, maintains that it conducted a thorough investigation and took appropriate action in response to Frederick's allegations. Simpson College had a disseminated policy prohibiting sex discrimination under Title IX and effective grievance procedures in place at the time of the incident. 

Frederick filed her complaint against Simpson College and Professor Rose on February 18, 1999, and amended it on February 23, 2001. She alleges violations of Title IX, breach of contract, and negligent hire, supervision, and/or retention against Simpson College. Against Professor Rose, she brings claims of assault, battery, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The parties disagree on the adequacy of Simpson College's response to Frederick's complaints and the appropriateness of the actions taken by the college and Professor Rose.

Larry Jefferies, Perry Golden, and Patricia Chatman, all supervisors at General Motors Corporation (GM), alleged that they were subjected to racial and sexual harassment by Robert Wilson, a Committeeman for Local 25 of the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (the union) and a GM employee. The alleged harassment occurred from July 1992 to July 1994. Jefferies and Golden, who are black males, claimed that Wilson made several racist comments, including referring to them as "boy" and making statements about their race. Chatman, a black female, alleged that Wilson made racist and sexist comments, including telling her that "women should be at home and not in positions of authority." The supervisors also testified that Wilson repeatedly shouted at them, used profanity, and made threatening gestures.

Plaintiff alleges that GM and the union failed to take appropriate action to end the harassment, despite being aware of Wilson's behavior. The EEOC contends that GM officials met with union officials and Wilson in July 1992 to discuss his behavior, but no meaningful action was taken. The EEOC also points to an undated draft letter from J.D. Rietzke, the manager of the Hazelwood plant, outlining several instances of harassment by Wilson, which was not sent. Instead, a shorter letter was sent in October 1992 stating that minority employees were still being subjected to derogatory and harassing behavior. The supervisors testified that they were instructed to place Wilson on notice for harassing conduct, but he often did not receive discipline, and when he did, it was later removed.

Defendant GM contends that the harassment was not based on the charging parties' protected status, but was instead directed at all management employees. The union argues that it has no liability under Title VII for a hostile work environment claim and that it did not cause GM to discriminate against its supervisors. The union also claims that it is not liable for alleged discriminatory conduct directed at or affecting individuals it does not represent. The parties dispute the extent to which GM and the union took action to address the harassment, with the EEOC alleging that they failed to take proper remedial action, and GM and the union arguing that they took sufficient steps to address the issue.

In November 2017, Keith, a black woman, applied for a position at the Clinic, a healthcare provider in Gadsden, Alabama, which she believed was for a Certified Medical Assistant (CMA). The Clinic describes the position as a "front desk receptionist with a CMA certification." The job posting on the Clinic's internal job posting website, Taleo, described the position as "Certified Medical Assistant – Etowah Family Practice – Full Time" and listed duties such as assisting in examination and treatment of patients, measuring vital signs, and recording information on patients' charts. 

Keith interviewed with the Clinic shortly after applying, and the parties dispute what happened during the interview. Keith alleges that Marie McGinnis, the Clinic's former office manager, appeared surprised when she saw Keith and asked about her age, but did not ask to see her CMA certification, resume, or transcript. Keith claims that McGinnis told her the position was for a front desk receptionist and did not mention any potential CMA duties. The Clinic, on the other hand, contends that McGinnis did not act surprised, and that Keith did not perform well during the interview, lacking interpersonal skills and having pay expectations that were too high. The Clinic also claims that Keith had less-relevant experience than the candidate they ultimately hired, Judy Clowdus-Huntington, a white woman of American Indian/Alaskan Native descent.

The Clinic hired Clowdus-Huntington for the position, and about a month later, posted another opening for a CMA without receptionist duties. Keith did not apply for this position, and the Clinic ultimately hired Dalana Abercrombie, a black woman. In April 2018, Keith filed a charge with the EEOC alleging discrimination based on race and age. The Clinic provided statements to the EEOC that were later construed as contradictory, stating that they had hired Clowdus-Huntington for the position Keith applied for, but later saying they had hired Abercrombie for a CMA position. The EEOC also attempted to conduct an on-site visit, but the Clinic's legal counsel, Rhea Garrett, did not show up as scheduled, leading to further confusion. The Clinic claims that they never confirmed the date for the visit, and that Garrett had proposed scheduling a visit after sending some personnel documents to the EEOC's investigator, Iran Cruz.

Harvey Ross, an African-American man, worked as a general mechanic (grade 5) at the United States Postal Service (Postal Service) since 1987. Prior to joining the Postal Service, Ross worked for 11 years installing, repairing, and maintaining electrical and electronic systems. In August 1989, the Mail Equipment Shops (MES) section of the Postal Service posted a vacancy announcement for a MES technician position. Ross and six other applicants, including four African-Americans, one Caucasian, and one Asian-American, submitted applications for the position. To qualify for an interview, each applicant had to pass the mandatory Postal Test 500 (PT 500), which Ross passed with the highest score.

The selecting panel, consisting of three members, interviewed the six qualified applicants, including Ross, and rated them based on the qualification standards for the position. Ross's interview took place on October 13, 1989, during which he admitted to being ill and nervous. The panel also reviewed Ross's application form and his Supervisory Appraisal form, which showed that his immediate and second-line supervisors, Reginald Carnegie and Steve Cohout, had recommended him only "with reservation" due to his poor attendance and human relations. The appraisal form noted that Ross had "fair human relations and poor attendance." After the interview process, the selecting panel ranked the applicants based on their composite scores, with Arthur Taylor, a Caucasian applicant, receiving the highest score and being selected for the position. Ross was ranked fifth overall and was notified on October 23, 1989, that he had not been selected.

Plaintiff Ross alleges that the Postal Service discriminated against him on the basis of his race when it failed to promote him to the MES technician position. He claims that he was more qualified than the selectee, Arthur Taylor, and that the selection process was flawed. Ross contends that the procedures used during the selection process were in violation of postal regulations and that he was unfairly rated on areas not within the scope of the vacancy announcement, including his past leave record and his experience with heating, air-conditioning, and ventilation. Defendant Postal Service contends that Ross did not receive the promotion because he did not score as well as other applicants during the interview process and had a history of attendance problems at work. The Postal Service also notes that Ross's immediate and second-line supervisors had recommended him only "with reservation" due to his poor attendance and human relations. Ross had filed a formal complaint of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Office of the Post Office, which was initially filed as a national origin discrimination complaint but was later amended to a racial discrimination complaint. The EEOC ultimately found no discrimination, and Ross appealed the decision, which was denied.

Sharone Hubert, an African-American woman, has been an employee of the Connecticut Department of Correction (DOC) since February 13, 1998, initially as a Correction Officer. She was promoted to Lieutenant on September 11, 2009. However, on January 27, 2010, she was demoted back to her former position as a Correction Officer. Plaintiff alleges that after her demotion, she was subjected to sexual harassment, employment discrimination, and retaliation, which created a hostile work environment. Specifically, she claims that high-ranking officers sent her inappropriate pictures, male co-workers stalked and harassed her, and male supervisors and administrators subjected her to sexual harassment, embarrassment, and retaliation.

Plaintiff alleges several incidents that gave rise to her claims, including an August 7, 2017, incident where an inmate exposed himself to her, and her supervisor, Lieutenant Hernandez, refused to take action. She also alleges that on an unspecified date, she was asked to prepare a "Page 3" supplemental report regarding an incident that supposedly occurred in December 2017, but she had no knowledge of the incident. When she expressed her concerns and requested to speak to a union steward, Lieutenant Schwartz and Lieutenant Hernandez allegedly became hostile and relieved her of her duties. Plaintiff contends that she has been continuously subjected to harassment, discrimination, and retaliation, which has affected her emotionally, physically, and financially.

Defendant contends that Plaintiff was placed on administrative leave with pay effective July 22, 2019, and received paychecks until her leave was changed to unpaid leave on October 7, 2019. Plaintiff had filed a complaint with the Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities (CHRO) on February 2, 2018, and received a right to sue letter on April 17, 2019. She also received a right to sue letter from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on May 28, 2019. Plaintiff alleges that she has been unable to work and has not received any income, while Defendant claims that she made false representations about her employment status and income in her affidavit.

Christine A. Bergerson began her employment at the New York State Office of Mental Health, Central New York Psychiatric Center (the Center) on September 10, 2004, as a probationary employee subject to a 52-week probationary period. During her employment, Bergerson was evaluated five times, with her performance rated in various categories. Plaintiff alleges that from the time she began her employment, she was subjected to derogatory sexual comments and jokes by coworkers, including comments about her alleged promiscuity and attraction to African-American men. Bergerson also contends that she was exposed to lewd posters and computer screen savers, and that rumors were spread about her dating and sex life.

Plaintiff alleges that she made multiple complaints to supervisors about the harassment, but they were largely ignored, with one female supervisor telling her to "just deal with it" because it was a "man's environment." Bergerson also claims that she was told by her evaluator that her friendship with an African-American coworker, Keith Richardson, was not in her best interest to continue. Plaintiff eventually began an interracial dating relationship with Richardson, which she alleges was a factor in her termination. Defendant contends that Bergerson's termination was due to her poor performance, including her excessive use of "mutuals" (shift swaps with other employees), which resulted in her not being on the job on her assigned shift often enough.

Bergerson's fifth and final evaluation, completed on January 18, 2006, resulted in her being ranked below average or unacceptable in several categories, leading to her termination on January 24, 2006. Plaintiff alleges that the reason for her termination was pretextual and that she was actually terminated due to her race and sex. Defendant contends that Bergerson's termination was due to her poor performance and that she cannot establish a prima facie case of discrimination. The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding Bergerson's termination, with plaintiff alleging that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and disparate treatment, and defendant arguing that her termination was based on legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons.

The plaintiffs, a group of individuals, claim to have been subjected to discriminatory practices by the defendant, their employer, in violation of the Equal Employment Opportunities Act. Plaintiff alleges that the defendant engaged in a pattern of discriminatory behavior, including acts of discrimination in a company layoff commencing October 1, 1969. The plaintiffs further contend that these violations were constant and continuous, with several specific acts set forth as illustrative of the pattern. Defendant contends that the charges of discrimination, other than the charge related to the layoff, were untimely filed. 

The plaintiffs initially filed charges of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on October 10, 1969. However, some of the plaintiffs, including Ms. Sandra K. Webb, Ms. Ellen Hughes, and Ms. Johnnie L. Young, did not sign the original charges. The EEOC investigated the claims and ultimately notified the plaintiffs of their right to bring suit on December 22, 1970. The plaintiffs then filed this lawsuit on January 22, 1971, within 30 days of receiving the notice. Defendant contends that the Court lacks jurisdiction over the subject matter and that the plaintiffs failed to state a claim on which relief can be granted.

The plaintiffs and the defendant have a relationship as employer and employees, with the defendant being the employer of the plaintiffs. The nature of the dispute is a claim of discriminatory practices under the Equal Employment Opportunities Act. The plaintiffs allege that the defendant's actions were discriminatory and in violation of their civil rights, while the defendant contends that the claims are untimely and that the Court lacks jurisdiction. Relevant pre-litigation events include the filing of the initial charges with the EEOC, the investigation by the EEOC, and the notification to the plaintiffs of their right to bring suit. The plaintiffs amended their complaint to cure the defendant's claim that the Court lacks jurisdiction by alleging that the defendant is an "employer" under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b).

FedEx employs drivers in the Chicago area, including the plaintiff, an African American man who began working for FedEx in April 2015, and Don Romero, a non-African American driver. On August 10, 2017, after completing his deliveries, the plaintiff was filling out paperwork in the drivers' lounge when Romero called him "dumb" or "stupid" and hit him on the side of his headphones, knocking them off. The plaintiff told Romero to "back off" and yelled to Matt Terrence, an operations supervisor, to get Romero away from him, stating that if Romero did not leave, "things are about to go down." Terrence eventually arrived and asked Romero to leave, which he did after dancing around the plaintiff and teasing him.

Plaintiff alleges that he was physically attacked by Romero and complained to FedEx's Alert Line about the incident. Defendant FedEx relieved the plaintiff of duty, sending him home without pay during an investigation, but did not relieve Romero of duty. The investigation, conducted by security specialist Brian Simikoski, resulted in plaintiff being given corrective action for allegedly violating defendant's policy against workplace violence, while Romero was suspended for three days for "provoking or threatening behavior." Plaintiff contends that he was treated unfairly compared to Romero, who was not discharged despite admitting to touching the plaintiff's headphones. 

Defendant FedEx contends that it followed its employee-conduct and performance-improvement policies in responding to the incident, and that the plaintiff's comments to Romero were threatening and inappropriate, warranting termination. FedEx also notes that Romero's actions, while inappropriate, did not rise to the level of workplace violence. The plaintiff disputes this, arguing that he was the victim of Romero's provocation and that FedEx's response was discriminatory. Prior to this incident, neither the plaintiff nor Romero had been subject to corrective action, and another non-African American employee, Bill Lyon, was not discharged after being accused of pushing an employee in 2016.

Will Grimes, the sole named plaintiff who filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), worked for the defendant employer. On January 18, 1979, Grimes filed a charge with the EEOC, alleging employment discrimination. His attorney requested a Notice of Right to Sue from the EEOC on January 30, 1979, stating that further delay in filing the action would be fruitless. The EEOC issued the Notice of Right to Sue on February 6, 1979, after only 19 days, stating that it would be unable to complete its administrative process within 180 days and was terminating further processing of the charge. Grimes then filed this lawsuit on May 7, 1979, as a class action on behalf of himself and "all others similarly situated," alleging violations of 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1985, and 2000e, et seq.

Plaintiff Grimes alleges that he and other black employees were discriminated against by the defendant employer, including being denied employment benefits due to their race. Defendant contends that Grimes failed to wait the required 180 days after filing his charge with the EEOC before bringing this action, and that the EEOC's issuance of the Notice of Right to Sue after only 19 days was premature. Defendant also argues that Grimes lacks standing to raise the claim regarding denial of employment benefits because he was employed for close to four years and thus would have been eligible for such benefits.

The parties disagree on the interpretation of the 180-day waiting period under Title VII, with defendant arguing that it is a mandatory period of exclusive EEOC jurisdiction, and plaintiff arguing that it is not a prerequisite to filing a private action. The EEOC's practice of issuing a right-to-sue notice before the expiration of the 180-day period is also at issue. The defendant employer has moved to dismiss the complaint on various grounds, including lack of jurisdiction, vagueness of the complaint, and failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.

Leilani Kryzhanovskiy was hired by Amazon in January 2020 as an Onsite Medical Representative at the Stockton, California warehouse location. Her husband, with comparable qualifications and experience, was hired for the same position in April 2020 but was offered substantially more in wages. Kryzhanovskiy and her husband have identical primary responsibilities in their positions. On May 27, 2021, Kryzhanovskiy sent a notification letter to the California Labor & Workforce Development Agency and Amazon, outlining alleged violations of the California Labor Code, including the Equal Pay Act, based on disparate treatment on the basis of gender.

Plaintiff alleges that after her supervisors became aware of her complaint, they began retaliating against her. In May 2021, Kryzhanovskiy had applied for a promotion to the position of Workplace Health & Safety Specialist at the Stockton warehouse. Although an interview was scheduled, her direct supervisor, Brent Butterfield, later told her the position had been filled and her interview was canceled. Kryzhanovskiy contends that Butterfield's actions were in retaliation for her complaints about Amazon's Labor Code violations and gender discrimination. She also alleges that since submitting her complaint, Butterfield has been dismissive of her, including not responding to her request for information about modifying her work schedule and informing her that schedule assignments are based on seniority, despite her being the most senior Onsite Medical Representative at the Stockton warehouse.

Amazon contends that its policies and practices are lawful. The company had uniform written policies and practices for calculating the regular rate of pay, and its wage statements provided to California employees were accurate. Amazon's position is that it did not violate the California Labor Code or engage in gender discrimination. The dispute between Kryzhanovskiy and Amazon involves allegations of unequal pay, retaliation, and violations of California labor laws, with Kryzhanovskiy seeking to represent a class of non-exempt California employees who may have been similarly affected by Amazon's practices. Relevant pre-litigation events include Kryzhanovskiy's notification letter, her application for a promotion, and the subsequent interactions with her supervisor, Brent Butterfield.

Marvin M. Redding, an African-American employee of Anne Arundel County's Public Works Department, alleges that he was discriminated against by the county in the granting of overtime benefits. Plaintiff alleges that the county engaged in a pattern of ongoing or continuous discrimination against him, which is sometimes referred to as a "serial violation". Defendant Anne Arundel County, Maryland, contends that Redding did not bring his claim within Maryland's general three-year limitations period. Redding claims that his complaint alleges a continuing pattern and practice of discrimination, which tolls the statute of limitations. 

Redding was employed by the Public Works Department, where he claims to have been denied overtime opportunities, including the assignment of "leak week". Redding's original complaint failed to allege an act occurring within the limitations period, which is after March 11, 1994. Redding's counsel was retained only three days before the deadline to file suit and did not have sufficient time to conduct a full investigation. Redding now seeks to amend his complaint to include additional allegations of discrimination, including allegations of discrimination within the relevant limitations period.

The parties have engaged in discovery, and Redding's deposition was taken in December. Redding's counsel had eight months to develop this information through discovery but waited until after the close of discovery and the court's earlier opinion to make the motion to amend. The court heard oral argument concerning the motions on March 11, 1998. Defendant argues that considerable additional discovery would be needed, new motions would need to be filed, and the trial would be postponed if the amendment is permitted, which would be highly prejudicial to the county.

Zuhdija Napreljac, a green card holder from Bosnia, worked as an engineer at the Embassy Suites hotel in Des Moines, Iowa, owned by John Q. Hammons Hotels, Inc. (JQH), from September 2000 until his termination on September 24, 2003. Napreljac's duties included collecting trash, inspecting and repairing hotel rooms, and conducting general maintenance tasks. In November 2001, Napreljac injured his neck and back while moving a wet piece of carpet at work, and he underwent neck surgery in January 2002. He was subject to physical restrictions, including a twenty-five pound lifting restriction and a reaching restriction, but was released from all work restrictions on March 6, 2003.

Plaintiff Napreljac alleges that he suffered another workplace injury on August 4, 2003, and was placed on "light duty" status, which allowed him to perform tasks within his physical restrictions. Defendant JQH contends that Napreljac was accommodated and able to perform his job duties, albeit with some limitations. On September 18, 2003, Napreljac claims he hurt his back while descending a staircase at the hotel, but the circumstances and extent of the injury are disputed. Defendant JQH asserts that Napreljac did not report the incident as a work-related injury and continued to work, folding towels in the hotel's laundry department. Napreljac denies telling his supervisor, Kevin Beaver, that he had fallen, while Beaver recalls Napreljac saying he had slipped and fallen on the loading dock.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Napreljac working under the supervision of various JQH staff, including Scott Johnston, Kevin Beaver, and Shannon Kaufman, the hotel's general manager. The nature of the dispute involves Napreljac's workplace injuries, his ability to perform his job duties, and the circumstances surrounding his termination on September 24, 2003. Relevant pre-litigation events include Napreljac's performance reviews, which were generally favorable, and the hotel's handling of his workplace injuries, including the implementation of light duty status and the investigation into the September 18, 2003, incident. Napreljac's interactions with his supervisors and colleagues, including Johnston, Beaver, and Postier, are also relevant to the dispute.

Plaintiff, an individual of a protected class, was employed by defendant, an entity subject to federal and state anti-discrimination laws. Plaintiff alleges that during their employment, they were subjected to discriminatory treatment based on their race and national origin. Specifically, plaintiff contends that they experienced disparate treatment in the workplace, including being passed over for promotions and being assigned to less desirable tasks. Plaintiff also alleges that they were retaliated against after complaining about the discriminatory treatment.

Defendant contends that plaintiff's allegations are unfounded and that any adverse employment actions taken against plaintiff were based on legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons. Defendant asserts that plaintiff's performance was subpar and that they had difficulty working with colleagues. Defendant also claims that plaintiff's complaints about discrimination were thoroughly investigated and found to be without merit. The parties' relationship began to deteriorate after plaintiff's initial complaints, with plaintiff alleging that defendant took steps to further marginalize and exclude them from workplace opportunities.

Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff engaged in internal complaint procedures, reporting their concerns about discrimination to defendant's human resources department. Defendant responded by conducting an investigation, which plaintiff alleges was inadequate and biased. The pre-litigation events culminated in plaintiff's termination, which plaintiff contends was a direct result of their protected activity in complaining about discrimination. Defendant, on the other hand, maintains that the termination was based on legitimate business reasons, unrelated to plaintiff's protected characteristics or activities. The parties' dispute ultimately led to the filing of the complaint on November 17, 2017, asserting claims under Title VII and the PHRA.

In November 2015, Sgt. Hood, then a corporal, took the DOCR promotional examination to qualify for promotion to sergeant. However, her computer malfunctioned during the exam, and she was given four to five additional minutes to complete the relevant portion with the assistance of an IT specialist. Despite this, Sgt. Hood was not promoted to sergeant based on her score. Plaintiff alleges that the computer malfunction and the subsequent handling of her exam results were improper.

Sgt. Hood sent an email to DOCR officials in December 2015, complaining about the computer malfunction and expressing her refusal to accept the results of the promotion-exam process. However, she did not allege impermissible discrimination at that time. Sgt. Hood contends that she filed a complaint of race discrimination with the Montgomery County Office of Human Rights (MOHR) in April 2016, based on the 2015 promotion exam, and received a Right-to-Sue Letter after a cursory investigation. Defendant contends that Sgt. Hood's complaints were confined to perceived issues with the exam-scoring process.

In July 2016, Sgt. Hood, through her union, filed a grievance with the Offices of the County Executive, asserting that the examination process caused her undue hardship and placed her at an unfair disadvantage. The grievance was denied in October 2016. Sgt. Hood filed a second complaint with MOHR in September 2016, alleging race discrimination and retaliation. She received a Right-to-Sue Letter on September 29, 2016. Sgt. Hood alleges that she experienced retaliation in the form of altered time sheets, citations for tardiness, discouragement from taking sick leave and FMLA leave, and efforts to remove her from a prestigious Audit Team assignment. Defendant contends that these allegations are unfounded and that Sgt. Hood's time sheets were altered to give her more overtime, that the citations for tardiness were justified, and that she was not removed from the Audit Team.

Robert Burton, an African American male, is employed at the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) as a GS-12 budget analyst. He first met Lisa Bevels, a white female, in December 2000 when she began employment at NLRB as the Deputy Budget Chief. Bevels indicated in January 2001 that she intended to write performance plans to upgrade all GS-12 positions in the Budget Branch to GS-13. Burton and Bevels began to have coffee together each morning, and Burton alleges that during these meetings Bevels began to discuss intimate details of her personal life. In April 2001, Bevels asked Burton if he would ever marry a white woman, to which he responded "No". 

Plaintiff alleges that Bevels' behavior towards him changed after this conversation. Another budget analyst, Bill Snuggs, was hired in April 2001 as a GS-12 and had his position upgraded to GS-13 within 90 days, despite having no prior budget experience. Burton claims that when he inquired about his own potential upgrade, Bevels stated that she planned to upgrade all positions soon and asked him to remain at NLRB. Burton contends that he was not upgraded, while other budget analysts, including Angie Jones, were. 

Burton alleges that in January 2002, Bevels terminated all personal conversations of a sexual nature with him. He asked Bevels for a performance rating in January 2002 and contacted the EEO office of NLRB to inquire about filing a formal complaint. Burton claims that Bevels threatened to issue him a poor evaluation after he inquired at the EEO office about the lack of a performance appraisal. He also alleges that Bevels took several discriminatory and retaliatory actions against him, including failing to provide performance appraisals, providing him a minimally successful rating, denying him a within-grade increase, yelling at him in the office, and sending harassing emails. Defendant NLRB contends that Bevels' actions were legitimate and non-discriminatory, and that Burton's performance issues were the reason for the lack of upgrades and poor evaluations.

South Central Bell Telephone and Telegraph Company (Bell) had an Employee Benefits Plan in effect from October 13, 1971, to August 7, 1977, which provided non-occupational sickness and accident benefits to its employees. However, the plan did not cover pregnancy-related absences, except in cases of physical complications. Female employees who took maternity leave accrued only thirty additional days of service credit, while sick or disabled employees received full seniority credit for up to fifty-two weeks. Harriet Wilhite, a female employee of Bell, requested a leave of absence for maternity reasons in 1972 and was not guaranteed reinstatement to the same or equal position upon returning to work. Betty Dubose, another female employee, was granted a six-month maternity leave in 1975 and accrued only thirty days of service credit during her leave.

Plaintiff Wilhite alleges that Bell's policy of not providing mandatory reinstatement rights to female employees returning from maternity leave for a normal pregnancy violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Plaintiff Dubose alleges that Bell's policy of denying full seniority credit to female employees on maternity leave for a normal pregnancy, compared to its treatment of other temporarily disabled employees, also violates Title VII. Bell contends that its policies are facially neutral and do not discriminate against female employees. The Communication Workers of America, AFL-CIO, filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission on April 12, 1972, alleging violations of Title VII by Bell.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Bell being the employer and Wilhite and Dubose being female employees. The nature of the dispute is a claim of sex discrimination in employment practices, specifically regarding Bell's maternity leave and seniority policies. Relevant pre-litigation events include the filing of complaints with the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission and the issuance of right-to-sue letters to Wilhite and Dubose. The employees' union, the Communication Workers of America, AFL-CIO, is also a party to the lawsuit, representing Wilhite and other similarly situated female employees.

Laurie Campbell began working as a distribution clerk at the United States Postal Service's Blue Valley branch in Overland Park, Kansas, in March 1997. She was supervised by Daniel Strauss, among others. Plaintiff alleges that Mr. Strauss created a hostile work environment by sexually harassing her and other female employees. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Mr. Strauss patted her inner thigh in July 1995, grabbed and firmly held her wrist in September 1998, grabbed and held her upper arms for 10 to 15 seconds in February 1999, occasionally hit her on the back or arm, and bumped into her or rubbed his shoulder against her back on several occasions. Plaintiff also claims that she witnessed Mr. Strauss's harassment of other women in the workplace, including Leticia Stumpner and Rhonda Ford, and that she saw him hugging and giving back rubs to these women.

Plaintiff alleges that she was forced to avoid Mr. Strauss's efforts to touch her at least 20 to 30 times, or several times each month. On March 2, 1999, Plaintiff contacted an EEO counselor to discuss Mr. Strauss's conduct. Defendant contends that the conduct of which Plaintiff complains was not based on her sex and/or was neither sufficiently severe nor sufficiently pervasive to alter the conditions of her employment and create an abusive working environment. Defendant also maintains that Plaintiff cannot establish a prima facie case of retaliation because she cannot show that she suffered any adverse employment action.

After Plaintiff contacted the EEO counselor, she claims that Mr. Strauss retaliated against her by trying to convince her to drop her complaint on March 4, 1999, and by walking by her work station and staring at her. Plaintiff interpreted Mr. Strauss's statements on March 4, 1999, as an attempt to intimidate her into dropping her complaint. Defendant's employees, including Ms. Stumpner and Ms. Ford, have provided statements that contradict Plaintiff's allegations, stating that they did not feel uncomfortable with Mr. Strauss's conduct and that it was consensual. Ms. Stumpner described herself as a "hugger" and stated that she had a good rapport with Mr. Strauss, while Ms. Ford recalled one occasion when Mr. Strauss rubbed her shoulder to help with stress in her neck.

Homi Amirmokri, an Iranian immigrant and a GS-15 level nuclear engineer, was employed by the United States Department of Energy (DOE) and acted as Program Manager for the Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), a nuclear facility located in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. On May 5, 2003, Amirmokri visited ORNL to review safety measures and raised concerns over the adequacy of a Transportation Safety Document (TSD) prepared by Cathy Simmons, a member of the ORNL research and development staff. Amirmokri voiced his concerns to Ray Bond, the facility manager, who arranged a meeting between Amirmokri and Simmons. The meeting did not go well, with Simmons later complaining that Amirmokri addressed her in a "hostile, condescending manner."

Plaintiff alleges that he was neither rude nor discourteous towards Simmons, while Simmons contends that she was shaken by the exchange. Several days after the meeting, Amirmokri's supervisor, Owen Lowe, was contacted by George Malosh, a manager at ORNL, and advised of Amirmokri's allegedly unprofessional conduct towards Simmons. Lowe was also informed of an incident where Amirmokri allegedly refused to identify his employer when seeking entry into a limited access area at the facility. Lowe spoke to Amirmokri and advised him to be "on his best behavior" during the remainder of his visit to ORNL.

On May 15, 2003, Amirmokri met with Larry Boyd, a GS-14 general engineer at ORNL, and allegedly asked him if he knew that he could be sued for libel, which Boyd viewed as a thinly-veiled threat. Boyd contacted Lowe to complain, and Lowe decided to conduct his own investigation into Amirmokri's conduct at ORNL. After receiving approval from his supervisor, William Magwood, Lowe traveled to ORNL and interviewed Simmons, Bond, and several other individuals, but did not interview Michael Woods, who had accompanied Amirmokri on part of his tour and later testified that he had not observed Amirmokri's behavior to be rude or unprofessional.

Lowe issued Amirmokri a memorandum of reassignment and a letter of reprimand, which provided that Amirmokri would no longer have oversight duties at ORNL and was not to have any direct contact with anyone at the facility. The letter of reprimand discussed Amirmokri's "inappropriate behavior" at ORNL, specifically referencing his meeting with Simmons, his meeting with Boyd, and his conduct when seeking entry into the limited access area. Amirmokri contends that after his reassignment, he was given "unattainable deadlines" to complete a Documented Safety Analysis (DSA) review and was deprived of meaningful work until April 2005, while Defendant maintains that Amirmokri was given ample work and that his post-reassignment responsibilities were not significantly diminished.

Amirmokri filed a formal complaint with the DOE, which was advanced to the administrative hearing stage, claiming that his reassignment and letter of reprimand constituted discrimination on the basis of national origin and retaliation for the filing and litigation of an earlier EEO complaint. The administrative judge issued a bench ruling denying Amirmokri's claims, which was followed by a written order. Amirmokri then filed suit in the United States District Court, asserting claims of retaliation and discrimination on the basis of national origin. Defendant filed a Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, for Summary Judgment, which is currently pending before the Court.

John W. Bradley, the plaintiff, received his EEOC right-to-sue letter on December 12, 2017. He then filed a complaint against American Electric Power, the defendant, in the Eastern District of Texas. Plaintiff alleges that he was entitled to bring this action under Title VII. Defendant contends that the 90-day time bar applies to the action. However, plaintiff amended his complaint to reflect the correct date of receipt of his EEOC right-to-sue letter, which potentially avoids the time bar.

Plaintiff initially filed the suit pro se but is now represented by counsel. Defendant notes that it took over eight months for plaintiff to serve process, with no effort at service made during that time. Plaintiff's counsel appeared on June 22, 2018, but plaintiff does not claim that defendant was evading service or concealing a defect in attempted service. Plaintiff's counsel mentions health issues and the need to investigate the case, but provides few specifics. Defendant states an intent to dispute the pleaded facts, including the date of receipt of the EEOC right-to-sue letter.

The parties have engaged in pre-litigation communications, including the exchange of motions and briefs. Defendant filed a motion to dismiss, which plaintiff opposed. The court reserved judgment on the question of whether a discretionary extension of the deadline for service of process is warranted. The parties have also discussed the potential application of the 90-day time bar and the consequences of a Rule 4(m) dismissal. Plaintiff's counsel has not provided evidence of when the attorney-client relationship was formed, making it difficult to assess the weight to attach to plaintiff's initial pro se filing status.

Elizabeth Burciaga began working for Channel Prime Alliance, a business unit of Ravago Americas, LLC, in Des Moines, Iowa, as a Customer Service Representative (CSR) in August 2007. Her supervisor was Customer Service Manager Jeremy Howe. Burciaga's responsibilities included contact with sales representatives and customers, receiving and processing orders, scheduling shipments, and fixing customer issues. Throughout her employment, Burciaga used Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave multiple times, including in 2008 after the birth of her oldest son and in 2011 after the birth of her twin children.

Burciaga had several performance-related issues during her employment. Howe began taking notes about Burciaga's employment on May 23, 2011, after she took a longer than normal lunch break without notifying him. He also noted an issue regarding an order that needed to be triggered, which he considered significant but not requiring a corrective action form. In February 2012, Burciaga made a shipping mistake by reshipping an order that had already been shipped, and Howe counseled her to take her time and ensure she entered orders correctly, warning her of the possibility of termination if she continued to make mistakes. 

In July 2012, Burciaga requested FMLA paperwork authorizing intermittent FMLA leave to care for her son, who had a medical condition requiring several medical appointments and a hospital stay. Her request was granted, and she took half days off related to appointments for her son on August 8, 2012; September 5, 2012; and September 6, 2012. However, it is unclear whether Howe was notified of Burciaga's FMLA leave at the time of the requests. Burciaga made a series of mistakes prior to her termination, including errors on September 16, 2012, September 11, 2012, September 18, 2012, and September 27, 2012. Howe met with Stephen Kramer, a controller at Ravago, to discuss the possibility of terminating Burciaga's employment due to her mistakes and poor performance. On September 28, 2012, Burciaga was informed that she was terminated from Ravago because of her mistakes and poor performance, with neither Howe nor Kramer making any reference to her FMLA leave or time missed during the termination process. Plaintiff alleges that she was discharged based on her use of FMLA leave, while Defendant contends that the termination was due to her poor performance and mistakes.

Carrie Spangler was a fellow in the Department of Surgery, Division of Cardio-Thoracic (CT) Surgery fellowship program at the University of Utah, under the supervision of Division Chief Craig H. Selzman and Program Director Thomas K. Varghese, Jr. Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to various forms of discrimination and harassment during her time in the program. Plaintiff contends that she was not accommodated in violation of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and that she was retaliated against in violation of § 504. 

Plaintiff also alleges that she was sexually harassed in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and that she was discriminated against based on her gender in violation of Title VII. Plaintiff further contends that she was retaliated against in violation of Title VII. Additionally, Plaintiff alleges that she was discriminated against based on her gender in violation of Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, and that she was retaliated against in violation of Title IX. 

Defendant University of Utah, Selzman, and Varghese contend that Plaintiff's claims are without merit and seek dismissal of several of her claims. The parties engaged in pre-litigation communications and filings, including a Motion to Dismiss filed by Defendants, to which Plaintiff responded. Relevant pre-litigation events include Plaintiff's involvement in the fellowship program and her interactions with Selzman and Varghese. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the University of Utah being the employer and Spangler being the employee. The nature of the dispute is one of alleged discrimination, harassment, and retaliation.

The plaintiff, a female, was employed by the defendant from December 1979 to March 1995, as a collection manager. In September 1992, the defendant hired Janet Muse, also a female, as the division collection manager, who became the plaintiff's immediate supervisor. The plaintiff considered several incidents of Muse's conduct to be inappropriate and believed them to be sexual in nature, including unwanted sexual advancements. In 1992, the plaintiff complained to Susan Ponessa, a human resource specialist, about Muse's conduct, stating that she considered it to be inappropriate. The plaintiff again complained about Muse's conduct in 1995, telling Cynthia Johnson, the defendant's human resources manager, about an incident where Muse had partially exposed her breast while leaning over the plaintiff's desk.

The relationship between the plaintiff and Muse deteriorated over time, with Muse complaining that the plaintiff was uncommunicative and wouldn't keep her informed about business issues. In March 1995, Muse decided to meet with the plaintiff to discuss her job performance, and the meeting was attended by Tim Donovan from the human resource department. During the meeting, the plaintiff became upset and stated that the meeting was another example of Muse harassing her because she had spurned Muse's sexual advances. The plaintiff also claimed that she was afraid of Muse and that Muse's conduct made it difficult for her to do her job. After the meeting, Donovan met with Johnson and told her about the specific instances of Muse's conduct that the plaintiff claimed were sexual harassment. Johnson then met with Muse and subsequently recommended that the plaintiff be terminated. The plaintiff was fired by Johnson the next day, on March 17, 1995.

Plaintiff alleges that her discharge was in retaliation for her complaints about Muse's conduct, which she believed constituted sexual harassment. Defendant contends that the plaintiff was fired due to her persistent communication problems and uncommunicative attitude, which affected her job performance. The defendant argues that the plaintiff's complaints about Muse's conduct were not protected activity, as the court had previously found that the plaintiff was not sexually harassed. However, the plaintiff argues that her complaints were made in good faith and that she had a reasonable belief that Muse's conduct was discriminatory. The plaintiff also contends that the temporal proximity between her complaints and her discharge justifies an inference of retaliatory motive.

In October 2016, Burmans Medical Supplies Inc. hired Patrick Lienhard as the Director of Competitive Intelligence at an annual salary of $80,000, with an annual bonus of $20,000. In the Spring of 2017, CHC Solutions acquired Burmans and retained Lienhard in its employ. As part of his job duties, Lienhard sent detailed financials to all upper management on a daily basis, handled reporting for the sales team, and worked with operations and purchasing. During his employment, Lienhard received good performance reviews but was never paid the promised annual bonuses.

In February 2020, Lienhard informed his supervisor, Garrett Moon, that he and his wife were expecting a baby and that he intended to take twelve weeks of unpaid leave under the FMLA. Lienhard offered to take his leave on an intermittent basis to reduce the burden of his absence and requested a cost-of-living salary adjustment, as he had never received a raise during his employment with CHC Solutions. Moon indicated that he would need to consult with human resources and denied Lienhard's request for a raise but promised that Lienhard would be eligible for bonuses based on the company's performance.
