Lienhard also spoke to Maryn Allen, his assigned human resources representative, to inquire into the process for taking the full twelve weeks of FMLA leave. Allen remarked that the request was "odd" and that she could think of only one other person who had done so, which made Lienhard believe he may be punished if he took the full twelve weeks.

Lienhard had to repeatedly follow up with Moon regarding his FMLA leave request, and eventually, Allen advised him that CHC Solutions would not grant his request to take intermittent FMLA and that he would need to take his leave in an uninterrupted twelve-week block. Lienhard completed the required paperwork and trained a colleague to fulfill his job responsibilities in his absence. On April 30, 2020, when Lienhard's son was born, he immediately went out on leave. On July 22, 2020, two days before he was expecting to return to work, Lienhard received a call from Allen, who advised him that CHC Solutions was terminating his employment. Plaintiff alleges that his employment was terminated in violation of the FMLA, while Defendant contends that the termination was lawful. Following his separation from CHC Solutions' employment, Lienhard did not search, apply, or interview for any available positions, but instead reached out to his professional contacts and worked as a consultant with Gaboro Medical Supply and Sleek Consulting, LLC. Defendant contends that Lienhard had access to a labor market of over 13,000 jobs in the Philadelphia, Camden, and Wilmington area, and that his skills were particularly marketable during the pandemic because he could work remotely.

Ruth McClure was employed by Valmac Industries, Inc. in June 1968. Plaintiff alleges that during her employment, she was denied advancement to positions for which she was qualified, compelled to train male employees for positions to which she should have been promoted, denied educational opportunities on the same basis as male counterparts, and paid less than a male of equal value to the company. McClure contends that she was discharged on January 29, 1979, under circumstances that would not have resulted in the discharge of a male employee. Valmac Industries, Inc. is faced with two suits simultaneously concerning Ruth McClure, one filed by McClure under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and another filed by the EEOC under the Equal Pay Act, both seeking back pay, reinstatement, declaratory and injunctive relief.

Valmac contends that many of McClure's allegations are time-barred, specifically the allegedly discriminatory actions by the defendant in 1969 relating to the training of a male employee. The defendant argues that the filing of a suit by the EEOC under the Equal Pay Act bars any private right of action by McClure under Title VII. Prior to her discharge, McClure filed a charge of discrimination with the EEOC, which elected to pursue her case under the Equal Pay Act instead of Title VII. The EEOC's suit, filed pursuant to Section 16(c) and 17 of the Fair Labor Standards Act, seeks the same relief as McClure's suit but is based on the Equal Pay Act rather than Title VII.

The relationship between McClure and Valmac Industries, Inc. is that of employer and employee, with McClure alleging discriminatory employment practices by Valmac. The nature of the dispute is a claim of sex discrimination under Title VII, with McClure alleging that she was subjected to various forms of discrimination, including denial of promotion, unequal pay, and discharge. The EEOC's involvement in the case adds a layer of complexity, as the agency's suit under the Equal Pay Act raises questions about the relationship between the two statutes and the rights of individual employees to bring private actions. Relevant pre-litigation events include McClure's initial employment by Valmac in 1968, her filing of a charge of discrimination with the EEOC, and the EEOC's decision to pursue her case under the Equal Pay Act.

Ward, a nontenured instructor, was employed by Kentucky State University. His teaching contract was not renewed. Plaintiff alleges that the nonrenewal was racially motivated and violated his rights to free speech and due process. Defendants contend that the University was not acting "under color of law" as required by 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and that Ward, as a nontenured instructor, is not entitled to notice and hearing. The University also argues that the Kentucky courts are suitably equipped to adjudicate Ward's claim and that the federal judiciary should abstain from exercising jurisdiction.

Prior to the nonrenewal, Ward had been employed by the University, but the exact terms of his employment, including any implied contract, are disputed. Plaintiff alleges that his termination was motivated by his exercise of free speech, while defendants contend that the nonrenewal was lawful. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the University being a state institution. The nature of the dispute is a claim of racial discrimination and violation of constitutional rights.

The pre-litigation events include the nonrenewal of Ward's contract, which led to the filing of this lawsuit. Relevant documents and communications may include Ward's employment contract, any notices or warnings given to him, and any discussions or meetings between Ward and University officials regarding his employment. The workplace facts include the University's policies and procedures for renewing or terminating contracts, as well as any relevant state laws or regulations governing employment and discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that he was not given notice or a hearing prior to the nonrenewal, while defendants contend that such procedures are not required for nontenured instructors.

On October 17, 1974, a consent decree was entered, enjoining the Milwaukee Fire Department from engaging in any employment practice that has the purpose or effect of discriminating on the basis of sex against applicants to or employees of the Fire Department. The decree was later modified in October 1976 to provide that 5 per cent of the firefighter appointments would go to females. The Milwaukee Fire Department conducts a paramedic program, selecting and training paramedics exclusively from among firefighters serving in the department. However, no woman has ever passed the Milwaukee Fire Department's training course and become a firefighter, and consequently, no woman has ever served as a paramedic in the Milwaukee Fire Department.

Plaintiff alleges that the requirement for potential paramedics to first pass the Fire Department's training course and become a firefighter has excluded all women from becoming paramedics. Plaintiff contends that this requirement is not justified by business necessity and disproportionately excludes women. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that paramedics must be able to fight fires should it become necessary and that due to the high stress encountered in their jobs, paramedics must be trained firefighters so that they can be returned to firefighter duties after they "burn out" as paramedics. Defendants also argue that the paramedic program requires individuals to have the skills and training of a firefighter.

Prior to the lawsuit, the Milwaukee Fire Department had a shortage of paramedics, with only 44 paramedics in the department, despite a full complement of 48. The department's paramedic program involves extensive training in emergency medicine, and paramedics work full-time providing emergency medical services under the supervision of physicians. Paramedics seldom perform firefighting duties during their regular work week, and their job is different in kind from that of firefighters. Other cities, such as Chicago, have successfully employed non-firefighters, including women, as paramedics, and there is no showing that civilian paramedics could not assist firefighters in the ways paramedics now occasionally do without being full-fledged firefighters.

Billy Porter, a black man, began working for the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) in 2013 as a supervisory contracting specialist, supervising employees, assigning and reviewing work, and providing training and direction. Initially, he supervised around sixteen employees in Little Rock, and later, he supervised employees in other states, while continuing to supervise at least five employees in Little Rock until his retirement in 2017. In October 2015, Porter applied for a promotion to division chief, but was not selected for the position after interviews. The VA compiled information about each candidate, including federal contracting experience, supervisory experience, VA experience, and certification level, and each candidate was interviewed by a panel of three people. Porter was not one of the top two candidates, and a white man ultimately got the job.

Porter alleges that a higher-ranking VA employee made a comment that the person who received the job was a "better fit" for the role, which Porter views as a racist remark. Meanwhile, Porter's health issues began impairing his ability to do his job, and he repeatedly requested an accommodation to work from home, providing documentation from medical providers in support of this request. The VA offered alternative accommodations, including an ergonomic workstation, an ergonomic assessment, a sit/stand workstation, hybrid telework, and leave for medical and physical therapy appointments, but Porter rejected these offers, stating that working from home was the only accommodation acceptable to him. Porter contends that the VA's proposed accommodations did not address the impact his disabilities had on his daily life activities, such as caring for himself and attending medical appointments.

The VA denied Porter's requests for advanced leave in April 2016, citing that he had applied for disability retirement and might not return to duty or be able to earn the leave amount by the end of the remaining leave year. Porter's position required him to maintain a certain certification level, and he was temporarily detailed to a position that did not require that certification level after he failed to complete training hours. Porter believes he was subjected to a hostile work environment based on his disability and treated differently than others based on his race, and he also alleges that he was retaliated against for requesting accommodations. The VA and Porter have different contentions about the events and circumstances surrounding his employment, including the reasons for the denial of his promotion, accommodation requests, and leave requests, as well as the impact of these events on his work and well-being.

Samuel Daniels and Leticia Anderson, both black, began working as casual drivers for Traditional Logistics and Cartage, LLC (TLC) in early 2018. TLC provides drive away services for Ford Motor Company at its Claycomo, Missouri, manufacturing facility. As casual drivers, they were only called into work on an as-needed basis, did not receive the same benefits as full-time drivers, and were not eligible to join the union. Approximately once a year, TLC goes through a "hiring" process to transition casual drivers to full-time drivers. Despite receiving positive performance reviews, neither Daniels nor Anderson was ever offered a position as a full-time driver. 

Plaintiff Daniels alleges that TLC's "hiring" process is a pattern or practice of intentional discrimination against black employees, and that the company has repeatedly "hired" less qualified non-black casual drivers with less seniority over more qualified, more senior black casual drivers. Daniels filed an amended charge of discrimination against TLC with the Equal Opportunity Employment Commission (EEOC) and the Missouri Commission on Human Rights (MCHR), checking boxes for "race" and "sex" discrimination. The EEOC terminated its processing of his charge and notified him of his right to sue in court. 

Daniels and Anderson, on behalf of themselves and a class of others, allege putative class action race discrimination claims against TLC, RCS Transportation, LLC, and Valiant Management and Holdings, LLC. They contend that the defendants are their joint employers and/or a common enterprise. Defendants argue that Anderson failed to exhaust administrative remedies on her Title VII race discrimination claims because Daniels's amended charge was directed at and limited to alleged discrimination against black males and did not contemplate discrimination against black females. Plaintiff Anderson contends that she was subjected to the same discriminatory "hiring" process as Daniels and that her claims are like or reasonably related to the substance of charges timely brought before the EEOC.

Plaintiff, a female law enforcement officer with over twenty years of experience, has been employed by the Wright County Sheriff's Office since 1996. She has a bachelor's degree in Criminal Justice and a master's degree in Criminal Justice Leadership, as well as several certificates related to court security. In July 2014, a sergeant position opened in the Court Services department, and Plaintiff applied for the position. She met the minimum qualifications, which included having an associate's degree in criminal justice or law enforcement. 

Plaintiff alleges that despite her qualifications and experience, she was not selected for the promotion. She contends that she was invited to interview for the position, but her interview performance was not fairly evaluated. Plaintiff alleges that she was nervous during the interview and gave short answers, which she claims was a result of her nervousness. She also alleges that one of her answers, in which she mentioned having trouble going to the bathroom while wearing her duty belt as a woman, was misinterpreted by the interviewers. 

Defendant contends that the interview panel, which included Chief Deputy Todd Hoffman, Captain Dan Anselment, and Human Resources Representative Judy Brown, fairly evaluated all candidates based on their communication skills, thought processes, articulation, and overall presentation. Defendant claims that Plaintiff's answers were brief and lacked depth, and that she did not outline how the barrier she mentioned prevented her from doing her job effectively. The panel ultimately recommended Drew Scherber for the position, and Sheriff Hagerty selected him after considering the panel's recommendations and discussing the finalists with his Command Staff. Plaintiff later asked Sheriff Hagerty for advice on what she needed to do to be promoted to Sergeant, and he told her that he seeks qualities such as good attitude, attendance, experience, and personality specific to the position. Defendant contends that Sheriff Hagerty's decision was based on legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons.

Charles Ojih Oji, a Black citizen of Nigeria, was hired by Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation in June 2017 as a Software Engineer II, with a salary of $76,000. Oji had a master's degree in electrical engineering and computer science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, but had limited work experience in his field. During his three months of employment, Oji worked on a team with a team leader and two coworkers. However, issues with his performance arose, and his coworkers reported that he lacked fundamental understanding in basic computer networking. Oji's functional manager also informed him that he was not adequately performing his job.

Plaintiff Oji alleges that he faced racial harassment and discrimination during his employment, including a video of Neil Degrasse Tyson being played in the lab, which he claims was mocking Black people. He also claims that his team leader advised him to avoid a certain branch of the DMV located in a predominantly Black neighborhood because it was a "zoo," and that his coworkers made comments about him smelling "too good" for a person who was Black and of Nigerian origin. Oji reported this conduct in August 2017, but an employee relations investigator found no evidence to support his allegations of racial harassment and hostile work environment.

Defendant Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation contends that Oji was discharged due to his inability to perform the duties of his job, citing his lack of experience and poor performance. Northrop's functional manager decided to discharge Oji based on his own observations and the reports of Oji's team, concluding that Oji was not capable of performing the duties of his job. The "Termination of Employment" letter stated that the decision was based on Oji's "ongoing performance issues and not being able to meet [his] deliverables in a timely manner." Oji challenges his discharge, claiming that Northrop violated Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 by discharging him due to his race, color, and national origin, and in retaliation for complaining about racial harassment and a hostile work environment. Oji also claims that Northrop paid him less than his non-Black counterparts in violation of Section 1981.

Godfrey Biggers, Carlton Brantley, Henry Crawford, Larry Dowdell, Melvin Griffin, Pondiel Mabry, William Marshall, Connie McCoy, Hayward Parham, Reginal Richardson, Jerry Starks, Patrick Stroud, Larry Thompson, and Calvin Williams (collectively, "Plaintiffs") are current and former plant services and custodial employees of the Muscogee County School District ("School District"). Plaintiffs allege that the School District engaged in a pattern of racial discrimination, relegating certain black employees to the Public School Employees Retirement System ("PSERS") while making the more generous Teachers Retirement System ("TRS") available to similarly-situated white employees. Plaintiffs, who are black, claim they were placed in the PSERS because of their race and that some School District employees, including Kinard Latham, fraudulently prevented them from being placed in the TRS.

Plaintiffs assert that Latham's testimony regarding TRS eligibility requirements establishes that each Plaintiff was eligible for TRS enrollment but was denied an opportunity to enroll. However, Defendant Latham contends that he never had responsibility for approving or rejecting TRS applications and that his understanding of TRS eligibility requirements was incorrect. The School District Defendants, including Don A. Cooper, Jr., Carolyn French, Marie Stringfellow, and Jerry Duck, argue that Plaintiffs were not eligible for TRS enrollment based on their job titles and duties. Latham's mistakes in the 1980s led to several plant services employees being accepted into the TRS despite being unqualified, and subsequent investigations and process changes were implemented in the School District's personnel department.

The events in question began in 1974 when Latham became the School District's director of plant services, a position he held until his retirement in 1996. During his tenure, Latham permitted some employees to inflate their job titles on TRS applications, allowing them to enroll in the TRS. However, when Latham attempted to help more employees, including several Plaintiffs, join the TRS in 1993, the TRS found them ineligible due to their actual job titles. The TRS provided the School District with a clear definition of the terms "supervisor" and "manager," which are required for TRS eligibility. Plaintiffs made several complaints over the years, including a complaint to the NAACP in 1998 and a state court lawsuit in 2007, alleging unfair exclusion from the TRS. The Plaintiffs and the School District Defendants have exchanged various documents and communications, including summary judgment motions, with the Plaintiffs seeking to establish their eligibility for the TRS and the School District Defendants arguing that the Plaintiffs were not eligible due to their job titles and duties.

Hope Quaintance worked as a temporary bus driver for the City of Columbia-COMO Connect, beginning in February 2013. Her route operated on the University of Missouri, Columbia campus, and she worked only when students were present. Quaintance alleges that she was subject to harassment from her co-workers, which made her feel physically unwell. On April 4, 2014, she filed a complaint with her supervisors about the harassment. 

On May 8, 2014, Quaintance left work early to visit her primary care doctor due to high blood pressure. Although she was released to return to work with no restrictions, Columbia required her to undergo a "fitness for duty examination" because of the blood pressure results. As part of this examination, Dr. Michael Szewczyk, a certified DOT Medical Examiner, reviewed Quaintance's medical records and learned that she had a history of bipolar disease and was not receiving treatment. Quaintance disputed this diagnosis, claiming she had attention deficit disorder instead. Dr. Szewczyk informed her that she needed to establish care with a mental health professional, be stable, and be cleared to operate a commercial vehicle by both a mental health professional and himself.

Quaintance was restricted from driving due to the need for additional medical treatment, and a follow-up exam was scheduled for July 15, 2014, but was ultimately cancelled and never rescheduled. On August 18, 2014, Quaintance was supposed to be recalled to work, but she received a letter from Columbia stating that she was not eligible for recall because she was not DOT certified. Plaintiff alleges that her former employer discriminated against her on the basis of her race, gender, and disability, and in retaliation for her complaints of harassment in the workplace. Defendant contends that Quaintance was not recalled due to her lack of DOT certification, which is a requirement for all Columbia Transit Bus driver positions.

Sydney Watson began working for Blaze in May 2021 under a Talent Services Agreement, where she was hired to cohost the internet-based show "You Are Here" (YAH) focused on politics and culture, alongside Elijah Schaffer. The show started production in September 2021 and was initially successful. However, the relationship between Watson and Schaffer quickly deteriorated. Plaintiff alleges that Schaffer's persona on the show became increasingly aggressive and misogynistic, and he selected guests who were "grossly misogynistic." One of these guests shouted at Watson during the show, and Schaffer continued to book similar guests without consulting her. Watson felt she was the target of sexist comments from both Schaffer and the show's guests, and the audience would routinely harass her with "grossly sexist" and "anti-Jewish" comments.

Watson began reporting Schaffer's behavior to Blaze management on a weekly basis starting in January 2022. She experienced significant stress and vertigo, which caused her to miss shows. On March 4, 2022, Watson told Schaffer and other Blaze employees, including president Gaston Mooney, that the behavior was making it impossible for her to do her job. After the meeting, Blaze management promised to address the issues. Despite this promise, the problems continued, and things escalated when Schaffer tweeted that he hoped Watson would "sleep with" a certain conservative media personality on April 7, 2022. Watson then stopped participating in YAH, and the show was officially put on hiatus in May 2022. In the following months, Schaffer continued to make disparaging comments about Watson.

Plaintiff alleges that Blaze either constructively terminated her in the spring of 2022 or actively terminated her in July 2022 after she complained about Schaffer's conduct through counsel. Defendant contends that the parties had an agreement that included arbitration provisions. Watson sued Blaze in February 2023, and Blaze moved to compel arbitration under the parties' Agreement. The parties' relationship and the nature of the dispute center around the alleged harassment and discrimination Watson faced while working on YAH, and the question of whether these claims are subject to arbitration under the parties' Agreement.

Kess Tani, the plaintiff, entered into an open-ended written and verbal contract with defendants, including Florida Power and Light (FPL), Myriad Technical Service Corp. (Myriad), and Guidant Group, Inc. (Guidant), in April 2010, to perform work for FPL in Palo, Iowa, for a period of not less than thirty-six months. On May 14, 2010, defendants verbally instructed Tani to travel from North East, Maryland to Palo, Iowa, and told him that all background investigations had been completed, and the contract was valid for him to begin work. Tani arrived in Palo, Iowa, was processed, and was issued an access badge/photo ID. 

On May 19, 2010, Tani discovered deficiencies at the nuclear power plant and reported them to his immediate supervisor. Later, on May 25, 2010, defendants required Tani to produce pre-employment medical records from age eighteen through the present as a condition of performing his contract with FPL. Tani advised defendants that this demand was discriminatory because white employees were not required to produce medical records from age eighteen to the present as a condition of employment. He notes that the demand for records is not found in the contract or FPL employment policies. On the same day, defendants terminated Tani's contract "on the spot." 

Plaintiff alleges that the decision to terminate his employment was due to his refusal to provide pre-employment medical records and not the result of job performance issues or violations of federal and state laws or company policies. Tani also alleges he engaged in protected whistle-blowing activities and was subjected to racial profiling and discrimination. Defendants, including FPL and Myriad, contend that they were not properly served and that the court lacks personal jurisdiction over them. Myriad sought an extension of time to answer or otherwise plead, which was granted by the court. FPL has filed a motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, presuming that Tani intended to name it as a defendant rather than the non-existent entity FPL/NextEraEnergy.

On April 17, 1967, Celio Diaz, Jr. applied for a position as a flight cabin attendant with Pan American World Airways, Inc. (Pan Am). His application was rejected because Pan Am had a policy of only hiring females for that position, which had been in place since 1965. Diaz then filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) under Section 703 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, alleging that Pan Am had discriminated against him based on his sex. The EEOC found probable cause and attempted conciliation, but it was unsuccessful. 

Diaz filed a complaint with the court on February 14, 1969, on behalf of himself and others similarly situated, alleging that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants was discriminatory. The parties stipulated that Diaz had applied and been rejected for the position because he was male, and that other males had also been rejected for the same reason. They also stipulated that Pan Am's policy was to not hire males for the position, and that the class of plaintiffs would consist of males who had applied for the position within the United States and been rejected because of their sex. 

Plaintiff alleges that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants is discriminatory and violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Defendant Pan Am contends that being a female is a bona fide occupational qualification for the position of flight cabin attendant, reasonably necessary to the normal operation of its business. The EEOC, as amicus curiae, supports the plaintiff's position. The Transport Workers Union of America, representing Pan Am's cabin attendants, and the Air Line Pilots Association, International, also filed amicus curiae briefs. The parties disagree on the criteria for determining which males who applied for the position in the past should be entitled to preferential consideration for hire and back pay. Plaintiff contends that this group should include all males who filed written applications between July 2, 1965, and November 18, 1971, while defendant Pan Am argues that it should only include those who applied between November 16, 1968, and April 24, 1970.

Rosello, an attorney, represented an individual who received treatment from Defendant Rivera Chiropractic, Inc. ("Rivera") for two car accidents. Rivera was never paid for the treatment. Plaintiff alleges that Rivera sued the individual who received treatment, Rosello personally, and Rosello's law firm in state court, seeking reimbursement. Defendants Fresh Legal Perspective, PL ("FLP") and Keathel Chauncey, FLP's managing attorney, represented Rivera in the state court case. 

Rivera voluntarily dismissed the state court case about ten months after it was filed. Plaintiff alleges that Rivera wrongly claimed he personally owed a debt and that the state court action was an attempt to coerce him into providing compensation. Rosello also alleges that Chauncey and FLP accused him of unethical and illegal conduct through a bar complaint in order to force him into paying a debt he had no obligation to pay. 

The parties' relationship is that of a debt collector (Rivera) and a debtor's attorney (Rosello), with FLP and Chauncey representing Rivera. The nature of the dispute is over whether Rivera, FLP, and Chauncey violated the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act and the Florida Consumer Collection Practices Act in their attempts to collect the debt from Rosello's client. Defendant contends that their actions were lawful and that Rosello had no basis for his claims. Relevant pre-litigation events include the state court lawsuit, the voluntary dismissal of that case, and the bar complaint filed against Rosello.

Yao Etienne Kouakou, an African marketing representative, was employed by New York State Catholic Health Plan, Inc., d/b/a FidelisCare New York, from June 2008 until his involuntary discharge on August 20, 2010. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, he was discriminated against because he was the only African marketing representative in a department where the remainder of the staff was Hispanic. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that his former supervisor, Hector Hernandez, constantly spoke in Spanish with another supervisor, Efrain Vargas, making Plaintiff feel uncomfortable. 

Plaintiff requested a transfer from Hernandez's team in 2008, but was denied. After the transfer request, Plaintiff alleges that Hernandez "turned the marketing department against him" and "falsely accused him of creating a fraudulent application" for a government healthcare program. Plaintiff also alleges that Hernandez forced him to sign a disciplinary letter stating that he did not meet sales quota requirements, which Plaintiff claims was untrue. Defendant terminated Hernandez after Plaintiff showed the letter to the Human Resources Department. 

Plaintiff alleges that, following Hernandez's termination, the marketing department became "angry and retaliated against him." For instance, Vargas allegedly forced Plaintiff to sign documents stating that if he ended up back in Vargas's office, he would be terminated. Another supervisor, Ana Roposo, allegedly continued Plaintiff's mistreatment, and on one occasion, Vargas called Plaintiff an "Africano negro." Other co-workers allegedly "verbally attacked" Plaintiff and were "closer to physically harming him" at work in support of their cause as Spanish speakers. Plaintiff also alleges that he was involved in two specific confrontations with co-workers over gifts that were frequently made available for marketing representatives to give to their clients. In both incidents, Plaintiff was allegedly denied gifts for his clients, while Hispanic applicants received them. Plaintiff notified his supervisor about both incidents, but claims that his supervisor chose to do nothing about them. Plaintiff also alleges that he was investigated for submitting another "fraudulent application," which resulted in his involuntary termination, and that other marketing representatives who were suspected of creating fraudulent applications were not disciplined, investigated, or fired. Defendant contends that there is no evidence that the adverse employment actions against Plaintiff were motivated by his race or national origin.

Chasity King, a corrections officer, worked at a facility operated by the Pennsylvania Department of Corrections. Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and gender-based discrimination at the facility. Specifically, Plaintiff contends that she was repeatedly reassigned to work outside of the control bubble by Sergeant Bloss, and that he also played pranks on women. Plaintiff also alleges that the women's bathroom door was unlocked while she was indisposed, and that her coworkers replayed her reaction to a incident where a corrections officer's pants fell down after he took off his belt to enter a metal detector. Additionally, Plaintiff claims that she and another female coworker were locked out in sub-zero temperatures.

Defendant contends that there was an incident where a corrections officer's pants inadvertently fell down, and a video of the incident was shown to other corrections officers for training purposes. However, Defendant disputes that the officers viewing this video made fun of Plaintiff's reaction to the incident. Defendant also notes that Plaintiff made numerous complaints to her coworkers and supervisors about her treatment, but argues that these complaints do not establish a pattern of discriminatory behavior.

The parties have a complex and disputed history, with multiple incidents and interactions that are central to the lawsuit. Plaintiff filed a complaint against the Pennsylvania Department of Corrections, alleging violations of Title VII. The parties have engaged in extensive pre-litigation interactions, including the filing of a Joint Statement of Undisputed Facts, as well as separate statements of additional facts and responses thereto. These submissions highlight the parties' disagreements about the facts and their interpretations of the events in question. Relevant pre-litigation events include the incident with the corrections officer's pants falling down, the showing of the video to other officers, and Plaintiff's complaints to her coworkers and supervisors. Employment and workplace facts relevant to the case include the facility's policies and procedures, as well as the relationships between Plaintiff and her coworkers and supervisors.

Darlene Atta, a black female, was a management-level employee of Sun Company, Inc. (also known as Sun Refining and Marketing Company) from 1969 to January 17, 1983. Plaintiff alleges that despite performing competently, her performance rating was lowered in May 1982, and her employment status was changed from "permanent exempt, salaried employee" to "temporary, nonexempt employee". Plaintiff further alleges that from 1981 to January 17, 1983, the defendant discriminated against her based on her race and gender by changing her status, excluding her from office conferences, failing to provide necessary performance feedback, and subjecting her to higher standards and lower pay than similarly situated whites and/or males. Plaintiff contends that she was terminated on January 17, 1983, due to her race and gender, and that the defendant's procedures for reducing its employee pool were designed to discriminate against blacks and/or females.

Defendant Sun Company, Inc. employed Darlene Atta in various capacities from 1969 to 1983. Defendant contends that it did not discriminate against Atta based on her race or gender. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Atta alleging that the defendant's actions constituted employment discrimination. Relevant pre-litigation events include the change in Atta's employment status in May 1982 and her termination in January 1983. The complaint alleges that the defendant made false and misleading representations to Atta concerning the terms and conditions of her employment, which induced her to accept employment and a temporary assignment in May 1982.

The plaintiff has alleged that the defendant's conduct violated various federal laws, including Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Equal Pay Act of 1963, and the Civil Rights Act of 1866. The defendant has moved to dismiss certain claims and strike certain damages, but the underlying factual dispute concerns the defendant's treatment of Atta during her employment, including the change in her employment status, her exclusion from office conferences, and her termination. The plaintiff alleges that these actions were taken due to her race and gender, while the defendant contends that it did not discriminate against her.

Jannette Rae Olson, a female resident of Minnesota, applied for employment with Minneapolis Electric Steel Casting Company on July 29, 1979. She was interviewed by the company's labor relations assistant, Dwayne Christiansen, on August 8, 1979, and again by Daniel Donovan, the finishing room superintendent, on August 28, 1979. During the second interview, Olson was considered for employment as a chipper-grinder in the cleaning department on the second or third shift. Donovan explained the duties of a chipper-grinder, which include removing excess metal from steel castings using various grinding tools, including a large grinder that weighs approximately twenty to twenty-five pounds.

Olson was hired and started working as a chipper-grinder on September 4, 1979. She was introduced to her supervisor, Bill Schofield, who told her to focus on performing her job safely. Schofield assigned experienced chipper-grinders, Thomas Holley and Steven Beals, to demonstrate the operation of the grinding equipment and proper procedures to Olson. The company claims to have an unwritten safety policy that requires chipper-grinders to operate the large grinder with both feet on the ground, but this policy was not posted anywhere in the work area. Plaintiff alleges that she was not adequately trained on the safe use of the large grinder and was not given sufficient time to learn how to operate it properly. Defendant contends that Olson was warned repeatedly about violating the safety policy, but Olson alleges that she was only warned one or two times.

The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding Olson's termination on September 13, 1979. Defendant claims that Olson was discharged due to her inability to handle the large grinders safely, while Plaintiff alleges that the termination was discriminatory. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) commenced this suit on November 2, 1981, on behalf of Olson, alleging that the company subjected her to different terms and conditions of employment and discharged her because of her sex. The company denies these allegations, contending that it uniformly enforced its safety policy against all employees, regardless of sex. However, several male employees, including Beals and Aussing, testified that they regularly violated the company's unwritten safety policy without being warned or disciplined, which Plaintiff alleges suggests that the company's enforcement of the policy was not uniform and was instead discriminatory against Olson.

Ms. Holley, an African-American woman with hypertension, was hired by BBS/Mendoza, a McDonald's franchisee, in January 2019. She worked in the kitchen at the Sinclair Road location for over two and a half years without receiving written discipline. In March 2021, a new General Manager, Brett Wilson, was appointed, and Ms. Holley reported to him and his supervisor, Steven Kunz, that she had overheard derogatory language used against African-American employees. She also reported that Mr. Wilson had referred to his African-American colleagues as "you people" or "them people." Mr. Kunz denies receiving these reports.

On August 27, 2021, Ms. Holley arrived at work at 4:00 a.m. and soon experienced hypertension symptoms. She advised the shift manager, Yakaday Sankoh, who told her that she could not leave but would advise Mr. Wilson. Ms. Holley and Mr. Wilson disagree about what happened next. According to Ms. Holley, she told Mr. Wilson that she needed to leave due to her symptoms, but he accused her of malingering and directed her to continue working. The situation escalated, and Mr. Wilson told Ms. Holley that she was "fired" as she left. Mr. Wilson, on the other hand, claims that Ms. Holley was over-stuffing cabinets in violation of food safety regulations, and when she said she was sick, he told her to clock out and leave. He also claims that Ms. Holley became agitated and harassed a customer, which led to her termination.

The parties also disagree about the events that followed Ms. Holley's termination. Mr. Kunz claims that he overrode Mr. Wilson's decision and offered Ms. Holley continued employment at a different location, but Ms. Holley denies speaking with Mr. Kunz or receiving such an offer. BBS/Mendoza's response to the incident is also disputed, with the company stating that Ms. Holley was terminated due to her harassment of a customer, while Ms. Holley alleges that she was terminated due to her reports of racist behavior and her medical condition. Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and retaliation, while Defendant contends that it took appropriate action in response to Ms. Holley's behavior. The parties' accounts of the events are vastly different, with each side presenting conflicting evidence and testimony.

Nazeem Stanazai was employed as an international broadcaster and copy editor at the Voice of America, a media network that provides news in 47 languages to an estimated 278 million people worldwide. He worked with the Afghan Service, within the South and Central Asian Division, and was compensated at the General Schedule pay scale (GS) level 12. The division's director, Akbar Ayazi, oversaw a reorganization of the Afghan Service's management in 2016, which involved reconfiguring the three radio and television services into two services organized by language. 

The Board maintains that prior to the reorganization, each of the four groups within the Afghan Service was led by a GS-13 employee, and that after the reorganization, Ayazi made Lina Rozbih and Shaista Sadat Lami managing editors of the two resulting divisions, both of which were GS-13 positions. The Board also asserts that Ayazi assigned several "new tasks" as part of the reorganization, including designating four individuals as "senior editors" on the Dari and Pashto teams, but that these designations were not new GS-13 positions and the individuals remained GS-12 International Broadcasters. 

Plaintiff Stanazai alleges that Ayazi not only reconfigured the services but also changed the editorship of the two new services, promoting Ms. Rozbih and Ms. Lami to managing editor positions, despite Stanazai being more qualified for those positions. Stanazai also disputes the Board's assertions regarding the "senior editor" positions, arguing that he was overlooked for those positions and that most of the individuals who took those positions were later benchmarked to GS-13. Stanazai filed this action on December 11, 2017, alleging discrimination and retaliation under the ADEA, and the parties have engaged in discovery and motions practice, with the Board moving for summary judgment on the grounds that Stanazai cannot make out a prima facie case for retaliation.

The plaintiffs, former commercial airline pilots, were forced to retire from their positions as first pilots (also known as captains or pilots in command) at American Airlines, Inc. ("American") following their sixtieth birthdays. Before reaching age sixty, the plaintiffs had been employed as first pilots, working alongside second pilots and flight officers or flight engineers in the cockpit of large commercial aircraft. Unlike pilots, flight engineers are permitted to work beyond their sixtieth birthdays. The plaintiffs sought to continue their employment with American in the position of flight officer/flight engineer, but American refused their request.

Plaintiff alleges that American's refusal to allow them to continue working as flight officers/flight engineers constitutes age discrimination in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act ("ADEA"). Defendant American contends that the plaintiffs' claims to the position of flight officer are contrary to the Tripartite Agreement of 1965, a collective bargaining agreement between American, the Allied Pilots Association ("APA"), and the Flight Engineers' International Association ("FEIA"). American also contends that the plaintiffs have failed to exhaust their applicable remedies within the Allied Pilots Association or under the Railway Labor Act as a condition precedent to bringing suit.

The plaintiffs filed charges with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission ("EEOC") alleging age discrimination and subsequently filed this lawsuit on July 3, 1979. The Tripartite Agreement, which was approved by the Secretary of Labor and the National Mediation Board on March 8, 1965, guarantees priority in the third cockpit position to flight engineers until retirement and requires that all third crew members hired after July 1, 1964, be pilots represented by the APA. American maintains that the plaintiffs' claims to the position of third crew member are contrary to this agreement. The plaintiffs had been employed as pilots and were members of the Allied Pilots Association, which has a collective bargaining agreement with American that governs the terms and conditions of their employment, including the process for bidding on available positions.

Terrance Green, a Black man, was hired by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) as a bank examiner in the mid-sized bank division on June 11, 2012. Plaintiff alleges that he was not sufficiently paid during his employment with OCC, specifically claiming that two other individuals, Dwanda Asberry, a Black woman, and Ryan de France, a White man, received higher salaries than him despite being hired for the same or similar positions. Asberry had six years of prior experience and was paid $107,942 at OCC, while de France had over ten years of experience and was paid $140,941. In contrast, Plaintiff had five years of experience and was hired at a starting salary of $85,652.

Plaintiff requested an Administratively Determined Pay Increase (ADPI) on June 21, 2016, which involved an analysis of his performance, experience, and pay data compared to his peers. The Compensation and Benefits team gathered data, including resumes and previous new hire salary justification forms, and compared Plaintiff's salary to that of his peers. After conducting the analysis, the team decided to raise Plaintiff's salary to $106,602, which was nearly equivalent to the salary of another colleague, Neha Gosalia, an Asian woman with the same position but more experience and better performance ratings. Despite this pay increase, Plaintiff alleged that his new salary was still lower than that of Asberry and de France.

Plaintiff also alleges various non-pay-related claims, including that his supervisor, Marva Cummings, a Black woman, issued a memorandum on January 27, 2015, advising him that his performance might result in a lower rating on his evaluation if it did not improve. Plaintiff filed an EEO complaint on May 18, 2015, alleging racial discrimination based on four theories, but the claims were dismissed as untimely or for lack of evidence. Plaintiff appealed the decision, but the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) upheld the findings. On April 11, 2018, Plaintiff filed this action, asserting several theories of employment discrimination under the Equal Pay Act, Title VII, and the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination. Defendant, Scott Bessent, Secretary of the Department of the Treasury, contends that the salary differential is based on legitimate reasons, such as Plaintiff's lower-level positions, less relevant experience, and lower previous salary, and that Plaintiff cannot meet his burden to prove pretext.

Plaintiff, a Clinical Laboratory Scientist, was hired by Defendant, Redwood Toxicology Laboratory, with a start date of January 8, 2018. Plaintiff alleges that during her term of employment, a co-worker made one sexual remark to her. She also claims that she was bullied by her co-workers, which led her to resign in May 2018. However, after discussing her concerns with her supervisor, Plaintiff retracted her resignation. 

In July 2018, Plaintiff notified her supervisor that she was experiencing back pains, shoulder hurt, and had sprained her ankle in the lab. Her physician restricted her activity, and Redwood accommodated these restrictions. Plaintiff requested an additional 30 days of leave, which was denied by Redwood, as it had not been requested by her physician. Plaintiff also alleges that she requested a printer at her desk, but Redwood does not have a record of this request. Additionally, Plaintiff claims that two co-workers called her "old" several times.

During her employment, Plaintiff was issued both verbal and written warnings citing several instances of inappropriate conduct or performance issues. Plaintiff resigned from her job on September 27, 2018, and Redwood accepted her resignation. Two days later, Plaintiff tried to rescind her resignation, but Redwood refused to allow her to retract it. Defendant contends that it accommodated Plaintiff's restrictions and did not discriminate against her based on her disability. 

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute involves claims of disability discrimination, harassment, and retaliation. Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and was wrongfully terminated, while Defendant contends that it acted lawfully and reasonably in its treatment of Plaintiff. Relevant pre-litigation events include Plaintiff's resignation and attempted rescission, as well as the warnings and accommodations provided by Redwood. The employment records and communications between Plaintiff and her supervisor are also relevant to the dispute.

Ms. Linda Matarese and her husband, Mr. Domenic Matarese, have been renting an apartment at Archstone Parc Vista (APC) in Arlington, Virginia, for over 18 years. Ms. Matarese has chemical sensitivities to paint fumes, tobacco smoke, and mold, which can cause her severe reactions, including dizziness, coughing, and debilitating headaches. She has informed Archstone managers of her sensitivities on multiple occasions and has requested accommodations to avoid exposure to these chemicals. In 2006, APC began a renovation project that involved painting the exterior surfaces of the windows, doors, and handrails of every unit, using paint containing volatile organic compounds (VOC paint). Ms. Matarese became ill from the exterior painting and complained of a respiratory infection that lasted for several months.

Plaintiff Ms. Matarese alleges that she met with Defendant Malcolm McGregor in May 2007 to discuss the painting inside her apartment and presented him with letters from herself and her doctor, requesting that APC refrain from painting inside her unit due to her chemical sensitivities. Defendant McGregor allegedly became visibly angry and denied her request for accommodations. Plaintiffs contend that Defendants discriminated against them on the basis of Ms. Matarese's handicap by non-renewing their lease, converting them to a month-to-month tenancy, and refusing to allow them to rent at a different Archstone location. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that they did not discriminate against Plaintiffs and that their actions were taken for legitimate business reasons.

The parties have a long history of disputes over Ms. Matarese's chemical sensitivities and the accommodations she has requested. Ms. Matarese has become extremely afraid of exposure to chemicals and has sanitized her apartment to avoid exposure. She has also limited her activities outside the apartment due to her sensitivities. The dispute between the parties escalated over time, with Plaintiffs alleging that Defendants failed to provide reasonable accommodations and discriminated against them on the basis of Ms. Matarese's handicap. Defendants, however, contend that they have made efforts to accommodate Ms. Matarese's requests and that their actions were not discriminatory. The parties' relationship and the nature of the dispute are complex, with multiple incidents and communications between them over the years. Relevant pre-litigation events include the renovation project, the meeting between Ms. Matarese and Defendant McGregor, and the various requests for accommodations made by Ms. Matarese.

John Hancock was employed by Securitas Security Services USA, Inc. as the Vice President of Response Services of North America, a position he was promoted to in April 2017, with a salary of $170,000 per year and the potential to earn up to $250,000 per year. In February 2018, Hancock discovered he had fractured his back and was required by his doctor to wear a back brace at all times, except when sleeping. Plaintiff alleges that in April 2018, Securitas demoted him to the position of Branch Manager of Central Texas and reduced his salary to $75,000. Hancock claims this demotion and salary reduction were due to his disability and that Securitas failed to accommodate his needs.

Plaintiff alleges that he had requested accommodations for his disability and had also reported incidents of racial discrimination against other employees, as well as discrimination against military servicemembers, which he believes led to the retaliation against him. Securitas, on the other hand, contends that Hancock failed to exhaust his administrative remedies regarding his failure-to-accommodate claims under the ADA and the Texas Labor Code. Securitas also argues that Hancock's Title VII retaliation claim is without merit because he did not engage in any protected activity recognized under Title VII's anti-retaliation statute.

The events leading up to the lawsuit include Hancock's promotion, his back injury, and his subsequent demotion and salary reduction. Hancock had filed a Charge of Discrimination detailing the alleged disability discrimination he personally suffered, as well as the racial discrimination and discrimination against military servicemembers he witnessed against other employees. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the nature of the dispute centering on allegations of disability discrimination, retaliation, and failure to accommodate under federal and state laws.

Theodore R. Lucas, a 62-year-old employee of the United States Department of Education (DOE), applied for the GS-13 position of Management & Program Analyst in the DOE's Office of Civil Rights in 1998. The position was advertised through Vacancy Announcement No. 98-087VB, which required applicants to have at least 52 weeks of specialized experience at the GS-12 level and to address their previous work experience and educational accomplishments in their applications. Lucas, who was then serving as a GS-343-12 in the Office of Civil Rights, submitted his application along with other candidates, including Jerelyn Berry, a 43-year-old GS-343-12 employee.

Plaintiff alleges that during his interview, the selecting official, Dr. Paul Fairley, made a comment, "You old timer, you've been around here," which Lucas claims is a reference to his age and evidence of discriminatory intent. Defendant contends that Fairley does not recall making such a statement and suggests that even if he did, it was merely an acknowledgment of Lucas's long tenure with the DOE. Defendant also argues that Berry was the most qualified candidate for the position, as determined by Verna Braxton of the DOE personnel office, and that the selection panel unanimously recommended her for the position.

The selection process involved a panel of OCR employees, including David Berkowitz, Jan Gray, Janice Pottker, and Gloria Threadgill, who interviewed each of the candidates and asked the same questions. After the interviews, the panel sent a memorandum to Fairley recommending Berry for the position, and Fairley certified his selection of Berry on July 23, 1998. Lucas contacted the DOE's EEO office regarding his non-selection on July 22, 1998, and eventually filed a lawsuit on November 16, 2001, alleging age discrimination in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA).

Glenn Duckworth was employed by Mid-State Machine Products as a Gage Control Technician from 1995 until 2002, when his employment was terminated due to a workforce reduction, not his performance. At the time of his termination, Mid-State informed him that he was eligible to be rehired. Between May and July 2005, Mr. Duckworth contacted Mid-State about re-employment but was not hired. Instead, Mid-State hired a 26-year-old applicant for a Gage Control Technician position on July 6, 2005. Mr. Duckworth alleges that this 26-year-old was significantly less qualified for the position than he was.

In April 2008, Mr. Duckworth, then 60 years old, applied to Mid-State for the advertised position of Gage Control Technician. He was interviewed for the position, but claims that Mid-State's managers treated him with hostility and incorrectly told him that his work quality from 1995 to 2002 was poor. A Mid-State manager informed him that the company was looking to hire someone who would be with the company for a long time. Mid-State did not hire Mr. Duckworth for this position and instead hired someone 34 years old, who Mr. Duckworth contends was less qualified than him.

Plaintiff alleges that Mid-State's decision not to hire him in 2005 and 2008 was motivated by age discrimination. Defendant contends that Mr. Duckworth never actually applied for the Gage Control Technician position in 2005 and that there was no open position for a Gage Control Technician in 2005 since Mid-State only posted the position internally. Mid-State also claims that even if Mr. Duckworth made out a prima facie case, he failed to prove that age was the "but-for" cause of Mid-State's decision not to hire him in 2005 and 2008. Mr. Duckworth responds that he has sustained his burden to make out a prima facie case of age discrimination in 2008 and that Mid-State's explanations for its decision are pretexts.

In 1991, agents of the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) began investigating Richard Clark Gardner in connection with his activities as a tax preparer. On March 11, 1997, a grand jury returned an indictment charging Mr. Gardner with eighteen counts of assisting in the preparation of false and fraudulent tax returns, three counts of fraudulently concealing an asset during a bankruptcy proceeding, and two counts of bankruptcy fraud. A superseding indictment was returned on May 8, 1997, which realleged the eighteen tax fraud counts and alleged three violations of 18 U.S.C. § 152. 

Plaintiff alleges that the IRS investigation and subsequent indictment were vexatious, frivolous, or in bad faith. Defendant, the United States, contends that its position was substantially justified. The Government moved to dismiss without prejudice several counts of the superseding indictment, and on January 5, 1998, moved to dismiss the remaining counts without prejudice, except for counts 1-3, which were dismissed with prejudice. Mr. Gardner argues that the dismissal of the counts should have been with prejudice. Prior to the dismissal, the Court addressed the Government's proposal regarding its expert witness and denied the request, ordering the Government to produce an expert report. However, the Government did not produce the report and instead decided to dismiss the charges against Mr. Gardner.

The parties' relationship is that of a defendant (Mr. Gardner) and the United States Government, which prosecuted him. The nature of the dispute is Mr. Gardner's claim for attorneys' fees and expenses under the Hyde Amendment, which allows for such awards in criminal cases where the court finds that the position of the United States was vexatious, frivolous, or in bad faith. Mr. Gardner seeks $108,332.91 in fees and expenses, contending that he has satisfied all requirements of the Hyde Amendment. The Government's position is that its actions were substantially justified, and Mr. Gardner is not entitled to the requested fees and expenses. Relevant pre-litigation events include the IRS investigation, the grand jury indictments, and the pretrial hearings and motions.

Jill Mehrberg worked as the Managing Director, Performance Management in the Office of Accountability at the Illinois Department of Commerce & Economic Opportunity (the Department) until her termination on April 8, 2016. She had joined the Department in May 2009 as Deputy Director of the Bureau of Technology and Industrial Competitiveness and moved to her final position in September 2011. Plaintiff alleges that she met the Department's legitimate performance expectations at all times relevant to her claims. 

Plaintiff alleges that her treatment and recovery from breast cancer left her with disabilities as defined by the Americans with Disabilities Act, and that the Department never fulfilled her reasonable requests for accommodation in light of those disabilities. She also claims that the Department intentionally micro-managed her movements, including monitoring her comings and goings, breaks, bathroom breaks, meal times, and authorized medical appointments, and that none of her similarly-situated peers or other Department employees who do not suffer from disabilities were subject to this treatment or monitoring. Plaintiff further alleges that the Department harassed her for making requests for reasonable accommodations by pejoratively referring to her as an "entitled" and "privileged" employee.

Plaintiff contends that starting in January 2016, the Department began taking away her job duties because of her disabilities, requests for accommodations, and age in an attempt to get her to quit, and in retaliation for exercising her legal rights. In March 2016, Plaintiff complained again about the Department's failure to reasonably accommodate her, and on April 8, 2016, the Department fired her. The Department contends that Plaintiff did not file her complaint against it within the applicable statute of limitations. Plaintiff filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), which mailed her a right to sue letter on February 20, 2018, naming the Department as the respondent. The Department received a copy of the letter. Plaintiff initiated this lawsuit on March 21, 2018, initially naming the State of Illinois as the defendant, but later amended her complaint to name the Department as the defendant on January 13, 2019. The Department argues that Plaintiff's claims against it are barred as untimely, while Plaintiff argues that her amended complaint "relates back" to her initial complaint under Rule 15(c).

Between 2008 and 2014, Plaintiff R.C.C. alleges she was trafficked for sex at the Phoenix Red Roof Inn (RRI) in Phoenix, Arizona, a branded property of Red Roof Inns, Inc., and Red Roof Franchising, LLC (collectively referred to as "Red Roof" or "Defendants"). Plaintiff alleges that her trafficker and customers rented rooms at the Phoenix RRI, where she was harbored and maintained for the purpose of sex trafficking, and that Defendants profited from each of these room rentals, as well as from Wi-Fi data collected from the rooms. Plaintiff contends that Red Roof failed to create, adopt, implement, and enforce company-wide policies and procedures regarding human trafficking at their branded properties, prioritizing profits over costs.

Plaintiff alleges that hotel staff at the Phoenix RRI interacted with her repeatedly and would have been aware of her deteriorating condition, including visible bruises. According to R.C.C., her stays at the Phoenix RRI raised several consistent red flags, including paying for stays in cash, requesting rooms away from other guests, and having large numbers of male visitors. Plaintiff also alleges that her trafficker used the hotel's Wi-Fi to post advertisements for the sale of her body and communicate with customers. Defendants, on the other hand, have not explicitly stated their version of events in the provided text, but their filing of a Motion to Dismiss in June 2023 suggests that they dispute Plaintiff's allegations.

The parties' relationship is that of a business and its customer, with Plaintiff alleging that Defendants benefited financially from her exploitation. The nature of the dispute is centered on whether Red Roof knowingly or should have known that their business was being used to facilitate human trafficking, and whether they took adequate steps to prevent or report such activities. Relevant pre-litigation events include the alleged trafficking activities at the Phoenix RRI, the hotel staff's interactions with Plaintiff, and the use of the hotel's Wi-Fi for illicit purposes. The lawsuit was commenced by Plaintiff in October 2022, with Defendants responding with a Motion to Dismiss in June 2023.

Betty Kulinski, the plaintiff, worked at Yates Dial-A-Ride, the defendant. Plaintiff alleges that she experienced employment discrimination and retaliation at the hands of the defendant. Defendant contends that it did not discriminate against or retaliate against the plaintiff. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is an employment discrimination and retaliation claim. 

Plaintiff alleges that she filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and received a right-to-sue notice, which included deadline requirements. Plaintiff contends that she did not know that the original charge was filed too late and that she relied on her attorney to keep track of dates and deadlines. Defendant contends that plaintiff received the EEOC right-to-sue notices, which included the deadline requirements, and that she cannot claim ignorance of the applicable deadline. 

Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff had communications with an attorney in Washington, D.C., who purportedly was working with her on this case. However, the documentation submitted by plaintiff fails to establish circumstances that warrant equitable tolling. Plaintiff submitted 81 pages of new evidence in support of her objection, including online communications with the attorney and a Retainer Agreement that limited the attorney's representation to mediation, which ultimately never occurred. Plaintiff filed her case pro se and does not provide evidence that she attempted to inform herself of the process to file the claim once she received the EEOC notice. The timeline in plaintiff's objection outlines that from June 23rd to December 20th, 2018, all plaintiff did was forward the notices to her attorney and request a copy of her file through the Freedom of Information Act.

Plaintiffs, including the Vulcan Society of Westchester County, challenged the job requirements for firefighters in four municipalities in Westchester County: Mount Vernon, New Rochelle, White Plains, and Yonkers. They alleged that the recruiting practices and policies, as well as the written tests for firefighter positions, discriminated against black individuals. The plaintiffs sought changes to these practices and policies to increase the number of black firefighters in these municipalities. 

The defendants, including the municipalities and the State of New York, contended that their practices and policies were not discriminatory and that they had made good-faith efforts to recruit and hire black firefighters. They also argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing to bring the lawsuit and that the court lacked jurisdiction over the case. The State of New York further argued that it was immune from liability under the eleventh amendment of the Constitution. 

Prior to the lawsuit, the plaintiffs had attempted to address these issues through other means, including filing complaints with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). The United States government also filed a separate lawsuit against the same defendants, alleging discrimination against blacks, Hispanics, and women. The parties engaged in settlement negotiations, which were complex and difficult due to the involvement of local, state, and federal policies and laws, as well as collective bargaining agreements. The negotiations ultimately led to changes in the written tests, physical agility tests, recruitment and training practices, and the establishment of hiring and promotional goals. The plaintiffs also sought damages for some named plaintiffs and unnamed class members. 

The plaintiffs' attorneys spent a total of 3,288.25 hours working on the case, with hourly rates ranging from $80 to $110 per hour. The defendants opposed the plaintiffs' motion for attorneys' fees, arguing that the fees were excessive and that the plaintiffs had not achieved significant benefits for the class they represented. The defendants also argued that they had made good-faith efforts to settle the case and that the plaintiffs had obstructed these efforts. The plaintiffs countered that they had achieved substantial benefits for the class and that the defendants' opposition to the fee motion was frivolous and excessive.

Plaintiff began working for Assurant in 2004 and was promoted to senior quality control specialist around January 2019, while working on manager Brandi Howard's team. On July 25, 2019, Plaintiff had a telephone call with Howard about attending training on the following Saturday, during which Howard allegedly spoke to Plaintiff in a disrespectful manner. Plaintiff reported this incident to Brian Kovach, David Susag, and Christine Bieller, and subsequently met with Kovach on August 8, 2019, to discuss the alleged retaliation and harassment by Howard. 

Plaintiff alleges that after reporting the incident, she was subjected to retaliation, including being assigned additional tasks inconsistent with her job description, which she believes was pretext for discrimination based on her race. Plaintiff filed a Charge of Discrimination with the EEOC on November 22, 2019, alleging retaliation, but did not check the "continuing violation" box. The EEOC dismissed the charge, finding that the facts alleged failed to state a claim under any of the statutes enforced by the EEOC. 

Plaintiff filed a second EEOC charge on March 19, 2020, alleging race-based discrimination and retaliation, stating that her duties had increased substantially and she had been assigned tasks inconsistent with her job description since filing the first charge. Defendant contends that the assignments were part of workflow development and not based on race. The EEOC dismissed the second charge as well, finding insufficient evidence to show a nexus between the previous complaint and the assignment of additional job duties, or that any employee was treated more favorably based on race. Plaintiff sent a formal written complaint to Defendant's executives in June 2020, detailing her concerns of discrimination and retaliation, which was investigated by the then-VP of Employee Relations, Georgie Cummins. Defendant contends that Plaintiff's allegations are unfounded and that the company took appropriate actions to address her concerns.

Edwin J. Krystof, Sr. ("Krystof") was hired by Hyatt Corporation ("Hyatt") in February 1969 as a Night Auditor and Night Manager at the Hyatt Lincolnwood. Over the years, Krystof held various positions, including Night Manager at the Hyatt Regency Chicago and General Cashier at the same hotel. As General Cashier, Krystof was responsible for handling accounting procedures, operating the hotel's vaults, and managing cash transactions. Krystof's supervisors during his tenure included Controller Bob McCall and Assistant Controllers Pam Seiter and Bikas Pandy. 

Krystof received satisfactory evaluations for production, but also received criticisms concerning his accuracy and management skills. He was cautioned about the importance of maintaining 100% accuracy in bank audits and following established procedures to control funds. Despite these warnings, Krystof continued to experience performance issues, including a written warning in March 1987 for failure to comply with house bank audit guidelines. In the fall of 1989, James Barnish replaced McCall as Controller, and Krystof's performance issues persisted. In May 1990, Krystof was cited for failure to count the vault for three days, and in September 1990, he was cited for failure to follow procedures for issuing a loan to a cashier. 

In May 1991, Krystof was relieved of his responsibility for auditing house banks, and in July 1991, he was placed on 60 days' probation due to his failure to complete all deposits by month-end. After completing his probation, Krystof continued working until he was discharged on October 16, 1991, as part of Hyatt's reduction-in-force (RIF). Krystof was 65 years old at the time of his termination. His position was consolidated with that of Faneeza Shaw, who was 47 years old and became the new General Cashier/Food and Beverage Cashier Supervisor. Krystof alleges that he was discharged due to age discrimination, while Hyatt contends that the RIF was economically motivated and that Shaw was chosen for the consolidated position because she was better qualified. Krystof filed a charge of age discrimination with the Illinois Department of Human Rights and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in April 1992, and subsequently filed a complaint under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) in June 1992.

Melinda Markovich, the plaintiff, was an employee of Union Railroad Company, LLC, the defendant. The nature of their relationship is that of employer and employee. The dispute between them concerns allegations of discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that she was treated unfairly and disciplined by Union Railroad Company, while a younger, male employee, Gary Manges, was treated more favorably despite similar circumstances. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Mr. Manges lied to management at the direction of his supervisor but was not disciplined, whereas she was disciplined for similar actions. 

Plaintiff contends that she was treated differently than a similarly situated male and younger employee, which forms the basis of her Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA), Title VII, and Pennsylvania Human Relations Act (PHRA) discrimination claims. Defendant Union Railroad Company argues that the addition of a comparator employee, in this case, Gary Manges, does not satisfy Plaintiff's pleading requirements for her discrimination claims. 

The events leading to the lawsuit involve Plaintiff's employment with Union Railroad Company and the alleged discriminatory actions taken against her. The parties have engaged in pre-litigation activities, including the filing of a Second Amended Complaint by Plaintiff, which contains allegations regarding her comparator employee, Gary Manges. Defendant has moved to dismiss the complaint, arguing that it lacks sufficient factual detail to support Plaintiff's discrimination claims. The parties have also exchanged written objections and responses regarding the Report and Recommendation issued by Magistrate Judge Patricia Dodge, which recommended denying Defendant's Motion to Dismiss.

Dollar General, a national discount retailer, operates a distribution center in Bessemer, Alabama, where it hires general warehouse workers. To hire these workers, Dollar General uses a multi-step process that includes an online application, interviews with the HR department and a warehouse supervisor, and a contingent job offer based on a pre-employment background check, physical examination, and drug test. The physical examination and drug test are conducted by Middle Creek Medical Center, an urgent care center that has been providing pre-employment medical services for Dollar General since 2012.

As part of the physical examination, job candidates must complete a "Physical Encounter Questionnaire" designed by Dollar General, which includes questions about their medical history. Until August 22, 2014, the questionnaire asked about the candidate's family medical history, including whether their grandparents, parents, or children had significant medical problems. Middle Creek staff would also ask follow-up questions about the candidate's family medical history if they indicated that their relatives had significant medical problems. The results of the physical examination, including the candidate's medical history and family medical history, were then provided to Dollar General.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and Vincent Jackson, an unsuccessful job applicant, contend that Dollar General's use of the post-offer medical examination and the collection of family medical history information violated the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA). The EEOC and Jackson allege that Dollar General used the results of the medical examinations to screen out qualified individuals with disabilities, and that the collection of family medical history information was not job-related or consistent with business necessity. Dollar General contends that it did not violate the ADA or GINA, and that the medical examination and collection of family medical history information were necessary to ensure that job candidates were qualified for the position. The parties dispute whether Dollar General or Middle Creek set the requirements for the physical examination, including the benchmarks for vision and blood pressure.

Constance Guice-Mills was a nurse at the Montrose, New York, hospital of the United States Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) until she retired on disability in April or May 1986. Plaintiff alleges that the VA discriminated against her based on race, color, gender, handicap, and age, and also retaliated against her for prior complaints. Specifically, she claims that the chief personnel officer for the Montrose hospital stated on or about June 1, 1992, that he would not rehire her because she would file another Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint. Plaintiff alleges that she learned of this statement in early December 1992 while reviewing her occupational counselor's file. 

Plaintiff filed an administrative complaint of discrimination with the VA on or about December 21, 1992, which alleged that the most recent discriminatory event occurred on June 1, 1992. However, she did not contact an EEO counselor until March 4, 1993. The VA contends that plaintiff failed to exhaust her administrative remedies in a timely manner, as required by law. Plaintiff had previously filed at least three other Title VII actions against the VA, including Guice-Mills v. McGeowan, Guice-Mills v. Ferguson, and Guice-Mills v. Derwinski, which suggests that she was familiar with the EEO requirements and procedures.

Plaintiff alleges that the VA's failure to hire her, termination of her employment, failure to promote her, and reprisal were all discriminatory actions. The VA's chief personnel officer's statement on June 1, 1992, is the basis for her retaliation claim.
