Plaintiff's administrative complaint also states that she had not discussed her complaint with an EEO counselor prior to filing the complaint. The VA's response to plaintiff's allegations is that she failed to invoke and exhaust her administrative remedies in a timely fashion, which is a required step before filing a lawsuit.

Navdeep Singh, an inmate at Fishkill Correctional Facility, professes a belief in the Sikh faith and has made numerous requests related to the practice of his religion since his arrival at the facility. These requests include possession of certain religious articles, treatment of his religious articles, wearing religious garbs, grooming standards, dietary considerations, and accommodations regarding prayer. The New York State Department of Correctional Services (DOCS) designated Captain Arlin Pele to address many of Singh's requests due to the relatively small number of Sikh inmates housed by DOCS. While some of Singh's requests have been accommodated, he currently seeks additional accommodations.

Plaintiff alleges that he has been denied certain rights, including the right to wear a Kacchera (a religious undergarment) at all times, to possess more than three Kaccheras, to wash and dry Kaccheras and turbans in his cell, to be present when his religious articles and books are searched or touched, and to shower three hours before dawn. Defendant contends that Singh has not formally exhausted administrative requirements with respect to these claims. Singh argues that his failure to exhaust administrative remedies is justified because defendants' actions precluded him from using administrative grievance procedures. However, defendants claim that Singh was advised to resolve his complaints through channels available to him other than the formal grievance system and that he was not prevented from filing a formal grievance.

Singh claims to have filed grievances on certain issues, including his right to use a reading lamp at night for prayer purposes, his right to remain in continuous contact with his religious articles, and his right to work assignments that do not violate his religious beliefs. However, defendants argue that Singh has not exhausted his administrative remedies with respect to these claims. Specifically, defendants contend that Singh's grievance regarding the use of a reading lamp was actually a complaint about harassment, and that he did not appeal the decision of the Superintendent regarding his request to remain in contact with his religious articles. Additionally, defendants claim that Singh did not file a grievance on the issue of work assignments that violate his religious beliefs, but rather was disciplined for refusing to perform a work assignment that conflicted with his religious convictions.

Kleinfelter, the plaintiff, was an employee of the United States Postal Service, the defendant. Plaintiff alleges that she was paid unequally compared to her male colleagues for performing the same work. Defendant contends that the pay difference was due to legitimate factors. The dispute between the parties centers around the issue of equal pay for equal work, with Kleinfelter claiming that she was not paid fairly and the Postal Service arguing that the pay difference was justified.

Plaintiff alleges that she worked the same hours and performed the same job duties as her male colleagues, but was paid less. Defendant contends that the male employees had different job titles, responsibilities, or levels of experience, which justified the pay difference. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the Postal Service being Kleinfelter's employer. The nature of the dispute is a claim of unequal pay under the Equal Pay Act (EPA). 

Prior to filing the lawsuit, Kleinfelter was employed by the Postal Service, and the events giving rise to the lawsuit occurred during her employment. The lawsuit was filed in May 2020, and during the discovery process, Kleinfelter stipulated that her complaint only included a claim under the EPA. Relevant documents and communications include Kleinfelter's deposition testimony and the complaint filed in the lawsuit. The workplace facts relevant to the dispute include the job duties, hours worked, and pay received by Kleinfelter and her male colleagues.

Inova, a healthcare provider, implemented an Influenza and COVID-19 Vaccination Policy (IPP) requiring its employees to receive COVID-19 vaccinations. Plaintiffs, Ellison and Graham, who are employees of Inova, objected to the COVID-19 vaccine due to their religious beliefs, specifically their objections to abortion, as they claim the available vaccines are connected to abortion. Ellison alleges that he has a sincere religious objection to the vaccine based on his religious objections to abortion. Graham contends that her religious beliefs also prohibit her from receiving the vaccine due to its connection to abortion. 

Inova refused to grant exemptions to the IPP for Ellison and Graham, leading to a dispute between the parties. Plaintiffs claim that Inova's refusal to accommodate their religious objections constitutes unlawful religious discrimination under Title VII. Inova, on the other hand, contends that it cannot reasonably accommodate the plaintiffs' religious needs without undue hardship. The parties engaged in pre-litigation communications, and Inova received notice of the plaintiffs' religious objections to the vaccine. 

The plaintiffs provided Inova with information about their religious beliefs and their objections to the vaccine, which they claim conflict with Inova's vaccine requirement. Inova, however, maintains that it has a legitimate interest in requiring its employees to be vaccinated against COVID-19. The parties' dispute ultimately led to the filing of a class action complaint, with the plaintiffs seeking relief for Inova's alleged failure to accommodate their religious practices. The case proceeded to discovery, with the plaintiffs and Inova exchanging information and evidence related to their claims.

Desius and Harris, two female employees, were hired to work at a restaurant in 2021, with Desius as a server and Harris as a cashier. At the time, Himes was the general manager of the restaurant, and Wright was the shift manager of the kitchen. Plaintiff alleges that Wright sexually harassed them on a regular basis, making vulgar sexual comments, physically touching them, and drawing sexually explicit pictures of them and other female employees. Plaintiffs allege that they repeatedly told Wright to stop such behavior, but he did not do so. They also complained about Wright to Himes, but claim that Himes did not take any action to stop the behavior.

Plaintiff alleges that on or about September 18, 2021, Himes interviewed Desius, Harris, and two female coworkers concerning their complaints about Wright, but instead of disciplining Wright, Himes accused the employees of lying. The next day, the Company's district manager, James Farrance, told plaintiffs that they could not retain a lawyer without notifying him. Plaintiffs allege that after they complained to Himes, defendants began retaliating against them. Desius's schedule was changed, resulting in her working fewer hours and losing income, which led to her resignation in October 2021. Harris alleges that Himes scheduled her to work on days she was unavailable, in retaliation for her complaints about Wright, and that she also resigned due to Wright's "menacing presence" and her "retaliatory schedule".

Defendant Wright's employment was terminated in October 2021, but the circumstances of his termination are unclear. Plaintiffs allege that even after his termination, Wright would still come to the restaurant and "hang out". The parties' relationship is that of employer and employees, with Himes and Wright in supervisory roles, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of sexual harassment and retaliation. Plaintiff alleges that the defendants created and maintained a hostile work environment, while Defendant's contentions are not explicitly stated, but it can be inferred that they may dispute the allegations of harassment and retaliation. Relevant pre-litigation events include the complaints made by plaintiffs to Himes, the interview with Himes, and the change in Desius's schedule.

Professor Janay Garrick was employed as an instructor of secular courses at Moody Bible Institute, a post-secondary Christian educational institution. Moody adheres to a "complementarian" doctrine that forbids women from acting as religious leaders, while Professor Garrick subscribes to "egalitarian Christian" beliefs regarding gender equality in the ministry. Plaintiff alleges that she suffered pervasive sex discrimination during her employment and that Moody ultimately fired her because of her sex, but under the guise that she was "not aligned with Moody's doctrinal statement as it related to gender roles in ministry." Defendant Moody contends that Professor Garrick's claims are barred because she qualified as a "minister" within the meaning of the ministerial exception under Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church and School v. EEOC.

Professor Garrick initially filed a complaint alleging retaliatory discharge and breach of contract under Illinois law, and retaliation under Title IX. Moody moved to dismiss, prompting Professor Garrick to amend her complaint to assert claims for sex discrimination, retaliation, and religious discrimination under Title VII, and hostile work environment under both Titles VII and IX. Moody again moved to dismiss, arguing that principles of "church autonomy" precluded these claims. The court rejected Moody's ministerial exception argument, pointing out that the exception was an affirmative defense and that the facts Moody relied upon came from Moody's submissions, not the complaint.

Prior to the lawsuit, Professor Garrick worked at Moody, where she experienced antagonistic treatment by male colleagues and preferential treatment of male faculty members with respect to job duties and performance. Moody's employment decision-making process and the circumstances surrounding Professor Garrick's termination are disputed. Moody provided a reason for Professor Garrick's termination, stating that she was "not aligned with Moody's doctrinal statement as it related to gender roles in ministry." Professor Garrick disputes this reason, alleging that it was a pretext for gender discrimination. The parties' pre-litigation communications and any relevant employment or workplace documents are not detailed in the provided text, but it is clear that the parties had disagreements regarding Moody's religious views and Professor Garrick's role at the institution.

Kathryn M. Smith was hired as the director of catering at the Capitol City Club of Montgomery in August 1991, after being contacted by the club's manager, Timothy Shepardson, and taking a test for the position. In November 1991, Smith informed the defendants that she was pregnant. Plaintiff alleges that after learning of her pregnancy, Shepardson subjected her to discriminatory terms and conditions of employment, including harsh treatment and offensive remarks about her pregnancy. Despite her satisfactory work performance, Smith was terminated on January 7, 1992. Defendant Shepardson contends that he cannot be held individually liable under Title VII. 

Prior to her termination, Smith had been working at the club, and her employment was managed by Shepardson. The club is owned by Club Corporation of America, and Shepardson is the manager of the Capitol City Club. Smith claims that she suffered physical pain, a miscarriage, emotional anguish, and loss of reputation due to the defendants' discriminatory employment actions. 

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Shepardson being Smith's supervisor at the Capitol City Club. The nature of the dispute is a claim of employment discrimination, specifically pregnancy discrimination, under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Smith alleges that the defendants discriminated against her in the terms and conditions of her employment and in discharging her without good cause because she became pregnant. Defendant Shepardson argues that individual capacity suits under Title VII are inappropriate, relying on the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals' opinion in Busby v. City of Orlando. 

Relevant pre-litigation events include Smith's hiring, her notification to the defendants of her pregnancy, and her subsequent termination. There were also communications between Smith and Shepardson regarding her employment and her pregnancy. The employment and workplace facts relevant to the case include Smith's job duties, her work performance, and the actions taken by Shepardson and the other defendants in response to her pregnancy.

Dawud Habib Taylor El, the plaintiff, was employed by the Regional Transportation District (RTD). Plaintiff alleges that he was subjected to certain actions by his coworkers and supervisors, including Will Adams and Amerie Gagliardi, which led to his filing of this lawsuit. The nature of the dispute involves claims under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Plaintiff contends that he was treated unfairly and suffered harm as a result of the actions of the individual defendants, who were his colleagues at RTD. 

Defendants Will Adams and Amerie Gagliardi, who are individual employees of RTD, contend that they cannot be held liable under Title VII, as the statute does not impose individual liability on non-employer employees. RTD, as the employer, is also a defendant in the case. The events giving rise to the lawsuit occurred while plaintiff was working at RTD, although the specific details of what happened are not specified. 

Prior to the lawsuit, it is unclear what, if any, internal actions or complaints were made by the plaintiff to RTD regarding the alleged treatment. The lawsuit was filed by the plaintiff, who is proceeding without an attorney, against RTD and the individual defendants, including Will Adams and Amerie Gagliardi. The individual defendants filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that they cannot be held liable under Title VII. The motion to dismiss was considered by the magistrate judge, who issued a recommendation that it be granted.

Mack, an employee at the Chicago Department of Aviation (CDA), alleges that her supervisor, Robert May, made disparaging remarks about her age and singled her out due to her age. Plaintiff alleges that she obtained statements from several witnesses, including Denise Arnold, Madeline Orok, William H. Cruse, Sr., Robert M. Kelly, Jr., James Rufus, Priscilla Crowder, and Marilyn Bracy, which support her claims of age discrimination. Defendants contend that Mack failed to produce these statements during the discovery period, despite their written discovery requests asking for such information. 

Defendants served Mack with an interrogatory asking her to identify any statements related to her allegations or employment with the City, and a request to produce documents concerning communication between her and any City employee related to her allegations or employment. Mack does not contend that she complied with her obligation to supplement her written discovery responses, but instead argues that her production of the statements was timely under a different rule. Defendants assert that they were prejudiced by Mack's late disclosure of the witness statements, which prevented them from examining the witnesses, gathering additional evidence, or becoming aware of a potentially material fact dispute before they moved for summary judgment.

Mack was represented by counsel until after discovery closed and Defendants moved for summary judgment. During discovery, Mack did not identify Orok, Rufus, or Bracy in her Rule 26(a)(1) disclosures, and although she identified Arnold, Cruse, Kelly, and Crowder, she did not indicate that they had knowledge of May's alleged age discrimination against her. Mack obtained all but Cruse's statement before discovery closed on June 13, 2018, and Cruse prepared his statement more than two weeks before Defendants moved for summary judgment. Mack produced the witness statements, along with her summary judgment opposition papers, which Defendants contend was a violation of her obligation to supplement her written discovery responses.

Catherine Johnson was a teacher for School District 158. In February 2017, her immediate supervisor was Jessica Lombard. On several occasions, Mrs. Lombard informed Adam Zehr, the Assistant Superintendent for Human Resources, that Johnson was sending her text messages about Mrs. Lombard and her family that Mrs. Lombard found inappropriate. On February 10, 2017, Johnson allegedly sent Mrs. Lombard additional "inappropriate" messages, which Mrs. Lombard showed to Mr. Zehr. That same day, Mr. Zehr emailed Johnson, instructing her to come to a meeting at his office, but Johnson did not attend, instead emailing Mr. Zehr that she was at the police station filing a report about an incident at an employee's house.

Johnson alleged that while at Mrs. Lombard's home in November 2016, she was drugged and sexually assaulted by Mrs. Lombard's husband. The police were unable to make a report due to Johnson's apparent mental state. Defendant commenced an investigation, which included a review of Johnson's employee file and a formal interview with her on February 15, 2017. On February 16, 2017, Defendant's superintendent informed Johnson that she was being placed on paid administrative leave while the investigation was conducted. Johnson retained the Patterson Law Firm to represent her regarding Defendant's treatment of her allegations and the decision to place her on administrative leave.

In June 2017, Johnson filed a Charge of Discrimination with the EEOC against Defendant. From August 24, 2017, to September 6, 2017, the parties negotiated a settlement agreement via email, which culminated in a "Separation Agreement." Defendant contends that Johnson signed the Separation Agreement on September 6, 2017, and that she agreed to withdraw the 2017 Charge and voluntarily resign with an effective date on the earlier of obtaining alternative employment or December 31, 2017. In consideration, Johnson was required to release the Board, its board members, employees, and agents from claims she had or might have had against them arising under the ADA, Title VII, the Rehabilitation Act, and other specified state and federal laws.

Johnson disputes the series of events, asserting that she did not execute the Separation Agreement and that she remains employed by School District 158 and is on disability. She relies on appendices to support her position, including the unsigned and undated Separation Agreement, an affidavit stating that she did not meet with Defendant's counsel or board president regarding a Separation Agreement, and a letter from Defendant's superintendent informing her that she was being placed on administrative leave. Communications between Johnson, Defendant, and other school officials stalled after December 31, 2017. On January 27, 2021, Johnson emailed Scott Iddings, stating that she had been "raped by several colleagues in November of 2016" and that she had been "illegally fired for reporting." Defendant responded, explaining that Johnson had entered into a Separation Agreement and had not been illegally fired. On April 13, 2021, Johnson filed her second Charge with the EEOC against Defendant, alleging that she was discharged after filing her first EEOC Charge and that she had been discriminated against based on her disability. The next month, Johnson filed this lawsuit against Defendant, alleging that her employment was terminated after she filed a Charge with the EEOC and that she was discriminated against based on her disability.

Jennifer Champagne, the plaintiff, worked for the defendant, where she was allegedly subjected to sexual harassment by her supervisor, Dr. John Stanko, a dentist. Plaintiff alleges that Dr. Stanko threw items and raised his voice in a profane manner, referred to her as his "hot assistant" and "daytime wife," massaged her shoulders several times, grabbed her hand during a dental procedure, and thrust a drill into her hand during another procedure. These incidents allegedly occurred during her employment, which ended on March 27, 2017. Plaintiff contends that she complained to the district manager, Ochrim, about Dr. Stanko's behavior, but Ochrim did not address or attempt to remedy the issue. Instead, Ochrim told Plaintiff that if she did not work with Dr. Stanko, she would not have a job. Plaintiff also mentioned to other employees that Dr. Stanko's conduct caused her anxiety to be "through the roof."

Defendant contends that even if all the alleged incidents are considered, they do not constitute sexual harassment as a matter of law. Defendant also argues that the alleged incidents of harassment that occurred before March 24, 2017, should not be considered because Plaintiff did not file her complaint with the applicable governmental entity within 300 days of those incidents. Defendant further argues that it did not constructively discharge Plaintiff, as a reasonable person in Plaintiff's position would not have perceived the working conditions to be so intolerable as to compel separation.

Plaintiff filed her initial complaint on November 17, 2018, and an amended complaint on November 21, 2018, alleging sexual harassment. Defendant filed a motion to dismiss, which was denied. Plaintiff then filed a complaint with the CHRO/EEOC on January 2, 2018, which Defendant argues was outside the 300-day time limit for filing such a complaint. Relevant pre-litigation events include Plaintiff's complaints to Ochrim and her conversations with other employees about Dr. Stanko's behavior. Employment facts include Plaintiff's role as an assistant to Dr. Stanko and her eventual departure from the defendant's employ on March 27, 2017.

Plaintiff Bikram Sharma was a member of the Sacramento Independent Taxi Owners' Association (SITOA) from 2006 until his membership was terminated in April 2018. Plaintiff alleges that his membership was wrongfully terminated because of his religion, as all the defendants are Muslim and he is a strict Hindu. Defendants are the board members of SITOA, including Asif Mehmood, Farhad Muhaiudin, Mohammad Hawarneh, Mushtq A. King, and Zahid Khan. 

Plaintiff alleges that he worked as a taxi driver providing services to the Sacramento International Airport as a member of SITOA, and that his termination was in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Plaintiff contends that the reasons given for his termination, including his alleged failure to abide by the association's rules and offering assistance to a competing taxi company, were pretextual and that the real reason was his religion. Defendants respond that plaintiff's complaint asserts a federal claim and removal to federal court was proper. 

Defendants contend that plaintiff was not an employee of SITOA, but rather an independent business owner who was a member of the association, and that they did not have control over the manner in which plaintiff owned and operated his taxi business. Defendants also argue that they are not a covered entity subject to liability under Title VII, as they are individuals and not an employment agency or labor organization. Plaintiff, on the other hand, alleges that his termination was discriminatory and that defendants' actions were motivated by his religion. The parties disagree on the nature of their relationship and the circumstances surrounding plaintiff's termination, with plaintiff claiming discrimination and defendants claiming that plaintiff was not an employee and that they are not liable under Title VII.

Larissa Hairgrove was hired by Lane Bailey, the City Manager of Salisbury, as the Downtown Development Director in 2017. Her employment began in October of that year, and she reported to Zack Kyle, the Assistant City Manager. As part of her job, she worked closely with the Downtown Salisbury Incorporated Nonprofit (DSI) board and was responsible for the day-to-day operations of DSI. 

Plaintiff alleges that her tenure at the City was marked by difficulties, including concerns about her job performance raised by Mr. Kyle and DSI Board members. She contends that she was subjected to unfair treatment, including disciplinary actions, and that she was expected to work excessively long hours, essentially performing two full-time jobs. Ms. Hairgrove also alleges that DSI Board members were dismissive and demeaning towards her, and that Mr. Kyle bullied her at times. 

Defendants contend that Ms. Hairgrove's performance was unsatisfactory, citing instances of lateness, failure to follow instructions, and unsatisfactory work quality. They also point to a February 2020 incident in which Ms. Hairgrove inadvertently left a recording device in a DSI board meeting, which captured a closed session discussion. After realizing the device still contained the recording, Ms. Hairgrove listened to it, which led to accusations of a "deliberate breach of the Board's trust" by DSI board members. The board members wrote to city officials, stating that Ms. Hairgrove's actions showed a "lack of integrity and good character" and that they did not see a "workable scenario" where the existing board could continue to work with her as Executive Director. Relevant pre-litigation events include a series of disciplinary actions and performance reviews, as well as communications between Ms. Hairgrove, Mr. Kyle, and DSI board members regarding her employment and performance.

Borden's, Inc., a New Jersey corporation, closed its Phoenix, Arizona, dairy operation on December 31, 1979, resulting in the termination of all dairy employees except for a few management personnel. Prior to the closure, on July 27, 1979, Borden's had renewed its collective bargaining agreements with two unions representing the dairy employees, which included a severance pay formula in the event of closure. The formula, added to the agreements in November 1979, excluded employees eligible for normal or early retirement, who had to have at least ten years of continuous service with Borden's and be at least fifty-five years old. Fourteen employees, including eleven named in the original complaint, were excluded from receiving severance pay due to their eligibility for retirement.

Plaintiff EEOC alleges that Borden's denial of severance pay to these employees constitutes age-based discrimination in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA). The EEOC contends that the severance pay policy either discriminates against fifty-five-year-old employees or has a disparate impact on them. Defendant Borden's argues that eligibility for retirement, not age, was the determining factor in denying severance pay and that the policy is part of a bona fide employee benefit plan exempt from the ADEA. Borden's also claims that the severance pay policy was intended to provide benefits to employees not otherwise covered by retirement plans.

The parties have stipulated to the facts, including the amounts of severance pay the eleven affected employees would have received under the severance pay formula. The EEOC seeks these amounts with interest, as well as injunctive relief to prevent Borden's from denying severance pay in similar circumstances in the future. Borden's requests that it not be required to pay interest if judgment is found against it and claims that injunctive relief is unnecessary. The evidence shows that there were no fifty-five-year-old employees who received severance pay, and Borden's has not provided evidence of business necessity for the severance pay policy. The EEOC argues that the affected employees were adversely affected by the policy, as they were forced to give up a newly created benefit (severance pay) in exchange for benefits they already had (retirement benefits).

The Plaintiffs, Harding, Goff, and Williams, were employees of the United States Postal Service. They filed compensation claims for injuries allegedly received on the job, but the Postal Service employed a presumption of fraud when processing these claims. Plaintiff alleges that this presumption denied them their Fifth Amendment right to due process. The Plaintiffs had two different grievance systems available to them: one under 5 U.S.C. § 7501, et seq. (the merit system), and another under their union's collective bargaining agreement with the Postal Service, which provided a five-step procedure for resolving disputes. 

Plaintiff Harding and Goff proceeded to final arbitration, while Plaintiff Williams went to step 2 of the arbitration process but then apparently abandoned his claim. The Defendants contend that Williams was dismissed for cause because he could no longer perform his duties as a mail handler and had not worked for the Postal Service for at least five years, which meant he had no right to be assigned to lighter duty. The Plaintiffs argue that the alternative remedies available to them, including the merit system and the collective bargaining agreement processes, have been "perverted by the due process violations" of which they complain, and therefore should not be barred from bringing a constitutional tort claim.

The Plaintiffs' union was initially a party to the lawsuit, but has since been voluntarily dismissed. The Plaintiffs now proceed under a constitutional tort theory, alleging that the Postal Service's use of a presumption of fraud when processing their compensation claims denied them their Fifth Amendment right to due process. The Defendants argue that the Plaintiffs have alternative remedies available to them, including the merit system and the collective bargaining agreement processes, and that these remedies should be exhausted before a constitutional tort claim can be brought.

Nancy Shaffer was employed at National Can Corporation's Morrisville plant from March 13, 1975, until March 27, 1981, first as a secretary-receptionist and then as a billing clerk. In June 1977, Pat Dettorre was hired as the plant manager, and Shaffer alleges that he engaged in a continuing course of sexual harassment from that point until she left the company. Dettorre allegedly attempted to induce Shaffer to go out with him socially, made verbal sexual advances, and discussed the relative sizes of female employees' chests. When Shaffer refused his advances, Dettorre began to retaliate by mistreating and ignoring her, excluding her from certain luncheons and being overly friendly towards other female employees. Shaffer claims that Dettorre's conduct made it impossible for her to carry out her responsibilities, caused her severe mental anguish, and ultimately led to her resignation on March 27, 1981, which she characterizes as a constructive discharge.

Plaintiff alleges that she sent complaints to both the EEOC and the PHRC, although the exact dates are disputed. National claims that Shaffer's charge was not filed with the PHRC within the 90-day statute of limitations, while Shaffer contends that her charge was received by the PHRC on October 27, 1981, 214 days after her termination. National also argues that Shaffer's common law claims for wrongful discharge and intentional infliction of emotional distress have been supplanted by the remedies provided under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act. Shaffer contends that her claims are valid and that the PHRA does not preclude her from pursuing other remedies.

Shaffer and National have different contentions regarding the timing and filing of her complaints with the EEOC and PHRC. Shaffer alleges that she filed her complaints simultaneously with both agencies, while National claims that the filing date was November 5, 1981, 223 days after termination. The parties also disagree on the applicability of the 300-day exception for filing with the EEOC, with Shaffer arguing that she is entitled to invoke this exception and National arguing that she is not. The dispute centers on the interpretation of the relevant statutes and the timing of the filing of Shaffer's complaints.

A group of current and former sheriffs' deputies, dispatchers, and jailers with the Stone County, Missouri Sheriffs Department claim they were not paid overtime as required by the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). The plaintiffs, including Baker, Janie Beck, Jimmy Beck, Bolin, Branstetter, Carr, Doucey, Gideon, Heagerty, Heinzl, Kinser, Miller, Myers, Outhouse, Rinehart, Stuart, Stults, Thompson, Turner, and Warren, were employed by the Sheriffs Department at various times between 1988 and 1997. They allege that they worked overtime hours without receiving proper compensation.

The plaintiffs were employed in various roles, including deputy sheriffs, dispatchers, and jailers, and were paid hourly wages ranging from $6.25 to $14.42 per hour. Some plaintiffs, such as Bolin, Heagerty, Miller, and Stults, received payment for accrued compensatory time upon their termination, but claim that this payment did not fully compensate them for their overtime work. The defendants, including the Stone County Commission, current and former Commissioners Tony DeLong, Alden Hembree, and Duane Clark, County Clerk Carolyn Dean, and current and former Sheriffs Richard Hill and Lonnie Mease, are responsible for setting the budget and determining the compensation for Sheriffs Department employees.

The Stone County Commission, as the governing body of the county, is responsible for balancing the budget and ensuring that the county does not run a deficit. The Commission sets wage guidelines for Sheriffs Department employees, but the Circuit Judge has final authority to set wages. The plaintiffs contend that the defendants failed to properly compensate them for their overtime work, while the defendants argue that they followed the applicable laws and regulations in setting the budget and determining employee compensation. The plaintiffs and defendants disagree on the interpretation of the FLSA and the application of Missouri state laws governing county budgets and employee compensation.

Linda Ortega was a tenured teacher in the Chicago Public School system, teaching fifth grade at Hedges Elementary. She was terminated by the principal of that school on June 19, 2009, after being determined to no longer meet the requirements for her position. Ortega alleges that her termination was the result of intentional discrimination by the principal and her employer, the Chicago Board of Education, in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The principal and the Board are the defendants in this case. 

Ortega contends that she was removed from her teaching position without justification and that the Board failed to provide her with reasonable accommodations for her disability. The Board, on the other hand, argues that Ortega's termination was lawful and that she was provided with opportunities to find alternative employment within the school system. After her termination, Ortega was placed in the reassigned teacher's pool for one year, during which she received full pay and applied for open teaching positions. She then moved to the substitute teacher's cadre, where her pay was substantially less, and eventually found a part-time job as a professor at City Colleges of Chicago. Ortega's employment with the Board ended in 2011, and she later found a job as a human services caseworker with the State of Illinois in 2013.

Ortega alleges that she has suffered economic losses as a result of her termination and seeks compensation for back pay, lost pension benefits, and other damages. The Board contends that Ortega's entitlement to back pay should be limited due to her failure to mitigate her damages and because of a stipulation to a back pay amount agreed upon during trial. The Board also disputes Ortega's calculation of net lost wages and argues that she should not recover prejudgment interest due to her purported delay in litigating the case. Ortega, on the other hand, seeks an award of net lost wages through August 15, 2016, and pre-judgment interest, as well as lost pension benefits representing the estimated present value of her total monthly teacher's pension payments. The parties have presented evidence and arguments regarding Ortega's job history, her efforts to mitigate her damages, and the calculation of her lost wages and benefits.

Geleta was a Health Systems Administrator for the DMH Office of Policy and Planning, serving as the Project Director for the D.C. Children Inspired Now Gain Strength (DCCINGS) mental health program from approximately 2002 through March 2005. His salary was $77,965 (grade 13, step 8). In the fall of 2004, his immediate supervisor was Velva R. Taylor-Spriggs, who filed a discrimination complaint, and Geleta provided a written statement in support of her complaint in November 2004. 

Plaintiff alleges that his reassignment to a series of "non-supervisory" positions starting in March 2005 was retaliation for his statement in support of Taylor-Spriggs' EEO complaint. Defendant counters that the reassignments were due to DMH's decision to realign DCCINGS following an HHS site visit in October 2004. Geleta was initially temporarily reassigned to the Oak Hill Youth Detention Center for about thirty days, then detailed to the DMH Office of Accountability, where he reported to Deputy Director Susan Curran. His position as Health Systems Administrator was formally transferred to the DMH Office of Accountability, and he became the Residential Treatment Center Certification and Monitoring Projects Manager. 

Geleta's salary increased to $84,658 (grade 14, step 5) as of April 27, 2005, and later to $87,148 (grade 14, step 6) in March 2006. He filed a charge of discrimination based on retaliation with the EEOC on September 1, 2005, and received a Right to Sue Letter on July 24, 2006. In September 2007, DMH advised Geleta that his position was being converted to the Management Supervisory Service (MSS), and he accepted the appointment on October 1, 2007, with a salary of $95,781.76 as of October 14, 2007. Plaintiff alleges that his reassignments were retaliatory, while defendant claims they were part of a legitimate realignment of DCCINGS.

Ms. Dickerson, an African-American female approximately 72 years old, works as a customer service representative in the human resources department at New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT). She suffers from a permanent chronic respiratory condition that occasionally requires her to request temporary leave under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA). Plaintiff alleges that her supervisor, Annie Crawford, and other defendants, Staci Mongelli and Lauren Rubitz, who are members of the employment division of NJIT, did not want to work with her and retaliated against her, discriminated against her, denied her opportunities, created a hostile environment, and suppressed her positive relationships with faculty and staff.

Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to harassment and a hostile work environment by several employees, including Crawford, Mongelli, and Rubitz, from August 31, 2014, to September 20, 2018. She claims that she was denied opportunities to grow as an employee within her department by these individuals and that she complained to NJIT about these actions, but nothing was done. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that on one occasion, Crawford called her into her office and interrogated her about how she could be dancing if she had her disability, which she found harassing and uncalled for. Defendant NJIT contends that Plaintiff's amended claims should be dismissed because the Amended Complaint offers no new information and contains even fewer facts than her first pleading.

On November 23, 2018, Ms. Dickerson filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) asserting discrimination based on race, age, and disability. She also filed a complaint with the United States Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division alleging violations of the FMLA. The Department of Labor conducted an investigation and determined that Crawford had discriminated against Ms. Dickerson when she questioned her about how she could be on FMLA leave and yet dance at a retirement party. NJIT agreed to use proper recertification procedures moving forward and that if Crawford had questions about FMLA usage, she should ask for a recertification. Around the same time, Ms. Dickerson reported incidents to the Director of Labor Relations and Employment at NJIT and eventually filed a lawsuit.

Leroy Douglas, an African American man, was hired by M. Swift & Sons, Inc. ("Swift & Sons"), a gold leaf and hot stamping foil company in Hartford, Connecticut, as a machinist on December 4, 2000. Plaintiff alleges that he was hired to help maintain the company's production machinery and make replacement parts, while Defendant contends that the position also involved assisting with other maintenance tasks. The job advertisement Douglas responded to stated "MACHINIST With job shop experience," but Allen Swift, the owner and manager of Swift & Sons, claims that he explained to Douglas during interviews that the job would involve both machining and other duties, including carpentry.

Douglas alleges that he was not given machinist work, despite having approximately 10 years of experience with manual machining, and was instead assigned menial tasks such as sweeping, shingling a house, and repairing windows. He claims that Everett Overstrum, the head machinist, prevented him from doing machinist work and that another employee, Joe Profit, an African American who was close to Swift, also intimidated him and prevented him from working on machines. Douglas states that he complained to Swift multiple times about not being given machinist work, but Swift never intervened. On November 21, 2001, Douglas was laid off, along with three white female employees, with the company citing "lack of work" as the reason.

Plaintiff alleges that he was laid off because of his race, while Defendant contends that the layoff was due to a slowdown in business and that Douglas was relatively limited in the skills he could contribute to the company. After his layoff, Douglas saw an advertisement for a machinist position at Swift & Sons in January 2002 and called to ask for his job back, but was told that the company was not hiring. In April 2002, Swift & Sons hired a white male, Michael Haggerty, as a machinist. Douglas had discussed his concerns about racial discrimination with coworkers, including Ramona Petronio and Alberto, and had indirectly raised the issue with Profit, who responded in a way that Douglas interpreted as suggestive of racial bias. However, Douglas never directly raised the issue of racial discrimination with Swift or any other members of the company's management.

Michael Redick was employed by Kraft, Inc. as an engineering manager for the Kraft Dairy Group in April 1987. His supervisor was Mark Buchheim, who submitted his resignation with two weeks' notice in September 1988. After Buchheim's departure, he kept in touch with Redick and eventually offered him a job opportunity at John La-Batt, Ltd. (LaBatt) in November 1988. Redick was interested and sent his resume to Buchheim. He met with Buchheim and Neal Blackburn, LaBatt's Vice President for Engineering, on November 21, 1988, but no job offer was made at that time. Redick was later interviewed by Richard Cliff, Vice President for Human Resources of Tuscan Dairies, a LaBatt subsidiary, in early December 1988, but again, no job offer was made.

On December 10, 1988, Neal Blackburn offered Redick a position with LaBatt, and they discussed salary range and benefits. Redick did not accept the offer immediately, waiting for a written offer, which he received on December 14, 1988. He signed and dated the letter accepting employment with LaBatt, indicating a preferred starting date of January 16, 1989. Redick mailed his acceptance to LaBatt on December 17, 1988. On December 21, 1988, Redick met with Lawrence Gundrum, his supervisor, and Hugh Mazza, Vice President and Director of Human Resources for the dairy division of Kraft, at Logan Airport in Boston. Mazza and Gundrum were aware that Redick had received a job offer from another company and asked him about his plans. Redick responded that he had not accepted the offer but was planning to make a decision over the Christmas holidays. Gundrum mentioned that he and Mazza needed to make plans for the coming year and asked Redick to reveal his plans by the next day. Gundrum also commented on Redick's annual bonus under the Kraft Management Incentive Plan.

Plaintiff alleges that Gundrum told him that if he delayed his resignation until the turn of the year to secure a bonus, Gundrum would get him his bonus the next day. Defendant contends that Gundrum merely mentioned that the annual bonuses might be available the following day, but did not promise Redick that his bonus would be secure if he promptly revealed his employment plans. Redick submitted his resignation to Gundrum and Mazza on December 22, 1988, stating that he would terminate his employment with Kraft Dairy Group as of January 6, 1989. However, Gundrum and Mazza told him to leave immediately, citing the company's policy of immediately severing any employee who resigns to go to work for a competitor. Redick was not paid a bonus for 1988 under the Incentive Plan and did not receive a salary for the notice period, which prevented him from making contributions to the Kraft Section 401K Plan. The parties dispute the nature of Gundrum's comment about the annual bonus and whether a binding contract was formed. Redick claims that he was entitled to a bonus and two weeks of salary, while Kraft argues that no such contract existed and that Redick's statement about not having accepted the LaBatt offer was a misrepresentation.

Loretta Collins, a female police officer, began working at the Yonkers Police Department (YPD) in March 1985. During her rookie year, she claims to have been subjected to verbal abuse and derogatory comments from male colleagues, including being told that women did not belong on the job. Collins alleges that she was also denied assignment to the Emergency Services Unit (ESU) initially, with someone telling her that "cunts" were not wanted in that unit. However, she was eventually assigned to ESU in March 1986, where she claims to have experienced ongoing harassment, including being referred to in derogatory terms, finding a rubber chicken with female genitalia drawn on it in her truck, and being exposed to pornographic magazines and posters.

Plaintiff alleges that the harassment continued throughout her assignments, including during her time in the Inspectional Services Division of the Medical Control Unit (MCU) from 1993 to 1997. She claims that Sergeant Warren Cave, Captain Gerald Curtis, and Lieutenant Edward Barrette, among others, regularly called her and other women demeaning names. Collins also alleges that she was denied equal opportunities for training and assignments, and was given inferior tasks, such as being assigned to the Records Administration Unit, known as the "vegetable bin," during her pregnancy. Defendants deny these allegations, claiming that the derogatory statements were made in jest and that Collins herself participated in the name-calling and vulgar joking.

Collins claims that she complained about the harassment and discrimination to her superiors, including Police Commissioner Robert Olson, but her complaints were dismissed or ignored. She also alleges that she faced retaliation after filing a discrimination complaint with the United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in February 1996, including being moved to a windowless office, being denied necessary office supplies, and being ostracized by other members of the department. Defendants contend that Collins' allegations are unfounded and that she was treated fairly and equally during her time at the YPD. Collins' relationship with the defendants is that of an employee, and the nature of the dispute is her allegations of sexual harassment, discrimination, and retaliation against her employers.

The Whiting-Turner Contracting Co. (Whiting-Turner) and Express Services, Inc. (Express) entered into a contract on August 31, 2017, wherein Express agreed to provide staff for a construction project in Tennessee. The contract included a duty to defend provision, which required Express to defend Whiting-Turner in any litigation stemming from employees provided by Express. Express agreed to carefully screen its employees before placing them on the project and to ensure they provided services consistent with industry standards and complied with all applicable laws and regulations.

In 2018, Express placed employees Darren Riley, Clifford Powell, Jr., and Harold Thomas on the project. Thomas complained that Powell and Riley were bullying him and making fun of his religious beliefs. After Whiting-Turner learned of the complaints, it asked Express to remove Powell and Riley from the project, which Express did. Powell later submitted a complaint to Express alleging discrimination and retaliation on the basis of his race. Whiting-Turner conducted an internal investigation and concluded that Powell's claims were unfounded. 

The EEOC issued a Letter of Determination on August 17, 2021, indicating that there was reasonable cause to believe Whiting-Turner had violated Title VII with respect to Powell, Riley, and other African-American workers. The EEOC filed a class action lawsuit against Whiting-Turner on September 30, 2021, alleging a hostile work environment and retaliation on the basis of race. Whiting-Turner claims that Express and its employees caused or contributed to the alleged hostile work environment. Whiting-Turner alleges that Express has refused to defend it in the EEOC lawsuit despite the terms of the contract. Plaintiff alleges that Express employees, including Randy Spaulding and Nicole Boutiette, discriminated against Powell and Riley. Defendant Express contends that it reached a resolution with the EEOC during the administrative proceedings, but the nature of this resolution is not specified.

Aldon J. Anderson, a black man, was hired by Litton Systems, Inc. on January 3, 1986, as a Senior Industrial Relations Representative. Prior to joining Litton, Anderson worked as a Personnel Generalist at Sperry Univac in Salt Lake City, where he performed his job duties satisfactorily. Anderson holds a Bachelor of Science degree in human relations and was working on a master's degree in organizational communications when he was hired by Litton. His responsibilities at Litton included recruiting and placement of employees, employee relations, compensation, and affirmative action.

Plaintiff alleges that he was terminated from his position due to racial discrimination. Defendant Litton contends that Anderson was terminated because of repeated evaluations showing that he lacked initiative, organization, and writing skills, and that his job knowledge was below average. Litton claims that Anderson's work habits were unsatisfactory, and he failed to follow instructions, including hiring individuals without interviewing them and arranging for employees to start work without the supervisor's knowledge. Anderson, on the other hand, argues that he was never fully informed of his job responsibilities and was not responsible for hiring, but rather for conducting interviews and evaluating applicants. He also claims that he was given an inaccurate formula to complete a compensation survey, which led to errors.

The parties have different contentions about the circumstances surrounding Anderson's termination. Litton maintains that the decision to terminate Anderson was made by several managerial employees due to his poor performance. Anderson, however, alleges that Litton's allegations were part of a preconceived plan to discredit and racially discriminate against him. He claims that the "barrage" of negative evaluations he received was racially motivated and that another black employee was promoted to be his supervisor solely to terminate him. The parties also dispute the handling of a United Way Campaign and a compensation survey, with Litton alleging that Anderson inadequately handled these tasks and Anderson arguing that he was not given the necessary resources or support to complete them successfully.

Myra Johnson began working at Walmart as a CAP Team Associate on April 9, 2019. On July 2, 2019, Johnson reported to Walmart that a coworker, Tayvionna Blade, had threatened her, and Blade was subsequently terminated. However, Blade then attacked Johnson while she was working. After the attack, Johnson was transferred to a Salesfloor Team Associate position within Store 5244, which Johnson claims was not a voluntary transfer. Plaintiff alleges that this transfer was retaliatory. 

Johnson contends that she accumulated attendance points during her time as a Sales Floor Team Associate, but Defendant Walmart claims that she exceeded the allowed number of attendance points under the company's Attendance and Punctuality Policy. The parties dispute Johnson's termination date, with Walmart claiming it was December 3, 2019, and Johnson claiming it was December 6, 2019. Johnson filed a charge of discrimination with the EEOC on December 11, 2020, alleging age and race discrimination. Defendant Walmart asserts that Johnson's EEOC charge was untimely, as it was filed more than 180 days after her termination. Johnson argues that she is entitled to equitable tolling or equitable estoppel, claiming that Walmart did not inform her of her rights and failed to cooperate in her attempts to bring criminal charges related to the Blade incident.

Johnson alleges that her termination was the result of age and race discrimination, as well as retaliation for reporting the threat from Blade. Defendant Walmart denies these allegations, citing Johnson's attendance record and the company's policies. The parties also dispute the circumstances surrounding Johnson's transfer and termination, with Johnson claiming that she was treated unfairly and Walmart asserting that its actions were lawful and justified. Johnson's EEOC charge did not include a claim of retaliation, which she now argues is part of her claims for age and race discrimination. Walmart contends that Johnson's failure to include retaliation in her initial charge precludes her from advancing on this claim.

On June 25, 1996, a bombing occurred at the Khobar Towers in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, killing 19 U.S. Air Force personnel, including Airman Rimkus, and injuring many others. Plaintiff Joseph J. Rimkus, the father of Airman Rimkus, alleges that the bombing was planned, funded, and sponsored by senior leadership in the government of the Islamic Republic of Iran, with the IRGC and MOIS participating in the planning and funding of the attack. 

Plaintiff alleges that Iran and other defendants provided material support and resources that caused and facilitated the terrorist bombing, which was an extrajudicial killing within the meaning of 28 U.S.C. § 1605A. Plaintiff contends that he suffered injuries as a direct and proximate result of the defendants' conduct. Defendant Iran, MOIS, and IRGC have not responded to the allegations. Prior to this lawsuit, there were other related cases, including Blais v. Islamic Republic of Iran and Heiser v. Islamic Republic of Iran, in which the court heard extensive evidence concerning the Khobar Towers bombing, including testimony from Louis Freeh, Dale Watson, Dr. Bruce Tefft, and Dr. Patrick Clawson.

In the current case, plaintiff filed a complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1605A(c) on September 19, 2009, and served the defendants through diplomatic channels. The defendants failed to respond within the 60-day period, and the Clerk of the Court entered default on January 25, 2010. Plaintiff then requested that the court take judicial notice of the proceedings in Blais, Heiser, and Rimkus I, and moved for default judgment, seeking $2 billion in punitive damages. Defendant contends that the court should not enter default judgment without evaluating the evidence and ensuring that plaintiff has established his claim or right to relief.

The plaintiff, a multi-racial woman, worked as a Licensed Practical Nurse for the defendant from May 2022 until her constructive discharge in January or March 2024. Plaintiff alleges that she experienced different treatment than coworkers of different races and sexes when it came to discipline. For example, in November 2022, she received a "write-up" for a medication error, but the lead nurse, who authorized the administration of the medication, was not disciplined. Later, Plaintiff was involved in another "medication mix-up," and her supervisor, Audrey Aldrich, initially told her to write an occurrence report, but changed her mind when she learned that a coworker, Adam Cooke, was partially responsible for the error.

Plaintiff alleges that Aldrich regularly compared her to Cooke in a critical manner, saying things like, "You ask questions, Adam doesn't." Plaintiff also alleges that when she reported a racially charged incident to Aldrich, Aldrich either ignored her or told her not to write an incident report. On December 27, 2023, Aldrich asked Plaintiff to move a "med cart" from one building to another with no assistance, resulting in Plaintiff's physical injury and her need to leave work. Plaintiff had other interactions with supervisors that she found offensive, including receiving a text message with a sex toy from supervisor Brittany Washington, and being told that "groceries and such" were "women's work" by supervisor Christina Davila.

Plaintiff presented a discrimination complaint to the Delaware Department of Labor (DDOL) on March 8, 2024, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) accorded substantial weight to DDOL's findings, dismissed Plaintiff's charge, and issued her a Notice of Right to Sue on September 19, 2024. Defendant contends that it did not discriminate against Plaintiff based on her race or sex, but the specific contentions of the defendant are not detailed in the available information. Plaintiff filed a complaint with the Superior Court for the State of Delaware on October 18, 2024, alleging employment discrimination in the form of constructive discharge, discipline, harassment, and hostile work environment.

The plaintiff worked for the defendant as a visual display person and janitor from April 1994 to October 1994. In October 1994, the plaintiff left the defendant to pursue other employment opportunities. The plaintiff then applied for a part-time sales associate position with the defendant in May, July, and August 1996, but was not rehired. Plaintiff alleges that he was not rehired because of his religious convictions. Defendant contends that the plaintiff's applications were not successful due to other reasons. 

On or about December 2, 1996, the plaintiff filed a claim of religious discrimination with the United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). The EEOC investigated the plaintiff's charge and concluded that there was no violation of Title VII. On March 26, 1998, the EEOC mailed the plaintiff a Dismissal and Notice of Rights letter stating that the evidence obtained during their investigation did not indicate that the defendant violated Title VII. Plaintiff claims that he did not actually receive the right-to-sue letter until April 28, 1998, because it was sent to an address where he was no longer welcome. Defendant argues that the plaintiff's claim was not timely filed, as the 90-day time period for filing a lawsuit began on the date the EEOC letter was mailed, not on the date the plaintiff actually received it.

The plaintiff and the defendant have a history of employment and attempted re-employment, with the plaintiff having worked for the defendant in the past and attempting to be rehired. The nature of the dispute is a claim of religious discrimination under Title VII, with the plaintiff alleging that the defendant did not rehire him due to his religious convictions. The defendant contends that the plaintiff's claim is untimely and that there is no evidence to support the claim of religious discrimination. Relevant pre-litigation events include the plaintiff's applications for employment, the EEOC investigation, and the mailing of the Dismissal and Notice of Rights letter. The plaintiff instituted this action by filing a complaint in court on July 8, 1998, and the defendant filed its answer and a motion for judgment on the pleadings on August 14, 1998.

Tracy Randle, Allison Taylor, Arthur Boyd, and Tahir Johnson, all former financial advisors for SunTrust, allege that the company maintains discriminatory policies governing compensation, teaming, and assignment of territory, resources, designations, and business opportunities. Plaintiff alleges that these policies result in higher rates of attrition and lower pay for African Americans and segregate the SunTrust workforce by race. Specifically, Plaintiffs claim that SunTrust "race matches" and assigns African American financial advisors to branches with higher African American and minority populations, while white financial advisors are assigned to wealthier, predominantly white territories with greater opportunities. 

Plaintiffs contend that African American financial advisors are assigned branches with fewer licensed bankers, are often assigned to multiple smaller branches, and are disproportionately excluded from assignments to "Premier Banks" in affluent areas. They also allege that African American financial advisors are almost entirely excluded from title designations needed to serve high net worth clients and from favorable teams and pools that can increase compensation. SunTrust, on the other hand, has not explicitly contested these allegations in the provided text, but the company's actions and the lawsuit's progression suggest a dispute over the existence and impact of these policies.

The parties have a history of employment and litigation, with the Plaintiffs having worked as financial advisors for SunTrust between June 24, 2014, and February 17, 2021. During this time, SunTrust allegedly implemented and maintained the discriminatory policies in question. The lawsuit concerns the alleged discriminatory treatment of African American financial advisors, including the four named Plaintiffs, and seeks relief for the class of affected individuals. Prior to the lawsuit, there is no indication of any settlement or resolution of the dispute between the parties. The parties engaged in substantial discovery, exchanging documents and data related to the policies and practices challenged by the lawsuit, and Plaintiffs retained experts to analyze this data. Mediation lasted over two years, ultimately leading to a proposed settlement agreement.

Kimberly Guereca was an employee of Sweeping Maids Cleaning Services, a residential and commercial cleaning service in Hobbs, New Mexico, owned and managed by Zulema Cordero and Eduardo Lara, during the second quarter of 2019. As an employee, Guereca performed manual, non-management work, including vacuuming, sweeping, mopping, and scrubbing, alongside other employees who performed similar tasks. These employees, including Guereca, spent the majority of their time performing manual tasks in customers' residences or commercial buildings, handling tools and equipment manufactured outside of New Mexico. Their job functions required little to no official training and did not necessitate a college education or advanced degree.

Plaintiff alleges that she and other employees typically worked in excess of forty hours per week, often working fifty hours or more, but were paid "straight time" for all hours worked without receiving an overtime premium for hours worked over forty per week. Defendants contend that they properly classified cleaning technicians, including Guereca, as exempt from overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) and the New Mexico Minimum Wage Act (NMMWA). However, Plaintiff alleges that Defendants failed to compensate her and other employees at a rate of not less than time-and-one-half their regular rates of pay for hours worked in excess of forty in a workweek.

Defendants had hiring and firing authority over Guereca and other cleaning technicians, and made decisions regarding their pay and classification. Prior to commencing the lawsuit, there is no indication of any settlement discussions or agreements between the parties. On June 20, 2019, Guereca commenced an opt-in collective action against Defendants, alleging violations of the FLSA and NMMWA. Relevant pre-litigation events include Defendants' decisions regarding employee classification and pay, as well as their failure to provide overtime compensation to Guereca and other employees. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Defendants exercising control over Guereca's work and pay. The nature of the dispute centers on whether Defendants properly compensated Guereca and other employees for overtime work under the FLSA and NMMWA.

Diane Larsen started working for Club Corporation of America, Inc. (CCA) affiliated clubs in 1978 and worked for a total of five such clubs by transferring from one to another. In 1989, she resigned as a pastry chef at the Metropolitan Club of Chicago to become the Food and Beverage Manager at the Lakeshore Athletic Club. Shortly after, she consented to become a plaintiff in a pending lawsuit, Avitia v. Metropolitan Club of Chicago, which charged Metropolitan with violations of the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for failure to pay overtime wages. 

Larsen alleges that she was told by CME manager Donna Kozak and head chef James Draveneck that a position would be available at the CME Club, but was later told by Draveneck that he couldn't hire her because Kozak said so. Larsen then applied for a sous chef position at Meadow, but was not hired. She claims that she was not hired at either CME or Meadow in retaliation for her involvement in the Avitia lawsuit. Defendant Clubs contend that the decision not to hire Larsen at CME was made by Kozak and Draveneck, who were unaware of her involvement in the Avitia lawsuit, and that the position was not filled due to cost-cutting measures. At Meadow, Clubs contend that the decision not to hire Larsen was made by manager Steve Strumpf, who decided not to incur the payroll expense of an additional employee, and that Larsen's involvement in the Avitia lawsuit was not a factor in the decision.

Larsen had previously worked at Lakeshore and had resigned to take the position at CME, which she claims was offered to her but later withdrawn. She had also spoken with Greg Carso, the chef at Meadow, about the sous chef position, but was told that he needed to discuss the matter with Strumpf. Larsen claims that she was told by Mark Condie, the restaurant manager at Meadow, that Carso said she would not be hired because she had a lawsuit against CCA or Metropolitan Club. However, Carso testified that the decision not to hire Larsen was due to the fact that Meadow's revenues were below budget, and that her involvement in the Avitia lawsuit was not a factor. The positions at CME and Meadow that Larsen applied for have not been filled, with Clubs citing cost-cutting measures as the reason.

Sonya Blackwell-Fripp, an African American woman, was employed as a GS-06 Practical Nurse at the Rock Island Arsenal Health Clinic from September 2, 2018, to October 2, 2019, under a 13-month term appointment. Her supervisors were Sergeant First Class Eugenio Lolli and Dr. Aaron Jacob. During the hiring process, Blackwell-Fripp signed a Statement of Understanding, which stated that her position was a term appointment with no guarantee of conversion to a permanent position. 

In June 2019, Blackwell-Fripp contacted an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) counselor and filed a claim against Lolli, which was later dismissed. On September 13, 2019, she received a memorandum stating that her term appointment would not be renewed beyond October 2, 2019. The decision not to extend her term appointment was made by Lolli, Colonel Gordon Prairie, and Major Elizabeth Hamilton, with Prairie and Hamilton working at a different location, Blanchfield Army Community Hospital at Fort Campbell, Kentucky. No one was hired to fill Blackwell-Fripp's position after her term appointment ended.

Plaintiff alleges that she was treated differently than similarly situated Caucasian employees and that the decision not to renew her term appointment was motivated by racial discrimination and retaliation for her earlier EEO claim. Defendant contends that the decision not to extend Blackwell-Fripp's term appointment was based on the needs of the organization and that there was no discriminatory intent. The parties' dispute centers on whether the non-renewal of Blackwell-Fripp's term appointment was lawful or discriminatory. Prior to filing this lawsuit, Blackwell-Fripp contacted the EEO office on October 3, 2019, and filed a formal complaint on November 15, 2019, which was followed by a request for a final agency decision letter on June 4, 2020.

The plaintiff, an employee of the defendant, requested annual leave for December 22, 23, and 28, 1998. His leave request was initially approved by his supervisors, but his leave request form was later voided, and he was asked to resubmit his request. The defendant's leave policy, as explained in a memorandum by Carole Grant, the plaintiff's immediate supervisor, required employees to check with their partners before requesting leave and only allowed one member of each pair to take leave at a time. The plaintiff did not follow this policy, as he did not consult with his partner, Roberta Melton, and requested leave dates both before and after Christmas. The plaintiff was granted leave for December 22 and 23, 1998, but claims he was required to work on December 28, 1998, although it was later added as a county-wide holiday.

The plaintiff alleges that he was treated differently than other employees with regard to obtaining annual leave and that this treatment was discriminatory. He also claims that he was required to use a sign-in board to inform his supervisors of his whereabouts during the workday, which he believes was unnecessary and a hassle. The plaintiff contends that other employees in his department did not have their names on the board and were not required to sign in and out. However, the defendant's evidence suggests that other employees, including all computer programmers, had their names on the board, and the plaintiff admitted that he did not know whether other employees were told they did not need to use the board.

The plaintiff also alleges that he engaged in protected activity under Title VII by complaining of alleged discrimination in the workplace to Marie Wauben, the Director of Human Resources. He claims that subsequent to these complaints, his supervisor, Carole Grant, took disciplinary actions against him on March 23, 1999, which he believes were retaliatory. The plaintiff contends that the temporal proximity between his protected activity and the adverse employment actions is sufficient to establish a causal connection between the two. The defendant, however, proffers legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for its disciplinary actions, which the plaintiff must show are pretexts for discrimination.

Darron Terry Smith, the plaintiff, was employed by the University of Tennessee, specifically the College of Health Professions, Department of Physician Assistant Studies. Plaintiff alleges that he experienced race discrimination and retaliation during his employment, including pay discrimination and other conditions of employment. Plaintiff contends that he was subjected to these discriminatory practices because of his race. 

The University of Tennessee, the defendant, contends that it did not discriminate against the plaintiff. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of employment discrimination. Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff filed charges with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on March 4, 2015, and amended them on July 30, 2015, alleging race discrimination, retaliation, and retaliatory discharge. He received a right to sue letter from the EEOC on July 19, 2016. Plaintiff filed another charge with the EEOC on October 24, 2016, alleging race discrimination and retaliation, and received a second right to sue letter on August 28, 2018.

Plaintiff alleges that the university's actions were motivated by discriminatory intent, while the university contends that its actions were lawful and non-discriminatory. The pre-litigation events include the plaintiff's employment with the university, the filing of charges with the EEOC, and the receipt of right to sue letters. The lawsuit was filed after the plaintiff received the right to sue letters, and the university has moved to dismiss the complaint. Relevant documents include the EEOC charges, the right to sue letters, and the complaint filed in this lawsuit. The workplace facts include the plaintiff's employment duties, the conditions of his employment, and the alleged discriminatory practices.

The plaintiff, a former federal employee, received a final agency decision on December 2, 1989, stating that there was no discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that she was discriminated against in violation of Title VII. The defendant contends that the plaintiff's lawsuit was not filed within the required 30-day time limit, as it was received by the court on January 11, 1990. However, the plaintiff had submitted her complaint to the court on January 2, 1990, which is within the 30-day time limit. The defendant argues that the 30-day time limit is jurisdictional and cannot be waived or tolled. The plaintiff, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, had filed a handwritten complaint and other pleadings, and the court notes that she has followed the complicated Title VII path without the assistance of a trained lawyer.

The parties agree that the plaintiff received the final agency decision on December 2, 1989. The defendant claims that the plaintiff's suit was not filed until January 11, 1990, which is 39 days after the final agency decision. However, the court's records indicate that the plaintiff's complaint was date-stamped January 2, 1990, when it was first received by the court. The court's procedures for in forma pauperis complaints resulted in a delay between the receipt of the complaint and its official filing on January 11, 1990. The plaintiff contends that she did everything she could to file her complaint in a timely manner, and the delay was due to the court's procedures.

The defendant cites two cases, Richardson v. Wiley and Coles v. Penny, to support its argument that the 30-day time limit is jurisdictional. However, the plaintiff points to a more recent case, Mondy v. Secretary of the Army, which held that the 30-day time limit is subject to equitable tolling. The court must decide whether to dismiss the plaintiff's complaint due to the alleged late filing, considering the circumstances of the case and the applicable law. The plaintiff's complaint alleges discrimination in violation of Title VII, and the defendant's motion to dismiss raises a question about the court's subject matter jurisdiction over the claim.

Leon Weiss and Timothy Engel were employed as warehousemen by Parker Hannifan Corporation at its distribution service center in Trenton, New Jersey. Weiss, who is Jewish, began working at the warehouse in March 1982 as a temporary employee and became a full-time employee in September 1982. Engel started working at the warehouse in October 1983. Weiss was the only Jewish warehouseman in the Trenton facility from 1982 until his termination in 1985. The warehouse was managed by a distribution service center manager, who reported to Parker Hannifan's manager of physical distribution in Cleveland, Ohio. At the time, Thomas Dickerson was the manager of physical distribution.

Weiss and Engel worked under the supervision of leadperson Fred Schmidt, who was selected for the job over Weiss in 1984. Schmidt had been a full-time Parker Hannifan employee longer than Weiss, although Weiss had started working in the Trenton facility as a temporary employee before Schmidt was hired. Weiss was the senior warehouseman in Trenton and had trained most of the new warehousemen, including Engel and Robin MacNeal. When Schmidt or the prior leadperson was away, Weiss acted as leadperson and assumed all the responsibilities of that position. In January 1985, Schmidt left his job as warehouse leadperson to take a sales position with Parker Hannifan, and the leadperson vacancy needed to be filled.

Plaintiff Weiss alleges that he was denied a promotion to leadperson due to his religion. Plaintiff Engel alleges that his employment was terminated in retaliation for his complaints about the alleged discrimination against Weiss. Defendant Parker Hannifan contends that the promotion was awarded to MacNeal based on his better attendance record, prior supervisory experience, and ability to communicate. The company also contends that Weiss and Engel's behavior after the promotion announcement, including their criticism of the decision and alleged threats against MacNeal, led to their termination. Weiss and Engel deny making any threats against MacNeal. The events leading up to the lawsuit include a series of meetings and conversations between Altmeyer, Weiss, and Engel, during which Altmeyer announced the promotion decision and warned Weiss and Engel about their behavior.

Women, including Lois Jenson, Patricia Kosmach, and Kathleen O'Brien Anderson, applied for or were employed in hourly positions at Eveleth Taconite Company's (Eveleth Mines) taconite mining facility. Plaintiff alleges that Eveleth Mines discriminated against them on the basis of their sex, including engaging in acts of sexual harassment, and created a hostile work environment. The women claim that they were subjected to discriminatory practices, including discrimination in hiring, job assignment, promotion, compensation, discipline, and training. 

Defendant Eveleth Mines and the Union deny these claims, stating that hiring practices and terms and conditions of employment are conducted in a non-discriminatory manner. Eveleth Mines also alleges that it has a practice of immediately investigating and correcting sexual harassment when it knows or reasonably should know of its existence. The company claims to have adhered to this practice at all relevant times. 

The named plaintiffs, Jenson, Kosmach, and Anderson, began their employment with Eveleth Mines in 1975, 1976, and 1976, respectively. Jenson filed a charge of sex discrimination with the Minnesota Department of Human Rights (MDHR) in 1984, and the MDHR found probable cause to credit her allegations. Kosmach and Anderson also filed charges of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in 1988. The plaintiffs received Right to Sue Notices from the EEOC, allowing them to proceed with their lawsuit.
