The lawsuit was bifurcated into two phases: a liability phase to determine whether Eveleth Mines violated Title VII and/or the Minnesota Human Rights Act, and a recovery phase to determine individual class members' eligibility for compensatory relief.

Wayne Galbreth, a Louisiana resident, worked for Bellsouth Telecommunications, Inc. (Bellsouth), a Georgia corporation. Galbreth's supervisor was Aaron Begnaud, and during Begnaud's absence, Barbara C. Johansen acted as his supervisor. In March 1995, Begnaud evaluated Galbreth's performance for 1994, giving him a rating that denied him a salary increase. Galbreth alleges that Begnaud's decision was influenced by Johansen's recommendations from 1994. Galbreth contends that Begnaud discriminated against him based on his race, favoring white employees over him in various aspects of his job and in awards and recognition. 

Plaintiff alleges that Begnaud and Johansen, as his supervisors, discriminated against him in violation of Louisiana statutes LSA-R.S. 23:1006 et seq. and LSA-R.S. 51:2231 et seq. Defendant Bellsouth removed the case to federal court, claiming diversity jurisdiction exists between Galbreth and Bellsouth, and that Begnaud and Johansen, both Louisiana residents, were fraudulently joined as defendants to prevent removal. Galbreth opposes the removal, arguing that Begnaud and Johansen were not fraudulently joined and that he has stated a valid cause of action against them under state law.

Galbreth originally filed the lawsuit in Civil District Court for the Parish of Orleans, State of Louisiana, naming Bellsouth, Begnaud, and Johansen as defendants. The lawsuit alleges racial discrimination and seeks relief under Louisiana law. The parties disagree on whether Begnaud and Johansen can be held liable under the relevant Louisiana statutes, with Galbreth arguing that they can be held liable as supervisors and Bellsouth arguing that only the employer, Bellsouth, can be held liable. Relevant pre-litigation events include Begnaud's performance evaluation of Galbreth and Johansen's recommendations, which Galbreth alleges were discriminatory. The parties have exchanged memoranda and the court has reviewed the applicable law, but no decision has been made on the motions to remand and dismiss.

Kathleen P. Arnold began working at Kimberly Quality Care Nursing Service in October 1988. In December 1988, Barbara Parks became her supervisor. Plaintiff alleges that over a period of seven months, Parks subjected her to various forms of sexual harassment, which she reported to Parks' superior. After reporting the harassment, Parks began issuing written warnings to Arnold. Arnold's employment was terminated on October 12, 1989, shortly after she informed the defendants that she would be contacting the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission about her situation. 

Plaintiff alleges that the sexual harassment and subsequent termination were retaliatory actions taken by Parks and Kimberly. Defendant Parks contends that she was acting within the scope of her agency for Kimberly at all times. Defendant Kimberly argues that the Pennsylvania Workmen's Compensation Act bars the claims for assault and battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and loss of consortium against it. 

Lynn Arnold, Kathleen's husband, claims loss of consortium due to the alleged harassment and retaliation his wife suffered. The defendants argue that the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over Lynn Arnold's state law claim for loss of consortium. The plaintiffs initiated this lawsuit, which includes claims under Title VII for retaliatory discharge, as well as state law claims for assault and battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and loss of consortium. Relevant pre-litigation events include Kathleen Arnold's reports of harassment to Parks' superior and her subsequent termination, as well as her intention to contact the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission.

Kathia E. Ennett, an African American woman, began working for Cumberland County Schools in August 1977. She served as principal of the Lewis Chapel Middle School from July 1, 2002, until her retirement on July 31, 2008. On April 14, 2005, Ennett entered into a contract with the Board of Education for her employment as principal from July 1, 2005, through June 30, 2009. Ennett alleges that Dr. William Harrison forced her to retire as principal on the basis of her race. 

Plaintiff alleges that Harrison asked Dr. Lavetta Henderson to develop an action plan for her, gave her a negative evaluation, told her that he wanted her to retire rather than attempt an action plan, threatened to investigate her and start dismissal proceedings if she did not retire, and informed the Board of Education that she had retired when she had not. Ennett contends that this conduct caused her to retire as principal and take a part-time position as a remediation tutor at Lillian Black Elementary. Defendant Harrison and the Board of Education contend that their actions were legitimate and not motivated by racial discrimination. 

Ennett filed a charge of discrimination with the EEOC on September 11, 2008, alleging discrimination based on race, and received a Notice of Right to Sue on May 1, 2009. She then filed a complaint against the Cumberland County Board of Education and Dr. William C. Harrison, in his individual capacity, on July 30, 2009, alleging claims of race discrimination, retaliation, breach of contract, negligent infliction of emotional distress, negligent supervision or retention, and tortious interference with contract. The Board of Education filed a Partial Motion to Dismiss and an Answer on September 11, 2009, which Ennett responded to on October 5, 2009, and Defendants replied on October 13, 2009.

Johnnie Mae Riggsbee, a black female, was hired by Diversity Services, Inc. ("Diversity"), a temporary staffing agency in Washington, D.C., in December 2004. She was immediately placed in a position as a temporary identification services clerk in the House of Representatives, earning $13.98 per hour. Plaintiff alleges that she worked at the House from December 2004 to April 2005, when she was told to leave that position by a Diversity employee. She contends that she was then hired in May 2005 for a receptionist/data entry position at the House, which would last until October 2005, but was terminated from this position in July 2005 after a Diversity employee told her to leave. 

Defendant Diversity asserts that it successfully negotiated with the House to transfer Riggsbee to a new temporary clerk position in April 2005, where she earned $16 per hour, and that her temporary assignment was complete by the end of June 2005. Diversity claims that it offered Riggsbee three temporary positions after her position with the House ended: proctoring exams in July 2005 at $10 per hour, photographing store fronts in September 2005 at $13 per hour, and distributing flyers in September 2005 at $9 per hour. However, Riggsbee alleges that she was only offered one position, distributing flyers in September 2005, and that the only other position Diversity offered her was a $9 per hour proctoring job in April 2005, before her second position at the House began, which she accepted.

Riggsbee filed a charge against Diversity with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on December 20, 2005, alleging "unlawful racial discrimination against me on the basis of my race and color." The EEOC investigated her charge, rejected her claim that violations of Title VII had occurred, and issued a right to sue letter allowing her to bring her claim in court. Riggsbee then filed her judicial complaint on November 21, 2007, alleging employment discrimination based on her race and sex in violation of Title VII. She contends that Diversity deliberately terminated her from her employment with the House despite her excellent work performance and replaced her with a white male, and that Diversity failed to make a reasonable effort to find comparable alternative employment for her. Diversity denies these allegations, asserting that it had little control over an employee's placement or tenure with a client and that it offered Riggsbee several temporary positions after her position with the House ended.

Richard Vankempen was employed by McDonnell Douglas Corporation until his termination on January 24, 1992. Plaintiff alleges that his employment was wrongfully terminated based on his age. Defendant contends that plaintiff's claim under the Missouri Human Rights Act (MHRA) is untimely, as the two-year statute of limitations would have expired but for defendant's agreement to extend the time for plaintiff to file his MHRA claim until July 1, 1995. Plaintiff filed his original complaint, including an MHRA claim, on June 23, 1995, but did not receive a right-to-sue letter from the Missouri Commission on Human Rights (MCHR) until October 3, 1995. Plaintiff then filed an Amended Complaint on November 2, 1995. 

Defendant contends that receipt of a notice of right to sue is a jurisdictional prerequisite to the maintenance of a civil action for violation of the MHRA, and that plaintiff's MHRA claim was time-barred at the time the Amended Complaint was filed. Plaintiff argues that no federal or state court has held that a right-to-sue letter from the MCHR is a jurisdictional prerequisite to filing an action under the MHRA, and that the statute should be liberally construed. 

Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff had filed a complaint with the MCHR, which had not completed its administrative processing within 180 days. Plaintiff had requested a right-to-sue letter, which was issued on October 3, 1995. The parties had also agreed to extend the time for plaintiff to file his MHRA claim until July 1, 1995. Defendant had moved to dismiss Count III of plaintiff's Amended Complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, arguing that plaintiff's MHRA claim was untimely and that the court lacked jurisdiction over the claim.

Six female employees, Antonopulos, Goldsmith, Greer, Johnson, Roberts, and Beach, worked as janitors for the defendant. On July 26, 1965, the defendant discharged Antonopulos, Goldsmith, Greer, Johnson, and Roberts from their jobs. Plaintiff Beach was discharged on September 9, 1966. The plaintiffs allege that they were discharged solely because they were female. 

Plaintiff Goldsmith filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on February 8, 1966, listing the names of the other four plaintiffs. The EEOC filed a decision on March 7, 1967, stating that there was reasonable cause to believe the defendant's actions were in violation of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Although Greer and Johnson were reinstated to their positions on August 15, 1967, and October 2, 1967, respectively, the EEOC notified each of the five plaintiffs on November 5, 1967, that conciliation efforts had failed, and they had 30 days to institute an action in court. 

Plaintiff Beach filed a charge with the EEOC on October 5, 1966, and the EEOC filed a decision on July 26, 1967, stating that there was reasonable cause to believe the defendant's actions were in violation of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Beach was reinstated to her former position on August 15, 1967, and was also notified by the EEOC on November 5, 1967, that further conciliation had failed, and she had 30 days to institute suit. The plaintiffs filed a joint lawsuit on December 4, 1967, seeking damages and reinstatement. Defendant contends that the plaintiffs did not comply with the legal prerequisites for filing the lawsuit, including filing individual charges with the EEOC and filing the charges within 90 days of the alleged unlawful practice. Plaintiff Goldsmith alleges that she and the other plaintiffs did not file individual charges because they were not aware that they had been discharged for an unlawful reason until after the 90-day period had expired. The plaintiffs also allege that the defendant and their labor union deceived them, which contributed to the delay in filing the charges.

From September 2023 through July 2024, Plaintiff, a Hispanic Puerto Rican with brown skin, was employed as an administrative assistant for The Oak Brook Club Association. She was supervised by the Property Manager and interacted with residents and co-workers, including the bookkeeper and Assistant Property Manager. Plaintiff alleges that one resident repeatedly gave her dirty looks, expressed dislike for "Spanish" people, and refused to interact with her. When Plaintiff sought help from the Property Manager, she was allegedly told to avoid the resident by going upstairs or to the cafeteria whenever the resident was in the office. Plaintiff's supervisor allegedly refused to address the resident's behavior, stating she didn't want to deal with the resident.

Plaintiff also alleges that the Assistant Property Manager engaged in discriminatory behavior, including not allowing employees to display flags from their countries of origin, making comments about Plaintiff's potential relationship to another Hispanic co-worker, and discussing "immigrants...coming in and taking everything from us." When Plaintiff pushed back on these comments, the Assistant Property Manager allegedly did not respond well. Plaintiff contends that within two months of complaining about the resident and two weeks of disagreeing with the Assistant Property Manager, she was terminated. Defendant contends that the reason for the termination was a complaint from an unknown employee that Plaintiff was taking calls using a speaker phone.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the Association being the employer and Plaintiff being the former employee. The nature of the dispute is a claim of discrimination and hostile work environment, with Plaintiff alleging that she was subjected to discriminatory behavior by a resident and a co-worker, and that her employer failed to address the behavior, ultimately leading to her termination. Plaintiff alleges that the stated reason for her termination was pretextual, while Defendant contends that the termination was based on a legitimate complaint about her use of a speaker phone.

Ricardo Tovar was hired by United Airlines Inc. as a Supervisor - Onboard Service in August 2009. He reported to Rita Donovan and Jackie Barnes, who were Operations Managers, and they in turn reported to Anthony Nicastro, Manager - Onboard Service. Tovar alleges that he was subjected to discrimination and harassment on the basis of his national origin and sex during his employment with United. Plaintiff alleges that he was placed on a performance improvement plan in February 2010 due to his performance, and that he received an "unsatisfactory" rating in his first performance review with Barnes in March 2010. 

Defendant United Airlines Inc. contends that Tovar's behavior towards his coworkers was a significant issue, citing several incidents where he allegedly yelled at, intimidated, or demeaned flight attendants, including Pedro Arreza, Karen Brown, Linda "Robbi" McMinn, and Judy Steinberg. United also contends that Tovar was given a disciplinary letter on October 10, 2010, stating that he was "viewed as intimidating, demeaning, demanding and difficult," and that he was offered support to help him handle situations better. However, Plaintiff alleges that the disciplinary actions taken against him were discriminatory and that he was singled out based on his national origin and sex.

The events leading to Tovar's termination on January 14, 2011, included an incident on November 10, 2010, where he allegedly spoke firmly to and followed Supervisor Wendy Biliskov, causing her to feel uncomfortable and upset. Tovar was suspended with pay pending an investigation into the incident, and he subsequently submitted a statement about the incident. Defendant United Airlines Inc. contends that Tovar's termination was due to his threatening and intimidating behavior towards coworkers, while Plaintiff alleges that the termination was retaliatory and discriminatory. Prior to his termination, Tovar had filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) against United, alleging discrimination based on his national origin, genetic information, and sex.

The plaintiff, a long-time employee of the Department of State, worked as a GS-12 Grants Specialist during the times relevant to this case. In 2003, he was responsible for preparing a final audit determination letter to close out an audit of the Mississippi Consortium for International Development (MCID Determination Letter), which took defendant more than six months to review and clear. Plaintiff alleges that in January 2004, after a GS-13 employee retired, he requested but did not receive "high-dollar" level reassignments, which were considered GS-13 level work, despite his direct supervisors reassigning these matters to the rest of the grant team with the approval of Fannie Lue Allen, the Division Chief of the Grants Division. 

Plaintiff contends that he received lower performance ratings in 2004 and 2005, with a rating of "Fully Successful", which is one level lower than the "Excellent" rating given to him in 2003. Defendant contends that the "Excellent" rating indicates "a level of unusually good performance" and that plaintiff's work was consistently above average. Plaintiff also alleges that his direct supervisors began to selectively review his work in 2003 and that he was required to attend various training programs to improve his communication and analytical skills and the quality of his work at the suggestion of Ms. Allen. 

Plaintiff alleges that the defendant tolerated a hostile work environment. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the plaintiff working under the supervision of various individuals, including Ms. Allen and his direct supervisors. The nature of the dispute is one of employment discrimination and retaliation, with the plaintiff alleging that he was treated unfairly and retaliated against in the workplace. Relevant pre-litigation events include the preparation and review of the MCID Determination Letter, the reassignment of grant work, and the plaintiff's performance evaluations.

Donald E. Pawley was employed by Bel Brands USA, Inc. at its facility in Leitchfield, Kentucky, where the company manufactures cheese. He was hired in April 2005, at the age of 49, and initially worked as a Warehouse Operator starting in June 2009. Around 2009, Mr. Pawley was diagnosed with high blood pressure. In August 2013, Rod Inman became Mr. Pawley's supervisor. Plaintiff alleges that on at least three occasions, he reported unsafe working conditions to his supervisors, including Mr. Inman, and that Mr. Inman was "verbally abusive" and made comments about his age or high blood pressure. However, Mr. Pawley never reported these comments to anyone in management or human resources, nor did he ever make any complaints that he believed he was being discriminated against or harassed by Mr. Inman.

Mr. Pawley received and reviewed Bel Brands' Employee Handbook when he was hired, which describes the company's progressive disciplinary system. He received infractions in July 2005, September 2006, and October 2012, but it was the four infractions he received in his last six months of employment that led to his termination. In December 2015, Mr. Inman gave Mr. Pawley a verbal warning for not pulling enough product. In mid-April 2016, Mr. Pawley received a written warning for failing to place pulled supplies into the staging area. In May 2016, Mr. Pawley received a three-day suspension related to a missing cage bolt on his forklift, and after his suspension, he had a fourth performance infraction when he pulled whey powder out of order.

Supply Chain Manager Paul Myers decided to terminate Mr. Pawley in accordance with the terms of Bel Brands' progressive discipline policy due to the fourth performance infraction within the previous twelve months. When Mr. Myers informed Mr. Inman of his decision to terminate Mr. Pawley, Mr. Inman asked that Mr. Pawley be given another chance, but Mr. Myers instructed Mr. Inman to deliver the termination decision to Mr. Pawley. At the time of his termination in May 2016, Mr. Pawley was 60 years old. Since June 2016, Mr. Pawley has been working as a truck driver for Otis Bryant. Defendant Bel Brands contends that Mr. Pawley's termination was based on his performance infractions and in accordance with the company's progressive discipline policy.

Elba Falto de Roman was the director of the Head Start Program in Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, until October 5, 2011. In June 2010, defendant Jose Guillermo Rodriguez, the mayor of Mayagüez, ordered her not to sign a lease contract with Rosaura Building Corporation, which had already been approved by Falto and other decision-makers at Head Start. Falto informed Rosaura of Rodriguez's order, and Rosaura subsequently sued Rodriguez in federal court for political discrimination in June 2011. After Rodriguez was served with the lawsuit in July 2011, he called Falto in a loud and threatening manner, scolding her for informing Rosaura that he was responsible for denying the contract. Rodriguez blamed Falto for Rosaura's lawsuit and told her that she had failed to protect him as mayor, stating that "women like her were not needed in his government" and that "women don't know how to be loyal." He asked if she was aware that the owners of Rosaura were his political enemies and said that her responsibility as director of Head Start was to protect him as mayor. 

Plaintiff alleges that Rodriguez's actions were retaliatory and that he ultimately had her terminated as director of the Head Start Program. On September 28, 2011, Falto received a letter signed by Rodriguez stating that the Board of Directors of Head Start and the Council had decided to dismiss her, effective October 5, 2011, due to the federal grant to the City of Mayagüez being threatened and because Rodriguez had lost trust in her. The Board members and the Council members, who are being sued in their personal and official capacities, contend that they are not municipal employees with the authority to terminate Falto and that the complaint fails to allege action pursuant to an official policy or custom. 

Falto alleges that her termination was the result of Rodriguez's exercise of his final policy-making authority as Mayor of Mayagüez and that she was subjected to harassment by Rodriguez. She also alleges that the Municipality of Mayagüez and its officers are liable for her termination. The parties are now engaged in a lawsuit, with the Head Start defendants moving to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim, and Falto opposing the motion. The case is before the court on the consent of the parties.

Mr. Ho, an Asian-American and a GS-level 13 criminal investigator at the Office of Strategic Intelligence and Information within the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), has worked for the agency since April 1999. Since 2015, Ho has filed several Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaints against his managers, including James McDermond, Kevin O’Keefe, and Edward Kropke, alleging race discrimination and non-selection for certain promotions. In 2018, Ho filed another EEO complaint, which was his last before bringing this case.

In June 2019, a GS-14 position for a "Criminal Investigator Program Manager" became available, and Ho applied for the promotion. He advanced through the hiring process and was interviewed by O'Keefe and Kropke, among others, in August 2019. However, the day after the interview, Human Resources notified Ho that he was not selected for the position. Plaintiff alleges that O'Keefe stated that all four applicants were qualified, but none were selected, with two having "outside factors" that disqualified them, and that Ho did not answer some questions well, although he "knocked it out of the park" on others. Plaintiff also alleges that McDermond intervened in the selection process, telling the panel they had the option of not hiring anyone. The position remains vacant, and Ho does not claim that it has been reopened for applications.

Plaintiff alleges that he was qualified for the promotion and that his non-selection was in retaliation for his prior complaints. Defendant contends that Ho was not selected due to his performance in the interview and that the position was not filled due to the lack of a suitable candidate. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Ho working under the supervision of McDermond, O'Keefe, and Kropke. The nature of the dispute is a claim of retaliation and potential discrimination in the hiring process. Relevant pre-litigation events include Ho's EEO complaints, his application and interview for the GS-14 position, and the notification of non-selection. Ho exhausted the administrative process and then filed this lawsuit, which the defendant has moved to dismiss.

Amanda Brennan was employed as a security guard by Century Security Services. During her employment, she reported an incident of sexual harassment by her supervisor. Brennan alleges that after making this report, she suffered adverse employment actions, including termination, reduction in hours, and denial of compensation. Plaintiff alleges that these actions were taken in retaliation for her report of sexual harassment. Defendant Century Security Services contends that Brennan was fired for excessive absenteeism, her hours were reduced in accordance with her own childcare schedule, and the withheld pay was due to a banking error. Brennan claims that she had never received negative feedback on her work performance before making the report, but after the report, she experienced issues with her schedule and compensation. The parties disagree on the circumstances surrounding Brennan's termination, with Brennan stating it occurred the day after her report, while Century provides paperwork with a different termination date. Brennan's report of sexual harassment is undisputed as a protected activity. The temporal proximity between the report and the alleged retaliatory actions, as well as evidence of ongoing antagonism, are disputed facts relevant to establishing a causal connection between the protected activity and the adverse actions. Brennan filed a complaint against Century on September 29, 2021, which was later amended on June 15, 2022, to include claims of disparate treatment, harassment, retaliation, sexual discrimination, negligent hiring and retention, and violations of the PHRA. Century filed a motion to dismiss the amended complaint, which was granted in part and denied in part, leaving only Brennan's Title VII retaliation claim pending. Century subsequently filed a motion for summary judgment on September 3, 2024, which Brennan opposed on September 17, 2024.

Kenion, an African American female, was hired by Skanska Civil Southeast, Inc. as a Carpenter Apprentice in April 2013. She received several promotions and additional responsibilities, becoming a Carpenter and Punch List Foreman in August 2014. By August 2015, Kenion was supervising a crew of 15 workers on the 1st Street Tunnel project in Washington, D.C. and was featured in Skanska's promotional advertisements. In May 2016, Kenion accepted a transfer, pay raise, and career development plan position as a Craft Foreman in Skanska USA Building, Inc. at its "American University Project."

Plaintiff alleges that she began experiencing discrimination in November 2016, after she was reassigned to Skanska's "DC Water Headquarters Project" and began working for Lemley and Leier, both Caucasian males. Plaintiff alleges that Lemley and Leier were "hostile, rude, or dismissive" towards her and Skanska's African American subcontractors, but did not treat White and Hispanic supervisors and workers in the same negative fashion. For example, Plaintiff alleges that Leier rejected her request for stone to compact a potentially unsafe worksite, citing budgetary concerns, but later requested and received two loads of stone for comparable work nearby. Plaintiff also alleges that Lemley made several disparaging remarks about African American laborers, including stating that "they're not that smart" and that African Americans were "lazy."

Plaintiff contends that Lemley and Leier stymied her professional development and caused her to fear for her job security. She alleges that Lemley denied her permission to attend a Skanska Women's Network professional development event, and that Leier refused to grant her permission to participate in a Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) training. Plaintiff also alleges that she was denied a 3% pay increase and the opportunity to complete a self-evaluation for her annual performance rating. Plaintiff claims that she was not promoted to the position of Assistant Superintendent, despite having more industry experience than the person who was hired for the position, James Moffitt, a Caucasian male. Plaintiff alleges that she was retaliated against for making complaints about the discrimination she experienced, including being prohibited from working overtime, being required to work on weekends, and being denied feedback on her self-assessment and career development guidance. Defendant Skanska contends that it took steps to address Plaintiff's concerns, including giving her the 3% pay raise she requested and allowing her to complete a self-assessment. However, Plaintiff alleges that these actions were insufficient and that she was ultimately forced to resign due to the ongoing retaliation and roadblocks to advancement.

Lorraine Lyons began working for New York Life Insurance Company (NYL) in January 2002 as an Agent and later as a Long-Term Care Consultant (LTCC) starting in 2009. She was laid off in 2013 but was rehired as an LTCC in January 2014 at the age of 48. At the time of her rehire, Brian Seguin, a Vice President and National Sales Officer, was 43 years old and made the decision to offer her the position. Lyons was assigned to eight general offices and was paid a base salary of $80,000, with the possibility of additional compensation based on sales performance.

Lyons alleges that during her tenure, she experienced age discrimination, citing comments made by NYL executives, the pattern of promotions, and her supervisors' failure to adequately support and coach her. She claims that there was a concerted effort at NYL to make the workforce younger. Plaintiff alleges that in 2015, she had a conversation with Seguin about her salary, during which he stated that he had to pay higher salaries to the "Genworth guys" he hired. Lyons also received memoranda of understanding (MOUs) in 2015, which she claims were unfair and incorrectly calculated her performance. Defendant contends that the MOUs were issued based on her performance and that she was given opportunities to improve.

In January 2018, Lyons's supervisor, Ray Singer, retired, and Courtney Crenshaw, a 41-year-old African-American woman, was promoted to the Regional Manager position. Lyons knew that the position was available and had been posted internally and externally. Defendant contends that Crenshaw was the best person for the role based on her experience and sales techniques. Plaintiff alleges that she was not considered for the promotion and that the company's actions were part of a larger pattern of age discrimination. The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding Lyons's performance evaluations, promotions, and ultimate termination in October 2018.

Frank T. Curto was hired by Sears, Roebuck and Co. as an "assistant to the Vice-President" on May 1, 1970. On April 21, 1980, at the age of 58, Curto was informed that he would be discharged effective July 31, 1980. Plaintiff alleges that he was a highly competent employee and that he was terminated because of his age, while younger employees in comparable positions who were no more competent than plaintiff were permitted to keep their jobs. On July 31, 1980, Curto lost his job as scheduled. 

On December 12, 1980, 235 days after the alleged discriminatory employment practice, counsel for Curto sent charges of age discrimination against Sears to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the Illinois Department of Human Rights (IDHR) by certified mail. On December 22, 1980, 245 days after the alleged discrimination took place, Curto signed a sworn charge, formally commencing proceedings before the IDHR. In April 1981, IDHR notified Curto that it had scheduled a conference on his charge, but the conference was postponed at his request. Curto never requested a new conference date, and throughout June and July, an investigator for IDHR attempted to contact him, but neither Curto nor his counsel returned the investigator's calls. On September 4, 1981, Curto's IDHR charge was dismissed at his request.

Defendant Sears contends that the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) requires Curto to file his EEOC charge within 300 days of the alleged discrimination and that he failed to do so. Plaintiff alleges that he was terminated due to his age and that Sears' actions were discriminatory. The parties' relationship is that of employer and former employee, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of age discrimination under the ADEA. Relevant pre-litigation events include Curto's termination, his filing of charges with the EEOC and IDHR, and the subsequent dismissal of his IDHR charge. Defendant argues that Curto's filing with the EEOC was untimely, while Curto contends that his commencement of proceedings before the IDHR was timely and that his EEOC filing was proper.

Mr. Young, a former corrections officer at the Colorado Department of Corrections (CDOC), received an online Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) training in 2021. Plaintiff alleges that this training created a hostile work environment so severe that it resulted in his constructive discharge when he opted to resign from his position in July 2021. Mr. Young had previously brought claims based on nearly identical facts against CDOC and other defendants in a separate lawsuit, Young v. Colo. Dep’t of Corrs., et al. (Young I), which raised hostile work environment and equal protection claims.

In the current case, Mr. Young contends that the EDI training he received was deeply racist and that he was forced to resign due to the hostile work environment it created. Defendant CDOC contends that Mr. Young's interests in proceeding expeditiously with discovery are reduced since he has found new employment and does not seek reinstatement to his previous position. CDOC also argues that it would be unduly burdened by discovery, especially since the court's ruling on their Motion to Dismiss may resolve the matter entirely. Mr. Young, on the other hand, argues that a delay in discovery would prejudice his ability to prove his claims, as the events relevant to his claims occurred between February and July 2021, and that his ability to gather evidence diminishes with time.

The parties have exchanged motions and responses regarding a stay of discovery, with CDOC seeking a stay pending the court's ruling on their Motion to Dismiss, and Mr. Young opposing the stay, arguing that it would increase the burden on CDOC, inconvenience the court, and harm the interests of non-parties, such as former colleagues who may have vital evidence to offer in the case. Mr. Young also claims that the public interest favors discovery, as his case has garnered attention across the country due to its broader impact on employers' use of potentially racist training materials under Title VII.

K.D. submitted a claim to Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, Inc. for out-of-network benefits under the Harvard Pilgrim – Lahey Health Select HMO. The claim was denied, prompting K.D. to challenge the decision. Plaintiff K.D. alleges that she is entitled to payment for care she received from Sierra Tucson, LLC, under the Plan. Defendant Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, Inc. contends that K.D.'s claim was properly denied. The parties' relationship is that of an insured (K.D.) and an insurance provider (Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, Inc.). 

K.D. alleges that she was entitled to the benefits and that the denial was improper. Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, Inc. contends that the denial was proper and that K.D. is not entitled to the benefits. Prior to the lawsuit, K.D. submitted her claim and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, Inc. denied it. The parties engaged in pre-litigation communications, but the details of these communications are not specified. K.D. is represented by Rosenfeld & Rafik, P.C., and has submitted billing records for the work performed by her attorneys, including Ms. Rafik, Ms. Burns, and Ms. MacKenzie.

Defendants Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, Inc., Harvard Pilgrim – Lahey Health Select HMO, and Lahey Clinic Foundation, Inc. oppose K.D.'s claim, arguing that the value of the court's remand order has not yet been determined and that an award of fees should be deferred until after remand. K.D. opposes this contention, arguing that postponing an award of fees undercuts the First Circuit's acknowledgment that interim fees serve an important purpose in ERISA cases. The parties have submitted their positions on the issue of attorney's fees, with K.D. requesting $81,047.00 in fees and $400.00 in costs, and Defendants disputing the quantum of the fee request.

Nicole D. Evans was employed as a full-time Lead Teacher in the Infant Room at Larchmont Baptist Church Infant Care Center, Inc. (Larchmont) starting in September 2006. In July 2009, one of Evans's co-workers was terminated, and this co-worker subsequently filed an age and disability discrimination charge with the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on July 16, 2009. Larchmont's Director, Kim Carmi, asked Evans to provide a written statement confirming that the terminated co-worker had been sleeping on the job, but Evans refused. Carmi made the same request to two other co-workers, who complied. Evans wrote a letter to the EEOC stating that her co-worker had been wrongfully terminated and that Carmi had forced staff to complete a survey and submit statements about the co-worker sleeping on the job.

Plaintiff Evans alleges that after she refused to provide the written statement, she was reassigned to the Toddler II Room as an Assistant Teacher on August 7, 2009, resulting in a decrease in her weekly work hours from forty to thirty-two hours per week and a reduction in her weekly pay. She also began receiving written reprimands, which she had not received prior to her reassignment. Evans filed her first retaliation charge with the EEOC on August 17, 2009. Nine and a half months later, on June 3, 2010, Larchmont terminated Evans, and she alleges that this termination was Larchmont's final retaliatory act related to her conduct surrounding her co-worker's termination in 2009. Defendant Larchmont contends that Evans's termination was not retaliatory.

Evans filed her second charge with the EEOC on July 15, 2010, claiming she had been subjected to a hostile work environment and discharged in retaliation for participating in protected activity under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The EEOC issued its Determination on August 26, 2010, finding that Larchmont had retaliated against Evans by demoting her and issuing her a Record of Discussion. The EEOC then issued Evans a Notice of Right to Sue letter on March 18, 2011, on her first retaliation charge. Evans timely filed a Complaint on June 9, 2011, against Larchmont, Carmi, and Laura Reed, Chairwoman of Larchmont's Board of Directors, alleging retaliation under the ADA and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The parties engaged in various pre-litigation events, including the filing of motions to dismiss and a motion for summary judgment, before the Court ordered Larchmont to retain legal counsel by November 12, 2012, or face default judgment. Larchmont failed to retain counsel, and the Clerk entered default against it on November 16, 2012.

Bryan R. Mudrich worked in the Tire and Lube Express department of Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. for approximately one year before his termination in the spring of 2010. Mudrich alleges that he was wrongfully terminated because Wal-Mart engaged in gender discrimination. He claims that he was accused of providing a free tire rotation on April 3, 2010, that his co-worker, Catherine Kinnonen, had provided, and that he was the victim of gender discrimination because Wal-Mart did not discipline Kinnonen. 

Mudrich was a "Service Writer" responsible for writing orders and performing services such as oil changes, tire replacements, and tire rotations. He contends that on April 3, 2010, Kinnonen used a scanner he was logged in on to scan in at least one customer vehicle, and as a result, he was unable to log into Wal-Mart's system and was sent to take his lunch break. Mudrich met with his supervisor, Regina Gilmore, and Kinnonen on April 4, 2010, and denied giving away services. Gilmore showed him two tickets from the previous day and told him that they indicated he was the service writer. Mudrich stated that Kinnonen had written up the tickets while he was at lunch.

Wal-Mart contends that it terminated Mudrich because he did not comply with a company policy that required him to write a corrective action plan as part of his discipline for violations that occurred on March 20, 2010. Mudrich received reprimands for violations of Wal-Mart policies, including a verbal coaching for inappropriately combining two customer discounts without manager approval and a written coaching for attendance and punctuality concerns. On March 20, 2010, Gilmore received a report indicating that Mudrich may have provided services without charging for them. Mudrich was given a D-Day, a one-day paid suspension, and was required to submit an action plan for improved performance, which he did not do. After his D-Day, Mudrich met with his support manager, Buck Wiley, and another assistant manager, Ahmed Jama, to finish his D-Day process, but Jama did not ask for Mudrich's action plan and instead told Wiley that Mudrich should not have been given a D-Day. Mudrich received a performance evaluation on April 24, 2010, which stated that he needed to improve in several areas but did not mention any disciplinary actions. On April 30, 2010, Gilmore met with Mudrich and asked him to complete an action plan, admission letter, and apology, which Mudrich refused to do, leading to his termination.

Northwest Airlines, Inc. employed female cabin attendants, who were subject to different pay and working conditions than their male counterparts. Plaintiff alleges that the company paid female cabin attendants lower salaries and benefits, including pension payments, and provided them with inferior lodging on layovers, requiring them to share double rooms. Defendant contends that the pay and benefits were based on legitimate factors, such as job requirements and seniority. The female cabin attendants were also subject to weight requirements, which they claim were discriminatory and not applied to male cabin attendants. 

The plaintiffs, female cabin attendants, claim that they were paid less than male cabin attendants, known as pursers, despite performing equal work. They allege that the company's pay practices violated the Equal Pay Act of 1963 and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The plaintiffs also claim that the company's weight requirements, which included weighing female cabin attendants and conditioning their employment on maintaining a prescribed weight, were discriminatory and not job-related. Defendant Northwest Airlines, Inc. contends that its pay practices were lawful and that the weight requirements were necessary for the job.

Prior to the lawsuit, the female cabin attendants were employed by Northwest Airlines, Inc. under collective bargaining agreements that governed their pay, benefits, and working conditions. The company had a system of seniority, which affected pay and benefits, and the plaintiffs claim that this system was used to discriminate against them. The plaintiffs filed written consents to become parties to the lawsuit, and the court certified a class of female cabin attendants who were employed by the company at various times. The parties engaged in pre-litigation communications and negotiations, but were unable to resolve their disputes, leading to the filing of the lawsuit.

Apple, a bank, uses the "available balance" method to calculate a customer's balance for overdraft purposes, which takes into account both settled and authorized but not yet settled transactions. Plaintiffs allege that Apple charges overdraft fees on "Authorize Positive, Settle Negative" (APSN) transactions, where a customer's account has sufficient funds to cover a transaction at the time of authorization, but subsequent intervening transactions cause the account to become overdrawn by the time the initial transaction settles. Plaintiff alleges that Apple reduces the customer's available balance as soon as a transaction is authorized, and then assesses overdraft fees if subsequent transactions would leave the available balance negative, even if the initial transaction had sufficient funds at the time of authorization.

Plaintiffs contend that this practice violates Apple's Membership and Account Agreement (the Contract), which they claim does not authorize Apple to charge overdraft fees on APSN transactions. Plaintiffs also allege that Apple's Opt-In Form, which allows customers to opt-in to overdraft protection, is misleading because it states that Apple determines the account's available balance for overdraft purposes when the merchant receives authorization for transaction payment. Instead, Plaintiffs claim that Apple authorizes transactions on positive funds, sets those funds aside on hold, and then fails to use those same funds to post those same transactions, resulting in additional overdraft fees.

The parties' relationship is that of a bank and its customers, with Apple providing banking services to Plaintiffs. The nature of the dispute is a breach of contract claim, with Plaintiffs alleging that Apple's APSN policy is not authorized by the Contract and is therefore a breach of the agreement. Apple's actions, as described by Plaintiffs, include authorizing transactions, setting aside funds, and assessing overdraft fees, all of which are relevant to the dispute. Relevant pre-litigation events include the execution of the Contract and Opt-In Form, as well as the assessment of overdraft fees on APSN transactions. The Contract and Opt-In Form are key documents in the dispute, and their terms and conditions are central to the parties' contentions.

Several former employees of Tri-State Plumbing, Heating & Air Conditioning Contractors, Inc. ("Tri-State") filed charges of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission ("EEOC"). The EEOC investigated these charges and found reasonable cause to believe that the employees had been unlawfully discriminated against on the basis of sex and race. Plaintiff alleges that African American employees were subjected to racially derogatory comments, graffiti, and other unwelcome conduct based on race, and were assigned less desirable jobs than similarly situated white employees. The EEOC also contends that a female employee was denied overtime work on the basis of her sex. Defendant Tri-State argues that the EEOC's attempt at conciliation was not in good faith.

The EEOC had sent Tri-State proposed conciliation agreements and letters inviting it to engage in conciliation discussions to resolve the charges of discrimination. Tri-State's attorney notified the EEOC that his client was interested in resolving the charges through conciliation but had some concerns. The parties exchanged letters, with Tri-State challenging the basis for the EEOC's determination that its employees were the subject of discrimination and requesting more information about the EEOC's calculation of damages and attorney's fees. The EEOC responded, refusing to reconsider its findings and expressing confusion at Tri-State's request for more information. The EEOC ultimately declared that the conciliation process had failed and filed the complaint in this case on September 29, 2005.

The EEOC's investigation and conciliation efforts were preceded by the filing of charges by several former Tri-State employees, including Donnell Addison, Karen Alexander, Eddie Anderson, Keith Clark, Billy Herring, Kendrick Hunt, Roy Oliver, and Fred Wiggins. These individuals were employed by Tri-State and were members of the United Association of Plumbers, Pipefitters & Sprinklerfitters, Plumbers Local Union No. 17 ("Local 17"). The EEOC's complaint alleges that Tri-State discriminated against these employees on the basis of sex and race, and that the company fired several employees either on the basis of race or because they complained about discriminatory treatment. Defendant Tri-State contends that the EEOC's conciliation effort was not in good faith, and that the complaint must be dismissed as a result.

Plaintiff, an African American male, began working as a payroll coordinator at Partners in Care, a home health aide and personal care worker service, on October 21, 1985. His responsibilities included compiling and recording data for Partners' payroll periods. However, he was discharged on November 8, 1985, less than three weeks after his employment commenced, due to poor performance, including untimely and inaccurate work. Plaintiff alleges that he was terminated because of his sex, and also claims to have experienced unsolicited encounters with a Caucasian male co-worker, Anthony, including receiving a note expressing personal interest, being sexually harassed at the copy machine, and being approached in the men's room.

Plaintiff filed an administrative complaint with the New York State Division of Human Rights (DHR) and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on November 13, 1985. The DHR issued a Determination and Order After Investigation on September 25, 1986, finding no probable cause that Partners engaged in unlawful discriminatory practice by terminating plaintiff. The investigation revealed that plaintiff was warned about performance problems, including unacceptable mistakes and delays, as early as one week into his employment. Plaintiff's supervisor, Lillian Pabon, advised him that his performance was unacceptable and that he needed to improve. Plaintiff responded that he was trying to be friendly, but was also advised to confine his social activities to non-work time.

Plaintiff alleges that he made occasional telephone calls to the DHR and EEOC between 1985 and 1996 to inquire about the status of his case, but was told that the matter was under investigation. In August 1996, plaintiff requested a Right to Sue Letter from the EEOC, which he received on October 1, 1996. Plaintiff then filed a complaint with the court on November 25, 1996, alleging that he was terminated in violation of Title VII. Defendant Partners contends that plaintiff's claims are barred by the doctrine of laches due to his delay in requesting a Notice of Right to Sue and filing his complaint, and argues that this delay has severely prejudiced Partners' ability to investigate and respond to plaintiff's allegations. Plaintiff contends that his delay was reasonable, given that he was waiting for the completion of the administrative process and was told that the matter was under investigation.

Charles Gregory Butta, a white male, applied for the position of executive secretary for the Human Relations Commission of Anne Arundel County in March 1973. The position had been occupied by Charles White, a black male, since 1967. Butta had a Master of Social Work degree and had accumulated eighteen graduate credits toward a doctorate in social administration. He had also worked as a social caseworker, family therapist, and personnel counseling specialist. The Human Relations Commission (HRC) reviewed and screened applications, and interviewed approximately six individuals, including Butta and Eurphan McLaughlin, a black male. The HRC concluded that Butta was its first choice for the position, and McLaughlin its second choice, based on Butta's poised and knowledgeable interview and his superior experience.

Plaintiff Butta alleges that he was rejected for the position because of his race. He contends that County Executive Joseph Alton, who had the sole power to select the executive secretary, offered the position to McLaughlin without interviewing Butta, and later told Butta that he preferred a black person for the position. Butta also alleges that Alton's stated reason for rejecting him, that he was emotionally immature, was a pretext for racial discrimination. Defendant Anne Arundel County contends that Butta was rejected because Alton and his assistants believed him to be emotionally immature, and that this was a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for the rejection.

Prior to the lawsuit, Butta had contacted Don Pennington, the County's personnel officer, seeking an explanation for his rejection and an opportunity to persuade Alton that he was qualified for the position. Alton did interview Butta, but ultimately selected Robert Nealy, a black male, for the position several months later. Nealy had worked in the County's budget office and had substantial contact with Alton, who was favorably impressed with him. The HRC had not reviewed Nealy's application, and some members of the HRC were displeased with Alton's rejection of Butta and appointment of Nealy. Alton told several members of the HRC that he wanted a black person for the position, but later testified that he said this only to justify his hiring decision in a way that would be least offensive to the HRC members. Butta worked for Montgomery County as its Director of Volunteer Services from 1973 to 1977, and later held part-time teaching positions at various local colleges and universities.

Louis G. Buttell was hired by the American Podiatric Medical Association (APMA) in July 1967 as the Director of Public Affairs. His duties included responsibility for the total communications programs for the APMA, and he supervised a staff of six. From 1967 until 1986, Buttell received no formal performance evaluations, although he typically would receive an annual bonus and salary increase at the end of each year. In early May 1986, Norman Klombers, Buttell's direct supervisor, warned Buttell that the Board of Trustees was not satisfied with his performance and that he was to be evaluated in three months. The APMA contracted with Peat, Marwick, an outside consulting agency, to conduct a management review of the APMA staff, which ultimately filed a report critical of Buttell. In September 1986, Buttell was fired for "performance-related reasons" at the age of 59. He was replaced by Dean Wakefield, who was 56 years old.

Buttell alleges that beginning in September 1984, Klombers engaged in a pattern of misconduct calculated to have him fired, including putting him in embarrassing positions, making misrepresentations to the Board of Trustees and the outside consulting firm regarding his job performance, creating erroneous records, altering memoranda, and generating inaccurate minutes of executive committee conferences. Buttell claims that this "misconduct" was brought to the attention of the Board of Trustees, which nevertheless affirmed Klombers' decision to terminate him. Buttell maintains that his termination was discriminatory, based on age, in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA). He also asserts state law claims for breach of contract and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

Defendants contend that Buttell was not qualified to continue as Director of Public Affairs, citing Klombers' assessment of his performance. However, Buttell challenges the evaluations of his work performance, relying on his nineteen years of service at APMA, with annual bonus and salary increases, as evidence of his continued "qualification". The Board of Trustees denied Buttell's request for a review of the termination, stating that "the procedures" were followed, and Buttell was not afforded a review of the merits of his termination nor given an opportunity to present his case to the Board. The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding Buttell's termination, with Buttell alleging age discrimination and defendants arguing that the decision was based on legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons.

Tracy Newell began working at the U.S. Treasury Department's Bureau of Engraving and Printing (BEP) in 1987. In 2004, she became a Plate Printer and worked on the day shift under the direct supervision of Bob Smith. In 2012, Newell applied for a Temporary Plate Printer Assistant Supervisor position, which was advertised as a temporary promotion not-to-exceed one year. She was selected for the position and switched to the evening shift, with Denita Simmons as her direct supervisor and Bob Smith as her second-line supervisor.

Newell's temporary promotion was set to end on September 22, 2013, but she continued in the position until March 2014, when she was reassigned to her former Plate Printer position. The circumstances surrounding her reassignment are disputed. Newell alleges that her position was made permanent after a one-year probationary period, in keeping with past BEP practices, and that her reassignment was a demotion. Defendant contends that there was no permanent assignment and that Newell's reassignment was a return to her prior position after the temporary term ended.

Newell also alleges that she experienced harassment and a hostile work environment during her time as a Temporary Assistant Supervisor. She claims that a male co-worker asked her to go to a strip club and engage in sexual activity with another female employee, and that she was referred to as "Baby" and "Honey" by another individual and touched on the buttock by a third male. Newell also alleges that she observed two unnamed superiors engaging in sexual behavior in the workplace on several occasions. Additionally, she claims that a male co-worker, Dennis Dunn, approached her at work, became aggressive, and referred to her as an "idiot." Newell reported the incident to her supervisor, Denita Simmons, who spoke with Dunn and told him to take a cooling-down period. Dunn was later disciplined with a one-day suspension and required to take an anger management class, although Newell disputes that he actually served the suspension. Newell also alleges that Dunn accused her of having an affair with a co-worker during a meeting to address the earlier incident. Other individuals present at the meeting have different recollections of the event. Newell also points to a separate conflict with a co-worker, Charles Wheelock, who raised his voice at her and treated her in a hostile manner following a dispute over an overtime schedule.

The plaintiffs, including Christine J. Amos, Judy L. Bawden, Deniece Kanon, April Joyce Riding, Ruth Arriola, and Shelleen Adamson, were employed by Beehive Clothing Mills, an unincorporated division of the Corporation of the Presiding Bishop of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The plaintiffs worked in various roles, including personnel, seamstressing, and other positions, from the 1970s to the early 1980s. The Mormon Church, also known as the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, is a religious association with headquarters in Salt Lake City, Utah, and has members worldwide. The Church conducts various activities, including worship services and ceremonies, and has temples where certain ceremonies and activities are reserved for members who have met worthiness requirements and have been granted a temple recommend.

Plaintiff alleges that they were terminated from their employment at Beehive Clothing Mills due to their inability or refusal to satisfy the worthiness requirements of the Mormon Church for temple recommends. The plaintiffs contend that they were employees performing non-religious activities and that their termination was a violation of federal and state antidiscrimination laws. The defendants, including the Corporation of the Presiding Bishop and the Corporation of the President of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, contend that the activities of Beehive Clothing Mills are religious in nature and that the plaintiffs' termination was lawful. The defendants also argue that the federal and state exemptions from antidiscrimination laws for religious organizations are constitutional.

The plaintiffs and defendants have engaged in discovery and have exchanged statements of facts, depositions, and affidavits. The plaintiffs have moved for summary judgment, arguing that the activities of Beehive Clothing Mills are not religious in nature and that their termination was unlawful. The defendants have opposed the motion, arguing that factual disputes remain and that the activities of Beehive Clothing Mills are indeed religious. The court must determine whether the activities of Beehive Clothing Mills are religious or secular and whether the plaintiffs' termination was a violation of federal and state antidiscrimination laws. Relevant pre-litigation events include the plaintiffs' employment and termination at Beehive Clothing Mills, as well as the Mormon Church's requirements for temple recommends and its policies regarding the manufacture and distribution of temple clothing and garments. The plaintiffs have also alleged that they were subjected to intentional infliction of emotional distress and invasion of privacy due to the defendants' conduct regarding the worthiness requirements and their termination.

Fourteen foreign seamen, all residents of the Philippines, worked on the M/V Fir Grove, a vessel owned by Japanese defendants. Plaintiff Edwin Jose and his wife, Augustine Jose, also brought a maritime personal injury claim under the Jones Act. The seamen allege that they were not paid their full wages and were subjected to various forms of mistreatment, including blacklisting, outrageous conduct, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The plaintiffs claim that the defendants deliberately misrepresented the pay scales to them and to the International Transport Workers Federation (ITF), and that they were deprived of "property" each month they received lower wages than those set forth in ITF wage schedules.

The plaintiffs and defendants have a complex and contentious relationship, with multiple claims and counterclaims. The plaintiffs allege that the defendants' actions were part of a "pattern of racketeering" and seek to recover damages under the federal racketeering law, 18 U.S.C. § 1961, et seq. The defendants contend that the plaintiffs' RICO claims are an attempt to "rekindle" previously dismissed fraud claims and that United States RICO laws should not be applied to the plaintiffs' claims due to the lack of contacts or connection to the United States. The defendants also argue that the alleged conduct took place outside of the U.S. territory, primarily in the Philippines and Japan.

The parties have engaged in extensive pre-litigation communications and discovery, with multiple motions and amendments to the complaint. The plaintiffs have sought to add new defendants and supplement the pretrial order with additional documents, while the defendants have moved to dismiss various claims, including the pendent common law claims and the RICO claims. The plaintiffs' counsel has submitted exhibits and affidavits in support of their claims, including expert opinions on Philippine law and its application to the case. The defendants have also submitted evidence, including proffers that they will submit to the jurisdiction of the Philippine courts if the pendent claims are dismissed. The case has a complex procedural history, with multiple opinions and rulings, but the underlying factual dispute remains centered on the seamen's allegations of unpaid wages and mistreatment.

Shula G. Elbaz, a United States citizen of Israeli national origin, was employed by Congregation Beth Judea, Inc., an Illinois not-for-profit corporation, as its education director from July 1, 1978, to June 30, 1991. She administered a religious school for the children of Congregation members. On October 25, 1990, Elbaz complained to her superiors about what she perceived to be discriminatory treatment, specifically the Congregation's practice of not timely making its employer contributions to her retirement plan, unlike its timely contributions to the retirement plans of the Congregation's rabbi and cantor, who were male and non-Israeli employees. Six weeks later, on December 12, 1990, Elbaz, unsatisfied with the Congregation's reaction, directed her attorney to demand that the Congregation remedy its discriminatory treatment. Within days, on December 20, 1990, the Congregation verbally informed Elbaz that it would not renew her employment contract. Elbaz's term of employment expired on June 30, 1991, and she was terminated.

Plaintiff Elbaz alleges that the Congregation's failure to renew her employment contract was in retaliation for her complaints about the retirement plan contributions. She also claims that she was not properly compensated according to contractual provisions dealing with severance pay, vacations, work-related expenses, and salary, and that she was demeaningly referred to as "the 'Israeli.'" Defendant Congregation contends that Elbaz's charge of discrimination was untimely filed and that it is not an "employer" as defined in 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b) because it does not have the required number of employees. The Congregation also argues that Elbaz's complaint is beyond the scope of her EEOC charge and that she has not alleged unlawful disparate treatment.

Elbaz filed charges against the Congregation with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the Illinois Department of Human Rights (IDHR) on August 30, 1991, alleging discrimination based on sex and national origin. The EEOC issued a right to sue notice on November 29, 1991, which Elbaz received on December 16, 1991. Elbaz maintains that her complaints about the retirement plan contributions were protected by federal laws, including Title VII and the Fair Labor Standards Act, and that her termination was a retaliatory discharge. The Congregation disputes these allegations, arguing that Elbaz has not shown that she was treated differently than other employees and that its decision not to renew her contract was not motivated by retaliatory intent.

Sean T. Wiley, an inmate, filed a pro se civil rights action against Warden Veronica Fernandez, Hospital Administrator Kim Burdo, and the United States of America. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant Burdo wrongfully denied him access to over-the-counter medication. Plaintiff contends that this denial was improper and violated his rights. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that the denial was proper and in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, including 28 C.F.R. § 549.31(c). 

Prior to the lawsuit, Plaintiff was an inmate at Raybrook F.C.I., where Defendants Fernandez and Burdo were employed. The events giving rise to the lawsuit occurred while Plaintiff was incarcerated at Raybrook F.C.I. Plaintiff submitted his complaint and amended complaint, to which Defendants responded with a motion for summary judgment. Magistrate Judge Christian F. Hummel issued a Report-Recommendation recommending that Defendants' motion be granted and that Plaintiff's remaining claims be dismissed with prejudice. Plaintiff then filed objections to the Report-Recommendation, which included arguments and evidence that had previously been presented to Magistrate Judge Hummel or could have been presented to him.

The parties have a relationship based on Plaintiff's incarceration at Raybrook F.C.I. and Defendants' employment there. The nature of the dispute is centered around the alleged wrongful denial of access to over-the-counter medication and the propriety of this denial under relevant laws and regulations. Plaintiff alleges that Defendants violated his rights, while Defendants contend that their actions were proper and lawful. The lawsuit has proceeded through various stages, including the filing of complaints, motions, and reports, with the parties presenting their arguments and evidence to the court.

Rohm and Haas Company ("Rohm and Haas") employed Greg Sailor at its waste water treatment plant in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where Nirav Panchal, an engineer, was Sailor's supervisor. On March 2, 2009, Bob Clark, a private contractor and friend of Sailor's, raised safety concerns with Panchal about a piece of rebar sticking up in the yard at the plant. According to Sailor, Panchal was "dismissive" of Clark's concerns. Two days later, on March 4, 2009, Sailor told Panchal that Clark was "angry and offended" at the way Panchal had treated him. Rohm and Haas alleges that Sailor said to Panchal, "let me give you some advice, you piss people off and you should treat people better. All the criminals are not in jail yet," and also that Clark "has some fucked up friends and that people get run over every day in here." Panchal felt threatened by these comments and reported them to his supervisor, Jeff Millman.

Plaintiff Rohm and Haas alleges that Sailor's comments constituted threatening behavior, and that it terminated Sailor on March 20, 2009, for violating Bristol Site Rules 15 and 21, which prohibit "using abusive, threatening, and obscene language," and "harassment .. or any behavior that threatens the safety or well being of another employee," respectively. Defendant United Steel, Paper and Forestry, Rubber, Manufacturing Energy, Allied Industrial and Service Workers International Union, and Defendant United Steelworkers Local 88 G (collectively, "the Union") contend that Rohm and Haas did not have just cause to terminate Sailor. The Union filed a grievance based on Sailor's termination, which was submitted to arbitration under the collective bargaining agreement ("CBA") between Rohm and Haas and the Union. During the arbitration proceedings, additional allegations of misconduct by Sailor were uncovered, including a private meeting with another plant employee, Robert Derr, on March 9, 2009, where Sailor allegedly produced a knife and made threatening comments about Panchal, referring to him as an "Indian boy."

The Union and Rohm and Haas have a collective bargaining agreement that provides for grievance and arbitration procedures, and the arbitrator's decision "shall be final and binding on both parties." The Union alleges that Rohm and Haas did not follow the procedures outlined in the CBA when it terminated Sailor, and that the termination was without just cause. Rohm and Haas contends that it had just cause to terminate Sailor due to his threatening behavior, and that the arbitrator's decision to reinstate Sailor with a sixty-day suspension was erroneous. The parties' dispute ultimately led to the filing of this lawsuit, with Rohm and Haas seeking to vacate the arbitration award and the Union seeking to confirm it.

Chris-Craft, a manufacturer of boats, and Seaward, a former dealer of Chris-Craft products, had a contractual relationship governed by written Dealer Agreements executed at annual sales conferences starting in July 1983 for Seaward's Portland store and in July 1984 for its Seattle store. The agreements described the basic relationship between the parties, with Chris-Craft appointing Seaward as its authorized dealer for the retail sale of its products, subject to the terms and conditions of the agreement. The appointment was non-exclusive, and Chris-Craft reserved the right to appoint other dealers and sell products directly to any person or entity. Seaward agreed to purchase and carry a representative inventory of Chris-Craft products, promote their sale, and maintain an acceptable floor plan and business practices.

Seaward alleges that Chris-Craft failed to adequately reimburse it for warranty repairs, boat show expenses, and advertising expenses, and that Chris-Craft wrongfully terminated the dealership agreements. Seaward claims that Chris-Craft owes it $40,000 in warranty claims and seeks compensatory and punitive damages. Chris-Craft contends that it terminated the agreements due to Seaward's poor sales performance and inability to maintain an adequate financing arrangement, as required by the agreements. Chris-Craft also argues that Seaward's actions, including withholding payment to Borg-Warner, the financing company, were in breach of the inventory security agreement.

The relationship between the parties began to deteriorate in 1985, when Seaward advised Chris-Craft that it wanted to cancel certain boat orders and delay production on others. Borg-Warner notified Seaward that it was delinquent in its payment for two yachts and demanded immediate payment of $185,000. Seaward sent a letter to Chris-Craft acknowledging serious sales problems and asking Chris-Craft to "put the brakes" on boat orders scheduled for 1986. A dispute arose concerning whether Chris-Craft had adequately reimbursed Seaward for certain warranty repairs and expenses, with Seaward demanding $33,843.74 and Chris-Craft offering $9,841.41. Chris-Craft eventually paid Seaward $7,445.83 for warranty claims owed to the Seattle store but demanded payment of $7,038.27 from the Portland store. Seaward withheld payment to Borg-Warner, hoping to pressure Chris-Craft to pay the money due for warranty claims directly to Borg-Warner. Borg-Warner issued another demand for payment to Seaward, asserting that a total of $46,945.86 was past due for interest on the Portland and Seattle inventory. The situation between Seaward and Borg-Warner deteriorated, leading to Borg-Warner filing a lawsuit against Seaward in August 1986. Chris-Craft terminated the dealership agreements with Seaward's Seattle store in November 1986 and with the Portland store in December 1986. Seaward asserts that the agreements were terminated in retaliation for its dispute with Chris-Craft over warranty claims, while Chris-Craft maintains that the termination was due to Seaward's poor sales performance.

Keyla Tosado Cotto was employed by General Accident Insurance Company of Puerto Rico (GAIC), where she worked under the supervision of Tomás Burgos Sánchez. Plaintiff alleges that Burgos subjected her to unwelcome sexual advances and harassment, including calling her into his office to ogle her, discussing his personal and sexual life with her, grabbing her hands, touching her thighs, and attempting to kiss her. These incidents allegedly occurred in Burgos' office, and Tosado claims she never reported them to anyone at GAIC except that she told her mother about the incidents. 

Tosado contends that after rejecting Burgos' attempt to kiss her, she took several days off work due to the emotional impact of the incident, and upon returning, found her desk moved and her job assignments altered without explanation. She was terminated approximately one week later. Plaintiff alleges that her termination was a direct result of her refusal to submit to Burgos' advances. Defendant General Accident Insurance Company of Puerto Rico asserts that it is not liable for the alleged harassment because Tosado failed to notify the company and the company had no actual or constructive knowledge of the alleged harassment. 

Defendant also claims that it has a written policy prohibiting sexual harassment, which Tosado was aware of but failed to invoke its procedures to address the alleged harassment. Furthermore, Defendant argues that Tosado's termination was not related to the alleged sexual harassment. The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding Tosado's employment, the events leading to her termination, and the company's knowledge and response to the alleged harassment. Tosado's deposition and an unverified copy of a receipt indicating she received a copy of GAIC's employment manual are part of the evidence submitted by the Defendant.

Joseph Graham, an employee of Bodine Electric Company, alleges that he was discriminated against by the company due to his race when he was not promoted. Graham filed a two-count complaint in August 1990, with Count I brought under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Count II brought under 42 U.S.C. § 1981. The company, Bodine Electric, argues that Graham does not have a viable Section 1981 claim under the tests enunciated by the United States Supreme Court in Patterson v. McLean Credit Union. Graham contends that the Patterson decision does not apply to his case because it was effectively overruled by the Civil Rights Act of 1991, which was passed on November 21, 1991. 

Graham alleges that he was subjected to racial discrimination by Bodine Electric, which led to his non-promotion. Bodine Electric contends that it did not discriminate against Graham and that its actions were lawful under the applicable laws at the time. The parties disagree on whether the 1991 Act applies to Graham's case, which was pending at the time the Act was passed. Graham claims that the 1991 Act should be applied retroactively, while Bodine Electric argues that it should only be applied prospectively. 

The dispute between Graham and Bodine Electric began when Graham was not promoted, leading him to file his complaint in August 1990. The case has been ongoing since then, with the parties exchanging arguments and evidence. The court must now decide whether the 1991 Act applies to Graham's case, which will determine the outcome of his Section 1981 claim. The legislative history of the 1991 Act and the principles of statutory construction will be crucial in determining the intent of Congress regarding the retroactive application of the Act.

Sergeant Peter Hansche, a Caucasian male police officer in the New Orleans Police Department's (NOPD) Homicide Unit, alleges that he was subjected to a toxic work environment and harassment by his supervisor, Lieutenant Jimmie Turner, an African American male. Sgt. Hansche claims that Lt. Turner made repeated sexual and racially inappropriate comments, including calling him names, making suggestive remarks, and initiating physical contact, such as kissing and embracing him. Plaintiff alleges that Lt. Turner also allowed a racially segregated work environment, assigning black detectives to work only with other blacks, and made comments about white people looking the same. 

Plaintiff alleges that he complained to his supervisors on multiple occasions, but no action was taken against Lt. Turner. Sgt. Hansche specifically alleges that Lt. Turner harassed him on three separate occasions: in September 2016, when Lt. Turner nonconsensually embraced him; in October 2016, when Lt. Turner kissed him on the head; and in November 2017, when Lt. Turner asked to call him a "cracker." Sgt. Hansche also alleges that Lt. Turner retaliated against him, restricting his time off, forcing him to take leave without pay, and assigning him less favorable work after he reported the harassment.

The City of New Orleans and Lt. Turner are the defendants in this case. Sgt. Hansche's relationship with Lt. Turner is that of supervisor and subordinate, with Lt. Turner commanding the Homicide Unit where Sgt. Hansche works. The nature of the dispute is Sgt.
