Hansche's allegations of sex and race discrimination, retaliation, and hostile work environment, as well as sexual assault, against Lt. Turner and the City. Defendant Lt. Turner's contentions are not explicitly stated, but it can be inferred that he denies the allegations made by Sgt. Hansche, as he filed a motion to dismiss the complaint. Relevant pre-litigation events include Sgt. Hansche's complaints to his supervisors, the NOPD's alleged inaction, and the dismantling of Sgt. Hansche's squad by Lt. Turner after Sgt. Hansche reported a family emergency through the NOPD Officer Assistance Program.

Diana Grastorf, a woman over 40, was employed as a Branch Manager at a bank for an unspecified period. Plaintiff alleges she was qualified for her position, had received good performance reviews, and was given a merit increase in pay in January 2019. At some point, the bank terminated her position, and her duties were subsequently performed by another person. The bank branch where Grastorf worked remained open after her termination. Grastorf contends that she experienced various negative consequences as a result of the bank's actions, including loss of income, fear, anxiety, severe humiliation, shame, embarrassment, emotional pain and suffering, loss of savings, and loss of enjoyment of life.

The parties' relationship was that of employer and employee, with Grastorf working as a Branch Manager at the bank. The nature of the dispute appears to be related to Grastorf's termination and the bank's subsequent actions. Plaintiff alleges that her termination was unjust, while the bank's actions and motivations are not specified in the complaint. The complaint does mention that Grastorf received good performance reviews and a merit increase in pay, which she contends suggests she was performing well in her role.

Prior to her termination, Grastorf had been performing her duties as Branch Manager, and the bank had been operating the branch where she worked. After her termination, the bank continued to operate the branch and had another person perform Grastorf's duties. The complaint does not specify the exact date of Grastorf's termination or the circumstances surrounding it, but it does allege that the bank's actions caused Grastorf significant harm and distress. Defendant's contentions regarding the termination and Grastorf's performance are not specified in the complaint.

In June 1989, Jaime and Graciela Barberis, a husband and wife residing in Ecuador, signed a "Property Management and Exclusive Rental Agreement" with Lewis & Silverman, Inc., a Maryland corporation, for their four-bedroom house located at 12 Leonard Court, Rockville, Maryland. Lewis & Silverman was acting as the property manager for the house through its agent, Gioia Mueller. Around the same time, Rosalie Coghill, a real estate agent employed by Dale Denton Realty, showed the house to Gilmore Thompson, a black male seeking to rent a home for himself and his family. Thompson tendered the requested rent and security deposit and signed a lease, but the Barberises later refused to sign the lease, allegedly because they learned that Thompson's family was black.

Plaintiff, the United States of America, alleges that the Barberises' refusal to rent the house to Thompson was based on his race. Thompson filed a complaint with the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) in June 1990, alleging that the Barberises had discriminated against him. He later amended his complaint to add familial status as an additional basis of discrimination. Although Thompson did not initially name Lewis & Silverman or Mueller in his complaint, he amended it in December 1990 to include them as respondents. Lewis & Silverman and Mueller contend that they were named as defendants outside the one-year statute of limitations period and that the complaint against them should be dismissed.

The parties' relationship and the nature of the dispute are centered around the alleged discriminatory housing practices. Lewis & Silverman and Mueller argue that they were not properly named in the administrative complaint and that the court lacks jurisdiction over them. The United States contends that Lewis & Silverman and Mueller were properly added to the complaint and that they participated in the administrative process, thereby waiving any objections to jurisdiction. Relevant pre-litigation events include Thompson's initial complaint to HUD, the investigation, and the amendments to the complaint. The employment and workplace facts relevant to the case include the roles of Lewis & Silverman and Mueller as property manager and agent, respectively, and their interactions with Thompson and the Barberises.

Tori Gandia was employed as a pilot by USAC Airways 693 LLC, a private aircraft rental and management company. Plaintiff alleges that she began working under Bradley Wernke, who was promoted to captain in approximately March 2020, and that Wernke started engaging in sexually harassing behavior towards her. Specifically, Plaintiff claims that Wernke hit her rear end, blocked the only exit to the airplane and demanded a kiss, and stopped her in the aisle of the airplane, grabbed her arm, and made her touch his private parts. Plaintiff asserts that she rebuffed Wernke's advances, after which he became belligerent and began taking actions that posed safety risks.

Plaintiff alleges that she complained about Wernke's harassment to the company's Chief Operating Officer, Matt Marci, and Chief Pilot, Fred Farid, but that her complaints were ignored. She then followed up with a text message to the human resources department complaining of harassment on or about July 7, 2020. Plaintiff also made safety complaints to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). Her employment with USAC Airways was terminated in August 2020, one month after she complained to the human resources department about harassment. The stated reason for her termination was a reduction in workforce due to the COVID-19 pandemic. However, Plaintiff contends that she was terminated in retaliation for the complaints she made, given the close temporal proximity of her termination to those complaints.

Defendant USAC Airways seeks dismissal of Plaintiff's retaliation claim, arguing that she "pleads no facts raising a plausible inference that she engaged in 'protected conduct.'" Defendant contends that reporting safety violations to the FAA or OSHA is not a "protected activity" under Title VII or the Texas Commission on Human Rights Act (TCHRA). Plaintiff, on the other hand, claims that she was the only pilot terminated at the time and that she could have been re-trained to fly other types of aircraft managed by Defendant. She maintains that she was not contacted when Defendant posted comparable open positions in the months following her termination.

Anthony W. Jackson, Sr., an African-American man, was employed in the housekeeping department of Cheyenne Mountain Conference Resort (CMCR) until his resignation in October 1998. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, he was disciplined more harshly than his Caucasian coworkers. Specifically, Jackson claims that he was suspended in April 1998 for allegedly being off-property without permission while on the clock, which he denies. Defendant CMCR contends that the suspension was based on a written statement from a coworker, Lisa Carter, which stated that she saw Jackson off-property on the dates in question. However, Jackson submits that numerous coworker statements rebut Carter's statement, asserting that Jackson was, in fact, at work at the times Carter allegedly saw him off-property.

Jackson also alleges that CMCR retaliated against him after he filed an EEOC complaint in July 1998, following his suspension. Plaintiff claims that CMCR continued to withhold his gratuities after the 90-day probationary period, suspended him for a second time in August 1998, and made life difficult for him and his family. Defendant CMCR maintains that the second suspension was due to Jackson's violation of company policy by making personal phone calls while on the clock. However, Jackson contends that the phone calls were work-related and that other employees were not similarly disciplined for making personal calls.

Prior to his resignation, Jackson had applied for a job with the Postal Service and had given CMCR two weeks' notice of his intent to leave. However, Jackson claims that CMCR took actions to be rid of him before the two weeks were up, scheduling him for work on a day he had previously been scheduled to be off and telling him that his last day would be earlier than expected. CMCR contends that Jackson's resignation was voluntary and that he was paid for the full two-week notice period, given a $100 bonus, and left on good terms with the company. The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding Jackson's resignation, with Jackson claiming that it was a constructive discharge due to CMCR's discriminatory treatment, while CMCR maintains that it was a voluntary resignation.

The plaintiff, an adult African-American citizen of the United States, is an employee of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) who began his career as an FBI agent in February 1991. He was first assigned to Los Angeles, California, where he worked in the bank robbery squad and later in the gang squad, focusing on African-American gangs. The plaintiff then served on the Joint Terrorism Task Force and was later selected to be a supervisor at FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C. in the Weapons of Mass Destruction Unit. After that assignment, he returned to Los Angeles to work as the International Terrorism supervisor, but only served in that capacity for one week before becoming a domestic terror and hate crimes coordinator.

In February 2001, the FBI posted a vacancy announcement for the position of Assistant Legal Attaché (ALAT) in Rome, Italy. The plaintiff timely submitted his application for the position, which was considered by the Investigative Services Division's Legat Screening Panel along with the application of Angelus Lagomarsino, a Caucasian applicant with an Italian surname. The Screening Panel rated the plaintiff as the highest among all applicants for the job, while Lagomarsino was ranked as tied for third place among the four recommended candidates. The Screening Panel's recommendations were then transmitted to the Special Agent Mid-Level Management Selection Board (SAMMS Board), which numerically ranked each candidate for the job on a zero to four point scale. The plaintiff earned the highest possible ranking from six of the seven SAMMS Board members and was the number one recommended candidate by the SAMMS Board. However, Director Louis J. Freeh bypassed the recommendation of the SAMMS Board and selected Lagomarsino over the plaintiff.

The plaintiff learned of this decision on June 7, 2001, and subsequently inquired about the details of the selection process. Within thirty days of learning of Lagomarsino's selection, the plaintiff contacted a DOJ Equal Employment Opportunity Counselor and initiated the counseling process, which concluded in August 2001. The plaintiff then filed a formal Complaint of Discrimination within fifteen days of his final counseling interview. The plaintiff alleges that he was rejected for the Rome ALAT position because of his race and national origin, and that Lagomarsino was selected because of his race and national origin. The plaintiff contends that he suffered and continues to suffer lost earnings and benefits, pain, suffering, humiliation, and mental distress as a result of this alleged discrimination. The defendant, on the other hand, argues that the plaintiff could not demonstrate that he was the victim of an adverse action and that the plaintiff had not shown that the legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons given for Director Freeh's decision to choose Lagomarsino over the plaintiff were pretextual.

Between 2008 and 2013, Plaintiff S.R. was trafficked for sex at several hotels in the Columbus area, including the Knights Inn by Wyndham. Plaintiff alleges that her traffickers rented rooms at these hotels, where she was forced to engage in commercial sex acts. Plaintiff contends that the hotel staff at the Knights Inn by Wyndham were aware of the trafficking, as there were several red flags, including paying for stays in cash, requesting rooms away from other guests, and frequent requests for linen changes. Plaintiff also alleges that her trafficker regularly paid off hotel staff to ignore signs of her trafficking and permitted her trafficker to rent rooms by the hour.

Plaintiff alleges that Defendant Wyndham profited from each room rental to her traffickers and customers, and that the company failed to create, adopt, implement, and enforce company-wide policies and procedures regarding human trafficking at its branded properties. Plaintiff contends that Wyndham's failure to prevent sex trafficking at its hotels constitutes participation in a venture that violated the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA). Defendant Wyndham, on the other hand, contends that it did not participate in a venture that violated the TVPRA, and that its failure to prevent sex trafficking cannot constitute "participation" under the law. Wyndham also argues that its relationship with the hotel operators, which are subject to franchise agreements, is too attenuated to support Plaintiff's claim.

Prior to commencing this action, Plaintiff alleges that she was a victim of sex trafficking at the Knights Inn by Wyndham, and that Wyndham's actions, or lack thereof, contributed to her trafficking. The parties' relationship is that of a hotel chain and a guest, with Plaintiff alleging that Wyndham's business practices and policies enabled her traffickers to operate at the hotel. The nature of the dispute is centered around Wyndham's alleged liability under the TVPRA for its role in facilitating sex trafficking at its hotels. Relevant pre-litigation events include the alleged trafficking of Plaintiff at the Knights Inn by Wyndham, as well as Wyndham's alleged failure to implement policies and procedures to prevent human trafficking at its hotels.

The plaintiff, a professor in the School of Interdisciplinary Studies at Miami University, suffers from lupus and has been granted accommodations by the University, including reduced advising responsibilities, reduced scholarly writing expectations, and scheduling accommodations. She was hired as a tenure-track professor in 1988, at the same time as Hays Cummins, a male professor, who was hired with a higher starting salary. The plaintiff and Cummins were of similar age and experience at the time of their hiring. In 1990, the plaintiff's lupus was diagnosed, and she did not immediately seek accommodations from the University. In 1991, the University granted the plaintiff tenure and promoted her to associate professor, and began making periodic adjustments to her salary to equalize it with Cummins'. 

The plaintiff sought accommodations for her medical condition in 1992, which the University agreed to provide. However, she believes that her salary has been negatively affected by these accommodations and/or by animus based on her handicap status or sex. The plaintiff contends that she has been paid a lower salary than male colleagues, including Cummins, and that this disparity is evidence of sex discrimination. She also argues that the University has unfairly considered the accommodations made for her handicap as detracting from her performance, and that she has been retaliated against for complaining about perceived gender bias in her compensation. The defendant, Miami University, has made periodic salary adjustments for the plaintiff, but she remains the lowest paid full professor in her department, with the second lowest paid being her only female colleague.

Plaintiff alleges that Defendant has engaged in sex discrimination in the terms of her employment by paying her a lower salary than it pays male colleagues, and that her sex must be the basis for the disparity. Defendant contends that the salary disparities are due to other factors, such as differences in job responsibilities and performance. The parties disagree on the extent to which the plaintiff's work is comparable to that of her male colleagues, including Cummins. The plaintiff points to evidence that she and Cummins have similar responsibilities and performance evaluations, while the defendant argues that there are significant differences in their job duties and qualifications. The plaintiff also alleges that she has been retaliated against for complaining about perceived gender bias in her compensation, citing smaller salary increases following her complaints. Defendant denies these allegations, and the parties' contentions regarding the salary disparities and the reasons for them are in dispute. Relevant pre-litigation events include the plaintiff's requests for accommodations, her complaints about perceived gender bias, and the defendant's responses to these complaints.

In 2005, Monika Starke, Christina Payne, and Robin Timmons, all female employees of CRST Van Expedited, Inc. (CRST), allegedly experienced sexual harassment by their lead drivers while training to become truck drivers. Specifically, Ms. Starke was allegedly harassed by Bob Smith and David Goodman in July and August 2005, Ms. Payne was allegedly harassed by Mark Hoagland between January and April 2005, and Ms. Timmons was allegedly harassed by John Boyle in December 2005 and January 2006. 

After these incidents, each of the women filed for bankruptcy. Ms. Starke and her husband filed a joint petition under Chapter 7 of the Bankruptcy Code in October 2005, listing CRST as a creditor but not disclosing any potential claim for sexual harassment. Ms. Payne filed a petition under Chapter 13 in October 2005, also not disclosing any claim for sexual harassment, and her plan was approved by the bankruptcy court in December 2005. Ms. Timmons and her husband filed a joint petition under Chapter 7 in March 2008, again not disclosing any potential claim against CRST. 

Plaintiff Monika Starke alleges that she was sexually harassed by her lead drivers while training to become a CRST truck driver, and that she did not intentionally fail to disclose her potential claim in her bankruptcy filing due to her limited English proficiency and reliance on an attorney. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) contends that it is categorically immune from the doctrine of judicial estoppel as a federal agency with its own interests, and that there is no evidence to suggest that Ms. Starke, Ms. Payne, or Ms. Timmons intended to mislead the bankruptcy court. Defendant CRST Van Expedited, Inc. contends that the three women made false assertions to the bankruptcy courts by not disclosing their potential claims and are now attempting to profit from those assertions in this lawsuit. CRST also argues that the EEOC's argument of categorical immunity is misplaced and contrary to Supreme Court precedent.

Plaintiff Boudreaux, a member of Local 1830 of the General Longshoremen Workers, International Longshoremen's Association, AFL-CIO, alleges that he and other members of his union, which is composed entirely of African American members, have been subjected to discriminatory employment practices by defendants Baton Rouge Marine Contractors, Inc. and Ryan Stevedoring Company, Inc. He contends that longshoremen's work at the dock is assigned in an alternating manner between Local 1830 and Local 1833, a union composed entirely of white members, resulting in individual white members receiving twice as many jobs as individual members of Local 1830. Boudreaux also alleges that undesirable jobs, such as those requiring heavy lifting and "dirty work," are always assigned to members of Local 1830, while desirable jobs, such as foreman and crane operator, are always assigned to members of Local 1833.

Plaintiff Boudreaux alleges that these practices have been ongoing and that he personally experienced discrimination as a result. He filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on January 26, 1967, which was more than 90 days after the alleged discriminatory practices occurred. Boudreaux had been physically injured on the job in March 1966 and had been receiving disability compensation under the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act from March 30, 1966, to January 30, 1969. During this time, he did not seek employment with any of the defendants and was physically incapacitated from working. Defendants contend that Boudreaux's complaint was not filed within the required 90-day timeframe and that he was not a "person aggrieved" as contemplated by the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Two other individuals, Henry Wells, Jr. and Daniel C. Collins, Jr., later intervened in the case, adopting Boudreaux's allegations as their own and alleging that the discriminatory practices continued from 1966 through February 1968. However, neither Wells nor Collins had filed a complaint with the EEOC. The defendants filed motions to strike and dismiss, arguing that Boudreaux's complaint failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted, and later filed motions for summary judgment, arguing that the record showed that Boudreaux did not file a complaint with the EEOC within the required 90-day timeframe and that the intervenors had never filed a charge with the EEOC.

Jabari Stafford, an African American student, joined the George Washington University (GWU) men's tennis team in the fall of 2014. Plaintiff alleges that shortly after joining the team, his teammates began using racial slurs, such as the n-word, and making derogatory comments about his race and American nationality. Stafford claims that he complained about this behavior to the head coach, Greg Munoz, at the beginning of his freshman year, but Munoz did nothing to address the issue and instead participated in and encouraged the mistreatment.

Stafford contends that the racial harassment continued throughout his freshman and sophomore years, with teammates using racial slurs and making derogatory comments about his race. He alleges that Munoz and other coaching staff singled him out because of his race and American nationality, and that he was suspended from the team in January 2015 after an altercation with a teammate. Stafford claims that he reported the racial harassment to Munoz and Nicole Early, the administrator for the tennis team, but they ignored his complaints.

Defendant GWU, on the other hand, contends that Stafford's suspension was due to his own behavior, including anger control issues and disrespect towards his teammates and coaches. The university also disputes Stafford's account of the meetings with Munoz and Early, claiming that the discussions focused on his suspension and playing time, rather than racial harassment. GWU also points out that Stafford did not formally report any incidents of racial harassment to the university during his time on the team, despite being informed of the procedures for doing so. Stafford's father, Tom, had discussions with Michael Tapscott, the Director of GWU's Multicultural Student Services Center, about his son's experiences on the team, but Tapscott's account of these conversations differs from Stafford's.

Tyler Gordon Ferrell was employed by EZPAWN Oklahoma, Inc. from August 2015 until his termination in February 2017. At the time of his termination, Ferrell was a 34-year-old male with a 90% disability rating due to his status as a military veteran. Ferrell alleges that his hiring constituted a contract, constructive contract, or quasi-contract between him and EZPAWN, which included terms that he would not be required to work on Sundays, would be allowed time off for medical appointments and Veterans' Administration services, and would not be asked to violate any laws or do anything unethical or immoral.

Ferrell filed a Charge of Discrimination with the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), alleging discrimination based on religion, disability, and retaliation. In his EEOC filing, Ferrell claimed that EZPAWN's management had agreed to accommodate his periodic absences due to medical appointments and his refusal to work on Sundays because of his religious beliefs. However, Ferrell alleged that a new store manager, who started more than a year after he was hired, harassed him when he sought time off due to his disability or religious beliefs, humiliated him in front of customers and co-workers, and complained about his requests to not work on Sundays. Ferrell reported the store manager's conduct to a district manager and the human resources department, but both the store manager and district manager allegedly retaliated against him by denying his request for a 10-day vacation, demoting him, and eventually terminating his employment.

Ferrell contends that he was told his demotion was because another employee had been hired to replace him, and that he was told his termination was due to labor costs. EZPAWN maintains that Ferrell filed his EEOC charge after his termination, while Ferrell alleges that he filed it before. Ferrell now asserts claims for gender discrimination, reverse age discrimination, disability discrimination, religious discrimination, national origin discrimination, breach of contract, and wrongful discharge in violation of public policy. EZPAWN has filed a motion to dismiss, and Ferrell has filed a motion to amend his complaint for a second time.

Latonia W. Lister, the plaintiff, is a former employee of the City of Las Vegas, the defendant. Lister alleges that she was subjected to discrimination and harassment throughout her career with the City, which she claims she was intimidated to report due to fear of mistreatment by her colleagues and supervisors. Lister contends that after she made complaints about her mistreatment, they were either ignored or resulted in derogatory or demeaning treatment by the Department. 

The City and Lister have a dispute regarding whether Lister suffered adverse employment actions in response to her protected activity of reporting the alleged incidents. Lister alleges that she suffered adverse employment actions after reporting two main incidents: the "dog taunting incident" on April 7, 2019, and the "cereal incident" on June 6, 2019. She claims that these incidents created a hostile work environment, citing various interactions with a coworker, Benneman, including being stared at, followed, and intimidated. Lister also identifies other incidents, such as being denied access to her personnel file and being placed behind a white male on a seniority list, as adverse actions.

Plaintiff Lister alleges that the City repeatedly violated its own zero-tolerance policy for acts of discrimination and its retaliation policy. Defendant City contends that Lister did not suffer any "loss of pay, seniority, benefits, or suffered any other materially adverse employment action" and that the minor employment actions that did occur were not pretext for retaliation. The City argues that Lister cannot establish a causal link between her protected activity and any adverse employment action. Lister's opposition to the City's motion for summary judgment argues that the City's actions were retaliatory and created a hostile work environment. Relevant pre-litigation events include Lister's reports of the alleged incidents to her Captain and the City's Human Resources office, as well as various interactions with Benneman and other coworkers.

Wesley Jarmon, an African-American employee in the Federal Communications Commission's (FCC) Audit Branch since 1987, alleges that he was subjected to race discrimination with respect to promotions. Plaintiff alleges that between 1987 and 1997, white employees were promoted above GS-13 without competitive application, while he was not. In 1997, when it was allegedly his "turn" to be promoted to GS-14, he was informed that any promotion would require competitive application. Jarmon also alleges that managers in the Audit Branch had a practice of identifying white male or female employees for promotion prior to an announcement of a vacancy. He points to particular instances in which white employees were hired for positions allegedly created for them, despite his allegedly better qualifications.

Plaintiff alleges that he was denied two specific promotional opportunities. The first was a GS-14 position for which he applied in 1998 under vacancy announcement # 98-91A. According to Jarmon, although the vacancy announcement specified that the position was in Washington, D.C., his manager selected Vincent Amalfitano, an FCC employee located in New York. When Jarmon complained to personnel about Mr. Amalfitano's ineligibility, the promotion was revoked, but no alternative promotion was issued. The second promotion involved a vacancy at GS-15 posted in August 1999, for which a white male was selected despite Jarmon's allegedly better qualifications. Jarmon also asserts that he was denied job assignments based on his race and that there was a correlation between job assignments, ratings, and promotions in the Audits Branch.

Defendant contends that Jarmon did not comply with administrative deadlines, as he did not contact an EEO counselor until December 1, 1999, more than 45 days after he became aware of the alleged discriminatory conduct. Jarmon opposes this contention, arguing that his efforts to contact the Office of Workplace Diversity (OWD) in May 1998 entitle him to waiver, estoppel, or equitable tolling of administrative deadlines. He claims that he was led to believe that an investigation was underway and that he relied on the advice of the OWD to his detriment. Defendant disputes this, stating that Jarmon's discussions with the OWD in May 1998 did not relate to a complaint about race discrimination, but rather to a complaint about a clerical error in vacancy announcement # 98-91A. The parties' contentions regarding the events of May 1998 are supported by conflicting declarations and exhibits, including emails between Jarmon and Harvey Lee of the OWD.

Deputy Sheriff Bozzi has been employed by the Cook County Sheriff's Office (CCSO) since 1993. In 1995, he was diagnosed with a panic disorder that makes him uncomfortable in confined spaces and crowded areas. The CCSO has been aware of Bozzi's disability since his diagnosis. Bozzi alleges that his panic disorder is episodic and substantially limits major life activities such as breathing, swallowing, and sleeping when it is active. His doctor has determined that his panic disorder does not impede his ability to handle emergency situations, but it can trigger post-incident anxiety.

Bozzi has worked with an ADA accommodation since June 2006, and as of 2009, the CCSO assigned him to work at two different security assignments and afternoon shifts at the Rolling Meadows Courthouse as ADA accommodations. Bozzi alleges that he has been able to perform the essential functions of his position with these accommodations. However, in 2017, Director of Human Resources Reierson informed Bozzi that he was no longer allowed to carry a firearm due to his disability, despite having documentation from his doctor stating that there was no medical reason keeping him from carrying a firearm. Plaintiff alleges that Reierson is a final policymaker and decision-maker for the CCSO, and that Sheriff Dart delegated final policymaking authority to her.

In 2019 and 2020, Reierson and other CCSO staff members, including Kimberly Pace, repeatedly asked Bozzi for information to help place him in a new position, and told him that his current assignment was not a reasonable accommodation and was not permanent. Bozzi's union complained to Human Resources on his behalf, stating that he was being discriminated against due to his disability. Bozzi alleges that the CCSO has a policy of discriminating against employees with disabilities, and that he has been prohibited from attending certain trainings, renewing certifications, working overtime, and bidding for lateral job positions. He also alleges that he was embarrassed and discriminated against when he was told he could no longer wear his deputy sheriff uniform at work due to his ADA accommodations. Defendant CCSO contends that it has been working to find a new position for Bozzi as a reasonable accommodation, and that Bozzi has been uncooperative in the process.

The plaintiffs, whose identities are not specified, worked for the County, with individual defendants Halcovage, Bender, Roth, Zula, and Kutzler allegedly involved in the events giving rise to the lawsuit. Plaintiff alleges that Halcovage intentionally inflicted emotional distress upon them. The plaintiffs also contend that Halcovage retaliated against them and aided and abetted discrimination in violation of the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act (PHRA). Furthermore, the plaintiffs claim that Halcovage discriminated against them and created a hostile work environment, violating their rights under the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection clause. Additionally, the plaintiffs assert that Halcovage retaliated against them in violation of their First Amendment rights.

The events leading to the lawsuit are not detailed, but it is clear that the plaintiffs and Halcovage had a workplace relationship, with Halcovage allegedly taking actions that led to the plaintiffs' claims. The plaintiffs filed their initial complaint on March 16, 2021, and an amended complaint on October 29, 2021, which named the County and the individual defendants. Halcovage filed motions to dismiss, resulting in the dismissal of the PHRA discrimination claims against them, but other claims were allowed to proceed. The plaintiffs' amended complaint is the operative complaint in the case.

Halcovage contends that the plaintiffs' claims of intentional infliction of emotional distress, retaliation and aiding and abetting under the PHRA, and Equal Protection claims fail as a matter of law, leading them to file a motion for partial summary judgment. The plaintiffs, on the other hand, maintain that there are genuine issues of material fact that preclude summary judgment in favor of Halcovage. The parties' contentions and the events leading to the lawsuit are now before the court for consideration.

Jennifer Christos was employed by Halker Consulting, LLC, until her termination in May 2015. Plaintiff alleges that her termination was due to sex and pregnancy discrimination, in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as well as retaliation under Title VII. She also claims that her employer interfered with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA). Defendant Halker Consulting, LLC, contends that Christos' termination was not discriminatory or retaliatory. 

Christos filed a complaint against Halker Consulting on July 19, 2016, asserting the aforementioned claims, as well as a Colorado state-law claim for intentional interference with contract against Halker Consulting's Chief Operations Officer, Travis Hutchinson, and owner, Matthew Halker. Prior to her termination, Christos had taken leave under the FMLA. The parties' relationship was that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute revolves around Christos' allegations of discriminatory and retaliatory actions by her employer. 

Defendant Halker Consulting argues that Christos' claims are without merit and that her termination was lawful. Plaintiff Christos alleges that she was subjected to discriminatory treatment due to her sex and pregnancy, and that her employer interfered with her rights under the FMLA. The pre-litigation events include Christos' employment with Halker Consulting, her taking of FMLA leave, and her subsequent termination. Relevant documents and communications include Christos' complaint, Halker Consulting's responses, and any relevant employment or workplace records. Christos received a right to sue letter on April 28, 2016, and Halker Consulting made a settlement offer of $50,000 on April 5, 2018, which Christos did not accept.

Five fair housing organizations, the National Fair Housing Alliance, Fair Housing of Marin, Fair Housing Napa Valley, Metro Fair Housing Services, and The Fair Housing Continuum, Inc., claim that A.G. Spanos Construction, Inc. and related entities (the Spanos Defendants) designed and constructed multifamily apartment complexes that do not comply with the accessibility requirements of the Fair Housing Act (FHA). The Spanos Defendants are alleged to have engaged in a continuous pattern and practice of discrimination against people with disabilities by designing and constructing apartment complexes that deny full access to and use of the facilities as required under the FHA. The plaintiffs allege that 82 apartment complexes located in 10 states, containing over 22,000 apartment units, do not comply with FHA requirements. 

Plaintiffs allege that they have been directly and substantially injured by the Spanos Defendants' actions, as they have been frustrated in their missions to eradicate discrimination in housing and have had to divert significant resources to identify, investigate, and counteract the Spanos Defendants' discriminatory practices. Each plaintiff conducted site visits, investigations, surveys, and/or tests at various properties, resulting in the diversion of staff time, salaries, and travel expenses. The plaintiffs claim that the Spanos Defendants' continuing discriminatory practices have forced them to expend resources that they would not have had to expend were it not for the Spanos Defendants' violations.

The Spanos Defendants are California corporations with principal offices in Stockton, and they allegedly engaged in land acquisition, development, construction, and management of multifamily apartment complexes throughout the United States. Highpointe Village, L.P. and Knickerbocker Properties, Inc. XXXVIII are also defendants, alleged to be owners of apartment complexes designed and/or constructed by the Spanos Defendants. The plaintiffs seek to certify a defendant class consisting of current owners of covered apartment complexes that were designed and/or built by the Spanos Defendants but are no longer owned by them. Plaintiffs allege that these properties do not fully comply with the accessibility and adaptability requirements of the FHA.

Gerard G. Pendas, Jr. was born on December 12, 1930, and worked for the United States Postal Service (Postal Service) from September 1980 to December 1, 1993. Initially, he was a part-time flexible (PTF) special delivery messenger, a position that did not guarantee work during specific times but ensured a minimum number of hours in a given week when called in to work. Pendas was represented by the American Postal Workers Union (APWU). In 1988, he contacted an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) counselor, alleging that he was improperly denied the ability to deliver express mail, that the special delivery messenger position was being eliminated, and that he should be given full-time status. This claim was settled.

Pendas again complained to an EEO counselor in 1990, making similar claims and alleging that the defendant was violating a 1989 pre-arbitration settlement. He withdrew this complaint on December 7, 1990. On December 29, 1990, Pendas was converted from a PTF special delivery messenger to a PTF city letter carrier because the special delivery messenger classification was being eliminated. The defendant argues that Pendas' time to object to the elimination of the special delivery messenger position accrued at this point, and that he failed to file an EEO complaint within the required 30 days.

After being converted to a PTF city letter carrier, Pendas fell and injured himself on January 6, 1991. His physician, Dr. Richard Boehler, stated that Pendas suffered from Osteoarthritis and recommended that he not be required to stand for more than one hour at a time, among other restrictions. Pendas filed a grievance regarding sick leave hours granted by the Postal Service and claimed that he was entitled to more hours of sick pay than he was given. In September 1991, his injury compensation claim was denied. Pendas underwent bypass surgery in October 1991 and was not working from approximately October 1, 1991, to February 1992. Upon his return, he was given light duty work.

On October 25, 1992, Pendas was notified that he was being assigned to the "carrier craft" with a four-hour day beginning at 4:00 a.m. His physician, Dr. Richard Lavigne, stated that he believed Pendas was capable of working that shift. However, Pendas refused to comply, citing his medical restrictions and physician recommendations. He received a letter of warning for failing to follow instructions and failing to report to his assigned duties. Pendas obtained a new physician, Dr. Michael J. Gardner, who recommended that he not work before 8:00 a.m. and made similar recommendations concerning reaching, limits on standing and sitting, working above shoulder height, and lifting only 20 pounds or less.

The defendant had Pendas see the postal contract physician, Dr. William Rogers, who found that he was capable of performing light duty work beginning at 4:00 a.m. Pendas received a seven-day suspension for failing to report to work. He then filed a grievance over the suspension and filed an informal complaint with an EEO counselor on December 7, 1992. In January 1993, Pendas reached an oral agreement with Reginald Poulin, the Postmaster at Albany, New York, to resolve the EEO complaint. However, Pendas claims that he never received the positions promised to him and was instead placed in the Central Forwarding Unit, a position he contends was detrimental to his health.

On March 12, 1993, Pendas filed a formal EEO complaint. On August 7, 1993, he was converted from PTF to a full-time city carrier with regular hours. Pendas contends that upon receiving full-time status, he was forced to work in a job that required him to stand for eight hours each day, which he found detrimental to his health and physically impossible. He notes that other less experienced and less qualified employees were given jobs that enabled them to walk, drive, and deliver mail, a combination of duties that his physician recommended. Pendas alleges that he was forced to leave the position on December 1, 1993, because he was incapable of performing the work assigned to him.

Plaintiff alleges that the defendant violated the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) by denying him "regular" status when other younger employees with less experience were granted such status. Pendas also alleges that the defendant regularly suggested that he retire, breached an agreement regarding early morning work hours, and required him to stand eight hours each day against his physician's orders, all in retaliation for filing a prior claim of age discrimination. Defendant contends that Pendas failed to file an EEO complaint within the required 30 days after the elimination of the special delivery messenger position and that he was capable of performing light duty work beginning at 4:00 a.m. as determined by Dr.

Nancy Holleman and Judy Wells, both employees of the Colonial Heights School Board, worked at North Elementary School in Colonial Heights, Virginia. Holleman was a kindergarten teacher, and Wells was a paraprofessional. In 2006, the school's principal, Bruce Seamster, retired, and Thomas Pond was hired as his replacement. Pond's management style was more direct and assertive than Seamster's, and he implemented changes at the school, which some employees, including Holleman and Wells, found intimidating and unwelcoming.

Plaintiff Holleman alleges that Pond treated women differently than men, while Defendant Colonial Heights School Board contends that Pond's behavior was not based on gender. A group of six female teachers and professionals, including Holleman, began meeting to discuss their frustrations with Pond's management style and behavior. They felt that Pond intimidated them, yelled at teachers, and was a micromanager. The group, which later included Wells, met with School Board member Joe Green to seek his advice and help in dealing with their issues. During these meetings, Wells reported an incident where Pond grabbed her by the arms in the cafeteria in front of students and teachers.

Holleman claims that she told Green that Pond treated women differently than men, but the other women in the group, and Green, deny that any of the women, including Holleman, made such a statement. The group members met with other School Board members, including Sandra Coleman and Cindy Shortlidge, to discuss their concerns about Pond. Holleman alone claims that she complained that Pond treated group members badly because they were women. On February 28, 2007, Wells told School Superintendent Dr. Joseph O. Cox, Jr. about the arm-grabbing incident, and on March 7, 2007, she filed a formal grievance about the incident. The grievance stated that Pond gripped both of her arms in front of other faculty and students in the cafeteria, while questioning her loudly and in a harsh and demeaning manner.

The group, excluding Wells, signed and submitted a 21-page grievance to Cox on March 16, 2007, which included complaints about Pond's treatment of group members, his management style, and incidents of physical contact. Cox discussed the complaints with Pond and conducted interviews with faculty and staff. After reviewing the results of the interviews, Cox expressed concern over the apparent movement to oust Pond and told the grievants that the conflict at North needed to end. On June 4, 2007, Cox told Wells that he did not find her accounts of the incidents to be credible and implied that he was considering nonrenewal of her contract. Wells received an email from Green the same day, stating that if she didn't change her story, she would likely be terminated. Wells submitted a letter of resignation on July 20, 2007. Holleman was transferred to teach kindergarten at another school, Tussing, and her yearly contract was renewed for greater pay, with no loss of benefits.

Bennie D. Jones, a Black-American male, worked at Glitsch, Inc. for twelve years, during which he had a good employment record. In 1976, while working as a fork lift operator, Jones injured his back, which made it painful for him to continue working. He attempted to return to his job several times but was unable to perform his duties due to his injury. On one occasion, he asked for lighter duty work but was told to go home. Several days later, on November 9, 1976, Glitsch terminated Jones, allegedly due to his "inability to perform assigned duties." 

Plaintiff Jones alleges that his termination was discriminatory, motivated by his race, and that Glitsch would have assigned him to a lighter duty job if he were white. Jones contends that he was qualified for several lighter duty jobs at Glitsch, including messenger/driver, and that he could have performed these jobs with minimal training. Defendant Glitsch, on the other hand, argues that Jones was not physically qualified for these jobs due to his back injury and lack of necessary skills. Glitsch also claims that there were no job openings available in lighter duty positions at the time of Jones' termination.

Prior to his termination, Jones had a good employment record at Glitsch, and there is evidence suggesting that black employees were treated differently than white employees when it came to job assignments and discipline. The company's progressive discipline system was not followed in Jones' case, and there were discrepancies in the treatment of black and white employees who had been injured on the job. Jones has been unable to find employment since his termination and has continued to experience difficulties due to his back injury. The parties disagree on the extent of Jones' physical capabilities and his qualifications for various jobs at Glitsch, with Jones claiming he could have performed lighter duty work and Glitsch arguing that he was not suited for such positions.

Outback Steakhouse of Florida, Inc., and OS Restaurant Partners, Inc., d/b/a Outback Steakhouse, are defendants in a lawsuit filed by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). The EEOC alleges that the defendants have engaged in a pattern or practice of discriminating against women by failing to hire and promote them and by discriminating against them in terms and conditions of employment. The lawsuit stems from charges of discrimination filed by two former employees, Jennifer Turner-Rieger and Kelly Altizer, who worked at Outback Steakhouse restaurants in Colorado. 

Turner-Rieger and Altizer alleged that they experienced sex discrimination while working at the restaurants, including being subjected to sexist remarks by their supervisor, Tom Flanagan, who is a Joint-Venture Partner (JVP) for the region. The EEOC commenced an investigation into their claims, which included requests for information about the defendants' hiring and promotion practices, as well as their policies regarding job assignments, pay, and training. The defendants submitted position statements in response to the charges, which included information about their national anti-discrimination policy. 

The EEOC and the defendants engaged in two separate conciliation efforts, which ultimately failed to resolve the matter. During these efforts, the parties discussed potential remedies, including changes to the defendants' policies and training programs. However, the parties disagree about the scope of the conciliation efforts, with the EEOC claiming that the discussions related to national changes to the defendants' policies, while the defendants claim that the discussions were limited to the three-state region managed by Flanagan. The EEOC alleges that the defendants' actions constitute a pattern or practice of discrimination against women, while the defendants contend that their policies and practices are fair and non-discriminatory. Plaintiff Turner-Rieger alleges that she was discriminated against in terms and conditions of employment, including hiring, firing, job assignments, promotions, and pay. Defendant Outback Steakhouse of Florida, Inc., contends that its national anti-discrimination policy is sufficient to prevent discrimination in the workplace. The EEOC alleges that the defendants' actions have affected a class of females, while the defendants argue that the EEOC's claims are limited to the specific allegations made by Turner-Rieger and Altizer.

Randy L. Greene began working as a truck driver for A. Duie Pyle, Inc. in March 2001. After an initial training period, he worked regularly at the Pyle terminal in York, Pennsylvania from July 2001 until April 2002. During his employment, Greene alleges that he was subjected to various inappropriate materials and comments that created a hostile work environment. Specifically, he claims to have observed a Penthouse magazine and a Playboy magazine in the cafeteria, a Playboy magazine in the men's restroom, and at least fifteen offensive faxes, cartoons, or emails, about half of which were observed near the public time clock. Greene also saw a joke list taped to the wall near the time clock on April 25, 2002, which contained several questionable jokes playing on gender stereotypes.

Greene reported the existence of these materials or comments to management at Pyle on three occasions. In February 2002, he reported to Eric McVeigh, the manager of the York terminal, that another employee, Gene Hart, had told an "off-color" joke. Approximately three months later, on April 5, 2002, Greene met with Tom Chambers, Pyle's Human Resources Director, to express his discomfort with the materials in the York terminal that he found offensive. Chambers indicated that such material was not condoned by Pyle. Following this meeting, Greene did not find any inappropriate material in the terminal until April 25, 2002, when he found the joke list. Greene took the list to McVeigh, who allegedly did not believe it was inappropriate and told Greene he was "just trying to cause... trouble." McVeigh then terminated Greene.

Plaintiff Greene alleges that he was terminated because he showed McVeigh the joke list, while Defendant Pyle maintains that Greene was terminated because he was argumentative. Other Pyle employees reported seeing FHM and Maxim magazines in the terminal, as well as hearing explicit jokes and supervisors making inappropriate sexual comments about female employees. However, no other employee complained about the allegedly sexually-charged nature of the Pyle facility in York. Pyle has a sexual harassment policy that protects third parties by prohibiting offensive "sexual conduct or communications of others" and maintains an "open-door" policy to encourage communication between managers and employees regarding these issues.

Jean Grover worked for Smarte Carte, Inc. from 1994 to 2007, starting as a sales representative and eventually rising to Vice President of Business Development and Operations of the company's domestic locker and retail business. Plaintiff Grover alleges that she was paid less than similarly situated male employees, specifically Johnny Chiu and Arthur Spring, and that she was overlooked for career- and compensation-enhancing opportunities that were awarded to male employees. Grover also alleges that she was fired in retaliation for complaining about her unequal treatment. 

Defendant Smarte Carte, Inc. contends that Grover's male peers were not paid more than she was and were not similarly situated to her. Smarte Carte's CEO, Edward Rudis, told Grover in 2005 that her current compensation was in line with her level of responsibility within the organization, but offered her additional incentives in the form of deferred salary and stock options. Grover had complained to Rudis about her unequal pay and treatment on several occasions, including in a May 28, 2004, memorandum, where she stated that she was underpaid compared to her male peers and that senior management perceived her comments and recommendations differently than those of her peers. 

Grover's reviews were largely positive, but Rudis noted that she had difficulty relating to her coworkers. In 2006 and 2007, Grover continued to complain to Rudis about her unequal pay and treatment, providing documentation to support her claims. On May 31, 2007, Smarte Carte terminated Grover without cause, citing a reduction in force, although it is unclear whether other employees were fired at the same time. Grover filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in February 2008, alleging violations of the Equal Pay Act and Title VII, and later filed a lawsuit against Smarte Carte in November 2009.

Martin, a probation officer for the Cook County Adult Probation Department and a practicing Muslim who wears a hijab, had been a steward for Local 3468 of the American Federation of County, State, and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) since 2006 and was promoted to chief steward in 2012. Plaintiff alleges that in 2013 or 2014, she filed a discrimination charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) claiming her then-supervisor had an issue with her hijab, but the Probation Department took no action regarding her complaint. Defendant contends that the charge was dropped. 

In January 2015, Martin received an anonymous letter expressing anti-union sentiment, which the president of Local 3468, James Dunaway, brought to the attention of Cook County Chief Judge Timothy Evans, but Evans did not respond. Beginning in October 2015, Deputy Chief Probation Officer Gray told Martin that unidentified coworkers had complained about her wearing a hijab, cautioning her that it was against department policy. Martin felt bullied by these interactions and consulted with Dunaway, who contacted the Probation Department's human resources department on her behalf. 

In December 2015, after Martin came to work without her hijab due to a scalp condition, Gray conveyed an anonymous complaint about her "apparent inconsistency" in wearing the hijab, prompting Martin to provide a doctor's note. On December 18, 2015, Martin discovered an anonymous note on her desk chair with an anti-Muslim message, and later that day, Gray publicly humiliated her in front of her supervisor. Martin reported the incident to the IDHR and emailed Chief Judge Evans, but received no response. Martin experienced additional harassment, including a suspension in September 2016 based on allegations by another probation officer, David Neeley, that she had interfered with his official duties. The union filed a grievance, charging that the suspension constituted retaliation for Martin's union activity and the agency charges she had filed. Martin's workstation was reassigned, and Gray shared confidential information about her with other employees, who later demonstrated hostility towards her. Martin also requested a quiet space to exercise her religious beliefs, including prayer, which was granted, but she found the conditions for using the space "unsettling." In March 2017, Martin discovered another anonymous message written on a wall of the employees-only women's restroom, causing her "tremendous emotional anxiety and mental discomfort."

Sandra Mohamed, a plaintiff, worked for the Atlantic County Special Services School District. Plaintiff alleges she was unlawfully discriminated against, harassed, and retaliated against in the workplace because of her race, color, national origin, and/or disabilities, and because of her repeated complaints concerning such conduct. Plaintiff contends that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and was terminated in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination, and the New Jersey Conscientious Employee Protection Act. 

Plaintiff filed a complaint against the School District and Eric Flecken, asserting various claims arising out of the alleged discrimination and retaliation. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the School District being the employer and Mohamed being the employee. The nature of the dispute is centered around the alleged discriminatory and retaliatory actions taken by the School District against Mohamed. 

Defendant School District contends that plaintiff is attempting to use her motion for pro bono counsel to further delay the case. Defendant argues that plaintiff deliberately failed to provide discovery responses by the Court-Ordered deadline and instead chose to file the motion. Defendant also contests plaintiff's basis for her request for counsel, which it argues is unsupported by the record and insufficient to justify granting plaintiff's motion. Plaintiff, on the other hand, alleges that she is unfamiliar with the law and does not have the full ability to present an effective case, and that financial and employment issues have prevented her from pursuing the case or obtaining counsel. Relevant pre-litigation events include plaintiff's repeated complaints concerning the alleged discriminatory conduct, and her subsequent termination. Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff had contacted the Atlantic County Bar Association Lawyer Referral Service in an attempt to find counsel, as advised by the Court.

E. Jean Carter, a black female, was hired by the Sedgwick County Board of Commissioners as an office associate for the Department of Sedgwick County Community Corrections on June 23, 1983. She worked under the supervision of Jon Cameron, the Community Corrections Director, and Michael Brand, the Assistant Director. Carter's duties were secretarial in nature and included tasks such as typing, handling correspondence, and acting as receptionist. During her employment, Carter received consistently above-average performance evaluations from Cameron and was rewarded with merit pay increases.

Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to numerous racial slurs and epithets by defendant Brand, including being referred to as "Jon's token nigger" and being told it was "nigger pick day." Carter also claims that Brand kept a picture of a black family in his office and boasted of his own "nigger blood" and sexual conquests of "black pussy." Additionally, Carter alleges that Brand presented her with a picture of "Long Dong Silver," a photo of a black male with an elongated penis, and pinned a postcard containing a picture of two black children on a bulletin board behind her desk. Carter believes these actions were intended to be racist and uncomplimentary.

Defendant Brand denies Carter's claims of race discrimination, stating that he fired her because she was too assertive, he was unsatisfied with her performance, and he wanted his "own person." Brand became the director of the department on February 25, 1985, after Cameron left the employ of the county, and terminated Carter's employment on his first day, giving her 15 minutes to clear out her things. Carter also alleges that she was sexually harassed by defendant Cameron, who gave her sexual objects as gifts, including a "Mr. Peter Party Mold" and a "Pecker Pop Top." Cameron's wife, Joan, testified that she and Carter were friends and that the gifts were part of a joking exchange between them, but Carter claims she found the gifts to be "hurtful, humiliating, embarrassing, angry and degrading."

Mr. Golatt is an employee at Southwood High School, which is under the Caddo Parish School Board. He alleges that the school's principal, Kim Pendleton, sexually harassed him, retaliated against him, and created a hostile work environment, violating his rights under Title VII. Plaintiff further alleges that Defendant Pendleton violated the ADA by suggesting drug abuse. Mr. Golatt filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and received a notice of right to sue. He then filed suit against Ms. Pendleton and the Caddo Parish School Board on June 23, 2023.

Plaintiff alleges that Ms. Pendleton's actions were discriminatory and harassing, while Defendant Pendleton contends that she cannot be held personally liable for Plaintiff's discrimination, harassment, or retaliation claims under Title VII or the ADA because she is an employee of the Caddo Parish School Board. Defendant Pendleton argues that Title VII's definition of employer does not include individual employees, and therefore, she should not be liable for the claims brought against her. She also alleges that the ADA does not impose individual liability.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Ms. Pendleton being the principal of the school where Mr. Golatt works. The nature of the dispute is centered around the alleged discriminatory and harassing behavior by Ms. Pendleton towards Mr. Golatt. Relevant pre-litigation events include Mr. Golatt's filing of a charge of discrimination with the EEOC and the subsequent notice of right to sue. The lawsuit was filed in court on June 23, 2023, and Defendant Pendleton filed a motion to dismiss on November 8, 2023, arguing that she should not be held personally liable for the claims brought against her.

In 2017, the Maryland General Assembly enacted a law aimed at preventing price gouging in the generic prescription drug market. The law prohibits drug manufacturers or wholesale distributors from introducing excessive and unjustified price increases for generic drugs, which could result in consumers having no meaningful choice but to purchase the drug at an excessive price due to its importance to their health and insufficient competition in the market. Each violation of this prohibition may be punished by a civil penalty of up to $10,000.

The Association for Accessible Medicines (AAM), a voluntary organization representing prescription drug manufacturers and wholesale distributors, filed a lawsuit on July 6, 2017, challenging the law under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. AAM alleged that the law regulated conduct occurring outside Maryland, violating the dormant Commerce Clause of the United States Constitution, and that the law was void for vagueness in violation of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Attorney General of Maryland and the Secretary of the Maryland Department of Health, defendants in the case, filed a motion to dismiss both counts.

Plaintiff AAM contends that the law's provisions would harm its members by restricting their ability to set prices for generic drugs. AAM argues that the law's language is too vague, making it difficult for its members to determine what constitutes an "excessive" price increase. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that the law is necessary to protect consumers from price gouging and that it does not violate the Constitution. The parties disagree on the law's impact on the pharmaceutical industry and the extent to which it regulates conduct outside Maryland. Relevant pre-litigation events include the enactment of the law and AAM's decision to challenge it in court. Prior to filing the lawsuit, there is no indication that the parties engaged in any significant negotiations or communications regarding the law's implementation or potential challenges.

Thomas Hopkins was employed by MacLellan as an assistant manager at their Nashville, Illinois location from approximately March 1, 2016, until his termination on March 4, 2020. His salary was based on a 40-hour workweek. In late 2019, Hopkins experienced severe back pain and visited the emergency room, where he was advised to follow up with Regional Brain & Spine. He informed his supervisor, David Jones, and regional manager, Scott Cone, about his condition and intention to seek medical attention. Despite this, Jones and Cone expected Hopkins to continue working 50-60 hours per week. Hopkins advised them that, due to his pain, he could no longer work such long hours and requested reasonable accommodations.

Plaintiff Hopkins alleges that he was diagnosed with a torn hip labrum, herniated discs, and hip impingement in late January 2020, and was told that surgery was required. He informed Jones and Cone about his diagnosis and requested 3-8 weeks off for surgery and recovery. Hopkins claims that he continued working with reasonable accommodations until late February 2020, when his schedule was altered without his input to four days a week, requiring him to work at least 10-hour days to complete a full week's worth of work. Defendant MacLellan contends that Hopkins did not exhaust his administrative remedies prior to filing the complaint, citing inconsistencies in the dates of his alleged injuries.

Hopkins filed a complaint with the EEOC, which he claims encompasses the ADA violations alleged in his complaint. MacLellan argues that the first amended complaint indicates that Hopkins' injuries began on November 13, 2019, more than two months before previously stated. Hopkins responds that the conduct did not change and MacLellan is not prejudiced by the allegations in the first amended complaint. The parties' dispute centers on whether MacLellan discriminated against Hopkins due to his disability and whether Hopkins was entitled to reasonable accommodations under the ADA.

Felicia Pickett Johnson worked at St. Barnabas Nursing Home. Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to unlawful employment practices, including discrimination and harassment, by her employer and a coworker, Ronald Granger. Johnson filed a complaint with the United States Equal Employment Commission (EEOC), which issued a right-to-sue letter on October 31, 2007. Defendant St. Barnabas contends that Johnson received this letter on or about November 3, 2007, based on the standard three-day mail delivery presumption. However, Johnson alleges that she actually received the letter on November 14, 2007. 

Johnson attached a copy of the right-to-sue letter to her complaint, which included a fax transmission confirmation dated November 8, 2007, with her name and telephone number. St. Barnabas argues that this document suggests Johnson had the letter at least by November 8, 2007. Johnson claims that, under her interpretation of federal court practice rules, the 90-day statutory period for filing a lawsuit does not include weekends and holidays, which would have given her until March 5, 2008, to file her complaint. 

Johnson filed her lawsuit on February 7, 2008. St. Barnabas moves for judgment on the pleadings, arguing that Johnson's claims under Title VII and the ADA are time-barred because she failed to file her lawsuit within the required 90-day period after receiving the right-to-sue letter. Johnson contends that she should be allowed more time due to extraordinary circumstances, but St. Barnabas argues that she has not demonstrated any such circumstances that would warrant equitable tolling of the 90-day period.

In Canton, Mississippi, a city with a majority black population, the municipal government's electoral system was challenged by two groups of citizens. The city had a population of 9,707 in 1960 and 10,503 in 1970, which led to changes in its electoral system. Initially, the city had five aldermen, one from each of four wards and one at-large. However, in 1962, the Mississippi legislature amended the statute, requiring one alderman to live in each of four wards but be elected at-large. After the 1970 census, the city switched to a seven-aldermen system, with one alderman from each of six wards and one at-large. 

The Hinton plaintiffs, a group of white and black citizens, filed a lawsuit on April 22, 1977, challenging the apportionment of the city's wards and alleging a violation of their rights under the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments. The NAACP plaintiffs, a group of black citizens, filed a separate lawsuit on April 28, 1977, also challenging the apportionment of the wards and alleging a dilution of black voting strength. The defendants include the City of Canton, its aldermen, the Canton Municipal Democratic Executive Committee, and the Canton Municipal Election Commission. 

Plaintiff Hinton alleges that the city's electoral system is unconstitutional because the wards are malapportioned, with significant population disparities between them. The NAACP plaintiffs contend that the city's electoral system dilutes the voting strength of black citizens. Defendant City of Canton acknowledges that its wards are malapportioned but claims it has taken steps to address the issue, including hiring a firm to prepare a redistricting plan. The city adopted a plan on October 11, 1977, which was unanimously approved by the Board of Aldermen, including its two black members. However, the NAACP plaintiffs have filed objections to the plan, arguing that it does not adequately address the voting strength of black citizens. The Hinton plaintiffs support the city's plan, while the defendants and the Hinton plaintiffs have objected to the NAACP's alternative plan. Prior to the filing of these lawsuits, the city had submitted a redistricting plan to the Attorney General of the United States for approval, but the plan was rejected due to concerns about inaccurate population figures. The city did not seek reconsideration or a declaratory judgment, and instead, these lawsuits were filed, leading to the court's injunction against holding the 1977 elections.

Vanessa L. Hobson, an African-American woman, worked in the operations department of a United States Postal Service facility. She was married to her immediate supervisor, who is white. After her manager received an anonymous phone call informing him of their marital relationship, Hobson was transferred to the marketing department of the same facility. Plaintiff alleges that this transfer was an adverse employment action, as she is now forced to perform an operations-related job under a supervisor whose specialty is marketing, her workspace was moved 300 feet down the hall, and the switch has made it more difficult for her to do her work. Defendant contends that Hobson is performing the same work, for the same pay, with the same title, in the same building, and that such a transfer is not adverse as a matter of law.

Hobson's husband had previously filed an EEO action and a union grievance when he was transferred to solve the conflict of interest created by the reporting relationship between Hobson and her husband. When that grievance was settled through his return to his old position, Hobson was transferred. Plaintiff alleges that her transfer was instituted in retaliation for her husband's complaint of racial discrimination. Defendant counters that the transfer was due to the conflict of interest that necessarily occurs when one spouse directly supervises another at work. The Manager of Human Resources for the Postal Service district acknowledged that at the time of Hobson's transfer, there were other non-interracial conjugal couples in direct supervisory relationships.

Plaintiff and defendant disagree on whether Hobson's transfer was an adverse employment action and whether it was motivated by racial discrimination or retaliation. Hobson's union representative acknowledged the need for her to report to someone other than her husband, but Hobson argues that her husband did not show her any favoritism and that she was treated unfairly because the Post Office handled cases of conflict of interest on a case-by-case basis rather than through an across-the-board inquiry. Defendant argues that avoiding the appearance of favoritism is a legitimate reason for transferring Hobson and that there is no evidence to suggest that the Post Office failed to act in cases of same-race spouses in supervisory relationships.

Kathleen Keys worked the night shift at Entergy's call center in Jackson, Mississippi, for approximately 10 years, monitoring activities and emergencies for Entergy's operations in four states: Mississippi, Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas. During her employment, Keys applied for over 70 vacancies within the Entergy system, received eight interviews, but was not hired for any of the positions. Plaintiff alleges that the majority of those positions were filled by white men, and that one manager explicitly told her the company was looking for men. Keys possesses a bachelor's degree in business, a master's degree in management, a leadership certificate from Cornell University, and several insurance licenses, which she claims made her overqualified for her position.

Keys alleges that her supervisor, Linda Butler, treated her in a discriminatory manner by instructing her to self-rate at a lower level than Keys felt appropriate on employee evaluations, denying her requested cross-training and educational opportunities, and failing to recommend or help her in applying for positions. Defendant contends that Keys was not treated unfairly, and that Butler did not discriminate against her. Keys also alleges that Butler offered preferential treatment to two darker-skinned colleagues, while denying Keys the same opportunities. 

In October 2017, Keys' position was outsourced to Alorica, and she was ordered to move to the day shift. She remained with Alorica until she quit in May 2018. Keys filed a charge of discrimination with the EEOC on May 3, 2018, alleging discrimination on the basis of race, gender, and age. The parties are now engaged in a lawsuit, with Entergy seeking summary judgment on the merits of Keys' discrimination claims, and other Entergy entities seeking summary judgment for an alleged lack of personal jurisdiction. Keys has responded in opposition to each motion, disputing the defendants' contentions and alleging that she was subjected to discriminatory treatment during her employment with Entergy.

The plaintiff was employed as an Approvals and Special Permits Assistant in the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) of the Department of Transportation (DOT) until her termination on October 8, 2016, for "AWOL and Improper Conduct." Plaintiff alleges that her removal was the result of unlawful retaliation and discrimination. On November 3, 2016, she appealed her removal to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) on various grounds, including that the penalty of removal was too severe and that the decision constituted a prohibited personnel practice. 

Plaintiff and defendant executed an agreement to settle the MSPB appeal on November 3, 2017, but plaintiff revoked the agreement within the allowed seven-day period. The MSPB hearing was rescheduled for January 25, 2018, at which point plaintiff chose to have a decision made on the written record rather than proceed with an in-person hearing. On February 5, 2018, plaintiff contacted an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) counselor about her alleged discriminatory removal and the "forced" settlement agreement. 

Defendant contends that plaintiff's EEO complaint, filed on June 13, 2018, was untimely because she failed to contact an EEO counselor within 45 days of the alleged acts or events. Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to discrimination and harassment based on her race and mental disability, as well as reprisal for her prior EEO activity, citing specific incidents including a delayed performance appraisal meeting in 2010, her termination on October 7, 2016, and the forced settlement agreement on November 3, 2017. The DOT dismissed the EEO complaint as untimely, and the EEOC affirmed this decision on December 13, 2018. Plaintiff requested reconsideration, which was denied by the EEOC on July 19, 2019. On October 17, 2019, plaintiff filed a complaint for employment discrimination in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland.

Gloria R. Jackson worked for the Veterans' Administration (VA) until she quit on September 22, 1979. Plaintiff alleges that she believed the VA was discriminating against her in early September 1979, prompting her to contact an EEOC representative. Informal settlement talks between Jackson and the VA were unsuccessful, leading Jackson to file an administrative charge. Defendant contends that Jackson's administrative charge failed to allege constructive discharge. Jackson participated in a hearing on her charge, during which evidence was presented on the issue of constructive discharge, including evidence from the VA attempting to prove that Jackson had not been constructively discharged. The hearing officer ultimately found that the VA had discriminated against and constructively discharged Jackson, but this decision was later rejected by the Office of the General Counsel, which concluded that the administrative charge did not allege constructive discharge.

Plaintiff alleges that she was discriminated against by the VA, leading to her constructive discharge. Defendant contends that Jackson's administrative charge was insufficient to support a claim of constructive discharge. The VA had the opportunity to challenge the sufficiency of Jackson's charge during informal settlement talks and the hearing, but did not do so until the Office of the General Counsel reviewed the charge over three years after it was filed. Jackson claims that she proceeded with her administrative charge and subsequent hearing under the assumption that her claim was properly stated.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and former employee, with the VA being the employer and Jackson being the former employee. The nature of the dispute is a claim of discrimination and constructive discharge under Title VII.
