Relevant pre-litigation events include the informal settlement talks, the filing of the administrative charge, and the hearing on the charge. Relevant documents include the administrative charge, the hearing officer's statement of findings and recommended decision, and the Office of the General Counsel's rejection of that decision. Communications between the parties include the informal settlement talks and the exchange of evidence during the hearing. Employment and workplace facts include Jackson's quit date and the VA's alleged discriminatory actions.

Anetha Barfield, a nurse, worked at Bellevue Hospital through three different nursing referral agencies from approximately August 2002 to May 2005. During this period, there were at least 16 weeks when she worked more than 40 hours at Bellevue in a given week, between October 30, 2003, and January 31, 2005. Plaintiff alleges that she did not receive overtime pay for those hours worked in excess of 40 hours. Defendant contends that the referral agencies, not Bellevue, were responsible for paying her overtime. 

Plaintiff worked exclusively at Bellevue during the period in question, using equipment provided by the hospital and performing work integral to its operation. The referral agencies generally did not shift their employees as a unit from one hospital to another, and plaintiff was assigned to work at Bellevue for an extended period. Bellevue provided plaintiff with tentative dates and times to work, required her to call in to confirm, and sometimes asked her to work double shifts, which were approved by the hospital. Bellevue also evaluated the performance of agency nurses, including plaintiff, and could prohibit them from working at the hospital if dissatisfied with their performance.

Plaintiff alleges that Bellevue exercised control over her work, including her schedule, and that she accurately reported all her worked hours on agency sign-in sheets, which Bellevue collected and cross-referenced. Defendant contends that plaintiff was informed by one of her referral agencies not to work more than 40 hours per week and that she prevented Bellevue from determining her total hours worked by signing in through multiple agencies. However, plaintiff claims that Bellevue never told her not to work more than 40 hours per week and that the hospital was aware of her overtime work through the sign-in sheets and verification forms.

In October 1994, plaintiffs, who are seamen, were employed on the merchant vessel S.S. Lake Charles, which was managed by Ahrenkiel Ship Management (U.S.), Inc. ("Ahrenkiel"). During that time, they allegedly experienced intense racial discrimination by other crew members. Plaintiffs reported the incidents to Ahrenkiel representatives, but claim that no adequate action was taken to address their concerns. In March and June 1995, plaintiffs filed formal complaints with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). After receiving their respective Notices of Right to Sue in March-April 1996, plaintiffs filed a lawsuit against Ahrenkiel, seeking relief under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Plaintiffs allege that they were subjected to racial discrimination while working on the S.S. Lake Charles, and that Ahrenkiel failed to take adequate remedial action. Ahrenkiel contends that plaintiffs' Title VII claim is subject to mandatory arbitration, citing the collective bargaining agreement between Ahrenkiel and the plaintiffs' union, District No. 4-NMU/MEBA ("Union"). The collective bargaining agreement, which was in effect in 1994 and 1995, includes provisions related to discrimination and arbitration. Ahrenkiel argues that these provisions require plaintiffs to submit their discrimination claims to arbitration, rather than pursuing a lawsuit.

The Union had filed a formal grievance with Ahrenkiel regarding minority discrimination in January 1995, but Ahrenkiel declined to take further action, and the Union did not pursue the matter. Plaintiffs claim that they are not able to unilaterally invoke arbitration under the collective bargaining agreement, and that the Union's failure to pursue their claims means that they have exhausted their limited arbitration opportunities. Ahrenkiel, on the other hand, argues that the collective bargaining agreement requires plaintiffs to submit their claims to arbitration, and that the court does not have subject matter jurisdiction over the Title VII claim.

On June 20, 1996, Advantage Systems, Inc., a transportation broker, accepted a shipment from Co-Pack Foods, Inc. in Iowa for delivery to a refrigerated storage facility in Kansas. The shipment consisted of 2260 cases of turkey, ham, and bologna that required refrigeration at 22 degrees during transportation. Advantage Systems engaged the services of D & S Trucking, Inc. to transport the meat. However, when the shipment arrived in Kansas on June 21, 1996, the temperature of the meats ranged between 52 and 65 degrees, allegedly rendering the shipment worthless for human consumption.

Plaintiff Swift-Eckrich, Inc., the intended recipient of the shipment, alleges that the failure to maintain the temperature of the meats at 22 degrees while in transit damaged the goods. Swift-Eckrich contends that Advantage Systems and D & S are liable for the damages. Defendant Advantage Systems asserts that it is not liable, arguing that the shipment was not damaged as alleged. Advantage Systems also claims that Swift-Eckrich owes it $9,103.80 for the shipment of other products. D & S Trucking, Inc. also denies liability, with its truck driver, Ken Gardner, stating in an interview that the refrigeration system in the trailer was working properly during the entire time the meat was in his possession.

The parties' relationship began when Swift-Eckrich hired Advantage Systems to transport its products. Advantage Systems, in turn, engaged the services of D & S to transport the meat. The dispute arose when the shipment arrived in Kansas at an allegedly improper temperature. Prior to the lawsuit, Advantage Systems had provided transportation services to Swift-Eckrich, and Swift-Eckrich had paid Advantage Systems for these services, except for the $9,103.80 that Advantage Systems claims is still owed. The lawsuit was filed on April 21, 1997, with Swift-Eckrich seeking damages for the allegedly damaged shipment. The parties have engaged in settlement discussions, but the terms of any potential settlement are disputed, with Advantage Systems denying that it agreed to a settlement that would permit Swift-Eckrich to set off its claim against Advantage Systems' claim for $9,103.80.

Citizens Bank, a small business with a net worth of less than $5,000,000 and fewer than 500 employees, paid an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) deficiency assessment for calendar years 1977 and 1978. The bank then sought recovery of the assessment in a lawsuit against the United States. The IRS opposed the bank's claim, and the case was litigated in the district court. The bank's attorneys spent 70.6 hours working on the case, including 1.5 hours at an evidentiary hearing, at a rate of $75 per hour, and incurred $188.31 in other expenses, such as long distance telephone charges, xerox, and postage. 

Plaintiff alleges that the IRS's position in the case was not substantially justified, as the bank's claim was supported by clear and controlling precedent, specifically the Fifth Circuit's decision in Bank of Coushatta v. United States. Defendant contends that its position was substantially justified, but the attorney who represented the IRS admitted at the evidentiary hearing that the IRS took its position in order to create an "appellate vehicle" to challenge the Bank of Coushatta decision. The IRS had given notice of appeal to the Eleventh Circuit but then voluntarily dismissed its appeal. 

The parties disagree on whether the IRS's position was substantially justified and whether special circumstances make an award of attorneys' fees and expenses unjust. The bank seeks $5,295.00 in attorneys' fees and $188.31 in other expenses, while the United States opposes the motion, arguing that its position was substantially justified. The bank's vice-president and cashier, E.N. Jones, III, submitted uncontroverted affidavits showing that the bank meets the financial eligibility requirements for an award of attorneys' fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA).

In February 2017, Hine applied to work as a volunteer firefighter and emergency medical technician (EMT) for the MVFD, a non-profit corporation located in Suitland, Maryland. Hine is deaf and substantially limited in the major life activities of hearing and speaking. Despite this, he had previously served as a volunteer firefighter in Pennsylvania with no restrictions on his duties. As part of the application process, Hine was referred for a physical examination. On March 8, 2018, Defendants informed Hine that he did not meet the standards set by the Prince George's County Fire Department to become a firefighter due to his hearing loss.

Plaintiff alleges that he submitted additional records relating to past hearing test results and requested an opportunity to receive another hearing test. However, on February 23, 2019, the County sent him a denial letter stating that he did not meet the standards to safely perform the essential functions of the position. Hine contends that the County and MVFD are joint employers because they were both involved in the hiring process, and that he would have been hired as a volunteer firefighter if not for Defendants' discriminatory policies, practices, and procedures. Defendant contends that Hine's hearing loss made him ineligible for the position.

On June 12, 2019, Hine filed a charge of discrimination with the United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights (MCCR). The EEOC issued a Notice of Right to Sue on July 28, 2020. Prior to filing the lawsuit, Hine had previously served as a volunteer firefighter in Pennsylvania, and he had applied to work with the MVFD, undergoing a physical examination as part of the application process. The parties' relationship is that of a job applicant and potential employer, with the nature of the dispute being allegations of discrimination based on Hine's disability.

Christine Alisen Radtke, born as Richard William Barker in 1965, underwent gender dysphoria treatment and sex-reassignment surgery in 2003. In 2005, she obtained a court order to change her birth certificate to reflect her female sex and married Calvin Radtke in a civil ceremony in Goodhue County, Minnesota. As Mr. Radtke's spouse, Ms. Radtke was enrolled in the Miscellaneous Drivers and Helpers Union Local #638 Health, Welfare, Eye and Dental Fund (the Fund) as an eligible family dependent, effective August 10, 2005. 

Plaintiff alleges that she is Mr. Radtke's legal spouse under Minnesota law and an eligible dependent under the Fund's Plan. Defendant contends that Ms. Radtke's marriage to Mr. Radtke is not valid under Minnesota law because Minnesota Statute section 517.01 states that "Lawful marriage may be contracted only between persons of the opposite sex." The Fund's counsel, Peter Rosene, instructed the Fund Office to terminate Ms. Radtke's benefits in April 2010, citing the Minnesota statutory definition of marriage as the basis for the decision. 

The Fund Office had knowledge of Ms. Radtke's transgender status since 2008, when her physician identified her as a transgender individual on a pre-authorization request for a gel breast implant replacement. However, the Fund continued to pay Ms. Radtke's other medical claims until her benefits were terminated in April 2010. Ms. Radtke appealed the termination, providing various exhibits, including her amended birth certificate, marriage certificate, and documents demonstrating that state and federal agencies recognize her as female and Mr. Radtke's legal spouse. The Trustees considered her appeal and voted to uphold the determination that Ms. Radtke was ineligible, leading to the current lawsuit.

A group of residents, including Lillian E. Bryant, Lillian W. Bryant, Carl Briscoe, Gustavia Ellis, Pierre Hollingsworth, Michael F. Johnson, and Elwood S. Davis, as well as several civic associations, filed a lawsuit against the State of New Jersey, the New Jersey Department of Transportation, the New Jersey Transportation Trust Fund Authority, the South Jersey Transportation Authority, the Casino Reinvestment Development Authority, and Mirage Resorts, Inc. The plaintiffs allege that the construction of a highway and tunnel through their neighborhood will have a disparate impact on their predominantly African-American community, causing flooding, noise, and traffic problems, and violating Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. 

The plaintiffs contend that the project will require the condemnation of several homes and will disproportionately affect their community. The State of New Jersey and other state defendants argue that they are immune from suit under the Eleventh Amendment, while the plaintiffs claim that Congress has abrogated state sovereign immunity under Title VI. The plaintiffs also allege that the defendants' actions will violate United States Department of Transportation regulations promulgated pursuant to Title VI, which prohibits racial discrimination by entities receiving federal funds. 

Prior to the lawsuit, the defendants had planned to construct the highway and tunnel, which would receive federal funding. The plaintiffs, who are residents of the affected neighborhood, had expressed concerns about the project's impact on their community. The United States Department of Justice has intervened in the case to defend the constitutionality of the abrogation provision. The plaintiffs had previously filed an amended complaint, which outlined their factual allegations, and the state defendants had moved to dismiss the complaint on Eleventh Amendment grounds. The court had previously dismissed the plaintiffs' claims against the Casino Reinvestment Development Authority without prejudice due to lack of evidence of their involvement in the project. Mirage Resorts, Inc. had withdrawn its motion to dismiss the amended complaint.

Rebecca Johnson, an African American woman, was employed at the Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities (CHRO) from 2004 to 2008 as an HRO Representative. During her employment, she alleges that she and several other women were subjected to verbal abuse and humiliation by the prior director, Hamisi Ingram, on the basis of gender, which ultimately led to her suspension. Following a series of actions, including a widely publicized hearing before the Connecticut legislature's Committee on Labor and Public Employees in May 2006, Johnson filed a federal court complaint for harassment, discrimination, and retaliation against CHRO and Ingram in 2007. The complaint resulted in a settlement favorable to her with both CHRO and Ingram.

Johnson left CHRO in 2008 to take a management role at Central Connecticut State University. Ten years later, in May and June 2018, she applied for the position of Regional Manager in two different CHRO regional offices but was not invited to interview for either position. Defendants Tanya Hughes, CHRO Executive Director, and Cheryl Sharp, CHRO Deputy Executive Director, both African American women, were involved in the hiring process. Hughes claims she did not participate in reviewing applications or determining which candidates would be interviewed but did review and approve the final selections. Sharp participated in the application review process, completed a checklist review for some candidates, and participated in candidate interviews and the selection memo.

Plaintiff Johnson alleges that she was qualified for the Regional Manager position and that the only reason Defendants could have had not to hire her was either racial discrimination or retaliation. Defendants contend that Johnson was not selected to interview because she lacked sufficient experience, rather than due to racial discrimination, and that neither Defendant could have retaliated against her because they lacked knowledge that Johnson applied for the regional manager positions or that she had engaged in protected activity. Johnson asserts that Hughes was aware of her prior lawsuit against CHRO and Ingram because they had conversations about it, and that the nature of the lawsuit was so publicized that "everyone in the agency knew about the suit." Defendants both claim they were unaware of Johnson's protected activity before the current lawsuit was brought.

Quamar, an Asian American Muslim, is an employee of HHA. On November 30, 2020, Quamar submitted a request to HHA's Human Resources Department for a hardship withdrawal from his pension. By December 8, 2020, Quamar had not received an update on his request and was informed that his application was sent to the Director of HR, Dianne Mitchel. Quamar sent emails to Mitchel over the next several days, but when he asked for updates, he was ignored. On December 14, 2020, Quamar spoke with Mitchel by phone, and he noticed that someone else, later identified as HHA's General Counsel, Keland Lewis, was also on the call. Quamar refused to discuss his request in Lewis's presence.

Quamar alleges that Mitchel and Lewis violated his privacy and discriminated against him. He filed a complaint against them for alleged violations of the Privacy Act and Invasion of Privacy, Discrimination, Aiding and Abetting in Discrimination, Harassment, Intimidation, Retaliation, and Breach of Personal Information. On May 10, 2022, Quamar submitted a second request to HR for a financial hardship withdrawal from his 401(k), explaining that he wanted this request to be kept "confidential." However, when HR emailed Quamar to ask for documents to process his request, Lewis was included in the email thread, despite Quamar's request for confidentiality. Quamar contends that Lewis's inclusion in the email thread was a violation of his request for confidentiality.

Quamar also alleges that he contracted COVID-19 after HHA failed to properly notify him of potential exposure to the virus. On August 18, 2021, HR sent an email to all employees informing them that two individuals in the building tested positive for COVID-19, but Quamar was not contacted by HR, and he later learned that one of the employees who tested positive worked in his department in close quarters with him. Quamar took a leave of absence from work under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) due to his COVID-19 symptoms, which spread to his entire family. Upon returning to work, Quamar reported to HR that a manager created a hostile work environment, but the problem went unresolved. Additionally, Quamar alleges that another manager, Mitchel Sykes, made discriminatory comments about his race and asked him if he was "collecting human dust in a cup." Quamar filed a complaint against Sykes on October 13, 2022. HHA contends that it properly handled Quamar's requests for hardship withdrawals and that it did not discriminate or retaliate against him.

John Edward Hightower, Jr., a bi-racial individual, was hired as a cook at Jet's Pizza, owned by Charles Riley II LLC, on March 11, 2020, and was later promoted to store manager. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, owner Robert Shearin subjected him to sexual harassment by making statements of a sexual nature towards him and touching him in a sexual manner, despite Hightower's requests to stop. Hightower contends that he told Shearin to cease this behavior, but it continued. On June 15, 2023, while Hightower was closing the store, it was robbed, and Shearin put his arm around him and hugged him, prompting Hightower to push him away and remind him not to touch him. Hightower then asked for a couple of days off due to the stress of the robbery, which Shearin granted, but when Hightower later said he was still unable to return to work, Shearin fired him. Hightower alleges that his termination was in retaliation for complaining about the sexual harassment and filing a charge with the EEOC, and that his race was also a factor in the decision to fire him.

Defendant Robert Shearin and Jet's Pizza contend that they are not covered by Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 because they do not employ at least 15 people, which is a requirement for Title VII liability. They also argue that Shearin, as an individual, cannot be held personally liable under Title VII. In support of their position, they provided an affidavit from Joelle Shearin, the business manager of Charles Riley II LLC, which includes payroll journals and a spreadsheet summarizing the number of employees at the pizzeria from October 6, 2022, to April 14, 2024.

Hightower disputes the Defendants' claim about the number of employees, stating that it is a question of fact that requires further examination and discovery. He asserts that he should be given the opportunity to investigate the alleged facts behind the Defendants' claim about the number of employees. Hightower filed an initial Charge of Discrimination with the Tennessee Human Rights Commission and EEOC on May 9, 2023, and a supplemental Charge on July 14, 2023, detailing the alleged harassment and retaliation. Prior to filing the lawsuit, Hightower had interactions with his employer, including requesting time off after the robbery and being fired by Shearin. The parties' dispute centers on the alleged sexual harassment, retaliation, and the applicability of Title VII to the Defendants.

Mills, an inmate with a history of serious mental illnesses, including schizophrenia, psychotic disorder, Parkinson's disease, and dementia, was housed in a single cell in the Special Needs Unit (SNU) at North Branch Correctional Institution (NBCI) from June 1, 2009, until June 20, 2019. Plaintiff alleges that on June 20, 2019, he was ordered to move to a double cell and be housed with another inmate who is also severely mentally ill. Mills claims that Defendants, including correctional officers and administrators, attempted to make him move to the double cell, which he refused, citing concerns about his mental health. 

Plaintiff alleges that as a result of his refusal, he was placed on disciplinary segregation for 43 days, which worsened his mental health conditions. Mills contends that he was again attempted to be moved to a double cell, but he refused and was again moved to disciplinary segregation. He claims that on October 21, 2019, correctional staff removed him from the SNU and put him in a protective custody cell, but then tried to move him to a double cell in general population with an inmate who was not mentally ill. Mills refused to go into the cell and was placed on disciplinary segregation, where he remained as of the filing of one of his complaints. 

Mills alleges that the Defendants knew or should have known about his severe mental illnesses and the effects of disciplinary segregation on his health. He claims that the Defendants' refusal to provide him a single cell violated his rights and worsened his mental health. Plaintiff contends that he should be granted a permanent "psychological single cell" because housing him with another inmate places him in "grave danger of maim and murder." Defendants, on the other hand, have filed motions to dismiss, which Mills has opposed, arguing that his complaints state valid claims for relief. The parties' relationship is that of inmate and correctional institution staff, with the dispute centering on the conditions of Mills' confinement and the adequacy of his mental health treatment.

The plaintiff, a black individual, was hired by Staples (also known as Office Superstore East, LLC) on October 29, 2019, as a store manager in training. Plaintiff alleges that he experienced discrimination by reason of race through failure to promote, unequal terms and conditions of employment, and retaliation. His employment was terminated on February 4, 2020. Prior to his termination, the plaintiff had completed his module training and had asked about his promotion to manager, but was rejected. The plaintiff contends that a manager in training of a different race seeking the same promotion was treated more favorably.

The plaintiff filed a charge of discrimination on October 23, 2020, and received a notice of suit rights from the EEOC on April 30, 2021. The defendant moves to dismiss the case, arguing that the plaintiff failed to properly serve the summons and complaint, and that the complaint fails to state claims upon which relief can be granted. The plaintiff responds that he thought the defendant was being served at the same time the case was being filed, and attached a certificate of mailing to the defendant dated May 12, 2022.

The plaintiff alleges that he was qualified for the manager position, but was rejected despite his qualifications. He also alleges that he complained to Human Relations about being treated less favorably than his white counterpart, and that shortly after, he was not allowed in the store, was not properly trained, and was written up for menial matters. The defendant contends that the plaintiff fails to state a failure to promote claim because he did not allege that he applied for and was qualified for any open position, and that he fails to plead the elements of a retaliation claim. The plaintiff's response to the motion to dismiss does not address whether the complaint states claims upon which relief can be granted.

Inez Frazier, a black female, worked for the Camden County Sheriff's Department from 1984 until her termination on August 1, 1995. During her tenure, she rose from the position of radio dispatcher to that of jail administrator and was promoted to the rank of captain in January 1993. As jail administrator, she was responsible for the operation of the Camden County jail and answered to either Sheriff William E. Smith or Charlie Easterling, Chief Deputy Sheriff. Frazier alleges that Easterling, a white man, used racial slurs in the workplace to refer to her and others, creating a hostile work environment. She complained of Easterling's behavior to Sheriff Smith and other employees.

Frazier also contends that she was discriminated against on the basis of her disability, carpal tunnel syndrome, which made it impossible for her to perform some of her job duties. She requested certain accommodations for her condition, but the Department did not comply with her requests. As a result, on July 24, 1995, she was placed on temporary medical leave. After an inmate escaped from the Camden County jail on July 25, 1995, Sheriff Smith ordered an investigation and subsequently terminated Frazier on August 1, 1995. Two other employees were given the option of resigning or facing termination in connection with the escape. Sheriff Smith contends that Frazier's termination was based on the escape and other complaints he had received about her performance. James Proctor, a white male, succeeded Frazier as jail administrator.

Plaintiff alleges that she was subjected to racial discrimination and a hostile work environment, while Defendants contend that her termination was based on legitimate reasons. The parties dispute whether Frazier was a member of Sheriff Smith's personal staff, which would exempt her from the coverage of Title VII. Frazier claims that she was not a member of the Sheriff's personal staff, while Defendants argue that she was. The Department's actions and decisions regarding Frazier's employment, including her promotion, accommodation requests, and termination, are central to the dispute. Relevant pre-litigation events include Frazier's complaints to Sheriff Smith and other employees about Easterling's behavior, her requests for accommodations due to her disability, and the investigation and termination following the inmate's escape.

Seth Hadley, the plaintiff, was employed by Walmart Stores East, LP, the defendant. Plaintiff alleges that, despite his satisfactory performance, he was subjected to discrimination based on his disability while working at Walmart. Specifically, he claims that disparaging remarks were made about his disability. In March 2024, Hadley reported the discriminatory conduct to Walmart's management, but he contends that the company failed to take appropriate corrective action. Instead, he alleges that Walmart continued to make disparaging remarks regarding his disability, creating a hostile work environment that ultimately led to his departure from the company.

Plaintiff contends that he has suffered damages, including lost wages and emotional distress, as a direct result of Walmart's alleged unlawful conduct. Defendant Walmart, on the other hand, has not explicitly stated its version of events in the provided text, but it has moved to dismiss the plaintiff's complaint, suggesting that it disputes the allegations made against it. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, and the nature of the dispute is a claim of disability discrimination and hostile work environment.

Prior to the lawsuit, Hadley reported the alleged discriminatory conduct to Walmart's management in March 2024. The complaint does not provide detailed information about the events leading up to the report or the specific actions taken by Walmart in response. The lawsuit was filed, and Walmart has moved to dismiss the complaint, arguing that it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. The plaintiff has responded to the motion, clarifying that he is attempting to state a disability discrimination claim under the Americans with Disabilities Act, as well as claims for hostile work environment and constructive discharge.

Robert M. Lopez, a 46-year-old Hispanic man with polio and post-polio syndrome, was employed as a layout draftsman/CAD operator at Union Tank Car Company's drafting department since October 1977. Lopez's supervisor, Dennis Chansler, who became the Chief Draftsman in March 1992, disagreed with Lopez's promotion to layout draftsman in February 1992. Chansler was responsible for evaluating employees' performance, and Lopez received high ratings in 1992 and 1993, but his rating decreased to 2.82 in 1994. Chansler prepared the 1994 evaluation without soliciting input from Lopez's group leader, Richard Benak, who had previously rated Lopez highly. 

Lopez alleges that he was subjected to racial and national origin harassment by his coworkers, including being called derogatory names such as "wetback," "cockroach," "fucking Mexican," and "fucking spic." He also claims that his physical handicap was criticized, with comments about his arms. Lopez reported this harassment to Benak, who witnessed some of the incidents. In March 1995, Lopez sent a memo to Union's Chief Engineer and Vice President of Engineering, complaining that Chansler's evaluation was "not objective," "demeaning," and "meant to defame" his ability as a layout draftsman. Lopez filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in April 1995, concerning Chansler's evaluation. 

Union Tank Car Company contends that Lopez was discharged on July 12, 1995, as part of a reduction-in-force, due to his poor performance. Chansler states that he decided to discharge Lopez because of his deteriorating performance in 1995, and that he would not have selected Lopez for discharge if his performance had remained at its pre-February 1995 level. However, Lopez alleges that his discharge was discriminatory, based on his race, national origin, age, and disability, and that Union retaliated against him for complaining about the harassment and filing the EEOC charge. Lopez also disputes Chansler's claim that his position was eliminated, noting that another employee, Tim Prasky, was promoted to the position of layout draftsman on the same day Lopez was discharged.

The Nutrition Program for the Elderly, established under Title VII of the Older Americans Act, provides funds to states to offer hot meals to elderly persons. The program was created in 1972 but did not begin until July 1973 due to Presidential vetoes of fiscal year 1973 appropriation bills. Congress initially authorized $100 million for FY 1973 and $150 million for FY 1974, with a supplemental appropriation of $100 million for FY 1973. The program became "advanced funded" or "forward funded," spending funds in the year following their appropriation. In 1974, Congress extended the program for three years, appropriating $150 million for FY 1974, $200 million for FY 1975, and $250 million for FY 1976.

In FY 1976, Congress appropriated $125 million in new funds and mandated a "level of operations" of $187.5 million per annum. Defendants, responsible for administering the program, interpreted this to mean a monthly expenditure rate that would result in a total of $187.5 million if continued over a full year. However, due to the late enactment of the appropriations bill and the delayed issuance of a Program Instruction, the $187.5 million annualized rate of expenditure would only be effective for the final three months of the fiscal year, resulting in a total expenditure of approximately $160 million. Plaintiffs, elderly persons who qualify for the program but are unable to participate due to inadequate funding, allege that defendants are impounding funds intended for the program. 

Plaintiffs contend that the Congressional mandate requires an actual expenditure of $187.5 million during FY 1976, and that defendants' limitation of actual expenditures to $160 million is an illegal impoundment of funds. Defendants argue that Congress intended to mandate only a $187.5 million annualized rate of expenditure, not an actual expenditure of that amount during the year. The parties disagree on the interpretation of the Labor-HEW Appropriations Act for Fiscal Year 1976 and the requirements of Title VII of the Older Americans Act. Relevant pre-litigation events include the Presidential veto of the appropriations bill in December 1975, which was later overridden by Congress, and the issuance of a Program Instruction by defendants on March 27, 1976, implementing the funding increase.

Mina Davari, a woman, applied for a car salesman position at Landers Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Norman, a dealership in Norman, Oklahoma. Plaintiff alleges that despite her qualifications, she was not hired for the position because of her gender. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) filed a complaint on behalf of Davari, naming five defendants, including Landers Chrysler of Norman, Motors Management Corporation, LL Glenn Road LLC d/b/a Landers Toyota, The Luther Holding Company d/b/a Luther Automotive Group, and LL Glenn Plaza Loop LLC d/b/a Landers Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Little Rock. The EEOC contends that these defendants collectively constitute a single employer and single integrated enterprise, and therefore, should be held liable for the alleged discriminatory acts.

Defendants, except for Landers Chrysler of Norman, filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that administrative remedies had not been exhausted as to them, as they were not named in the underlying EEOC charge filed by Davari. The EEOC responds that an exception applies, as the complaint alleges that all defendants constitute a single employer, and that they were all sent a Letter of Determination inviting them to join in conciliation efforts. The EEOC also argues that the complaint alleges numerous facts relevant to the single employer test, including interrelated operations, common management, centralized control of labor relations, and common ownership and financial control.

Before filing the lawsuit, Davari had filed a charge with the EEOC, which led to an investigation and a Letter of Determination. The EEOC alleges that during the transition of the Norman dealership from David Stanley Chrysler to Landers Chrysler of Norman, Davari overheard a conversation between a manager, Chris Chase, and another manager, in which Chase made a comment suggesting that the sales position was not suitable for a woman. The EEOC contends that this and other allegations demonstrate a pattern of discriminatory behavior and support the single employer theory of liability.

On March 12, 2012, Plaintiff was hired by the 781st Military Intelligence Battalion (781st MIB) as an Intelligence Specialist (Operations) at Fort Meade, Maryland, with the expectation that he would perform the basic duties as an interactive on-net operator (ION). However, Captain William Rhoades noted "ability gaps" in Plaintiff's background, leading to additional training, which Plaintiff completed between April and October 2012. Plaintiff successfully completed these trainings but failed the Remote Operations Center (ROC) assessment on November 16, 2012, a proprietary exam administered by the NSA, which meant he would not be an ION. 

Plaintiff alleges that he was not properly prepared for the ROC assessment and that his failure was used as a basis for separation. Defendant contends that Plaintiff's failure to pass the ROC assessment meant he was not qualified for interactive operations. After the failed assessment, Lieutenant Colonel Dietra Trotter attempted to place Plaintiff in an alternative position at Fort Gordon, Georgia, which Plaintiff declined. As a result, Plaintiff was scheduled for termination, as documented in a December 12, 2012, memorandum by Captain Rhoades. However, Senior Cyber Adviser Gregory Platt intervened, and Plaintiff was instead placed in an S6 role in the 780th MIB, which he began on January 3, 2013.

Plaintiff's work attendance became an issue, as he would often visit family in Georgia and arrive late to work on Mondays, initially being allowed to work late to make up for the lost time. However, on June 17, 2013, Plaintiff was required to submit a request for leave without pay for his late arrival. Plaintiff alleges that he was being singled out and discriminated against based on his race and age regarding the enforcement of leave policy. He contacted an EEO counselor, which led to an EEO Complaint, and discussed his concerns with his supervisor, Michael Young, and Young's supervisor, Major Ross. The EEO Complaint and subsequent discussions led to a change in the work environment, with coworkers testifying that the atmosphere became tense after Young and Major Ross discussed the complaint publicly. Plaintiff was then assigned to open and close the Deer Path Facility, which was being made operational as the headquarters for the 781st MIB and was subject to security restrictions. Plaintiff alleges that he was not formally briefed on these requirements and subsequently violated security protocols by bringing a personal cell phone into the facility and leaving equipment unattended.

The Plaintiff, 545 Halsey Lane Properties, LLC, purchased a 40.747 acre parcel of property in the Town of Southampton in 2003 for $15,150,000. The property, known as Suffolk County Tax Map No. 900-105.000-0001-001.030, is located in the R-80 Residential Zoning District and within an Agricultural Overlay District (AOD) established by the Town in 1972. The property had been utilized as agricultural farmland prior to its purchase by the Plaintiff. In 1980, the prior owners of the property, Raymond G. Wesnofske and Leonard Schulman, entered into an agreement with the Town pursuant to New York General Municipal Law § 247, which imposed certain understandings and agreements concerning the use of the property. This agreement, known as the Grant, reserved numerous property rights to the prior owners and their successors, including the right to utilize the property for farming operations, open space, recreational areas, and the construction of a single-family dwelling and accessory structures.

The Plaintiff alleges that the Grant permits the construction of a barn on the property, and in 2006, the Plaintiff sought to construct an 11,250 square foot barn on the property. The Plaintiff was directed to file an application for a permit with the Planning Board for site plan review. The Planning Board referred the application to the Agricultural Advisory Committee (AAC), which commented that the proposed size of the barn was "disproportionately large" for the proposed agricultural endeavor and that the ball field and playground equipment on the property were not an agricultural use. The AAC also questioned what equipment would be stored inside the barn and asserted that the equipment identified by the Plaintiff was "essentially landscaping equipment," which could not be stored on the property. The Plaintiff addressed the AAC's comments, noting that the ball field and playground equipment were recreational uses permitted by the Grant, and that the proposed structure size was consistent with other permits issued for barn constructions in the Town.

The Plaintiff and the Defendants, including the Town of Southampton, the Planning Board, and various members of the Planning Board and the AAC, have a dispute over the interpretation of the Grant and the Town Code, and whether the construction of the barn is permitted on the property. The Plaintiff contends that the Grant and the Town Code allow for the construction of the barn, while the Defendants argue that the proposed barn is not consistent with the agricultural use of the property and that the Grant does not permit such construction. The parties also disagree over the meaning of "agricultural production" and what structures are permitted on the property under the Town Code. The Plaintiff has submitted various studies and reports to support its application, including a review of public records and a study of the density of barns on parcels within the AOD. The Defendants have raised concerns about the size and location of the proposed barn, as well as the impact on the "view shed" of other preserved farmland.

Female employees, currently and formerly working as "cashiers" at parking lots owned by William Penn Parking Corporation, Inc. and Aleo Parking Corporation, allege that they have been discriminated against based on their sex. These employees, all of whom are female, claim that they perform essentially the same duties as "attendants," who are mostly male and receive higher pay. The female "cashiers" number around twenty-five and have requested equal pay and the same job classification without loss of seniority, but their requests have not been satisfied. The defendants have offered to allow "cashiers" to apply for "attendant" positions, but this would not guarantee a change in status and would result in a loss of seniority benefits.

Plaintiffs allege that the defendants' actions constitute sexual discrimination, and they seek damages, including back pay, and injunctive relief to end the discriminatory conduct. The plaintiffs define their class as all females who have been, are, or may be discriminated against in the payment of wages and terms and conditions of employment by the defendants. Defendants deny that any discrimination has occurred and argue that the plaintiffs have not met the requirements for class certification, particularly with respect to numerosity.

The plaintiffs claim that they have faced reprisals and retaliation from the defendants, which has made it difficult for them to find a current employee to represent the class as a named plaintiff. They also assert that the delay in filing their motion for class certification was due to their counsel's caution in locating proper representatives of the prospective class. The defendants, on the other hand, contend that the plaintiffs have not complied with the local rules regarding the timing of the motion for class certification and that the class is not numerous enough to warrant a class action. The plaintiffs and defendants have exchanged motions, with the plaintiffs seeking class certification and the defendants seeking to dismiss the action as a class action.

In 1995, some or all of the defendants, who were independent distributors of Amway products, disseminated a voice mail message via Amway's Amvox voice mail system. The message stated that a large portion of the profits of Procter & Gamble's products went to support a satanic church. This rumor is now acknowledged by all parties to be false. As a result of the Amvox messages, Procter & Gamble (P&G) filed the present action against the defendants, as well as a companion case in Texas. 

Plaintiff Procter & Gamble alleges that the defendants sent the Amvox messages, which contained the false rumor, and that these messages constituted commercial speech. Defendants admit that they sent the messages and that the rumor was false, but they contend that the messages were not commercial speech because they contained a significant theological component. The parties also disagree on whether the messages were sufficiently disseminated to constitute commercial advertising or promotion under the Lanham Act. 

Prior to the lawsuit, the defendants were independent distributors of Amway products, and Procter & Gamble was a competitor in the consumer goods market. The Amvox voice mail system was used by Amway distributors to communicate with each other and with potential customers. The false rumor about Procter & Gamble's products was spread through this system, allegedly damaging Procter & Gamble's reputation and business. The parties have engaged in extensive litigation, including multiple appeals to the Tenth Circuit, with the Lanham Act claim being the only claim remaining for the upcoming jury trial.

Joseph Jendusa was employed by Midwestern Regional Medical Center, Inc. and Cancer Treatment Centers of America, Inc. (CTCA) for over three years, serving as Vice President of Human Resources. In mid-March 1993, Jendusa informed Robert Mayo, then President of CTCA, that he had multiple sclerosis. He subsequently informed Richard Stephenson, Chairman of the Board and principal owner of CTCA and Midwestern, and R. Richard Wieland, President of CTCA's corporate parent, about his condition and requested a temporary reduction in his work week to 40 hours as an accommodation. Two days later, Jendusa was terminated from his position. The company then recruited a new Director of Human Resources to take over his duties, and Jendusa was not considered for the position. Plaintiff alleges that Stephenson participated directly in his termination. 

Jendusa contends that his termination was a result of discrimination based on his disability, in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Defendants CTCA and Midwestern have answered the complaint, while Stephenson moves to have the complaint against him dismissed, arguing that individual liability under the ADA may not be imposed on him as he is not a "covered entity" under the statute. 

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Jendusa having worked for CTCA and Midwestern for over three years before his termination. The nature of the dispute is Jendusa's allegation that he was terminated due to his disability, which he claims is a violation of the ADA. Jendusa alleges that he was discriminated against because of his multiple sclerosis, while defendants contend that they are not liable for any discrimination, with Stephenson arguing that he cannot be held personally liable under the ADA. Relevant pre-litigation events include Jendusa's disclosure of his condition to his superiors and his request for accommodation, which was followed by his termination.

Phyllis Kay Torbeck, a secretary at the Oklahoma City office of Ackerman, Hood & McQueen (AHM), an advertising and public relations firm, learned she was pregnant in January 1986 and announced the news to her coworkers. Prior to her pregnancy, Torbeck had never been disciplined at AHM and had a clean personnel file. As a pregnant employee, Torbeck would have been eligible for six weeks of paid maternity leave. However, four days after her pregnancy test, AHM's chairman, Raymond B. Ackerman, counseled Torbeck about her alleged unwillingness to work overtime, including evenings and weekends. 

Torbeck's obstetrician, Dr. James G. Cox, later sent a letter to AHM recommending that she work no more than 40 hours a week due to her pregnancy-related symptoms, such as fatigue, headaches, and lower back pain. Despite being in "good health," AHM discharged Torbeck on April 3, 1986, the day after she submitted her doctor's letter. The EEOC alleges that AHM fired Torbeck in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended by the Pregnancy Discrimination Act of 1978, claiming that AHM treated Torbeck's request to reduce her working hours differently than similar requests made by other employees. AHM contends that Torbeck was fired for insubordination because she intended to follow her doctor's recommendation and not work overtime, despite being in good health.

The parties have a history of interactions, including Torbeck's initial employment in December 1984, her request for time off for surgery in October 1985, and her subsequent return to work under different supervisors. AHM's management, including Ackerman, Angus McQueen, Bruce Anderson, and William Winkler, were involved in the decision to discharge Torbeck. The EEOC and AHM have exchanged correspondence and engaged in settlement discussions, with the EEOC ultimately filing a lawsuit on behalf of Torbeck. Torbeck's employment records, including time sheets and performance evaluations, are part of the evidence in the case, as well as the testimony of various witnesses, including Torbeck's coworkers, supervisors, and medical professionals.

John Dean Taylor was hired as a Rigger Helper by the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard (PNSY) on October 6, 1980, and was later promoted to Rigger Worker in 1984. On February 4, 1986, Taylor suffered a back injury while working at PNSY, which caused him to become a "handicapped individual" within the meaning of the Rehabilitation Act. As a result, Taylor was placed on leave status and began receiving benefits under the Federal Employees Compensation Act (FECA) on February 25, 1986. Taylor's physician, Dr. Schatzberg, indicated that Taylor could return to work in a light-duty capacity on October 3, 1986. 

Plaintiff alleges that the PNSY failed to accommodate his disability and discriminated against him because of it. Taylor contends that he was not reassigned to an appropriate permanent position after becoming disabled and was instead assigned to temporary details, including jobs inconsistent with his medical restrictions. Defendant Secretary of the Navy argues that Taylor was not qualified to work as a Rigger, the position for which he was hired, and therefore could not prevail on his claim of handicap-based discrimination. 

The parties' relationship began when Taylor was hired by PNSY, and the nature of the dispute arises from Taylor's allegations of disability-based discrimination and the Navy's actions in response to his injury and subsequent medical restrictions. Prior to the lawsuit, Taylor filed a complaint with the EEOC, which was rejected on February 28, 1990. Taylor then filed a pro se complaint on April 4, 1990, alleging harassment by PNSY personnel, and later filed an Amended Complaint on January 21, 1991, which included claims under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Relevant pre-litigation events include Taylor's back injury, his placement on leave status, and his receipt of FECA benefits, as well as the various medical examinations and job assignments he received after his injury. 

Defendant contends that Taylor was assigned to various jobs, including a Housekeeping position, which Taylor alleges was inconsistent with his medical restrictions. Taylor claims that he was removed from a job in the Purchasing Department and reassigned to the Housekeeping position despite his supervisor's desire to keep him in the Purchasing Department. The Navy also sent criminal investigators to interview Taylor's physicians, which Taylor alleges was a violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Taylor's contentions include that the Navy failed to accommodate his handicap, discriminated against him, and retaliated against him for filing a complaint with the EEOC. The Secretary of the Navy's contentions include that Taylor was not qualified to work as a Rigger and that the Navy's actions were lawful and reasonable.

Melani Deodhar Beattie, a 64-year-old female resident of Chicago, Illinois, began working as a salesperson for ST Media/HMG, also known as Boutique Design (BD), in March 2013. She worked remotely from her home in Chicago, operating in an assigned sales territory, and earned a salary plus commissions for any sale made within that territory. In October 2018, Emerald Expositions, a limited liability company headquartered in New York, purchased BD, and Beattie's employment transferred to Emerald. 

Beattie alleges that on January 12, 2019, Emerald EVP Joe Randall offered her a new employment contract that mimicked her prior contract with BD and assured her that Emerald intended to replicate her prior compensation structure. Randall emailed her a 2019 Sales Incentive Plan, which she signed, and which specified that she would earn a fixed base salary along with an opportunity to earn commissions on any "cumulative sales" generated by her during 2019. Beattie contends that her job responsibilities included working assigned trade shows and other events within an assigned geographic territory. 

Plaintiff alleges that sometime in early 2019, Emerald EVP Kevin Gaffney gave many of her trade show sales to three younger, less experienced salespeople, and that when she asked Gaffney how those assignments would impact her commissions and sales, she received no clear response. Defendant Gannon Brousseau, an Executive Vice President at Emerald, was not involved in drafting or negotiating the 2019 Sales Incentive Plan. The parties' relationship and the nature of the dispute center on Beattie's employment with Emerald, the terms of her employment contract, and the allocation of sales and commissions. Emerald's actions, including the purchase of BD and the subsequent changes to Beattie's sales territory and commission structure, are at the heart of the dispute.

Bishop Blanchet High School, a private Catholic high school, is located in a residential, single-family zone in North Seattle. The height limit for institutions in this zone is 30 feet. To better illuminate its athletic field, Bishop Blanchet sought to install four, 70-foot-tall light poles. The City of Seattle's Land Use Code requires institutions to apply for a variance if their proposed structures exceed the height limit. On April 25, 2013, the Director of the Department of Planning and Development (DPD) approved Bishop Blanchet's variance application, subject to 21 conditions addressing impacts such as noise, traffic, and light spill. However, on May 8, 2013, Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, an association of nearby homeowners and residents, appealed the DPD decision to the Hearing Examiner, who subsequently reversed the approval on July 17, 2013.

The City of Seattle has a Special Exception that exempts public schools in residential, single-family zones from the 30-foot height requirement for athletic field lighting. Under this exception, public schools can install higher light poles, up to 100 feet, if they demonstrate that the additional height is necessary for adequate illumination and that impacts from light and glare are minimized. Two public high schools in North Seattle, Nathan Hale High School and Ingraham High School, have utilized this Special Exception to install light poles on their athletic fields. Bishop Blanchet alleges that the City's requirement for a variance, while exempting public schools, violates the Equal Terms provision of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) and deprives Bishop Blanchet of substantive due process under the Washington State Constitution.

Plaintiff Bishop Blanchet contends that it is similarly situated to public schools like Nathan Hale and Ingraham High Schools, which have been allowed to install taller light poles under the Special Exception. Bishop Blanchet argues that the City's distinction between private religious schools and public schools is not justified by any legitimate regulatory purpose. Defendant City of Seattle argues that the Special Exception is justified by the accepted zoning criteria of "fostering the provision of public facilities by governmental agencies." Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, as an interested party, opposes Bishop Blanchet's variance request, citing concerns about noise, traffic, and light pollution. The parties have filed cross-motions for summary judgment, agreeing that there are no material facts in dispute.

The union representing approximately 6,000 flight attendants, IFFA, was engaged in contract negotiations with the defendant airline, TWA, starting in 1984. The negotiations aimed to amend the existing contract, known as the "Red Book," which was set to remain in effect until July 31, 1984. TWA sought mid-term concessions valued at $33 million, including work rules changes that would create a "new lifestyle" for its flight attendants and salary concessions. IFFA's general goal was to postpone adverse changes in the contract for as long as possible and to obtain some improvements in the agreement.

IFFA alleges that TWA engaged in bad faith bargaining, failing to provide necessary and relevant information during negotiations. IFFA's president, Victoria Frankovich, and its counsel, Jolley, adopted a strategy of "close and cautious scrutiny" and "cautious willingness to listen and entertain" TWA's proposals, while placing the burden of persuasion on TWA. TWA, on the other hand, contends that it made significant concessions, including reducing its demands by approximately one-half in February 1985, and that IFFA failed to react favorably to these concessions. TWA's president, C.E. Meyer, Jr., presented information showing that TWA's flight attendant costs were the highest in the industry, and that the company had suffered an operating loss of $72 million in the first quarter of 1984.

The parties' negotiations continued until May 1985, when IFFA sought release from further negotiations, which would have started a 30-day countdown and the possibility of a strike during the summer season. IFFA received "overwhelming authorization to strike" from its members in May 1985. The National Mediation Board scheduled a cooling-off period, which ended on March 6, 1986. After the cooling-off period, TWA implemented the proposed wage reductions and adverse changes in work rules, leading to a flight attendants' strike on March 7, 1986. IFFA offered to return to work under the new conditions imposed by TWA in mid-May 1986, but fewer than 200 of the full-term strikers were accepted back by TWA, and the majority of the pre-strike work force was displaced. The dispute centers on the issue of whether the strikers were "unfair labor practice strikers" entitled to return to their jobs after the strike, displacing all replacements, and enjoying back pay entitlement.

Marlene Thomas was hired by Southwestern Virginia Transit Management Company, Inc. (SVTMC) in June 2014 to work as an information officer at Valley Metro, a public transportation provider in the Roanoke Valley. Thomas' job duties included selling bus tickets, entering sales into a database, answering phone calls, and announcing buses. She worked in a confined space with a window for customer transactions and a single door for entry and exit. Thomas was employed as an information officer until July 24, 2019.

Beginning in February 2016, Valley Metro General Manager Carl Palmer began visiting Thomas' workspace approximately two to three times per week. Initially, the visits appeared to be work-related, but Palmer soon started giving Thomas unwanted attention, making sexually seductive facial expressions, and requesting that she call him. Thomas alleges that Palmer's behavior made her uncomfortable and that she believed he was not interested in discussing work-related matters. Plaintiff alleges that Palmer continued to visit and call her, making sexually suggestive comments and gestures, and propositioning her for sex. Thomas contends that she tried to avoid discussing Palmer's proposition and changed the subject or appeared busy to avoid him. 

Thomas alleges that Palmer's behavior affected her ability to perform her job and caused her significant emotional distress, including anxiety, stress, loss of sleep, and depression. Plaintiff alleges that she sought counseling to cope with the situation. Thomas also alleges that Palmer had promised to look into a raise for her but never followed through, and instead, told human resources administrators to deny her raise after she rejected his advances. Defendant Palmer contends that his interactions with Thomas were appropriate and that he did not engage in any wrongdoing. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Palmer being Thomas' supervisor. The nature of the dispute is a claim of quid pro quo sexual harassment and hostile work environment. Relevant pre-litigation events include Thomas' attempts to report the harassment to human resources, which she alleges were not properly addressed, and her eventual filing of a discrimination charge with the EEOC on August 22, 2018. The EEOC issued a right-to-sue letter on June 28, 2019, indicating that it was closing its file on the charge because it was not timely filed.

In August 2007, the plaintiff received a conditional offer of employment as an Emergency Operations Specialist with the Transportation and Emergency Control Center (TECC) at the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) in Albuquerque, New Mexico. The offer was contingent upon the plaintiff receiving certification from the Human Reliability Program. As part of this process, the plaintiff underwent a psychological interview administered by Dr. Daniel Seagrave. Plaintiff alleges that Dr. Seagrave provided "intentionally false information" in his report to Dr. Anthony Traweek, Dr. John Sloan, and Dennis Reese, which led to the denial of the necessary certification and the subsequent rescission of the employment offer.

Plaintiff contends that Dr. Seagrave's report contained false statements about the plaintiff's answers during the interview, and that Dr. Seagrave improperly contacted the plaintiff's former supervisor and fabricated allegations that the plaintiff had been reprimanded while serving in the United States Air Force. The plaintiff believes that Dr. Seagrave's actions were motivated by the plaintiff's race. The plaintiff also claims that there are no African Americans currently employed at TECC/NNSA in Albuquerque and that other Department of Energy employees have filed discrimination complaints against Dr. Seagrave.

The plaintiff filed a complaint of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) on April 22, 2008. The EEOC complaint alleged discrimination by the defendant, which the defendant denies. Prior to filing the lawsuit, the plaintiff and the defendant were involved in an EEOC proceeding, during which the EEOC Administrative Judge made a decision regarding the plaintiff's allegations of discrimination. The parties had exchanged communications and documents related to the plaintiff's employment application and the certification process, including the report prepared by Dr. Seagrave and the plaintiff's responses to the allegations contained therein.

Joseph Canada, a Black man, began working at Samuel Grossi & Sons, Inc. (Grossi), a steel producer, in 2009. Throughout his employment, he held various positions, including Helper, Painter, Saw Operator, and Material Handler. Canada was a member of a collective bargaining unit represented by the Shopmen's Local Union No. 502 of the International Association of Bridge, Structural, Ornamental and Reinforcing Iron Workers. The terms and conditions of his employment were governed by both a Collective Bargaining Agreement and Grossi's Employee Conduct and Disciplinary Action Policy.

Canada suffers from serious back problems, including herniated discs and arthritis, and informed Grossi of his need for medical accommodation. He obtained Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) forms himself and submitted them to Elena Osorio, Grossi's Director of Human Resources. Canada alleges that Osorio initially did not want to accept his FMLA forms but eventually did so. He utilized FMLA leave throughout the remainder of his employment. However, Osorio testified that she never approved FMLA leave for Canada and that he took leave without proper authorization. Canada claims that he was harassed when he returned to work after taking FMLA leave, with Osorio talking to him in a condescending manner and not responding to his messages.

Canada also alleges that he experienced racial discrimination and a hostile work environment. He testified that his coworker, Steve Carlberg, called him the N-word on two occasions, and that other employees reported that Joseph Beck, Grossi's shop foreman/shop superintendent, used the N-word as well. Canada claims that Beck used the slur in a crude story about sleeping with a Black woman and also to describe players on the Philadelphia 76ers NBA basketball team. Additionally, Canada alleges that Osorio used the N-word and told him to "stop fuckin' harassing me" during a meeting. Canada reported these incidents to Grossi's management, but he claims that no action was taken to address the harassment. Canada's employment was eventually terminated due to text messages found on a cellphone in a locker on Grossi's shop floor, which Canada contends was not a legitimate reason for his termination. Defendant claims that Canada's termination was based on a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason, and that the text messages were a valid basis for terminating his employment.

Christina Ryan, a Caucasian woman born in 1960, has worked for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) at Baltimore Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI) since 2004, and as a Master Behavior Detection Officer (MBDO) since 2014. Between 2007 and 2012, Ryan filed several Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaints against TSA, and she filed another EEO complaint on June 13, 2015. Ryan alleges that she met and/or exceeded TSA's legitimate job expectations at all relevant times and received an overall rating of "Exceeded Expectations" for the period from October 1, 2014, to September 30, 2015.

Ryan's first-line supervisor from May 2014 to October 2014 was Erica Foster Gibbs, an African American female born in 1985. John Chambers III, an African American born in 1962, became Ryan's first-line supervisor on or about October 30, 2014. Scott Wood, a Caucasian born in 1961, was Ryan's second-level supervisor throughout the relevant period. Ryan claims that upper management officials micromanaged her work performance but did not do the same with her African-American colleagues. In May or June 2014, Ryan informed Gibbs that she had approximately ten online learning courses to complete, and Gibbs allegedly responded with hostility, putting her face within one inch of Ryan's face and preventing her from exiting the room.

Ryan alleges that she was subjected to various forms of mistreatment and retaliation, including being falsely accused of spraying an African American passenger with Lysol, being denied a transfer request while similar requests from African American employees were granted, and being issued a Letter of Reprimand (LOR) on January 29, 2015, for an incident on October 10, 2014, in which she allegedly made inappropriate comments to an Operational Test Team member. Ryan claims that the LOR was unjustified and that she was not given an opportunity to have a Pre-Decision Meeting before it was issued, which is allegedly a policy and procedure of TSA. Ryan also alleges that non-Caucasian and/or substantially younger Behavior Detection Officers (BDOs) who expressed anger towards other individuals regarding utilization of fatigue mats and made inappropriate comments were not disciplined for doing so.

Ryan applied for a vacant position of Supervisory Behavior Detection Officer (SBDO) in February 2015 and interviewed for the position via telephone on March 25, 2015, receiving a consensus score of 27. However, she was not chosen for the position, and five other employees, including four African Americans and one Caucasian under 40, were selected instead. Ryan claims that she was plainly superior to one of the selected candidates, Brandy Durant, who received a consensus score of 25, and that she should have received a promotion over Durant. Ryan contends that the LOR and the non-selection for the SBDO position were based on her race and age, in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967. Defendant Chad Wolf, the Acting Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, contends that Ryan's allegations are without merit and that the actions taken against her were justified and non-discriminatory.

The plaintiff, a retiree, had her retirement benefits cut off completely by the defendants due to a discrepancy between her claimed birth date and what they believed to be her actual birth date, resulting in a difference of $1.01 per month in her benefits. Plaintiff alleges that this termination of benefits was done without a pre-deprivation hearing, denying her due process. The defendants contend that they offered the plaintiff a hearing under § 74(d) of New York State's Retirement and Social Security Law on April 4, 1990, and again on April 19, 1990, which the plaintiff's counsel declined. 

The plaintiff's counsel responded with skepticism and confusion about the proffered hearing, and subsequent letters were exchanged between the parties, with the defendants reiterating and explaining the offer, and the plaintiff's counsel demanding to know the authority for the hearing and the written procedures and/or regulations governing it. The defendants' counsel offered to restore the plaintiff's pension at the diminished rate until her right to the higher rate was established, but the plaintiff's counsel continued to press for more. 

The plaintiff's counsel spent significant time and resources litigating the case, including drafting and redrafting the complaint, consulting with colleagues, and reviewing documents. The plaintiff's counsel, consisting of four lawyers, sought compensation for their time at rates ranging from $175 to $300 per hour. The defendants contend that the plaintiff could have achieved the same result in April 1990 without incurring significant legal fees, and that the plaintiff's counsel should not be compensated for time spent pursuing a result that was already within their grasp. The plaintiff alleges that she was denied due process and seeks compensation for her legal fees.

The Nebraska Public Power District (NPPD) and several wind energy project owners, including Laredo, Broken Bow, Crofton, and Elkhorn, entered into Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) between 2008 and 2010. The PPAs required NPPD to purchase all energy produced by each project for 20 years at a predetermined price. The agreements included provisions restricting the project owners' ability to consolidate, merge, or transfer ownership interests without NPPD's written approval. 

Plaintiff alleges that the original ultimate parent company of the project entities, Edison Mission Energy (EME), filed for bankruptcy in 2012, and affiliates of NRG Energy, Inc. (NRG) acquired interests in parent companies and upstream affiliates of the project entities in 2014. Plaintiff further alleges that in 2018, an affiliate of GIP III Zephyr Acquisition Partners, LLP (GIP) acquired interests in parent companies of the project entities from NRG. NPPD was aware of NRG's proposed acquisition of EME's renewable assets and executed documents in connection with the exchange of letters of credit after the NRG acquisition. 

Defendant NPPD contends that the project entities were in violation of the PPAs and sent written notice of default to the project entities in January 2019, stating its intention to terminate the PPAs. The project entities dispute this contention, arguing that they were not in default and that NPPD did not have the right to terminate the PPAs. The project entities had entered into various agreements with outside entities, including services agreements and operation and maintenance agreements, to meet their obligations under the PPAs. The project entities, except for Elkhorn, had entered into services agreements with Clearway Asset Services, and all project entities had entered into operation and maintenance agreements with Clearway Renewable Operation & Maintenance LLC. Crofton and Elkhorn also had agreements with Vestas-American Wind Technology, Inc. (Vestas) for maintenance and repair services.

Richard A. Wilson, a Jamaican-born man, began working for Columbia Gas of Pennsylvania as a Service Technician in 2008. He was the only African American and Jamaican employee at the company. Wilson alleges that he was singled out based on his race and national origin, subjected to a hostile work environment, and treated differently than similarly situated Caucasian employees. He claims that these incidents became more frequent over the years, starting around 2008, and included being asked derogatory questions, being sent to low-income neighborhoods, being referred to as "the black guy," and being assigned undesirable work tasks.

Plaintiff Wilson alleges that he maintained perfect attendance and performed his job skillfully, earning satisfactory performance reviews, annual incentives, bonuses, and raises. He also volunteered his time to give back to the community and received complimentary letters and phone calls from satisfied customers. However, he claims that he was subjected to various forms of harassment and discrimination, including being asked to remove his hat so a coworker could defecate in it, being ridiculed for wearing collared shirts, and being assigned to work in high-crime neighborhoods at night. Wilson also alleges that he was not invited to a company celebration for employees with perfect attendance, despite having perfect attendance throughout his career.

Wilson contends that he reported the discrimination and harassment to his supervisor, Darryl Wargo, and other company officials, including the head of Human Resources, multiple times starting in 2012. He claims that his reports were met with inaction, and the incidents worsened over time. In 2019, Wargo was promoted to manager, and Wilson alleges that Wargo's behavior towards him became more abusive and condescending. In January 2021, Wilson reported concerns about his company phone and feeling like he was being followed, which led to a telephone conference with company officials, who suggested that he undergo a medical exam. Wilson objected to the medical evaluation but was eventually required to undergo one, which concluded that he was not "fit for duty." Columbia Gas refused to allow him to return to work, citing the medical evaluation, and eventually terminated his employment in September 2021. Defendant Columbia Gas and Wargo contend that Wilson's allegations are unfounded and that they did not discriminate against him based on his race, national origin, or disability.

Karl Byrd, Sr., an African-American, began working for The Baltimore Sun Company's paper handling department in 1979. In June 1996, a note was placed in his employment record detailing an insubordinate act, which Byrd discovered in October 1997. Byrd requested that the note be removed from his file, but the company refused. Byrd then complained to the Baltimore Graphic Communications Union Local 31, which chose not to pursue the matter further after investigating. On August 20, 1998, Byrd filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) alleging racial discrimination by both The Sun and the Union, citing events dating back to 1985. The EEOC investigated but was unable to conclude that a violation had occurred, and Byrd received a "right-to-sue" letter.

Byrd was demoted from paperhandler foreman to paper-handler on March 11, 1999, with his supervisor, Glenn Davis, citing his "continuing failure to support and follow simple management directives" as the reason. Byrd filed a grievance with the Union protesting his demotion. After a series of meetings and discussions, Byrd was temporarily replaced as night-shift paperhandler foreman by Phyllis Asbury, an African-American woman, and later by Donald Green, also African-American. On May 5, 1999, The Sun detailed eight reasons for Byrd's demotion, including failure to follow procedures and unauthorized early departures from the workplace. Byrd suffered an outbreak of hives on June 16, 1999, allegedly due to work-related stress, and took a leave of absence. He returned to work on October 13, 1999, but was soon suspended for five days for refusing to attend a meeting with his supervisor, Davis.

Plaintiff alleges that his demotion, suspension, and eventual termination were discriminatory and retaliatory actions taken by The Sun and the Union. Byrd contends that he was treated differently than other employees outside of his protected class and that the reasons given for his demotion and suspension were pretextual. The Sun, on the other hand, claims that Byrd's demotion and suspension were due to his failure to follow management directives and his unsatisfactory conduct. The Union contends that it did not discriminate against Byrd and that its actions were taken in accordance with its collective bargaining agreement with The Sun. Byrd also alleges that he was subjected to a hostile work environment, but The Sun and the Union deny this claim, stating that there is no evidence of harassment based on Byrd's race.

Elizabeth Salsbury, a speech pathologist, was terminated by SunDance Rehabilitation Corporation on March 1, 1999, as part of a company-wide reduction in force. SunDance offered Salsbury 80 hours of severance pay, conditioned on her signing a Separation Agreement and General Release, which included a provision releasing SunDance from all claims arising before the date of the release. The agreement also prohibited Salsbury from instituting any proceeding or claim against SunDance in any administrative, judicial, or other forum. Salsbury called SunDance's Human Resources Department and asked if she could strike out the part of the agreement that prohibited her from filing a charge with the EEOC, but was told that any alterations would be null and void. Salsbury did not sign the agreement.

Salsbury subsequently filed a charge of discrimination with the EEOC on April 20, 1999, alleging that she was denied a promotion on the basis of her sex. The EEOC investigated Salsbury's charge and requested that SunDance submit its reduction in force policy and procedure and its severance policy. On September 30, 1999, the EEOC issued a determination finding no reasonable cause to believe that Salsbury was discriminated against on the promotion or lay-off issues, but stating that SunDance's waiver/release provision failed to meet the criteria for a knowing and voluntary waiver under the ADEA and may have a chilling effect on employees' willingness to cooperate with the EEOC.
