The EEOC alleges that SunDance's policy of requiring terminated employees to waive their rights to file a charge with the EEOC in exchange for severance payments constitutes retaliation in violation of Title VII, the EPA, the ADEA, and the ADA. SunDance contends that its severance payment policy is not retaliatory and that the waiver provision in the Separation Agreement is enforceable. Salsbury filed a second EEOC charge on February 12, 2000, alleging that SunDance's failure to recall her to two positions was retaliation for her filing her first charge of discrimination with the EEOC. The EEOC dismissed her claim and issued her a right to sue letter. On March 7, 2000, Salsbury signed the Separation Agreement, but SunDance had already gone bankrupt and she did not receive the severance pay.

The plaintiff, a resident of Alabama, enlisted in the United States Air Force in 1972 and was discharged in 1974 for medical reasons. He subsequently made claims for Veteran's benefits with the United States Department of Veterans Affairs ("VA"). Plaintiff alleges that his military records show the onset of his disabilities and that he raised the existence of racial disparity in educational and training opportunities, and in promotions. He claims that the Alabama Department of Veterans Affairs ("ADVA") in Montgomery, Alabama, delayed and denied his benefits, denied him proper medical treatment, and violated his civil rights. 

Plaintiff alleges that he commenced his claims in 1974 and appealed them to the Veteran's Appeals Court on July 25, 2014. He contends that the Veteran's Appeals Court concluded that there were issues of law cited by the plaintiff of U.S. Constitutional significance and pertinent in the just enforcement under U.S. Laws, and the Constitution of the United States. The Veteran's Appeals Court also reminded plaintiff of the original jurisdiction of district courts to hear such claims. Plaintiff asserts that when the Veteran's Appeals Court case was closed on October 7, 2015, he exhausted his administrative remedies.

Defendants contend that sovereign immunity and the Veterans' Judicial Review Act ("VJRA") preclude judicial review of the Veteran's benefits claim by the court. They also argue that plaintiff failed to file an administrative claim pursuant to the Federal Tort Claims Act ("FTCA") for his medical negligence claim. Additionally, defendants claim that 42 U.S.C. § 1983 only applies to the States, and the Supreme Court has refused to extend Section 1983 claims based upon the federal Constitution against the United States or its federal agencies. Defendants also argue that Title VII and the Civil Service Reform Act provide the exclusive judicial remedy for discrimination in federal employment, but plaintiff did not comply with those laws' administrative prerequisites. William Robert Boulware, an attorney with the VA Office of District Counsel in Montgomery, Alabama, declared that he has not received a tort claim filed by or on behalf of plaintiff and found no record of a tort claim by plaintiff in the electronic tracking system.

James N. Patnaude, a former employee of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), worked as an intelligence research specialist (IRS) from February 16, 1999. He participated in various investigations, including telemarketing fraud and child pornography, and also worked on the FBI's Hazardous Materials Response Team due to his experience as a volunteer fire fighter, HAZMAT responder, and emergency medical technician. In 2001, Patnaude applied for a supervisory IRS position but was not selected. Around the same time, his job performance was criticized by supervisors and case agents, leading to his removal from the HAZMAT team and orders to focus exclusively on his IRS responsibilities.

Plaintiff alleges that he was unfairly treated by his supervisors and, in April 2002, filed a grievance with his Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) counselor. Shortly after, he began taking materials related to the EEO complaint home each evening. On May 21, 2002, Patnaude received an unfavorable rating and review from his supervisors. On May 30, 2002, he was stopped and searched as he was leaving the FBI building, and various documents, including some classified as secret and sensitive, were found in his possession. A criminal search warrant was executed at his residence the following day, and his personal computer and ZIP diskettes were seized. Child pornography images were discovered on one of the diskettes, leading to a criminal investigation.

Defendants contend that Patnaude mishandled documents and possessed child pornography, while Patnaude claims he inadvertently removed other materials when taking home documents related to his EEO complaint. Patnaude was suspended from his job pending an investigation, and in April 2003, the United States Attorney's Office declined to prosecute him for mishandling classified information and possessing child pornography. Patnaude's suspension was upheld in June 2003, and he continued to seek reinstatement. In September 2004, his "Top Secret" security clearance was revoked, and he was terminated in November 2004 due to his inability to perform his IRS duties without the clearance. Patnaude challenged his termination through administrative remedies, filing a formal complaint with the EEOC, but the administrative process was dismissed with prejudice due to his failure to submit a prehearing statement and participate in the process. Patnaude also alleges that he was exposed to anthrax and seeks compensation for any associated illnesses, and that defendants engaged in unfair hiring practices by denying his application for employment as a special agent due to a color vision deficiency.

Michael Korzeniowski worked as a linehaul supervisor for ABF Freight Systems, Inc. from September 25, 1995, until his termination on August 6, 1997. Before his discharge, Korzeniowski took a medical leave of absence from October 28, 1996, to January 27, 1997, to undergo leg surgery on a blocked femoral artery. After his return to work, he still had cardiovascular heart disease and high blood pressure, for which he took medication, and experienced some dizziness and leg pain. On June 16, 1997, Korzeniowski's cardiologist, Dr. Surendra Avula, advised him to maintain a set schedule to follow his diet and medication schedule. Korzeniowski then asked his manager, Mike Brinker, to remove him from the rotating shift schedule, and Brinker complied, placing him on a day-shift-only schedule.

Plaintiff Korzeniowski alleges that he was discriminated against by ABF due to his arterio-sclerotic heart disease, which he claims is a disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Defendant ABF contends that Korzeniowski's health problems do not amount to a disability and that his termination was due to job abandonment, not discrimination. On August 6, 1997, Korzeniowski was assigned to work the road side shift, which he had previously expressed dissatisfaction with. Korzeniowski claims that he told his supervisor, Scott Mayberry, that he wasn't feeling well, while Mayberry testified that Korzeniowski was upset about the assignment and left work without approval. ABF's management, including Brinker and Directors of Transportation and Personnel, Columbus Dalmut and Dan Griesse, decided to terminate Korzeniowski's employment due to job abandonment.

The parties dispute the circumstances surrounding Korzeniowski's departure from work on August 6, 1997. Korzeniowski alleges that he left due to health concerns, including chest pains and tingling in one arm, and drove himself to the hospital. ABF, on the other hand, contends that Korzeniowski abandoned his job without a valid reason and only later claimed to have been experiencing health issues. Korzeniowski's wife called Brinker after his termination, informing him that her husband was in the emergency room with chest pains, but ABF's management did not change their decision to terminate his employment. Korzeniowski had previously worked as a road side linehaul manager for ABF and had expressed dissatisfaction with being assigned to that position again. He had also told Mayberry that he would quit if assigned to work road side again. After his termination, Korzeniowski obtained a new job as a road side dispatcher with another trucking company, which had a non-rotating schedule.

St. Luke's Methodist Hospital, a hospital-based skilled nursing facility (HB-SNF) in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, provided atypical services to Medicare patients in 1992. Plaintiff alleges that its costs for these services exceeded the applicable cost limits, and it is entitled to reimbursement for these costs under 42 C.F.R. § 413.30. Defendant contends that St. Luke's is not eligible for reimbursement because its costs did not exceed 112% of the peer group mean for HB-SNFs, as required by the Provider Reimbursement Manual (PRM) § 2534.5. 

Prior to 1992, St. Luke's had been granted exceptions to the cost limits for providing atypical services, but the Secretary of Health and Human Services had reinterpreted the regulation in PRM § 2534.5, effectively raising the threshold for exception eligibility. St. Luke's alleges that this reinterpretation is arbitrary, capricious, and not in accordance with law. The parties agree that the relevant facts are undisputed, and the dispute centers on the validity of PRM § 2534.5. 

The Medicare program reimburses skilled nursing facilities for the "reasonable cost" of covered services, and 42 C.F.R. § 413.30 provides for exceptions to the cost limits for facilities that provide atypical services. The regulation requires that the services be necessary for the special needs of the patients and be furnished efficiently. The Secretary had previously granted exceptions to St. Luke's based on its actual costs exceeding the routine cost limit (RCL), but the new interpretation in PRM § 2534.5 requires that the costs exceed 112% of the peer group mean. St. Luke's contends that its costs for 1992 exceeded the RCL but not the new threshold, and it is seeking reimbursement for the difference. Defendant argues that the new interpretation is a valid exercise of the Secretary's discretion and that St. Luke's does not meet the new criteria for exception eligibility.

Mina Davari, a woman, applied for a car salesman position at Landers Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Norman, a dealership in Norman, Oklahoma. Plaintiff alleges that despite her qualifications, she was not hired for the position because of her gender. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) filed a complaint on behalf of Davari, naming five defendants, including Landers Chrysler of Norman, Motors Management Corporation, LL Glenn Road LLC d/b/a Landers Toyota, The Luther Holding Company d/b/a Luther Automotive Group, and LL Glenn Plaza Loop LLC d/b/a Landers Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Little Rock. The EEOC contends that these defendants collectively constitute a single employer and single integrated enterprise, and therefore, should be held liable for the alleged discriminatory acts.

Defendants, except for Landers Chrysler of Norman, filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that administrative remedies had not been exhausted as to them, as they were not named in the underlying EEOC charge filed by Davari. The EEOC responds that an exception applies, as the complaint alleges that all defendants constitute a single employer, and that they were all sent a Letter of Determination inviting them to join in conciliation efforts. The EEOC also argues that the complaint alleges numerous facts relevant to the single employer test, including interrelated operations, common management, centralized control of labor relations, and common ownership and financial control.

Before filing the lawsuit, Davari had filed a charge with the EEOC, which led to an investigation and a Letter of Determination. The EEOC alleges that during the transition of the Norman dealership from David Stanley Chrysler to Landers Chrysler of Norman, Davari overheard a conversation between a manager, Chris Chase, and another manager, in which Chase made a comment suggesting that the sales position was not suitable for a woman. The EEOC contends that this and other allegations demonstrate a pattern of discriminatory behavior and support the single employer theory of liability.

The Nutrition Program for the Elderly, established under Title VII of the Older Americans Act, provides funds to states to offer hot meals to elderly persons. The program was created in 1972 but did not begin until July 1973 due to Presidential vetoes of fiscal year 1973 appropriation bills. Congress initially authorized $100 million for FY 1973 and $150 million for FY 1974, with a supplemental appropriation of $100 million for FY 1973. The program became "advanced funded" or "forward funded," spending funds in the year following their appropriation. In 1974, Congress extended the program for three years, appropriating $150 million for FY 1974, $200 million for FY 1975, and $250 million for FY 1976.

In FY 1976, Congress appropriated $125 million in new funds and mandated a "level of operations" of $187.5 million per annum. Defendants, responsible for administering the program, interpreted this to mean a monthly expenditure rate that would result in a total of $187.5 million if continued over a full year. However, due to the late enactment of the appropriations bill and the delayed issuance of a Program Instruction, the $187.5 million annualized rate of expenditure would only be effective for the final three months of the fiscal year, resulting in a total expenditure of approximately $160 million. Plaintiffs, elderly persons who qualify for the program but are unable to participate due to inadequate funding, allege that defendants are impounding funds intended for the program. 

Plaintiffs contend that the Congressional mandate requires an actual expenditure of $187.5 million during FY 1976, and that defendants' limitation of actual expenditures to $160 million is an illegal impoundment of funds. Defendants argue that Congress intended to mandate only a $187.5 million annualized rate of expenditure, not an actual expenditure of that amount during the year. The parties disagree on the interpretation of the Labor-HEW Appropriations Act for Fiscal Year 1976 and the requirements of Title VII of the Older Americans Act. Relevant pre-litigation events include the Presidential veto of the appropriations bill in December 1975, which was later overridden by Congress, and the issuance of a Program Instruction by defendants on March 27, 1976, implementing the funding increase.

Ward, a nontenured instructor, was employed by Kentucky State University. His teaching contract was not renewed. Plaintiff alleges that the nonrenewal was racially motivated and violated his rights to free speech and due process. Defendants contend that the University was not acting "under color of law" as required by 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and that Ward, as a nontenured instructor, is not entitled to notice and hearing. The University also argues that the Kentucky courts are suitably equipped to adjudicate Ward's claim and that the federal judiciary should abstain from exercising jurisdiction.

Prior to the nonrenewal, Ward had been employed by the University, but the exact terms of his employment, including any implied contract, are disputed. Plaintiff alleges that his termination was motivated by his exercise of free speech, while defendants contend that the nonrenewal was lawful. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the University being a state institution. The nature of the dispute is a claim of racial discrimination and violation of constitutional rights.

The pre-litigation events include the nonrenewal of Ward's contract, which led to the filing of this lawsuit. Relevant documents and communications may include Ward's employment contract, any notices or warnings given to him, and any discussions or meetings between Ward and University officials regarding his employment. The workplace facts include the University's policies and procedures for renewing or terminating contracts, as well as any relevant state laws or regulations governing employment and discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that he was not given notice or a hearing prior to the nonrenewal, while defendants contend that such procedures are not required for nontenured instructors.

On April 17, 1967, Celio Diaz, Jr. applied for a position as a flight cabin attendant with Pan American World Airways, Inc. (Pan Am). His application was rejected because Pan Am had a policy of only hiring females for that position, which had been in place since 1965. Diaz then filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) under Section 703 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, alleging that Pan Am had discriminated against him based on his sex. The EEOC found probable cause and attempted conciliation, but it was unsuccessful. 

Diaz filed a complaint with the court on February 14, 1969, on behalf of himself and others similarly situated, alleging that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants was discriminatory. The parties stipulated that Diaz had applied and been rejected for the position because he was male, and that other males had also been rejected for the same reason. They also stipulated that Pan Am's policy was to not hire males for the position, and that the class of plaintiffs would consist of males who had applied for the position within the United States and been rejected because of their sex. 

Plaintiff alleges that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants is discriminatory and violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Defendant Pan Am contends that being a female is a bona fide occupational qualification for the position of flight cabin attendant, reasonably necessary to the normal operation of its business. The EEOC, as amicus curiae, supports the plaintiff's position. The Transport Workers Union of America, representing Pan Am's cabin attendants, and the Air Line Pilots Association, International, also filed amicus curiae briefs. The parties disagree on the criteria for determining which males who applied for the position in the past should be entitled to preferential consideration for hire and back pay. Plaintiff contends that this group should include all males who filed written applications between July 2, 1965, and November 18, 1971, while defendant Pan Am argues that it should only include those who applied between November 16, 1968, and April 24, 1970.

Five fair housing organizations, the National Fair Housing Alliance, Fair Housing of Marin, Fair Housing Napa Valley, Metro Fair Housing Services, and The Fair Housing Continuum, Inc., claim that A.G. Spanos Construction, Inc. and related entities (the Spanos Defendants) designed and constructed multifamily apartment complexes that do not comply with the accessibility requirements of the Fair Housing Act (FHA). The Spanos Defendants are alleged to have engaged in a continuous pattern and practice of discrimination against people with disabilities by designing and constructing apartment complexes that deny full access to and use of the facilities as required under the FHA. The plaintiffs allege that 82 apartment complexes located in 10 states, containing over 22,000 apartment units, do not comply with FHA requirements. 

Plaintiffs allege that they have been directly and substantially injured by the Spanos Defendants' actions, as they have been frustrated in their missions to eradicate discrimination in housing and have had to divert significant resources to identify, investigate, and counteract the Spanos Defendants' discriminatory practices. Each plaintiff conducted site visits, investigations, surveys, and/or tests at various properties, resulting in the diversion of staff time, salaries, and travel expenses. The plaintiffs claim that the Spanos Defendants' continuing discriminatory practices have forced them to expend resources that they would not have had to expend were it not for the Spanos Defendants' violations.

The Spanos Defendants are California corporations with principal offices in Stockton, and they allegedly engaged in land acquisition, development, construction, and management of multifamily apartment complexes throughout the United States. Highpointe Village, L.P. and Knickerbocker Properties, Inc. XXXVIII are also defendants, alleged to be owners of apartment complexes designed and/or constructed by the Spanos Defendants. The plaintiffs seek to certify a defendant class consisting of current owners of covered apartment complexes that were designed and/or built by the Spanos Defendants but are no longer owned by them. Plaintiffs allege that these properties do not fully comply with the accessibility and adaptability requirements of the FHA.

South Central Bell Telephone and Telegraph Company (Bell) had an Employee Benefits Plan in effect from October 13, 1971, to August 7, 1977, which provided non-occupational sickness and accident benefits to its employees. However, the plan did not cover pregnancy-related absences, except in cases of physical complications. Female employees who took maternity leave accrued only thirty additional days of service credit, while sick or disabled employees received full seniority credit for up to fifty-two weeks. Harriet Wilhite, a female employee of Bell, requested a leave of absence for maternity reasons in 1972 and was not guaranteed reinstatement to the same or equal position upon returning to work. Betty Dubose, another female employee, was granted a six-month maternity leave in 1975 and accrued only thirty days of service credit during her leave.

Plaintiff Wilhite alleges that Bell's policy of not providing mandatory reinstatement rights to female employees returning from maternity leave for a normal pregnancy violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Plaintiff Dubose alleges that Bell's policy of denying full seniority credit to female employees on maternity leave for a normal pregnancy, compared to its treatment of other temporarily disabled employees, also violates Title VII. Bell contends that its policies are facially neutral and do not discriminate against female employees. The Communication Workers of America, AFL-CIO, filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission on April 12, 1972, alleging violations of Title VII by Bell.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Bell being the employer and Wilhite and Dubose being female employees. The nature of the dispute is a claim of sex discrimination in employment practices, specifically regarding Bell's maternity leave and seniority policies. Relevant pre-litigation events include the filing of complaints with the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission and the issuance of right-to-sue letters to Wilhite and Dubose. The employees' union, the Communication Workers of America, AFL-CIO, is also a party to the lawsuit, representing Wilhite and other similarly situated female employees.

Mr. Young, a former corrections officer at the Colorado Department of Corrections (CDOC), received an online Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) training in 2021. Mr. Young had previously brought claims based on nearly identical facts against CDOC and other defendants in a separate lawsuit, Young v. Colo. Dep’t of Corrs., et al. (Young I), which raised hostile work environment and equal protection claims.

In the current case, Mr. Young contends that the EDI training he received was deeply racist and that he was forced to resign due to the hostile work environment it created. Defendant CDOC contends that Mr. Young's interests in proceeding expeditiously with discovery are reduced since he has found new employment and does not seek reinstatement to his previous position. CDOC also argues that it would be unduly burdened by discovery, especially since the court's ruling on their Motion to Dismiss may resolve the matter entirely. Mr. Young, on the other hand, argues that a delay in discovery would prejudice his ability to prove his claims, as the events relevant to his claims occurred between February and July 2021, and that his ability to gather evidence diminishes with time.

The parties have exchanged motions and responses regarding a stay of discovery, with CDOC seeking a stay pending the court's ruling on their Motion to Dismiss, and Mr. Young opposing the stay, arguing that it would increase the burden on CDOC, inconvenience the court, and harm the interests of non-parties, such as former colleagues who may have vital evidence to offer in the case. Mr. Young also claims that the public interest favors discovery, as his case has garnered attention across the country due to its broader impact on employers' use of potentially racist training materials under Title VII.

South Central Bell Telephone and Telegraph Company (Bell) had an Employee Benefits Plan in effect from October 13, 1971, to August 7, 1977, which provided non-occupational sickness and accident benefits to its employees. However, the plan did not cover pregnancy-related absences, except in cases of physical complications. Female employees who took maternity leave accrued only thirty additional days of service credit, while sick or disabled employees received full seniority credit for up to fifty-two weeks. Harriet Wilhite, a female employee of Bell, requested a leave of absence for maternity reasons in 1972 and was not guaranteed reinstatement to the same or equal position upon returning to work. Betty Dubose, another female employee, was granted a six-month maternity leave in 1975 and accrued only thirty days of service credit during her leave.

Plaintiff Wilhite alleges that Bell's policy of not providing mandatory reinstatement rights to female employees returning from maternity leave for a normal pregnancy violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Plaintiff Dubose alleges that Bell's policy of denying full seniority credit to female employees on maternity leave for a normal pregnancy, compared to its treatment of other temporarily disabled employees, also violates Title VII. Bell contends that its policies are facially neutral and do not discriminate against female employees. The Communication Workers of America, AFL-CIO, filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission on April 12, 1972, alleging violations of Title VII by Bell.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Bell being the employer and Wilhite and Dubose being female employees. The nature of the dispute is a claim of sex discrimination in employment practices, specifically regarding Bell's maternity leave and seniority policies. Relevant pre-litigation events include the filing of complaints with the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission and the issuance of right-to-sue letters to Wilhite and Dubose. The employees' union, the Communication Workers of America, AFL-CIO, is also a party to the lawsuit, representing Wilhite and other similarly situated female employees.

St. Luke's Methodist Hospital, a hospital-based skilled nursing facility (HB-SNF) in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, provided atypical services to Medicare patients in 1992. Plaintiff alleges that its costs for these services exceeded the applicable cost limits, and it is entitled to reimbursement for these costs under 42 C.F.R. § 413.30. Defendant contends that St. Luke's is not eligible for reimbursement because its costs did not exceed 112% of the peer group mean for HB-SNFs, as required by the Provider Reimbursement Manual (PRM) § 2534.5. 

Prior to 1992, St. Luke's had been granted exceptions to the cost limits for providing atypical services, but the Secretary of Health and Human Services had reinterpreted the regulation in PRM § 2534.5, effectively raising the threshold for exception eligibility. St. Luke's alleges that this reinterpretation is arbitrary, capricious, and not in accordance with law. The parties agree that the relevant facts are undisputed, and the dispute centers on the validity of PRM § 2534.5. 

The Medicare program reimburses skilled nursing facilities for the "reasonable cost" of covered services, and 42 C.F.R. § 413.30 provides for exceptions to the cost limits for facilities that provide atypical services. The regulation requires that the services be necessary for the special needs of the patients and be furnished efficiently. The Secretary had previously granted exceptions to St. Luke's based on its actual costs exceeding the routine cost limit (RCL), but the new interpretation in PRM § 2534.5 requires that the costs exceed 112% of the peer group mean. St. Luke's contends that its costs for 1992 exceeded the RCL but not the new threshold, and it is seeking reimbursement for the difference. Defendant argues that the new interpretation is a valid exercise of the Secretary's discretion and that St. Luke's does not meet the new criteria for exception eligibility.

Five fair housing organizations, the National Fair Housing Alliance, Fair Housing of Marin, Fair Housing Napa Valley, Metro Fair Housing Services, and The Fair Housing Continuum, Inc., claim that A.G. Spanos Construction, Inc. and related entities (the Spanos Defendants) designed and constructed multifamily apartment complexes that do not comply with the accessibility requirements of the Fair Housing Act (FHA). The Spanos Defendants are alleged to have engaged in a continuous pattern and practice of discrimination against people with disabilities by designing and constructing apartment complexes that deny full access to and use of the facilities as required under the FHA. The plaintiffs allege that 82 apartment complexes located in 10 states, containing over 22,000 apartment units, do not comply with FHA requirements. 

Plaintiffs allege that they have been directly and substantially injured by the Spanos Defendants' actions, as they have been frustrated in their missions to eradicate discrimination in housing and have had to divert significant resources to identify, investigate, and counteract the Spanos Defendants' discriminatory practices. Each plaintiff conducted site visits, investigations, surveys, and/or tests at various properties, resulting in the diversion of staff time, salaries, and travel expenses. The plaintiffs claim that the Spanos Defendants' continuing discriminatory practices have forced them to expend resources that they would not have had to expend were it not for the Spanos Defendants' violations.

The Spanos Defendants are California corporations with principal offices in Stockton, and they allegedly engaged in land acquisition, development, construction, and management of multifamily apartment complexes throughout the United States. Highpointe Village, L.P. and Knickerbocker Properties, Inc. XXXVIII are also defendants, alleged to be owners of apartment complexes designed and/or constructed by the Spanos Defendants. The plaintiffs seek to certify a defendant class consisting of current owners of covered apartment complexes that were designed and/or built by the Spanos Defendants but are no longer owned by them. Plaintiffs allege that these properties do not fully comply with the accessibility and adaptability requirements of the FHA.

On April 17, 1967, Celio Diaz, Jr. applied for a position as a flight cabin attendant with Pan American World Airways, Inc. (Pan Am). His application was rejected because Pan Am had a policy of only hiring females for that position, which had been in place since 1965. Diaz then filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) under Section 703 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, alleging that Pan Am had discriminated against him based on his sex. The EEOC found probable cause and attempted conciliation, but it was unsuccessful. 

Diaz filed a complaint with the court on February 14, 1969, on behalf of himself and others similarly situated, alleging that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants was discriminatory. The parties stipulated that Diaz had applied and been rejected for the position because he was male, and that other males had also been rejected for the same reason. They also stipulated that Pan Am's policy was to not hire males for the position, and that the class of plaintiffs would consist of males who had applied for the position within the United States and been rejected because of their sex. 

Plaintiff alleges that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants is discriminatory and violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Defendant Pan Am contends that being a female is a bona fide occupational qualification for the position of flight cabin attendant, reasonably necessary to the normal operation of its business. The EEOC, as amicus curiae, supports the plaintiff's position. The Transport Workers Union of America, representing Pan Am's cabin attendants, and the Air Line Pilots Association, International, also filed amicus curiae briefs. The parties disagree on the criteria for determining which males who applied for the position in the past should be entitled to preferential consideration for hire and back pay. Plaintiff contends that this group should include all males who filed written applications between July 2, 1965, and November 18, 1971, while defendant Pan Am argues that it should only include those who applied between November 16, 1968, and April 24, 1970.

The plaintiff, a professor in the School of Interdisciplinary Studies at Miami University, suffers from lupus and has been granted accommodations by the University, including reduced advising responsibilities, reduced scholarly writing expectations, and scheduling accommodations. She was hired as a tenure-track professor in 1988, at the same time as Hays Cummins, a male professor, who was hired with a higher starting salary. The plaintiff and Cummins were of similar age and experience at the time of their hiring. In 1990, the plaintiff's lupus was diagnosed, and she did not immediately seek accommodations from the University. In 1991, the University granted the plaintiff tenure and promoted her to associate professor, and began making periodic adjustments to her salary to equalize it with Cummins'. 

The plaintiff sought accommodations for her medical condition in 1992, which the University agreed to provide. However, she believes that her salary has been negatively affected by these accommodations and/or by animus based on her handicap status or sex. The plaintiff contends that she has been paid a lower salary than male colleagues, including Cummins, and that this disparity is evidence of sex discrimination. She also argues that the University has unfairly considered the accommodations made for her handicap as detracting from her performance, and that she has been retaliated against for complaining about perceived gender bias in her compensation. The defendant, Miami University, has made periodic salary adjustments for the plaintiff, but she remains the lowest paid full professor in her department, with the second lowest paid being her only female colleague.

Plaintiff alleges that Defendant has engaged in sex discrimination in the terms of her employment by paying her a lower salary than it pays male colleagues, and that her sex must be the basis for the disparity. Defendant contends that the salary disparities are due to other factors, such as differences in job responsibilities and performance. The parties disagree on the extent to which the plaintiff's work is comparable to that of her male colleagues, including Cummins. The plaintiff points to evidence that she and Cummins have similar responsibilities and performance evaluations, while the defendant argues that there are significant differences in their job duties and qualifications. The plaintiff also alleges that she has been retaliated against for complaining about perceived gender bias in her compensation, citing smaller salary increases following her complaints. Defendant denies these allegations, and the parties' contentions regarding the salary disparities and the reasons for them are in dispute. Relevant pre-litigation events include the plaintiff's requests for accommodations, her complaints about perceived gender bias, and the defendant's responses to these complaints.

On October 17, 1974, a consent decree was entered, enjoining the Milwaukee Fire Department from engaging in any employment practice that has the purpose or effect of discriminating on the basis of sex against applicants to or employees of the Fire Department. The decree was later modified in October 1976 to provide that 5 per cent of the firefighter appointments would go to females. The Milwaukee Fire Department conducts a paramedic program, selecting and training paramedics exclusively from among firefighters serving in the department. However, no woman has ever passed the Milwaukee Fire Department's training course and become a firefighter, and consequently, no woman has ever served as a paramedic in the Milwaukee Fire Department.

Plaintiff alleges that the requirement for potential paramedics to first pass the Fire Department's training course and become a firefighter has excluded all women from becoming paramedics. Plaintiff contends that this requirement is not justified by business necessity and disproportionately excludes women. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that paramedics must be able to fight fires should it become necessary and that due to the high stress encountered in their jobs, paramedics must be trained firefighters so that they can be returned to firefighter duties after they "burn out" as paramedics. Defendants also argue that the paramedic program requires individuals to have the skills and training of a firefighter.

Prior to the lawsuit, the Milwaukee Fire Department had a shortage of paramedics, with only 44 paramedics in the department, despite a full complement of 48. The department's paramedic program involves extensive training in emergency medicine, and paramedics work full-time providing emergency medical services under the supervision of physicians. Paramedics seldom perform firefighting duties during their regular work week, and their job is different in kind from that of firefighters. Other cities, such as Chicago, have successfully employed non-firefighters, including women, as paramedics, and there is no showing that civilian paramedics could not assist firefighters in the ways paramedics now occasionally do without being full-fledged firefighters.

Richard A. Wilson, a Jamaican-born man, began working for Columbia Gas of Pennsylvania as a Service Technician in 2008. He was the only African American and Jamaican employee at the company. Wilson alleges that he was singled out based on his race and national origin, subjected to a hostile work environment, and treated differently than similarly situated Caucasian employees. He claims that these incidents became more frequent over the years, starting around 2008, and included being asked derogatory questions, being sent to low-income neighborhoods, being referred to as "the black guy," and being assigned undesirable work tasks.

Plaintiff Wilson alleges that he maintained perfect attendance and performed his job skillfully, earning satisfactory performance reviews, annual incentives, bonuses, and raises. He also volunteered his time to give back to the community and received complimentary letters and phone calls from satisfied customers. However, he claims that he was subjected to various forms of harassment and discrimination, including being asked to remove his hat so a coworker could defecate in it, being ridiculed for wearing collared shirts, and being assigned to work in high-crime neighborhoods at night. Wilson also alleges that he was not invited to a company celebration for employees with perfect attendance, despite having perfect attendance throughout his career.

Wilson contends that he reported the discrimination and harassment to his supervisor, Darryl Wargo, and other company officials, including the head of Human Resources, multiple times starting in 2012. He claims that his reports were met with inaction, and the incidents worsened over time. In 2019, Wargo was promoted to manager, and Wilson alleges that Wargo's behavior towards him became more abusive and condescending. In January 2021, Wilson reported concerns about his company phone and feeling like he was being followed, which led to a telephone conference with company officials, who suggested that he undergo a medical exam. Wilson objected to the medical evaluation but was eventually required to undergo one, which concluded that he was not "fit for duty." Columbia Gas refused to allow him to return to work, citing the medical evaluation, and eventually terminated his employment in September 2021. Defendant Columbia Gas and Wargo contend that Wilson's allegations are unfounded and that they did not discriminate against him based on his race, national origin, or disability.

Five fair housing organizations, the National Fair Housing Alliance, Fair Housing of Marin, Fair Housing Napa Valley, Metro Fair Housing Services, and The Fair Housing Continuum, Inc., claim that A.G. Spanos Construction, Inc. and related entities (the Spanos Defendants) designed and constructed multifamily apartment complexes that do not comply with the accessibility requirements of the Fair Housing Act (FHA). The Spanos Defendants are alleged to have engaged in a continuous pattern and practice of discrimination against people with disabilities by designing and constructing apartment complexes that deny full access to and use of the facilities as required under the FHA. The plaintiffs allege that 82 apartment complexes located in 10 states, containing over 22,000 apartment units, do not comply with FHA requirements. 

Plaintiffs allege that they have been directly and substantially injured by the Spanos Defendants' actions, as they have been frustrated in their missions to eradicate discrimination in housing and have had to divert significant resources to identify, investigate, and counteract the Spanos Defendants' discriminatory practices. Each plaintiff conducted site visits, investigations, surveys, and/or tests at various properties, resulting in the diversion of staff time, salaries, and travel expenses. The plaintiffs claim that the Spanos Defendants' continuing discriminatory practices have forced them to expend resources that they would not have had to expend were it not for the Spanos Defendants' violations.

The Spanos Defendants are California corporations with principal offices in Stockton, and they allegedly engaged in land acquisition, development, construction, and management of multifamily apartment complexes throughout the United States. Highpointe Village, L.P. and Knickerbocker Properties, Inc. XXXVIII are also defendants, alleged to be owners of apartment complexes designed and/or constructed by the Spanos Defendants. The plaintiffs seek to certify a defendant class consisting of current owners of covered apartment complexes that were designed and/or built by the Spanos Defendants but are no longer owned by them. Plaintiffs allege that these properties do not fully comply with the accessibility and adaptability requirements of the FHA.

Ward, a nontenured instructor, was employed by Kentucky State University. His teaching contract was not renewed. Plaintiff alleges that the nonrenewal was racially motivated and violated his rights to free speech and due process. Defendants contend that the University was not acting "under color of law" as required by 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and that Ward, as a nontenured instructor, is not entitled to notice and hearing. The University also argues that the Kentucky courts are suitably equipped to adjudicate Ward's claim and that the federal judiciary should abstain from exercising jurisdiction.

Prior to the nonrenewal, Ward had been employed by the University, but the exact terms of his employment, including any implied contract, are disputed. Plaintiff alleges that his termination was motivated by his exercise of free speech, while defendants contend that the nonrenewal was lawful. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the University being a state institution. The nature of the dispute is a claim of racial discrimination and violation of constitutional rights.

The pre-litigation events include the nonrenewal of Ward's contract, which led to the filing of this lawsuit. Relevant documents and communications may include Ward's employment contract, any notices or warnings given to him, and any discussions or meetings between Ward and University officials regarding his employment. The workplace facts include the University's policies and procedures for renewing or terminating contracts, as well as any relevant state laws or regulations governing employment and discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that he was not given notice or a hearing prior to the nonrenewal, while defendants contend that such procedures are not required for nontenured instructors.

On October 17, 1974, a consent decree was entered, enjoining the Milwaukee Fire Department from engaging in any employment practice that has the purpose or effect of discriminating on the basis of sex against applicants to or employees of the Fire Department. The decree was later modified in October 1976 to provide that 5 per cent of the firefighter appointments would go to females. The Milwaukee Fire Department conducts a paramedic program, selecting and training paramedics exclusively from among firefighters serving in the department. However, no woman has ever passed the Milwaukee Fire Department's training course and become a firefighter, and consequently, no woman has ever served as a paramedic in the Milwaukee Fire Department.

Plaintiff alleges that the requirement for potential paramedics to first pass the Fire Department's training course and become a firefighter has excluded all women from becoming paramedics. Plaintiff contends that this requirement is not justified by business necessity and disproportionately excludes women. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that paramedics must be able to fight fires should it become necessary and that due to the high stress encountered in their jobs, paramedics must be trained firefighters so that they can be returned to firefighter duties after they "burn out" as paramedics. Defendants also argue that the paramedic program requires individuals to have the skills and training of a firefighter.

Prior to the lawsuit, the Milwaukee Fire Department had a shortage of paramedics, with only 44 paramedics in the department, despite a full complement of 48. The department's paramedic program involves extensive training in emergency medicine, and paramedics work full-time providing emergency medical services under the supervision of physicians. Paramedics seldom perform firefighting duties during their regular work week, and their job is different in kind from that of firefighters. Other cities, such as Chicago, have successfully employed non-firefighters, including women, as paramedics, and there is no showing that civilian paramedics could not assist firefighters in the ways paramedics now occasionally do without being full-fledged firefighters.

Neil Taylor began working as a mechanic for Arlington Transit Mix, Inc. in June 1985. At the time of his hiring, he informed the plant manager, Kenneth Abraham Sr., that he would need to leave work early on Wednesdays to attend church services, which he believed were mandated by the Bible. Taylor was allowed to leave early on Wednesdays for approximately two years, from June 1985 until July 8, 1987. During this time, Taylor and the other three mechanics, Dana Justice, Charles Belcher, and Lee Roy Cox, worked the same hours and often stayed late to complete repairs on the company's trucks.

The company, which owns about 15 trucks, including large cement mixers, requires four full-time mechanics to inspect and repair the trucks when they return to the garage at the end of the day. In the spring of 1987, Arlington's management became concerned about the amount of overtime paid to the mechanics and decided to stagger their hours to maximize straight-time coverage. As part of this change, Belcher was appointed working foreman of the mechanics and was tasked with implementing a new schedule. The schedule change resulted in two mechanics starting at 6:00 a.m. and two starting at 9:00 or 10:00 a.m. Taylor, who had previously been allowed to leave early on Wednesdays, was assigned to the later shift.

Plaintiff alleges that Taylor's discharge on July 9, 1987, was due to his refusal to work late on Wednesday, July 8, 1987, in order to attend church services. Defendant contends that Taylor was discharged because he left work without permission, despite being told that his presence was needed to complete repairs on the trucks. Defendant also claims that it had accommodated Taylor's religious beliefs for two years, but was unable to do so on July 8, 1987, without incurring undue hardship. Prior to his discharge, Taylor had been involved in an incident in which he removed and destroyed a Playboy magazine centerfold and other similar photographs that had been posted in the garage by mechanic Cox, which had led to a reprimand from Abraham. Taylor had also been allowed to post notice of a Bible study group meeting in the garage area and distribute religious literature to his fellow employees.

On April 17, 1967, Celio Diaz, Jr. applied for a position as a flight cabin attendant with Pan American World Airways, Inc. (Pan Am). His application was rejected because Pan Am had a policy of only hiring females for that position, which had been in place since 1965. Diaz then filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) under Section 703 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, alleging that Pan Am had discriminated against him based on his sex. The EEOC found probable cause and attempted conciliation, but it was unsuccessful. 

Diaz filed a complaint with the court on February 14, 1969, on behalf of himself and others similarly situated, alleging that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants was discriminatory. The parties stipulated that Diaz had applied and been rejected for the position because he was male, and that other males had also been rejected for the same reason. They also stipulated that Pan Am's policy was to not hire males for the position, and that the class of plaintiffs would consist of males who had applied for the position within the United States and been rejected because of their sex. 

Plaintiff alleges that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants is discriminatory and violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Defendant Pan Am contends that being a female is a bona fide occupational qualification for the position of flight cabin attendant, reasonably necessary to the normal operation of its business. The EEOC, as amicus curiae, supports the plaintiff's position. The Transport Workers Union of America, representing Pan Am's cabin attendants, and the Air Line Pilots Association, International, also filed amicus curiae briefs. The parties disagree on the criteria for determining which males who applied for the position in the past should be entitled to preferential consideration for hire and back pay. Plaintiff contends that this group should include all males who filed written applications between July 2, 1965, and November 18, 1971, while defendant Pan Am argues that it should only include those who applied between November 16, 1968, and April 24, 1970.

Mina Davari, a woman, applied for a car salesman position at Landers Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Norman, a dealership in Norman, Oklahoma. Plaintiff alleges that despite her qualifications, she was not hired for the position because of her gender. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) filed a complaint on behalf of Davari, naming five defendants, including Landers Chrysler of Norman, Motors Management Corporation, LL Glenn Road LLC d/b/a Landers Toyota, The Luther Holding Company d/b/a Luther Automotive Group, and LL Glenn Plaza Loop LLC d/b/a Landers Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Little Rock. The EEOC contends that these defendants collectively constitute a single employer and single integrated enterprise, and therefore, should be held liable for the alleged discriminatory acts.

Defendants, except for Landers Chrysler of Norman, filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that administrative remedies had not been exhausted as to them, as they were not named in the underlying EEOC charge filed by Davari. The EEOC responds that an exception applies, as the complaint alleges that all defendants constitute a single employer, and that they were all sent a Letter of Determination inviting them to join in conciliation efforts. The EEOC also argues that the complaint alleges numerous facts relevant to the single employer test, including interrelated operations, common management, centralized control of labor relations, and common ownership and financial control.

Before filing the lawsuit, Davari had filed a charge with the EEOC, which led to an investigation and a Letter of Determination. The EEOC alleges that during the transition of the Norman dealership from David Stanley Chrysler to Landers Chrysler of Norman, Davari overheard a conversation between a manager, Chris Chase, and another manager, in which Chase made a comment suggesting that the sales position was not suitable for a woman. The EEOC contends that this and other allegations demonstrate a pattern of discriminatory behavior and support the single employer theory of liability.

The Nutrition Program for the Elderly, established under Title VII of the Older Americans Act, provides funds to states to offer hot meals to elderly persons. The program was created in 1972 but did not begin until July 1973 due to Presidential vetoes of fiscal year 1973 appropriation bills. Congress initially authorized $100 million for FY 1973 and $150 million for FY 1974, with a supplemental appropriation of $100 million for FY 1973. The program became "advanced funded" or "forward funded," spending funds in the year following their appropriation. In 1974, Congress extended the program for three years, appropriating $150 million for FY 1974, $200 million for FY 1975, and $250 million for FY 1976.

In FY 1976, Congress appropriated $125 million in new funds and mandated a "level of operations" of $187.5 million per annum. Defendants, responsible for administering the program, interpreted this to mean a monthly expenditure rate that would result in a total of $187.5 million if continued over a full year. However, due to the late enactment of the appropriations bill and the delayed issuance of a Program Instruction, the $187.5 million annualized rate of expenditure would only be effective for the final three months of the fiscal year, resulting in a total expenditure of approximately $160 million. Plaintiffs, elderly persons who qualify for the program but are unable to participate due to inadequate funding, allege that defendants are impounding funds intended for the program. 

Plaintiffs contend that the Congressional mandate requires an actual expenditure of $187.5 million during FY 1976, and that defendants' limitation of actual expenditures to $160 million is an illegal impoundment of funds. Defendants argue that Congress intended to mandate only a $187.5 million annualized rate of expenditure, not an actual expenditure of that amount during the year. The parties disagree on the interpretation of the Labor-HEW Appropriations Act for Fiscal Year 1976 and the requirements of Title VII of the Older Americans Act. Relevant pre-litigation events include the Presidential veto of the appropriations bill in December 1975, which was later overridden by Congress, and the issuance of a Program Instruction by defendants on March 27, 1976, implementing the funding increase.

The plaintiff, a professor in the School of Interdisciplinary Studies at Miami University, suffers from lupus and has been granted accommodations by the University, including reduced advising responsibilities, reduced scholarly writing expectations, and scheduling accommodations. She was hired as a tenure-track professor in 1988, at the same time as Hays Cummins, a male professor, who was hired with a higher starting salary. The plaintiff and Cummins were of similar age and experience at the time of their hiring. In 1990, the plaintiff's lupus was diagnosed, and she did not immediately seek accommodations from the University. In 1991, the University granted the plaintiff tenure and promoted her to associate professor, and began making periodic adjustments to her salary to equalize it with Cummins'. 

The plaintiff sought accommodations for her medical condition in 1992, which the University agreed to provide. However, she believes that her salary has been negatively affected by these accommodations and/or by animus based on her handicap status or sex. The plaintiff contends that she has been paid a lower salary than male colleagues, including Cummins, and that this disparity is evidence of sex discrimination. She also argues that the University has unfairly considered the accommodations made for her handicap as detracting from her performance, and that she has been retaliated against for complaining about perceived gender bias in her compensation. The defendant, Miami University, has made periodic salary adjustments for the plaintiff, but she remains the lowest paid full professor in her department, with the second lowest paid being her only female colleague.

Plaintiff alleges that Defendant has engaged in sex discrimination in the terms of her employment by paying her a lower salary than it pays male colleagues, and that her sex must be the basis for the disparity. Defendant contends that the salary disparities are due to other factors, such as differences in job responsibilities and performance. The parties disagree on the extent to which the plaintiff's work is comparable to that of her male colleagues, including Cummins. The plaintiff points to evidence that she and Cummins have similar responsibilities and performance evaluations, while the defendant argues that there are significant differences in their job duties and qualifications. The plaintiff also alleges that she has been retaliated against for complaining about perceived gender bias in her compensation, citing smaller salary increases following her complaints. Defendant denies these allegations, and the parties' contentions regarding the salary disparities and the reasons for them are in dispute. Relevant pre-litigation events include the plaintiff's requests for accommodations, her complaints about perceived gender bias, and the defendant's responses to these complaints.

Mr. Young, a former corrections officer at the Colorado Department of Corrections (CDOC), received an online Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) training in 2021. Plaintiff alleges that this training created a hostile work environment so severe that it resulted in his constructive discharge when he opted to resign from his position in July 2021. Mr. Young had previously brought claims based on nearly identical facts against CDOC and other defendants in a separate lawsuit, Young v. Colo. Dep’t of Corrs., et al. (Young I), which raised hostile work environment and equal protection claims.

In the current case, Mr. Young contends that the EDI training he received was deeply racist and that he was forced to resign due to the hostile work environment it created. Defendant CDOC contends that Mr. Young's interests in proceeding expeditiously with discovery are reduced since he has found new employment and does not seek reinstatement to his previous position. CDOC also argues that it would be unduly burdened by discovery, especially since the court's ruling on their Motion to Dismiss may resolve the matter entirely. Mr. Young, on the other hand, argues that a delay in discovery would prejudice his ability to prove his claims, as the events relevant to his claims occurred between February and July 2021, and that his ability to gather evidence diminishes with time.

The parties have exchanged motions and responses regarding a stay of discovery, with CDOC seeking a stay pending the court's ruling on their Motion to Dismiss, and Mr. Young opposing the stay, arguing that it would increase the burden on CDOC, inconvenience the court, and harm the interests of non-parties, such as former colleagues who may have vital evidence to offer in the case. Mr. Young also claims that the public interest favors discovery, as his case has garnered attention across the country due to its broader impact on employers' use of potentially racist training materials under Title VII.

Richard A. Wilson, a Jamaican-born man, began working for Columbia Gas of Pennsylvania as a Service Technician in 2008. He was the only African American and Jamaican employee at the company. Wilson alleges that he was singled out based on his race and national origin, subjected to a hostile work environment, and treated differently than similarly situated Caucasian employees. He claims that these incidents became more frequent over the years, starting around 2008, and included being asked derogatory questions, being sent to low-income neighborhoods, being referred to as "the black guy," and being assigned undesirable work tasks.

Plaintiff Wilson alleges that he maintained perfect attendance and performed his job skillfully, earning satisfactory performance reviews, annual incentives, bonuses, and raises. He also volunteered his time to give back to the community and received complimentary letters and phone calls from satisfied customers. However, he claims that he was subjected to various forms of harassment and discrimination, including being asked to remove his hat so a coworker could defecate in it, being ridiculed for wearing collared shirts, and being assigned to work in high-crime neighborhoods at night. Wilson also alleges that he was not invited to a company celebration for employees with perfect attendance, despite having perfect attendance throughout his career.

Wilson contends that he reported the discrimination and harassment to his supervisor, Darryl Wargo, and other company officials, including the head of Human Resources, multiple times starting in 2012. He claims that his reports were met with inaction, and the incidents worsened over time. In 2019, Wargo was promoted to manager, and Wilson alleges that Wargo's behavior towards him became more abusive and condescending. In January 2021, Wilson reported concerns about his company phone and feeling like he was being followed, which led to a telephone conference with company officials, who suggested that he undergo a medical exam. Wilson objected to the medical evaluation but was eventually required to undergo one, which concluded that he was not "fit for duty." Columbia Gas refused to allow him to return to work, citing the medical evaluation, and eventually terminated his employment in September 2021. Defendant Columbia Gas and Wargo contend that Wilson's allegations are unfounded and that they did not discriminate against him based on his race, national origin, or disability.

She was hired as a tenure-track professor in 1988, at the same time as Hays Cummins, a male professor, who was hired with a higher starting salary. The plaintiff and Cummins were of similar age and experience at the time of their hiring. In 1990, the plaintiff's lupus was diagnosed, and she did not immediately seek accommodations from the University. In 1991, the University granted the plaintiff tenure and promoted her to associate professor, and began making periodic adjustments to her salary to equalize it with Cummins'. 

The plaintiff sought accommodations for her medical condition in 1992, which the University agreed to provide. However, she believes that her salary has been negatively affected by these accommodations and/or by animus based on her handicap status or sex. The plaintiff contends that she has been paid a lower salary than male colleagues, including Cummins, and that this disparity is evidence of sex discrimination. She also argues that the University has unfairly considered the accommodations made for her handicap as detracting from her performance, and that she has been retaliated against for complaining about perceived gender bias in her compensation. The defendant, Miami University, has made periodic salary adjustments for the plaintiff, but she remains the lowest paid full professor in her department, with the second lowest paid being her only female colleague.

Plaintiff alleges that Defendant has engaged in sex discrimination in the terms of her employment by paying her a lower salary than it pays male colleagues, and that her sex must be the basis for the disparity. Defendant contends that the salary disparities are due to other factors, such as differences in job responsibilities and performance. The parties disagree on the extent to which the plaintiff's work is comparable to that of her male colleagues, including Cummins. The plaintiff points to evidence that she and Cummins have similar responsibilities and performance evaluations, while the defendant argues that there are significant differences in their job duties and qualifications. The plaintiff also alleges that she has been retaliated against for complaining about perceived gender bias in her compensation, citing smaller salary increases following her complaints. Defendant denies these allegations, and the parties' contentions regarding the salary disparities and the reasons for them are in dispute. Relevant pre-litigation events include the plaintiff's requests for accommodations, her complaints about perceived gender bias, and the defendant's responses to these complaints.

The Nutrition Program for the Elderly, established under Title VII of the Older Americans Act, provides funds to states to offer hot meals to elderly persons. The program was created in 1972 but did not begin until July 1973 due to Presidential vetoes of fiscal year 1973 appropriation bills. Congress initially authorized $100 million for FY 1973 and $150 million for FY 1974, with a supplemental appropriation of $100 million for FY 1973. The program became "advanced funded" or "forward funded," spending funds in the year following their appropriation. In 1974, Congress extended the program for three years, appropriating $150 million for FY 1974, $200 million for FY 1975, and $250 million for FY 1976.

In FY 1976, Congress appropriated $125 million in new funds and mandated a "level of operations" of $187.5 million per annum. Defendants, responsible for administering the program, interpreted this to mean a monthly expenditure rate that would result in a total of $187.5 million if continued over a full year. However, due to the late enactment of the appropriations bill and the delayed issuance of a Program Instruction, the $187.5 million annualized rate of expenditure would only be effective for the final three months of the fiscal year, resulting in a total expenditure of approximately $160 million. Plaintiffs, elderly persons who qualify for the program but are unable to participate due to inadequate funding, allege that defendants are impounding funds intended for the program. 

Plaintiffs contend that the Congressional mandate requires an actual expenditure of $187.5 million during FY 1976, and that defendants' limitation of actual expenditures to $160 million is an illegal impoundment of funds. Defendants argue that Congress intended to mandate only a $187.5 million annualized rate of expenditure, not an actual expenditure of that amount during the year. The parties disagree on the interpretation of the Labor-HEW Appropriations Act for Fiscal Year 1976 and the requirements of Title VII of the Older Americans Act. Relevant pre-litigation events include the Presidential veto of the appropriations bill in December 1975, which was later overridden by Congress, and the issuance of a Program Instruction by defendants on March 27, 1976, implementing the funding increase.

Mr. Young, a former corrections officer at the Colorado Department of Corrections (CDOC), received an online Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) training in 2021. Plaintiff alleges that this training created a hostile work environment so severe that it resulted in his constructive discharge when he opted to resign from his position in July 2021. Mr. Young had previously brought claims based on nearly identical facts against CDOC and other defendants in a separate lawsuit, Young v. Colo. Dep’t of Corrs., et al. (Young I), which raised hostile work environment and equal protection claims.

In the current case, Mr. Young contends that the EDI training he received was deeply racist and that he was forced to resign due to the hostile work environment it created. Defendant CDOC contends that Mr. Young's interests in proceeding expeditiously with discovery are reduced since he has found new employment and does not seek reinstatement to his previous position. CDOC also argues that it would be unduly burdened by discovery, especially since the court's ruling on their Motion to Dismiss may resolve the matter entirely. Mr. Young, on the other hand, argues that a delay in discovery would prejudice his ability to prove his claims, as the events relevant to his claims occurred between February and July 2021, and that his ability to gather evidence diminishes with time.

The parties have exchanged motions and responses regarding a stay of discovery, with CDOC seeking a stay pending the court's ruling on their Motion to Dismiss, and Mr. Young opposing the stay, arguing that it would increase the burden on CDOC, inconvenience the court, and harm the interests of non-parties, such as former colleagues who may have vital evidence to offer in the case. Mr. Young also claims that the public interest favors discovery, as his case has garnered attention across the country due to its broader impact on employers' use of potentially racist training materials under Title VII.

Richard A. Wilson, a Jamaican-born man, began working for Columbia Gas of Pennsylvania as a Service Technician in 2008. He was the only African American and Jamaican employee at the company. Wilson alleges that he was singled out based on his race and national origin, subjected to a hostile work environment, and treated differently than similarly situated Caucasian employees. He claims that these incidents became more frequent over the years, starting around 2008, and included being asked derogatory questions, being sent to low-income neighborhoods, being referred to as "the black guy," and being assigned undesirable work tasks.

Plaintiff Wilson alleges that he maintained perfect attendance and performed his job skillfully, earning satisfactory performance reviews, annual incentives, bonuses, and raises. He also volunteered his time to give back to the community and received complimentary letters and phone calls from satisfied customers. However, he claims that he was subjected to various forms of harassment and discrimination, including being asked to remove his hat so a coworker could defecate in it, being ridiculed for wearing collared shirts, and being assigned to work in high-crime neighborhoods at night. Wilson also alleges that he was not invited to a company celebration for employees with perfect attendance, despite having perfect attendance throughout his career.

Wilson contends that he reported the discrimination and harassment to his supervisor, Darryl Wargo, and other company officials, including the head of Human Resources, multiple times starting in 2012. He claims that his reports were met with inaction, and the incidents worsened over time. In 2019, Wargo was promoted to manager, and Wilson alleges that Wargo's behavior towards him became more abusive and condescending. In January 2021, Wilson reported concerns about his company phone and feeling like he was being followed, which led to a telephone conference with company officials, who suggested that he undergo a medical exam. Wilson objected to the medical evaluation but was eventually required to undergo one, which concluded that he was not "fit for duty." Columbia Gas refused to allow him to return to work, citing the medical evaluation, and eventually terminated his employment in September 2021. Defendant Columbia Gas and Wargo contend that Wilson's allegations are unfounded and that they did not discriminate against him based on his race, national origin, or disability.

Mina Davari, a woman, applied for a car salesman position at Landers Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Norman, a dealership in Norman, Oklahoma. Plaintiff alleges that despite her qualifications, she was not hired for the position because of her gender. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) filed a complaint on behalf of Davari, naming five defendants, including Landers Chrysler of Norman, Motors Management Corporation, LL Glenn Road LLC d/b/a Landers Toyota, The Luther Holding Company d/b/a Luther Automotive Group, and LL Glenn Plaza Loop LLC d/b/a Landers Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Little Rock. The EEOC contends that these defendants collectively constitute a single employer and single integrated enterprise, and therefore, should be held liable for the alleged discriminatory acts.

Defendants, except for Landers Chrysler of Norman, filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that administrative remedies had not been exhausted as to them, as they were not named in the underlying EEOC charge filed by Davari. The EEOC responds that an exception applies, as the complaint alleges that all defendants constitute a single employer, and that they were all sent a Letter of Determination inviting them to join in conciliation efforts. The EEOC also argues that the complaint alleges numerous facts relevant to the single employer test, including interrelated operations, common management, centralized control of labor relations, and common ownership and financial control.

Before filing the lawsuit, Davari had filed a charge with the EEOC, which led to an investigation and a Letter of Determination. The EEOC alleges that during the transition of the Norman dealership from David Stanley Chrysler to Landers Chrysler of Norman, Davari overheard a conversation between a manager, Chris Chase, and another manager, in which Chase made a comment suggesting that the sales position was not suitable for a woman. The EEOC contends that this and other allegations demonstrate a pattern of discriminatory behavior and support the single employer theory of liability.

St. Luke's Methodist Hospital, a hospital-based skilled nursing facility (HB-SNF) in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, provided atypical services to Medicare patients in 1992. Plaintiff alleges that its costs for these services exceeded the applicable cost limits, and it is entitled to reimbursement for these costs under 42 C.F.R. § 413.30. Defendant contends that St. Luke's is not eligible for reimbursement because its costs did not exceed 112% of the peer group mean for HB-SNFs, as required by the Provider Reimbursement Manual (PRM) § 2534.5. 

Prior to 1992, St. Luke's had been granted exceptions to the cost limits for providing atypical services, but the Secretary of Health and Human Services had reinterpreted the regulation in PRM § 2534.5, effectively raising the threshold for exception eligibility. St. Luke's alleges that this reinterpretation is arbitrary, capricious, and not in accordance with law. The parties agree that the relevant facts are undisputed, and the dispute centers on the validity of PRM § 2534.5. 

The Medicare program reimburses skilled nursing facilities for the "reasonable cost" of covered services, and 42 C.F.R. § 413.30 provides for exceptions to the cost limits for facilities that provide atypical services. The regulation requires that the services be necessary for the special needs of the patients and be furnished efficiently. The Secretary had previously granted exceptions to St. Luke's based on its actual costs exceeding the routine cost limit (RCL), but the new interpretation in PRM § 2534.5 requires that the costs exceed 112% of the peer group mean. St. Luke's contends that its costs for 1992 exceeded the RCL but not the new threshold, and it is seeking reimbursement for the difference. Defendant argues that the new interpretation is a valid exercise of the Secretary's discretion and that St. Luke's does not meet the new criteria for exception eligibility.

On April 17, 1967, Celio Diaz, Jr. applied for a position as a flight cabin attendant with Pan American World Airways, Inc. (Pan Am). His application was rejected because Pan Am had a policy of only hiring females for that position, which had been in place since 1965. Diaz then filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) under Section 703 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, alleging that Pan Am had discriminated against him based on his sex. The EEOC found probable cause and attempted conciliation, but it was unsuccessful. 

Diaz filed a complaint with the court on February 14, 1969, on behalf of himself and others similarly situated, alleging that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants was discriminatory. The parties stipulated that Diaz had applied and been rejected for the position because he was male, and that other males had also been rejected for the same reason. They also stipulated that Pan Am's policy was to not hire males for the position, and that the class of plaintiffs would consist of males who had applied for the position within the United States and been rejected because of their sex. 

Plaintiff alleges that Pan Am's policy of only hiring females as cabin attendants is discriminatory and violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Defendant Pan Am contends that being a female is a bona fide occupational qualification for the position of flight cabin attendant, reasonably necessary to the normal operation of its business. The EEOC, as amicus curiae, supports the plaintiff's position. The Transport Workers Union of America, representing Pan Am's cabin attendants, and the Air Line Pilots Association, International, also filed amicus curiae briefs. The parties disagree on the criteria for determining which males who applied for the position in the past should be entitled to preferential consideration for hire and back pay. Plaintiff contends that this group should include all males who filed written applications between July 2, 1965, and November 18, 1971, while defendant Pan Am argues that it should only include those who applied between November 16, 1968, and April 24, 1970.
