Five fair housing organizations, the National Fair Housing Alliance, Fair Housing of Marin, Fair Housing Napa Valley, Metro Fair Housing Services, and The Fair Housing Continuum, Inc., claim that A.G. Spanos Construction, Inc. and related entities (the Spanos Defendants) designed and constructed multifamily apartment complexes that do not comply with the accessibility requirements of the Fair Housing Act (FHA). The Spanos Defendants are alleged to have engaged in a continuous pattern and practice of discrimination against people with disabilities by designing and constructing apartment complexes that deny full access to and use of the facilities as required under the FHA. The plaintiffs allege that 82 apartment complexes located in 10 states, containing over 22,000 apartment units, do not comply with FHA requirements. 

Plaintiffs allege that they have been directly and substantially injured by the Spanos Defendants' actions, as they have been frustrated in their missions to eradicate discrimination in housing and have had to divert significant resources to identify, investigate, and counteract the Spanos Defendants' discriminatory practices. Each plaintiff conducted site visits, investigations, surveys, and/or tests at various properties, resulting in the diversion of staff time, salaries, and travel expenses. The plaintiffs claim that the Spanos Defendants' continuing discriminatory practices have forced them to expend resources that they would not have had to expend were it not for the Spanos Defendants' violations.

The Spanos Defendants are California corporations with principal offices in Stockton, and they allegedly engaged in land acquisition, development, construction, and management of multifamily apartment complexes throughout the United States. Highpointe Village, L.P. and Knickerbocker Properties, Inc. XXXVIII are also defendants, alleged to be owners of apartment complexes designed and/or constructed by the Spanos Defendants. The plaintiffs seek to certify a defendant class consisting of current owners of covered apartment complexes that were designed and/or built by the Spanos Defendants but are no longer owned by them. Plaintiffs allege that these properties do not fully comply with the accessibility and adaptability requirements of the FHA.

Ward, a nontenured instructor, was employed by Kentucky State University. His teaching contract was not renewed. Plaintiff alleges that the nonrenewal was racially motivated and violated his rights to free speech and due process. Defendants contend that the University was not acting "under color of law" as required by 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and that Ward, as a nontenured instructor, is not entitled to notice and hearing. The University also argues that the Kentucky courts are suitably equipped to adjudicate Ward's claim and that the federal judiciary should abstain from exercising jurisdiction.

Prior to the nonrenewal, Ward had been employed by the University, but the exact terms of his employment, including any implied contract, are disputed. Plaintiff alleges that his termination was motivated by his exercise of free speech, while defendants contend that the nonrenewal was lawful. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with the University being a state institution. The nature of the dispute is a claim of racial discrimination and violation of constitutional rights.

The pre-litigation events include the nonrenewal of Ward's contract, which led to the filing of this lawsuit. Relevant documents and communications may include Ward's employment contract, any notices or warnings given to him, and any discussions or meetings between Ward and University officials regarding his employment. The workplace facts include the University's policies and procedures for renewing or terminating contracts, as well as any relevant state laws or regulations governing employment and discrimination. Plaintiff alleges that he was not given notice or a hearing prior to the nonrenewal, while defendants contend that such procedures are not required for nontenured instructors.

Neil Taylor began working as a mechanic for Arlington Transit Mix, Inc. in June 1985. At the time of his hiring, he informed the plant manager, Kenneth Abraham Sr., that he would need to leave work early on Wednesdays to attend church services, which he believed were mandated by the Bible. Taylor was allowed to leave early on Wednesdays for approximately two years, from June 1985 until July 8, 1987. During this time, Taylor and the other three mechanics, Dana Justice, Charles Belcher, and Lee Roy Cox, worked the same hours and often stayed late to complete repairs on the company's trucks.

The company, which owns about 15 trucks, including large cement mixers, requires four full-time mechanics to inspect and repair the trucks when they return to the garage at the end of the day. In the spring of 1987, Arlington's management became concerned about the amount of overtime paid to the mechanics and decided to stagger their hours to maximize straight-time coverage. As part of this change, Belcher was appointed working foreman of the mechanics and was tasked with implementing a new schedule. The schedule change resulted in two mechanics starting at 6:00 a.m. and two starting at 9:00 or 10:00 a.m. Taylor, who had previously been allowed to leave early on Wednesdays, was assigned to the later shift.

Plaintiff alleges that Taylor's discharge on July 9, 1987, was due to his refusal to work late on Wednesday, July 8, 1987, in order to attend church services. Defendant contends that Taylor was discharged because he left work without permission, despite being told that his presence was needed to complete repairs on the trucks. Defendant also claims that it had accommodated Taylor's religious beliefs for two years, but was unable to do so on July 8, 1987, without incurring undue hardship. Prior to his discharge, Taylor had been involved in an incident in which he removed and destroyed a Playboy magazine centerfold and other similar photographs that had been posted in the garage by mechanic Cox, which had led to a reprimand from Abraham. Taylor had also been allowed to post notice of a Bible study group meeting in the garage area and distribute religious literature to his fellow employees.

South Central Bell Telephone and Telegraph Company (Bell) had an Employee Benefits Plan in effect from October 13, 1971, to August 7, 1977, which provided non-occupational sickness and accident benefits to its employees. However, the plan did not cover pregnancy-related absences, except in cases of physical complications. Female employees who took maternity leave accrued only thirty additional days of service credit, while sick or disabled employees received full seniority credit for up to fifty-two weeks. Harriet Wilhite, a female employee of Bell, requested a leave of absence for maternity reasons in 1972 and was not guaranteed reinstatement to the same or equal position upon returning to work. Betty Dubose, another female employee, was granted a six-month maternity leave in 1975 and accrued only thirty days of service credit during her leave.

Plaintiff Wilhite alleges that Bell's policy of not providing mandatory reinstatement rights to female employees returning from maternity leave for a normal pregnancy violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Plaintiff Dubose alleges that Bell's policy of denying full seniority credit to female employees on maternity leave for a normal pregnancy, compared to its treatment of other temporarily disabled employees, also violates Title VII. Bell contends that its policies are facially neutral and do not discriminate against female employees. The Communication Workers of America, AFL-CIO, filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission on April 12, 1972, alleging violations of Title VII by Bell.

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Bell being the employer and Wilhite and Dubose being female employees. The nature of the dispute is a claim of sex discrimination in employment practices, specifically regarding Bell's maternity leave and seniority policies. Relevant pre-litigation events include the filing of complaints with the Equal Employment Opportunities Commission and the issuance of right-to-sue letters to Wilhite and Dubose. The employees' union, the Communication Workers of America, AFL-CIO, is also a party to the lawsuit, representing Wilhite and other similarly situated female employees.

Dan Williams has been a school social worker employed by the Board of Education of the City of Chicago (the "Board") since September 2008. He works in the Chicago Public Schools ("CPS") system, which has over 600 elementary and high schools with varying start and dismissal times. As a CPS social worker, Williams's primary job functions include assisting students, providing crisis intervention services, and developing Individualized Education Plans ("IEPs"). Williams suffers from depression, anxiety, and chronic sinusitis, which affect his ability to sleep, concentrate, and perform tasks. He requires a reasonably quiet workspace with adequate resources and a consistent work schedule to manage his conditions.

Plaintiff Williams alleges that he submitted an accommodation request on October 9, 2014, seeking consistent start and end times of 7:45 a.m. and 2:45 p.m. every day due to his health conditions. Defendant Board contends that Williams's healthcare provider did not provide enough information to support this request, and the Board denied it on November 14, 2014. Williams submitted two more accommodation requests, on May 7, 2015, and September 7, 2015, seeking various accommodations, including a consistent start time, reduced caseload, assignment to a single school, and a private office with specific equipment. The Board denied or partially denied these requests, citing reasons such as the lack of vacancies at 7:45 a.m.-start schools, the need for social workers to support all students in a school building, and the fact that some requests were unrelated to Williams's disability.

Williams's performance evaluations and disciplinary history are also relevant to the dispute. The Board uses the "REACH" tool to evaluate CPS teachers and social workers, and Williams received a "developing" rating for the 2013-2014 school year, which led to his placement on a professional development plan. During the 2014-2015 school year, Williams was placed on a Performance Improvement Plan ("PIP") due to complaints about his behavior at one of his assigned schools, Prescott. Williams disputes the effectiveness of the REACH tool in evaluating social workers, but the Board contends that it is a valid evaluation method. The parties' contentions regarding Williams's accommodation requests, performance evaluations, and disciplinary history are central to the dispute, with Williams alleging that the Board failed to provide reasonable accommodations and the Board contending that it made efforts to assist Williams while also considering the needs of the schools and students.

The plaintiff, an employee of the defendant, requested annual leave for December 22, 23, and 28, 1998. His leave request was initially approved by his supervisors, but his leave request form was later voided, and he was asked to resubmit his request. The defendant's leave policy, as explained in a memorandum by Carole Grant, the plaintiff's immediate supervisor, required employees to check with their partners before requesting leave and only allowed one member of each pair to take leave at a time. The plaintiff did not follow this policy, as he did not consult with his partner, Roberta Melton, and requested leave dates both before and after Christmas. The plaintiff was granted leave for December 22 and 23, 1998, but claims he was required to work on December 28, 1998, although it was later added as a county-wide holiday.

The plaintiff alleges that he was treated differently than other employees with regard to obtaining annual leave and that this treatment was discriminatory. He also claims that he was required to use a sign-in board to inform his supervisors of his whereabouts during the workday, which he believes was unnecessary and a hassle. The plaintiff contends that other employees in his department did not have their names on the board and were not required to sign in and out. However, the defendant's evidence suggests that other employees, including all computer programmers, had their names on the board, and the plaintiff admitted that he did not know whether other employees were told they did not need to use the board.

The plaintiff also alleges that he engaged in protected activity under Title VII by complaining of alleged discrimination in the workplace to Marie Wauben, the Director of Human Resources. He claims that subsequent to these complaints, his supervisor, Carole Grant, took disciplinary actions against him on March 23, 1999, which he believes were retaliatory. The plaintiff contends that the temporal proximity between his protected activity and the adverse employment actions is sufficient to establish a causal connection between the two. The defendant, however, proffers legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for its disciplinary actions, which the plaintiff must show are pretexts for discrimination.

Dollar General, a national discount retailer, operates a distribution center in Bessemer, Alabama, where it hires general warehouse workers. To hire these workers, Dollar General uses a multi-step process that includes an online application, interviews with the HR department and a warehouse supervisor, and a contingent job offer based on a pre-employment background check, physical examination, and drug test. The physical examination and drug test are conducted by Middle Creek Medical Center, an urgent care center that has been providing pre-employment medical services for Dollar General since 2012.

As part of the physical examination, job candidates must complete a "Physical Encounter Questionnaire" designed by Dollar General, which includes questions about their medical history. Until August 22, 2014, the questionnaire asked about the candidate's family medical history, including whether their grandparents, parents, or children had significant medical problems. Middle Creek staff would also ask follow-up questions about the candidate's family medical history if they indicated that their relatives had significant medical problems. The results of the physical examination, including the candidate's medical history and family medical history, were then provided to Dollar General.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and Vincent Jackson, an unsuccessful job applicant, contend that Dollar General's use of the post-offer medical examination and the collection of family medical history information violated the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA). The EEOC and Jackson allege that Dollar General used the results of the medical examinations to screen out qualified individuals with disabilities, and that the collection of family medical history information was not job-related or consistent with business necessity. Dollar General contends that it did not violate the ADA or GINA, and that the medical examination and collection of family medical history information were necessary to ensure that job candidates were qualified for the position. The parties dispute whether Dollar General or Middle Creek set the requirements for the physical examination, including the benchmarks for vision and blood pressure.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has required employers with 100 or more employees to file the Employer Information Report EEO-1 since 1966. The EEO-1 report collects data on the number of individuals employed by job category, sex, race, and ethnicity. In 2010, the EEOC began exploring ways to improve enforcement of federal laws prohibiting pay discrimination, including collecting pay data from employers. The EEOC commissioned a study by the National Academy of Sciences (NAS), which recommended collecting pay data through a survey such as the EEO-1. The EEOC also conducted a pilot study to identify the most efficient means to collect pay data.

In 2016, the EEOC published a Federal Register notice proposing a revised EEO-1 data collection, which included a new component (Component 2) to collect data on employees' W-2 earnings and hours worked. The EEOC estimated that the new pay data collection would increase the reporting time per filer by 3.4 hours. After a public comment period, the EEOC published a second Federal Register notice seeking a three-year approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for the revised EEO-1 data collection. OMB approved the proposed collection on September 29, 2016, and issued an OMB control number for the revised EEO-1.

Plaintiff alleges that OMB's subsequent decision to review and stay Component 2 of the EEO-1 report was improper. Defendant contends that the decision was made in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) and was based on a determination that the relevant circumstances related to the collection had changed and that the burden estimates provided by the EEOC were materially in error. Defendant also contends that the EEOC's data file specifications for submitting EEO-1 data were not contained in the Federal Register notices and were not outlined in the supporting statement for the collection of information, and that the public did not have an opportunity to provide comment on the method of data submission. The parties dispute the practical utility and burden of the revised EEO-1 data collection, as well as the adequacy of the EEOC's efforts to address privacy and confidentiality issues.

President Joseph R. Biden nominated Harris to be a member of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) in January 2022. The Senate confirmed her on May 25, 2022, and she was sworn in on June 1, 2022. Her term expires on March 1, 2028. The Senate later confirmed Harris as Chairman, and she was sworn in as Chairman on March 14, 2024. Harris has been efficient and effective in her role at the MSPB, and when the MSPB's quorum was restored in March 2022, the agency had a backlog of approximately 3,800 cases that had accrued since 2017. By January 2025, however, the MSPB had cleared nearly 99 percent of its backlog. From June 1, 2022, to February 10, 2025, Harris participated in nearly 4,500 decisions.

Plaintiff Harris alleges that on February 10, 2025, she received an email from Trent Morse, Deputy Assistant to the President and the Deputy Director of the White House Presidential Personnel Office, stating that her position on the Merit Systems Protection Board was terminated, effective immediately, on behalf of President Donald J. Trump. Defendants do not dispute that Harris received this email, but they contend that the President has the authority to remove her from her position. Plaintiff alleges that her firing was ultra vires, unconstitutional, and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Harris serving as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, an independent agency responsible for protecting the merit system principles and adjudicating conflicts between federal workers and their employing agencies. The nature of the dispute is Harris's termination from her position, which she claims was unlawful, and the Defendants' contention that the President has the authority to remove her. Relevant pre-litigation events include Harris's nomination, confirmation, and swearing-in as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, as well as her participation in nearly 4,500 decisions during her tenure. The email from Trent Morse to Harris on February 10, 2025, is also a relevant pre-litigation event.

The plaintiff, a multi-racial woman, worked as a Licensed Practical Nurse for the defendant from May 2022 until her constructive discharge in January or March 2024. Plaintiff alleges that she experienced different treatment than coworkers of different races and sexes when it came to discipline. For example, in November 2022, she received a "write-up" for a medication error, but the lead nurse, who authorized the administration of the medication, was not disciplined. Later, Plaintiff was involved in another "medication mix-up," and her supervisor, Audrey Aldrich, initially told her to write an occurrence report, but changed her mind when she learned that a coworker, Adam Cooke, was partially responsible for the error.

Plaintiff alleges that Aldrich regularly compared her to Cooke in a critical manner, saying things like, "You ask questions, Adam doesn't." Plaintiff also alleges that when she reported a racially charged incident to Aldrich, Aldrich either ignored her or told her not to write an incident report. On December 27, 2023, Aldrich asked Plaintiff to move a "med cart" from one building to another with no assistance, resulting in Plaintiff's physical injury and her need to leave work. Plaintiff had other interactions with supervisors that she found offensive, including receiving a text message with a sex toy from supervisor Brittany Washington, and being told that "groceries and such" were "women's work" by supervisor Christina Davila.

Plaintiff presented a discrimination complaint to the Delaware Department of Labor (DDOL) on March 8, 2024, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) accorded substantial weight to DDOL's findings, dismissed Plaintiff's charge, and issued her a Notice of Right to Sue on September 19, 2024. Defendant contends that it did not discriminate against Plaintiff based on her race or sex, but the specific contentions of the defendant are not detailed in the available information. Plaintiff filed a complaint with the Superior Court for the State of Delaware on October 18, 2024, alleging employment discrimination in the form of constructive discharge, discipline, harassment, and hostile work environment.

Rola Hamandi, a citizen and national of both France and Lebanon, has lived in the United States since 1990 and has been a legal permanent resident since October 2, 2001. She filed an application for naturalization (form N-400) with the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) on July 31, 2006. In May and July 2007, Hamandi contacted USCIS by telephone about the status of her application, but was given no information. On August 16, 2007, she visited the USCIS Miami District Office in person and was told that her application was delayed because the required FBI name check had not yet been completed. The office followed up with a letter dated September 15, 2007, stating that her case was not yet ready for decision due to the ongoing background investigation.

Hamandi alleges that USCIS failed to schedule her for the requisite interview and test of her language abilities and knowledge of U.S. history and culture. Plaintiff contends that the defendants, including the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, the Director of USCIS, and the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have a nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate her application within a reasonable time. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that they have no clear nondiscretionary duty to complete the adjudication of Hamandi's application prior to the receipt of her name check results and completion of her interview. They also claim that no statute or regulation gives USCIS a nondiscretionary duty to request expedited background checks or imposes any limitations on the FBI's discretion regarding the timetable for conducting name checks.

The FBI performs criminal background checks, including the FBI "name check," with respect to applicants for U.S. citizenship. Hamandi's application has been delayed due to the pending name check. The USCIS has a mandatory, nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate naturalization applications, which includes conducting a background investigation and examination of the applicant. The FBI, however, has no adjudicative responsibilities with respect to naturalization applications, and no statute or regulation cited by Hamandi expressly creates a mandatory duty owed by the FBI to individual naturalization applicants to process background and name checks. Hamandi filed this action seeking to compel defendants to process her naturalization application, which has been pending for over a year.

Robert M. Lopez, a 46-year-old Hispanic man with polio and post-polio syndrome, was employed as a layout draftsman/CAD operator at Union Tank Car Company's drafting department since October 1977. Lopez's supervisor, Dennis Chansler, who became the Chief Draftsman in March 1992, disagreed with Lopez's promotion to layout draftsman in February 1992. Chansler was responsible for evaluating employees' performance, and Lopez received high ratings in 1992 and 1993, but his rating decreased to 2.82 in 1994. Chansler prepared the 1994 evaluation without soliciting input from Lopez's group leader, Richard Benak, who had previously rated Lopez highly. 

Lopez alleges that he was subjected to racial and national origin harassment by his coworkers, including being called derogatory names such as "wetback," "cockroach," "fucking Mexican," and "fucking spic." He also claims that his physical handicap was criticized, with comments about his arms. Lopez reported this harassment to Benak, who witnessed some of the incidents. In March 1995, Lopez sent a memo to Union's Chief Engineer and Vice President of Engineering, complaining that Chansler's evaluation was "not objective," "demeaning," and "meant to defame" his ability as a layout draftsman. Lopez filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in April 1995, concerning Chansler's evaluation. 

Union Tank Car Company contends that Lopez was discharged on July 12, 1995, as part of a reduction-in-force, due to his poor performance. Chansler states that he decided to discharge Lopez because of his deteriorating performance in 1995, and that he would not have selected Lopez for discharge if his performance had remained at its pre-February 1995 level. However, Lopez alleges that his discharge was discriminatory, based on his race, national origin, age, and disability, and that Union retaliated against him for complaining about the harassment and filing the EEOC charge. Lopez also disputes Chansler's claim that his position was eliminated, noting that another employee, Tim Prasky, was promoted to the position of layout draftsman on the same day Lopez was discharged.

The plaintiff, a Black male, was hired by the Vance County Sheriff's Office as a patrol deputy on June 5, 2017. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, the Vance County Sheriff's Office discriminated against Black deputies, including himself, by not providing them with the same privileges as White deputies. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Black deputies were not provided with protective gear, were issued fewer new uniforms, received unsafe patrol vehicles, and were not given adequate training, whereas White deputies were afforded these benefits. Plaintiff contends that he personally experienced these forms of disparate treatment, including not being issued a laptop, having to use a patrol vehicle in need of repair, and not being provided opportunities for additional training.

Plaintiff alleges that he was also subjected to a hostile work environment, including being openly harassed and called gay. He further alleges that he was retaliated against for failing to discriminate in his policing and that his lieutenant created a paper trail to support a false narrative that plaintiff was insubordinate. In June 2018, plaintiff filed two internal written discrimination complaints against his lieutenant, alleging a hostile work environment based on race and gender discrimination. Plaintiff contends that Sheriff White ordered him to drop the discrimination complaints or face termination. Plaintiff then filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in August 2018, asserting race and gender discrimination and later retaliatory discharge.

The events leading to plaintiff's termination began on October 21, 2018, when he was serving warrants on an individual who allegedly refused multiple orders and became combative and physically aggressive. Plaintiff performed a takedown of the subject, and the subject's arm may have been broken in the process. The subject subsequently complained that plaintiff assaulted and harassed her. Plaintiff's supervisors determined that he had used excessive force, and on October 24, 2018, plaintiff was informed that his services were no longer needed. Defendant contends that plaintiff's termination was due to his use of excessive force, while plaintiff alleges that his termination was retaliatory and motivated by his prior discrimination complaints. Plaintiff also alleges that since his termination, the Vance County Sheriff's Office has made remarks that deputies who file complaints end up like him, and that he has been unable to gain employment in law enforcement due to the Vance County Sheriff's Office's characterization of his employment and termination.

Joseph Jendusa was employed by Midwestern Regional Medical Center, Inc. and Cancer Treatment Centers of America, Inc. (CTCA) for over three years, serving as Vice President of Human Resources. In mid-March 1993, Jendusa informed Robert Mayo, then President of CTCA, that he had multiple sclerosis. He subsequently informed Richard Stephenson, Chairman of the Board and principal owner of CTCA and Midwestern, and R. Richard Wieland, President of CTCA's corporate parent, about his condition and requested a temporary reduction in his work week to 40 hours as an accommodation. Two days later, Jendusa was terminated from his position. The company then recruited a new Director of Human Resources to take over his duties, and Jendusa was not considered for the position. Plaintiff alleges that Stephenson participated directly in his termination. 

Jendusa contends that his termination was a result of discrimination based on his disability, in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Defendants CTCA and Midwestern have answered the complaint, while Stephenson moves to have the complaint against him dismissed, arguing that individual liability under the ADA may not be imposed on him as he is not a "covered entity" under the statute. 

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Jendusa having worked for CTCA and Midwestern for over three years before his termination. The nature of the dispute is Jendusa's allegation that he was terminated due to his disability, which he claims is a violation of the ADA. Jendusa alleges that he was discriminated against because of his multiple sclerosis, while defendants contend that they are not liable for any discrimination, with Stephenson arguing that he cannot be held personally liable under the ADA. Relevant pre-litigation events include Jendusa's disclosure of his condition to his superiors and his request for accommodation, which was followed by his termination.

Bishop Blanchet High School, a private Catholic high school, is located in a residential, single-family zone in North Seattle. The height limit for institutions in this zone is 30 feet. To better illuminate its athletic field, Bishop Blanchet sought to install four, 70-foot-tall light poles. The City of Seattle's Land Use Code requires institutions to apply for a variance if their proposed structures exceed the height limit. On April 25, 2013, the Director of the Department of Planning and Development (DPD) approved Bishop Blanchet's variance application, subject to 21 conditions addressing impacts such as noise, traffic, and light spill. However, on May 8, 2013, Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, an association of nearby homeowners and residents, appealed the DPD decision to the Hearing Examiner, who subsequently reversed the approval on July 17, 2013.

The City of Seattle has a Special Exception that exempts public schools in residential, single-family zones from the 30-foot height requirement for athletic field lighting. Under this exception, public schools can install higher light poles, up to 100 feet, if they demonstrate that the additional height is necessary for adequate illumination and that impacts from light and glare are minimized. Two public high schools in North Seattle, Nathan Hale High School and Ingraham High School, have utilized this Special Exception to install light poles on their athletic fields. Bishop Blanchet alleges that the City's requirement for a variance, while exempting public schools, violates the Equal Terms provision of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) and deprives Bishop Blanchet of substantive due process under the Washington State Constitution.

Plaintiff Bishop Blanchet contends that it is similarly situated to public schools like Nathan Hale and Ingraham High Schools, which have been allowed to install taller light poles under the Special Exception. Bishop Blanchet argues that the City's distinction between private religious schools and public schools is not justified by any legitimate regulatory purpose. Defendant City of Seattle argues that the Special Exception is justified by the accepted zoning criteria of "fostering the provision of public facilities by governmental agencies." Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, as an interested party, opposes Bishop Blanchet's variance request, citing concerns about noise, traffic, and light pollution. The parties have filed cross-motions for summary judgment, agreeing that there are no material facts in dispute.

President Joseph R. Biden nominated Harris to be a member of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) in January 2022. The Senate confirmed her on May 25, 2022, and she was sworn in on June 1, 2022. Her term expires on March 1, 2028. The Senate later confirmed Harris as Chairman, and she was sworn in as Chairman on March 14, 2024. Harris has been efficient and effective in her role at the MSPB, and when the MSPB's quorum was restored in March 2022, the agency had a backlog of approximately 3,800 cases that had accrued since 2017. By January 2025, however, the MSPB had cleared nearly 99 percent of its backlog. From June 1, 2022, to February 10, 2025, Harris participated in nearly 4,500 decisions.

Plaintiff Harris alleges that on February 10, 2025, she received an email from Trent Morse, Deputy Assistant to the President and the Deputy Director of the White House Presidential Personnel Office, stating that her position on the Merit Systems Protection Board was terminated, effective immediately, on behalf of President Donald J. Trump. Defendants do not dispute that Harris received this email, but they contend that the President has the authority to remove her from her position. Plaintiff alleges that her firing was ultra vires, unconstitutional, and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Harris serving as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, an independent agency responsible for protecting the merit system principles and adjudicating conflicts between federal workers and their employing agencies. The nature of the dispute is Harris's termination from her position, which she claims was unlawful, and the Defendants' contention that the President has the authority to remove her. Relevant pre-litigation events include Harris's nomination, confirmation, and swearing-in as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, as well as her participation in nearly 4,500 decisions during her tenure. The email from Trent Morse to Harris on February 10, 2025, is also a relevant pre-litigation event.

Robert M. Lopez, a 46-year-old Hispanic man with polio and post-polio syndrome, was employed as a layout draftsman/CAD operator at Union Tank Car Company's drafting department since October 1977. Lopez's supervisor, Dennis Chansler, who became the Chief Draftsman in March 1992, disagreed with Lopez's promotion to layout draftsman in February 1992. Chansler was responsible for evaluating employees' performance, and Lopez received high ratings in 1992 and 1993, but his rating decreased to 2.82 in 1994. Chansler prepared the 1994 evaluation without soliciting input from Lopez's group leader, Richard Benak, who had previously rated Lopez highly. 

Lopez alleges that he was subjected to racial and national origin harassment by his coworkers, including being called derogatory names such as "wetback," "cockroach," "fucking Mexican," and "fucking spic." He also claims that his physical handicap was criticized, with comments about his arms. Lopez reported this harassment to Benak, who witnessed some of the incidents. In March 1995, Lopez sent a memo to Union's Chief Engineer and Vice President of Engineering, complaining that Chansler's evaluation was "not objective," "demeaning," and "meant to defame" his ability as a layout draftsman. Lopez filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in April 1995, concerning Chansler's evaluation. 

Union Tank Car Company contends that Lopez was discharged on July 12, 1995, as part of a reduction-in-force, due to his poor performance. Chansler states that he decided to discharge Lopez because of his deteriorating performance in 1995, and that he would not have selected Lopez for discharge if his performance had remained at its pre-February 1995 level. However, Lopez alleges that his discharge was discriminatory, based on his race, national origin, age, and disability, and that Union retaliated against him for complaining about the harassment and filing the EEOC charge. Lopez also disputes Chansler's claim that his position was eliminated, noting that another employee, Tim Prasky, was promoted to the position of layout draftsman on the same day Lopez was discharged.

Dan Williams has been a school social worker employed by the Board of Education of the City of Chicago (the "Board") since September 2008. He works in the Chicago Public Schools ("CPS") system, which has over 600 elementary and high schools with varying start and dismissal times. As a CPS social worker, Williams's primary job functions include assisting students, providing crisis intervention services, and developing Individualized Education Plans ("IEPs"). Williams suffers from depression, anxiety, and chronic sinusitis, which affect his ability to sleep, concentrate, and perform tasks. He requires a reasonably quiet workspace with adequate resources and a consistent work schedule to manage his conditions.

Plaintiff Williams alleges that he submitted an accommodation request on October 9, 2014, seeking consistent start and end times of 7:45 a.m. and 2:45 p.m. every day due to his health conditions. Defendant Board contends that Williams's healthcare provider did not provide enough information to support this request, and the Board denied it on November 14, 2014. Williams submitted two more accommodation requests, on May 7, 2015, and September 7, 2015, seeking various accommodations, including a consistent start time, reduced caseload, assignment to a single school, and a private office with specific equipment. The Board denied or partially denied these requests, citing reasons such as the lack of vacancies at 7:45 a.m.-start schools, the need for social workers to support all students in a school building, and the fact that some requests were unrelated to Williams's disability.

Williams's performance evaluations and disciplinary history are also relevant to the dispute. The Board uses the "REACH" tool to evaluate CPS teachers and social workers, and Williams received a "developing" rating for the 2013-2014 school year, which led to his placement on a professional development plan. During the 2014-2015 school year, Williams was placed on a Performance Improvement Plan ("PIP") due to complaints about his behavior at one of his assigned schools, Prescott. Williams disputes the effectiveness of the REACH tool in evaluating social workers, but the Board contends that it is a valid evaluation method. The parties' contentions regarding Williams's accommodation requests, performance evaluations, and disciplinary history are central to the dispute, with Williams alleging that the Board failed to provide reasonable accommodations and the Board contending that it made efforts to assist Williams while also considering the needs of the schools and students.

The plaintiff, a Black male, was hired by the Vance County Sheriff's Office as a patrol deputy on June 5, 2017. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, the Vance County Sheriff's Office discriminated against Black deputies, including himself, by not providing them with the same privileges as White deputies. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Black deputies were not provided with protective gear, were issued fewer new uniforms, received unsafe patrol vehicles, and were not given adequate training, whereas White deputies were afforded these benefits. Plaintiff contends that he personally experienced these forms of disparate treatment, including not being issued a laptop, having to use a patrol vehicle in need of repair, and not being provided opportunities for additional training.

Plaintiff alleges that he was also subjected to a hostile work environment, including being openly harassed and called gay. He further alleges that he was retaliated against for failing to discriminate in his policing and that his lieutenant created a paper trail to support a false narrative that plaintiff was insubordinate. In June 2018, plaintiff filed two internal written discrimination complaints against his lieutenant, alleging a hostile work environment based on race and gender discrimination. Plaintiff contends that Sheriff White ordered him to drop the discrimination complaints or face termination. Plaintiff then filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in August 2018, asserting race and gender discrimination and later retaliatory discharge.

The events leading to plaintiff's termination began on October 21, 2018, when he was serving warrants on an individual who allegedly refused multiple orders and became combative and physically aggressive. Plaintiff performed a takedown of the subject, and the subject's arm may have been broken in the process. The subject subsequently complained that plaintiff assaulted and harassed her. Plaintiff's supervisors determined that he had used excessive force, and on October 24, 2018, plaintiff was informed that his services were no longer needed. Defendant contends that plaintiff's termination was due to his use of excessive force, while plaintiff alleges that his termination was retaliatory and motivated by his prior discrimination complaints. Plaintiff also alleges that since his termination, the Vance County Sheriff's Office has made remarks that deputies who file complaints end up like him, and that he has been unable to gain employment in law enforcement due to the Vance County Sheriff's Office's characterization of his employment and termination.

The plaintiff, a multi-racial woman, worked as a Licensed Practical Nurse for the defendant from May 2022 until her constructive discharge in January or March 2024. Plaintiff alleges that she experienced different treatment than coworkers of different races and sexes when it came to discipline. For example, in November 2022, she received a "write-up" for a medication error, but the lead nurse, who authorized the administration of the medication, was not disciplined. Later, Plaintiff was involved in another "medication mix-up," and her supervisor, Audrey Aldrich, initially told her to write an occurrence report, but changed her mind when she learned that a coworker, Adam Cooke, was partially responsible for the error.

Plaintiff alleges that Aldrich regularly compared her to Cooke in a critical manner, saying things like, "You ask questions, Adam doesn't." Plaintiff also alleges that when she reported a racially charged incident to Aldrich, Aldrich either ignored her or told her not to write an incident report. On December 27, 2023, Aldrich asked Plaintiff to move a "med cart" from one building to another with no assistance, resulting in Plaintiff's physical injury and her need to leave work. Plaintiff had other interactions with supervisors that she found offensive, including receiving a text message with a sex toy from supervisor Brittany Washington, and being told that "groceries and such" were "women's work" by supervisor Christina Davila.

Plaintiff presented a discrimination complaint to the Delaware Department of Labor (DDOL) on March 8, 2024, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) accorded substantial weight to DDOL's findings, dismissed Plaintiff's charge, and issued her a Notice of Right to Sue on September 19, 2024. Defendant contends that it did not discriminate against Plaintiff based on her race or sex, but the specific contentions of the defendant are not detailed in the available information. Plaintiff filed a complaint with the Superior Court for the State of Delaware on October 18, 2024, alleging employment discrimination in the form of constructive discharge, discipline, harassment, and hostile work environment.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has required employers with 100 or more employees to file the Employer Information Report EEO-1 since 1966. The EEO-1 report collects data on the number of individuals employed by job category, sex, race, and ethnicity. In 2010, the EEOC began exploring ways to improve enforcement of federal laws prohibiting pay discrimination, including collecting pay data from employers. The EEOC commissioned a study by the National Academy of Sciences (NAS), which recommended collecting pay data through a survey such as the EEO-1. The EEOC also conducted a pilot study to identify the most efficient means to collect pay data.

In 2016, the EEOC published a Federal Register notice proposing a revised EEO-1 data collection, which included a new component (Component 2) to collect data on employees' W-2 earnings and hours worked. The EEOC estimated that the new pay data collection would increase the reporting time per filer by 3.4 hours. After a public comment period, the EEOC published a second Federal Register notice seeking a three-year approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for the revised EEO-1 data collection. OMB approved the proposed collection on September 29, 2016, and issued an OMB control number for the revised EEO-1.

Plaintiff alleges that OMB's subsequent decision to review and stay Component 2 of the EEO-1 report was improper. Defendant contends that the decision was made in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) and was based on a determination that the relevant circumstances related to the collection had changed and that the burden estimates provided by the EEOC were materially in error. Defendant also contends that the EEOC's data file specifications for submitting EEO-1 data were not contained in the Federal Register notices and were not outlined in the supporting statement for the collection of information, and that the public did not have an opportunity to provide comment on the method of data submission. The parties dispute the practical utility and burden of the revised EEO-1 data collection, as well as the adequacy of the EEOC's efforts to address privacy and confidentiality issues.

Bishop Blanchet High School, a private Catholic high school, is located in a residential, single-family zone in North Seattle. The height limit for institutions in this zone is 30 feet. To better illuminate its athletic field, Bishop Blanchet sought to install four, 70-foot-tall light poles. The City of Seattle's Land Use Code requires institutions to apply for a variance if their proposed structures exceed the height limit. On April 25, 2013, the Director of the Department of Planning and Development (DPD) approved Bishop Blanchet's variance application, subject to 21 conditions addressing impacts such as noise, traffic, and light spill. However, on May 8, 2013, Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, an association of nearby homeowners and residents, appealed the DPD decision to the Hearing Examiner, who subsequently reversed the approval on July 17, 2013.

The City of Seattle has a Special Exception that exempts public schools in residential, single-family zones from the 30-foot height requirement for athletic field lighting. Under this exception, public schools can install higher light poles, up to 100 feet, if they demonstrate that the additional height is necessary for adequate illumination and that impacts from light and glare are minimized. Two public high schools in North Seattle, Nathan Hale High School and Ingraham High School, have utilized this Special Exception to install light poles on their athletic fields. Bishop Blanchet alleges that the City's requirement for a variance, while exempting public schools, violates the Equal Terms provision of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) and deprives Bishop Blanchet of substantive due process under the Washington State Constitution.

Plaintiff Bishop Blanchet contends that it is similarly situated to public schools like Nathan Hale and Ingraham High Schools, which have been allowed to install taller light poles under the Special Exception. Bishop Blanchet argues that the City's distinction between private religious schools and public schools is not justified by any legitimate regulatory purpose. Defendant City of Seattle argues that the Special Exception is justified by the accepted zoning criteria of "fostering the provision of public facilities by governmental agencies." Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, as an interested party, opposes Bishop Blanchet's variance request, citing concerns about noise, traffic, and light pollution. The parties have filed cross-motions for summary judgment, agreeing that there are no material facts in dispute.

Joseph Canada, a Black man, began working at Samuel Grossi & Sons, Inc. (Grossi), a steel producer, in 2009. Throughout his employment, he held various positions, including Helper, Painter, Saw Operator, and Material Handler. Canada was a member of a collective bargaining unit represented by the Shopmen's Local Union No. 502 of the International Association of Bridge, Structural, Ornamental and Reinforcing Iron Workers. The terms and conditions of his employment were governed by both a Collective Bargaining Agreement and Grossi's Employee Conduct and Disciplinary Action Policy.

Canada suffers from serious back problems, including herniated discs and arthritis, and informed Grossi of his need for medical accommodation. He obtained Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) forms himself and submitted them to Elena Osorio, Grossi's Director of Human Resources. Canada alleges that Osorio initially did not want to accept his FMLA forms but eventually did so. He utilized FMLA leave throughout the remainder of his employment. However, Osorio testified that she never approved FMLA leave for Canada and that he took leave without proper authorization. Canada claims that he was harassed when he returned to work after taking FMLA leave, with Osorio talking to him in a condescending manner and not responding to his messages.

Canada also alleges that he experienced racial discrimination and a hostile work environment. He testified that his coworker, Steve Carlberg, called him the N-word on two occasions, and that other employees reported that Joseph Beck, Grossi's shop foreman/shop superintendent, used the N-word as well. Canada claims that Beck used the slur in a crude story about sleeping with a Black woman and also to describe players on the Philadelphia 76ers NBA basketball team. Additionally, Canada alleges that Osorio used the N-word and told him to "stop fuckin' harassing me" during a meeting. Canada reported these incidents to Grossi's management, but he claims that no action was taken to address the harassment. Canada's employment was eventually terminated due to text messages found on a cellphone in a locker on Grossi's shop floor, which Canada contends was not a legitimate reason for his termination. Defendant claims that Canada's termination was based on a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason, and that the text messages were a valid basis for terminating his employment.

The plaintiff, an employee of the defendant, requested annual leave for December 22, 23, and 28, 1998. His leave request was initially approved by his supervisors, but his leave request form was later voided, and he was asked to resubmit his request. The defendant's leave policy, as explained in a memorandum by Carole Grant, the plaintiff's immediate supervisor, required employees to check with their partners before requesting leave and only allowed one member of each pair to take leave at a time. The plaintiff did not follow this policy, as he did not consult with his partner, Roberta Melton, and requested leave dates both before and after Christmas. The plaintiff was granted leave for December 22 and 23, 1998, but claims he was required to work on December 28, 1998, although it was later added as a county-wide holiday.

The plaintiff alleges that he was treated differently than other employees with regard to obtaining annual leave and that this treatment was discriminatory. He also claims that he was required to use a sign-in board to inform his supervisors of his whereabouts during the workday, which he believes was unnecessary and a hassle. The plaintiff contends that other employees in his department did not have their names on the board and were not required to sign in and out. However, the defendant's evidence suggests that other employees, including all computer programmers, had their names on the board, and the plaintiff admitted that he did not know whether other employees were told they did not need to use the board.

The plaintiff also alleges that he engaged in protected activity under Title VII by complaining of alleged discrimination in the workplace to Marie Wauben, the Director of Human Resources. He claims that subsequent to these complaints, his supervisor, Carole Grant, took disciplinary actions against him on March 23, 1999, which he believes were retaliatory. The plaintiff contends that the temporal proximity between his protected activity and the adverse employment actions is sufficient to establish a causal connection between the two. The defendant, however, proffers legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for its disciplinary actions, which the plaintiff must show are pretexts for discrimination.

Rola Hamandi, a citizen and national of both France and Lebanon, has lived in the United States since 1990 and has been a legal permanent resident since October 2, 2001. She filed an application for naturalization (form N-400) with the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) on July 31, 2006. In May and July 2007, Hamandi contacted USCIS by telephone about the status of her application, but was given no information. On August 16, 2007, she visited the USCIS Miami District Office in person and was told that her application was delayed because the required FBI name check had not yet been completed. The office followed up with a letter dated September 15, 2007, stating that her case was not yet ready for decision due to the ongoing background investigation.

Hamandi alleges that USCIS failed to schedule her for the requisite interview and test of her language abilities and knowledge of U.S. history and culture. Plaintiff contends that the defendants, including the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, the Director of USCIS, and the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have a nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate her application within a reasonable time. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that they have no clear nondiscretionary duty to complete the adjudication of Hamandi's application prior to the receipt of her name check results and completion of her interview. They also claim that no statute or regulation gives USCIS a nondiscretionary duty to request expedited background checks or imposes any limitations on the FBI's discretion regarding the timetable for conducting name checks.

The FBI performs criminal background checks, including the FBI "name check," with respect to applicants for U.S. citizenship. Hamandi's application has been delayed due to the pending name check. The USCIS has a mandatory, nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate naturalization applications, which includes conducting a background investigation and examination of the applicant. The FBI, however, has no adjudicative responsibilities with respect to naturalization applications, and no statute or regulation cited by Hamandi expressly creates a mandatory duty owed by the FBI to individual naturalization applicants to process background and name checks. Hamandi filed this action seeking to compel defendants to process her naturalization application, which has been pending for over a year.

On April 25, 2013, the Director of the Department of Planning and Development (DPD) approved Bishop Blanchet's variance application, subject to 21 conditions addressing impacts such as noise, traffic, and light spill. However, on May 8, 2013, Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, an association of nearby homeowners and residents, appealed the DPD decision to the Hearing Examiner, who subsequently reversed the approval on July 17, 2013.

The City of Seattle has a Special Exception that exempts public schools in residential, single-family zones from the 30-foot height requirement for athletic field lighting. Under this exception, public schools can install higher light poles, up to 100 feet, if they demonstrate that the additional height is necessary for adequate illumination and that impacts from light and glare are minimized. Two public high schools in North Seattle, Nathan Hale High School and Ingraham High School, have utilized this Special Exception to install light poles on their athletic fields. Bishop Blanchet alleges that the City's requirement for a variance, while exempting public schools, violates the Equal Terms provision of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) and deprives Bishop Blanchet of substantive due process under the Washington State Constitution.

Plaintiff Bishop Blanchet contends that it is similarly situated to public schools like Nathan Hale and Ingraham High Schools, which have been allowed to install taller light poles under the Special Exception. Bishop Blanchet argues that the City's distinction between private religious schools and public schools is not justified by any legitimate regulatory purpose. Defendant City of Seattle argues that the Special Exception is justified by the accepted zoning criteria of "fostering the provision of public facilities by governmental agencies." Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, as an interested party, opposes Bishop Blanchet's variance request, citing concerns about noise, traffic, and light pollution. The parties have filed cross-motions for summary judgment, agreeing that there are no material facts in dispute.

Joseph Canada, a Black man, began working at Samuel Grossi & Sons, Inc. (Grossi), a steel producer, in 2009. Throughout his employment, he held various positions, including Helper, Painter, Saw Operator, and Material Handler. Canada was a member of a collective bargaining unit represented by the Shopmen's Local Union No. 502 of the International Association of Bridge, Structural, Ornamental and Reinforcing Iron Workers. The terms and conditions of his employment were governed by both a Collective Bargaining Agreement and Grossi's Employee Conduct and Disciplinary Action Policy.

Canada suffers from serious back problems, including herniated discs and arthritis, and informed Grossi of his need for medical accommodation. He obtained Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) forms himself and submitted them to Elena Osorio, Grossi's Director of Human Resources. Canada alleges that Osorio initially did not want to accept his FMLA forms but eventually did so. He utilized FMLA leave throughout the remainder of his employment. However, Osorio testified that she never approved FMLA leave for Canada and that he took leave without proper authorization. Canada claims that he was harassed when he returned to work after taking FMLA leave, with Osorio talking to him in a condescending manner and not responding to his messages.

Canada also alleges that he experienced racial discrimination and a hostile work environment. He testified that his coworker, Steve Carlberg, called him the N-word on two occasions, and that other employees reported that Joseph Beck, Grossi's shop foreman/shop superintendent, used the N-word as well. Canada claims that Beck used the slur in a crude story about sleeping with a Black woman and also to describe players on the Philadelphia 76ers NBA basketball team. Additionally, Canada alleges that Osorio used the N-word and told him to "stop fuckin' harassing me" during a meeting. Canada reported these incidents to Grossi's management, but he claims that no action was taken to address the harassment. Canada's employment was eventually terminated due to text messages found on a cellphone in a locker on Grossi's shop floor, which Canada contends was not a legitimate reason for his termination. Defendant claims that Canada's termination was based on a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason, and that the text messages were a valid basis for terminating his employment.

Rola Hamandi, a citizen and national of both France and Lebanon, has lived in the United States since 1990 and has been a legal permanent resident since October 2, 2001. She filed an application for naturalization (form N-400) with the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) on July 31, 2006. In May and July 2007, Hamandi contacted USCIS by telephone about the status of her application, but was given no information. On August 16, 2007, she visited the USCIS Miami District Office in person and was told that her application was delayed because the required FBI name check had not yet been completed. The office followed up with a letter dated September 15, 2007, stating that her case was not yet ready for decision due to the ongoing background investigation.

Hamandi alleges that USCIS failed to schedule her for the requisite interview and test of her language abilities and knowledge of U.S. history and culture. Plaintiff contends that the defendants, including the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, the Director of USCIS, and the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have a nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate her application within a reasonable time. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that they have no clear nondiscretionary duty to complete the adjudication of Hamandi's application prior to the receipt of her name check results and completion of her interview. They also claim that no statute or regulation gives USCIS a nondiscretionary duty to request expedited background checks or imposes any limitations on the FBI's discretion regarding the timetable for conducting name checks.

The FBI performs criminal background checks, including the FBI "name check," with respect to applicants for U.S. citizenship. Hamandi's application has been delayed due to the pending name check. The USCIS has a mandatory, nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate naturalization applications, which includes conducting a background investigation and examination of the applicant. The FBI, however, has no adjudicative responsibilities with respect to naturalization applications, and no statute or regulation cited by Hamandi expressly creates a mandatory duty owed by the FBI to individual naturalization applicants to process background and name checks. Hamandi filed this action seeking to compel defendants to process her naturalization application, which has been pending for over a year.

President Joseph R. Biden nominated Harris to be a member of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) in January 2022. The Senate confirmed her on May 25, 2022, and she was sworn in on June 1, 2022. Her term expires on March 1, 2028. The Senate later confirmed Harris as Chairman, and she was sworn in as Chairman on March 14, 2024. Harris has been efficient and effective in her role at the MSPB, and when the MSPB's quorum was restored in March 2022, the agency had a backlog of approximately 3,800 cases that had accrued since 2017. By January 2025, however, the MSPB had cleared nearly 99 percent of its backlog. From June 1, 2022, to February 10, 2025, Harris participated in nearly 4,500 decisions.

Plaintiff Harris alleges that on February 10, 2025, she received an email from Trent Morse, Deputy Assistant to the President and the Deputy Director of the White House Presidential Personnel Office, stating that her position on the Merit Systems Protection Board was terminated, effective immediately, on behalf of President Donald J. Trump. Defendants do not dispute that Harris received this email, but they contend that the President has the authority to remove her from her position. Plaintiff alleges that her firing was ultra vires, unconstitutional, and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Harris serving as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, an independent agency responsible for protecting the merit system principles and adjudicating conflicts between federal workers and their employing agencies. The nature of the dispute is Harris's termination from her position, which she claims was unlawful, and the Defendants' contention that the President has the authority to remove her. Relevant pre-litigation events include Harris's nomination, confirmation, and swearing-in as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, as well as her participation in nearly 4,500 decisions during her tenure. The email from Trent Morse to Harris on February 10, 2025, is also a relevant pre-litigation event.

Joseph Jendusa was employed by Midwestern Regional Medical Center, Inc. and Cancer Treatment Centers of America, Inc. (CTCA) for over three years, serving as Vice President of Human Resources. In mid-March 1993, Jendusa informed Robert Mayo, then President of CTCA, that he had multiple sclerosis. He subsequently informed Richard Stephenson, Chairman of the Board and principal owner of CTCA and Midwestern, and R. Richard Wieland, President of CTCA's corporate parent, about his condition and requested a temporary reduction in his work week to 40 hours as an accommodation. Two days later, Jendusa was terminated from his position. The company then recruited a new Director of Human Resources to take over his duties, and Jendusa was not considered for the position. Plaintiff alleges that Stephenson participated directly in his termination. 

Jendusa contends that his termination was a result of discrimination based on his disability, in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Defendants CTCA and Midwestern have answered the complaint, while Stephenson moves to have the complaint against him dismissed, arguing that individual liability under the ADA may not be imposed on him as he is not a "covered entity" under the statute. 

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Jendusa having worked for CTCA and Midwestern for over three years before his termination. The nature of the dispute is Jendusa's allegation that he was terminated due to his disability, which he claims is a violation of the ADA. Jendusa alleges that he was discriminated against because of his multiple sclerosis, while defendants contend that they are not liable for any discrimination, with Stephenson arguing that he cannot be held personally liable under the ADA. Relevant pre-litigation events include Jendusa's disclosure of his condition to his superiors and his request for accommodation, which was followed by his termination.

Dan Williams has been a school social worker employed by the Board of Education of the City of Chicago (the "Board") since September 2008. He works in the Chicago Public Schools ("CPS") system, which has over 600 elementary and high schools with varying start and dismissal times. As a CPS social worker, Williams's primary job functions include assisting students, providing crisis intervention services, and developing Individualized Education Plans ("IEPs"). Williams suffers from depression, anxiety, and chronic sinusitis, which affect his ability to sleep, concentrate, and perform tasks. He requires a reasonably quiet workspace with adequate resources and a consistent work schedule to manage his conditions.

Plaintiff Williams alleges that he submitted an accommodation request on October 9, 2014, seeking consistent start and end times of 7:45 a.m. and 2:45 p.m. every day due to his health conditions. Defendant Board contends that Williams's healthcare provider did not provide enough information to support this request, and the Board denied it on November 14, 2014. Williams submitted two more accommodation requests, on May 7, 2015, and September 7, 2015, seeking various accommodations, including a consistent start time, reduced caseload, assignment to a single school, and a private office with specific equipment. The Board denied or partially denied these requests, citing reasons such as the lack of vacancies at 7:45 a.m.-start schools, the need for social workers to support all students in a school building, and the fact that some requests were unrelated to Williams's disability.

Williams's performance evaluations and disciplinary history are also relevant to the dispute. The Board uses the "REACH" tool to evaluate CPS teachers and social workers, and Williams received a "developing" rating for the 2013-2014 school year, which led to his placement on a professional development plan. During the 2014-2015 school year, Williams was placed on a Performance Improvement Plan ("PIP") due to complaints about his behavior at one of his assigned schools, Prescott. Williams disputes the effectiveness of the REACH tool in evaluating social workers, but the Board contends that it is a valid evaluation method. The parties' contentions regarding Williams's accommodation requests, performance evaluations, and disciplinary history are central to the dispute, with Williams alleging that the Board failed to provide reasonable accommodations and the Board contending that it made efforts to assist Williams while also considering the needs of the schools and students.

The plaintiff, a multi-racial woman, worked as a Licensed Practical Nurse for the defendant from May 2022 until her constructive discharge in January or March 2024. Plaintiff alleges that she experienced different treatment than coworkers of different races and sexes when it came to discipline. For example, in November 2022, she received a "write-up" for a medication error, but the lead nurse, who authorized the administration of the medication, was not disciplined. Later, Plaintiff was involved in another "medication mix-up," and her supervisor, Audrey Aldrich, initially told her to write an occurrence report, but changed her mind when she learned that a coworker, Adam Cooke, was partially responsible for the error.

Plaintiff alleges that Aldrich regularly compared her to Cooke in a critical manner, saying things like, "You ask questions, Adam doesn't." Plaintiff also alleges that when she reported a racially charged incident to Aldrich, Aldrich either ignored her or told her not to write an incident report. On December 27, 2023, Aldrich asked Plaintiff to move a "med cart" from one building to another with no assistance, resulting in Plaintiff's physical injury and her need to leave work. Plaintiff had other interactions with supervisors that she found offensive, including receiving a text message with a sex toy from supervisor Brittany Washington, and being told that "groceries and such" were "women's work" by supervisor Christina Davila.

Plaintiff presented a discrimination complaint to the Delaware Department of Labor (DDOL) on March 8, 2024, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) accorded substantial weight to DDOL's findings, dismissed Plaintiff's charge, and issued her a Notice of Right to Sue on September 19, 2024. Defendant contends that it did not discriminate against Plaintiff based on her race or sex, but the specific contentions of the defendant are not detailed in the available information. Plaintiff filed a complaint with the Superior Court for the State of Delaware on October 18, 2024, alleging employment discrimination in the form of constructive discharge, discipline, harassment, and hostile work environment.

Dollar General, a national discount retailer, operates a distribution center in Bessemer, Alabama, where it hires general warehouse workers. To hire these workers, Dollar General uses a multi-step process that includes an online application, interviews with the HR department and a warehouse supervisor, and a contingent job offer based on a pre-employment background check, physical examination, and drug test. The physical examination and drug test are conducted by Middle Creek Medical Center, an urgent care center that has been providing pre-employment medical services for Dollar General since 2012.

As part of the physical examination, job candidates must complete a "Physical Encounter Questionnaire" designed by Dollar General, which includes questions about their medical history. Until August 22, 2014, the questionnaire asked about the candidate's family medical history, including whether their grandparents, parents, or children had significant medical problems. Middle Creek staff would also ask follow-up questions about the candidate's family medical history if they indicated that their relatives had significant medical problems. The results of the physical examination, including the candidate's medical history and family medical history, were then provided to Dollar General.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and Vincent Jackson, an unsuccessful job applicant, contend that Dollar General's use of the post-offer medical examination and the collection of family medical history information violated the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA). The EEOC and Jackson allege that Dollar General used the results of the medical examinations to screen out qualified individuals with disabilities, and that the collection of family medical history information was not job-related or consistent with business necessity. Dollar General contends that it did not violate the ADA or GINA, and that the medical examination and collection of family medical history information were necessary to ensure that job candidates were qualified for the position. The parties dispute whether Dollar General or Middle Creek set the requirements for the physical examination, including the benchmarks for vision and blood pressure.

The plaintiff, an employee of the defendant, requested annual leave for December 22, 23, and 28, 1998. His leave request was initially approved by his supervisors, but his leave request form was later voided, and he was asked to resubmit his request. The defendant's leave policy, as explained in a memorandum by Carole Grant, the plaintiff's immediate supervisor, required employees to check with their partners before requesting leave and only allowed one member of each pair to take leave at a time. The plaintiff did not follow this policy, as he did not consult with his partner, Roberta Melton, and requested leave dates both before and after Christmas. The plaintiff was granted leave for December 22 and 23, 1998, but claims he was required to work on December 28, 1998, although it was later added as a county-wide holiday.

The plaintiff alleges that he was treated differently than other employees with regard to obtaining annual leave and that this treatment was discriminatory. He also claims that he was required to use a sign-in board to inform his supervisors of his whereabouts during the workday, which he believes was unnecessary and a hassle. The plaintiff contends that other employees in his department did not have their names on the board and were not required to sign in and out. However, the defendant's evidence suggests that other employees, including all computer programmers, had their names on the board, and the plaintiff admitted that he did not know whether other employees were told they did not need to use the board.

The plaintiff also alleges that he engaged in protected activity under Title VII by complaining of alleged discrimination in the workplace to Marie Wauben, the Director of Human Resources. He claims that subsequent to these complaints, his supervisor, Carole Grant, took disciplinary actions against him on March 23, 1999, which he believes were retaliatory. The plaintiff contends that the temporal proximity between his protected activity and the adverse employment actions is sufficient to establish a causal connection between the two. The defendant, however, proffers legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for its disciplinary actions, which the plaintiff must show are pretexts for discrimination.
