The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has required employers with 100 or more employees to file the Employer Information Report EEO-1 since 1966. The EEO-1 report collects data on the number of individuals employed by job category, sex, race, and ethnicity. In 2010, the EEOC began exploring ways to improve enforcement of federal laws prohibiting pay discrimination, including collecting pay data from employers. The EEOC commissioned a study by the National Academy of Sciences (NAS), which recommended collecting pay data through a survey such as the EEO-1. The EEOC also conducted a pilot study to identify the most efficient means to collect pay data.

In 2016, the EEOC published a Federal Register notice proposing a revised EEO-1 data collection, which included a new component (Component 2) to collect data on employees' W-2 earnings and hours worked. The EEOC estimated that the new pay data collection would increase the reporting time per filer by 3.4 hours. After a public comment period, the EEOC published a second Federal Register notice seeking a three-year approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for the revised EEO-1 data collection. OMB approved the proposed collection on September 29, 2016, and issued an OMB control number for the revised EEO-1.

Plaintiff alleges that OMB's subsequent decision to review and stay Component 2 of the EEO-1 report was improper. Defendant contends that the decision was made in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) and was based on a determination that the relevant circumstances related to the collection had changed and that the burden estimates provided by the EEOC were materially in error. Defendant also contends that the EEOC's data file specifications for submitting EEO-1 data were not contained in the Federal Register notices and were not outlined in the supporting statement for the collection of information, and that the public did not have an opportunity to provide comment on the method of data submission. The parties dispute the practical utility and burden of the revised EEO-1 data collection, as well as the adequacy of the EEOC's efforts to address privacy and confidentiality issues.

The plaintiff, a Black male, was hired by the Vance County Sheriff's Office as a patrol deputy on June 5, 2017. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, the Vance County Sheriff's Office discriminated against Black deputies, including himself, by not providing them with the same privileges as White deputies. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Black deputies were not provided with protective gear, were issued fewer new uniforms, received unsafe patrol vehicles, and were not given adequate training, whereas White deputies were afforded these benefits. Plaintiff contends that he personally experienced these forms of disparate treatment, including not being issued a laptop, having to use a patrol vehicle in need of repair, and not being provided opportunities for additional training.

Plaintiff alleges that he was also subjected to a hostile work environment, including being openly harassed and called gay. He further alleges that he was retaliated against for failing to discriminate in his policing and that his lieutenant created a paper trail to support a false narrative that plaintiff was insubordinate. In June 2018, plaintiff filed two internal written discrimination complaints against his lieutenant, alleging a hostile work environment based on race and gender discrimination. Plaintiff contends that Sheriff White ordered him to drop the discrimination complaints or face termination. Plaintiff then filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in August 2018, asserting race and gender discrimination and later retaliatory discharge.

The events leading to plaintiff's termination began on October 21, 2018, when he was serving warrants on an individual who allegedly refused multiple orders and became combative and physically aggressive. Plaintiff performed a takedown of the subject, and the subject's arm may have been broken in the process. The subject subsequently complained that plaintiff assaulted and harassed her. Plaintiff's supervisors determined that he had used excessive force, and on October 24, 2018, plaintiff was informed that his services were no longer needed. Defendant contends that plaintiff's termination was due to his use of excessive force, while plaintiff alleges that his termination was retaliatory and motivated by his prior discrimination complaints. Plaintiff also alleges that since his termination, the Vance County Sheriff's Office has made remarks that deputies who file complaints end up like him, and that he has been unable to gain employment in law enforcement due to the Vance County Sheriff's Office's characterization of his employment and termination.

Plaintiff contends that he personally experienced these forms of disparate treatment, including not being issued a laptop, having to use a patrol vehicle in need of repair, and not being provided opportunities for additional training.

Plaintiff alleges that he was also subjected to a hostile work environment, including being openly harassed and called gay. He further alleges that he was retaliated against for failing to discriminate in his policing and that his lieutenant created a paper trail to support a false narrative that plaintiff was insubordinate. In June 2018, plaintiff filed two internal written discrimination complaints against his lieutenant, alleging a hostile work environment based on race and gender discrimination. Plaintiff contends that Sheriff White ordered him to drop the discrimination complaints or face termination. Plaintiff then filed a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in August 2018, asserting race and gender discrimination and later retaliatory discharge.

The events leading to plaintiff's termination began on October 21, 2018, when he was serving warrants on an individual who allegedly refused multiple orders and became combative and physically aggressive. Plaintiff performed a takedown of the subject, and the subject's arm may have been broken in the process. The subject subsequently complained that plaintiff assaulted and harassed her. Plaintiff's supervisors determined that he had used excessive force, and on October 24, 2018, plaintiff was informed that his services were no longer needed. Defendant contends that plaintiff's termination was due to his use of excessive force, while plaintiff alleges that his termination was retaliatory and motivated by his prior discrimination complaints. Plaintiff also alleges that since his termination, the Vance County Sheriff's Office has made remarks that deputies who file complaints end up like him, and that he has been unable to gain employment in law enforcement due to the Vance County Sheriff's Office's characterization of his employment and termination.

Robert M. Lopez, a 46-year-old Hispanic man with polio and post-polio syndrome, was employed as a layout draftsman/CAD operator at Union Tank Car Company's drafting department since October 1977. Lopez's supervisor, Dennis Chansler, who became the Chief Draftsman in March 1992, disagreed with Lopez's promotion to layout draftsman in February 1992. Chansler was responsible for evaluating employees' performance, and Lopez received high ratings in 1992 and 1993, but his rating decreased to 2.82 in 1994. Chansler prepared the 1994 evaluation without soliciting input from Lopez's group leader, Richard Benak, who had previously rated Lopez highly. 

Lopez alleges that he was subjected to racial and national origin harassment by his coworkers, including being called derogatory names such as "wetback," "cockroach," "fucking Mexican," and "fucking spic." He also claims that his physical handicap was criticized, with comments about his arms. Lopez reported this harassment to Benak, who witnessed some of the incidents. In March 1995, Lopez sent a memo to Union's Chief Engineer and Vice President of Engineering, complaining that Chansler's evaluation was "not objective," "demeaning," and "meant to defame" his ability as a layout draftsman. Lopez filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in April 1995, concerning Chansler's evaluation. 

Union Tank Car Company contends that Lopez was discharged on July 12, 1995, as part of a reduction-in-force, due to his poor performance. Chansler states that he decided to discharge Lopez because of his deteriorating performance in 1995, and that he would not have selected Lopez for discharge if his performance had remained at its pre-February 1995 level. However, Lopez alleges that his discharge was discriminatory, based on his race, national origin, age, and disability, and that Union retaliated against him for complaining about the harassment and filing the EEOC charge. Lopez also disputes Chansler's claim that his position was eliminated, noting that another employee, Tim Prasky, was promoted to the position of layout draftsman on the same day Lopez was discharged.

Joseph Canada, a Black man, began working at Samuel Grossi & Sons, Inc. (Grossi), a steel producer, in 2009. Throughout his employment, he held various positions, including Helper, Painter, Saw Operator, and Material Handler. Canada was a member of a collective bargaining unit represented by the Shopmen's Local Union No. 502 of the International Association of Bridge, Structural, Ornamental and Reinforcing Iron Workers. The terms and conditions of his employment were governed by both a Collective Bargaining Agreement and Grossi's Employee Conduct and Disciplinary Action Policy.

Canada suffers from serious back problems, including herniated discs and arthritis, and informed Grossi of his need for medical accommodation. He obtained Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) forms himself and submitted them to Elena Osorio, Grossi's Director of Human Resources. Canada alleges that Osorio initially did not want to accept his FMLA forms but eventually did so. He utilized FMLA leave throughout the remainder of his employment. However, Osorio testified that she never approved FMLA leave for Canada and that he took leave without proper authorization. Canada claims that he was harassed when he returned to work after taking FMLA leave, with Osorio talking to him in a condescending manner and not responding to his messages.

Canada also alleges that he experienced racial discrimination and a hostile work environment. He testified that his coworker, Steve Carlberg, called him the N-word on two occasions, and that other employees reported that Joseph Beck, Grossi's shop foreman/shop superintendent, used the N-word as well. Canada claims that Beck used the slur in a crude story about sleeping with a Black woman and also to describe players on the Philadelphia 76ers NBA basketball team. Additionally, Canada alleges that Osorio used the N-word and told him to "stop fuckin' harassing me" during a meeting. Canada reported these incidents to Grossi's management, but he claims that no action was taken to address the harassment. Canada's employment was eventually terminated due to text messages found on a cellphone in a locker on Grossi's shop floor, which Canada contends was not a legitimate reason for his termination. Defendant claims that Canada's termination was based on a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason, and that the text messages were a valid basis for terminating his employment.

Joseph Jendusa was employed by Midwestern Regional Medical Center, Inc. and Cancer Treatment Centers of America, Inc. (CTCA) for over three years, serving as Vice President of Human Resources. In mid-March 1993, Jendusa informed Robert Mayo, then President of CTCA, that he had multiple sclerosis. He subsequently informed Richard Stephenson, Chairman of the Board and principal owner of CTCA and Midwestern, and R. Richard Wieland, President of CTCA's corporate parent, about his condition and requested a temporary reduction in his work week to 40 hours as an accommodation. Two days later, Jendusa was terminated from his position. The company then recruited a new Director of Human Resources to take over his duties, and Jendusa was not considered for the position. Plaintiff alleges that Stephenson participated directly in his termination. 

Jendusa contends that his termination was a result of discrimination based on his disability, in violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Defendants CTCA and Midwestern have answered the complaint, while Stephenson moves to have the complaint against him dismissed, arguing that individual liability under the ADA may not be imposed on him as he is not a "covered entity" under the statute. 

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Jendusa having worked for CTCA and Midwestern for over three years before his termination. The nature of the dispute is Jendusa's allegation that he was terminated due to his disability, which he claims is a violation of the ADA. Jendusa alleges that he was discriminated against because of his multiple sclerosis, while defendants contend that they are not liable for any discrimination, with Stephenson arguing that he cannot be held personally liable under the ADA. Relevant pre-litigation events include Jendusa's disclosure of his condition to his superiors and his request for accommodation, which was followed by his termination.

Dollar General, a national discount retailer, operates a distribution center in Bessemer, Alabama, where it hires general warehouse workers. To hire these workers, Dollar General uses a multi-step process that includes an online application, interviews with the HR department and a warehouse supervisor, and a contingent job offer based on a pre-employment background check, physical examination, and drug test. The physical examination and drug test are conducted by Middle Creek Medical Center, an urgent care center that has been providing pre-employment medical services for Dollar General since 2012.

As part of the physical examination, job candidates must complete a "Physical Encounter Questionnaire" designed by Dollar General, which includes questions about their medical history. Until August 22, 2014, the questionnaire asked about the candidate's family medical history, including whether their grandparents, parents, or children had significant medical problems. Middle Creek staff would also ask follow-up questions about the candidate's family medical history if they indicated that their relatives had significant medical problems. The results of the physical examination, including the candidate's medical history and family medical history, were then provided to Dollar General.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and Vincent Jackson, an unsuccessful job applicant, contend that Dollar General's use of the post-offer medical examination and the collection of family medical history information violated the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA). The EEOC and Jackson allege that Dollar General used the results of the medical examinations to screen out qualified individuals with disabilities, and that the collection of family medical history information was not job-related or consistent with business necessity. Dollar General contends that it did not violate the ADA or GINA, and that the medical examination and collection of family medical history information were necessary to ensure that job candidates were qualified for the position. The parties dispute whether Dollar General or Middle Creek set the requirements for the physical examination, including the benchmarks for vision and blood pressure.

The plaintiff, a multi-racial woman, worked as a Licensed Practical Nurse for the defendant from May 2022 until her constructive discharge in January or March 2024. Plaintiff alleges that she experienced different treatment than coworkers of different races and sexes when it came to discipline. For example, in November 2022, she received a "write-up" for a medication error, but the lead nurse, who authorized the administration of the medication, was not disciplined. Later, Plaintiff was involved in another "medication mix-up," and her supervisor, Audrey Aldrich, initially told her to write an occurrence report, but changed her mind when she learned that a coworker, Adam Cooke, was partially responsible for the error.

Plaintiff alleges that Aldrich regularly compared her to Cooke in a critical manner, saying things like, "You ask questions, Adam doesn't." Plaintiff also alleges that when she reported a racially charged incident to Aldrich, Aldrich either ignored her or told her not to write an incident report. On December 27, 2023, Aldrich asked Plaintiff to move a "med cart" from one building to another with no assistance, resulting in Plaintiff's physical injury and her need to leave work. Plaintiff had other interactions with supervisors that she found offensive, including receiving a text message with a sex toy from supervisor Brittany Washington, and being told that "groceries and such" were "women's work" by supervisor Christina Davila.

Plaintiff presented a discrimination complaint to the Delaware Department of Labor (DDOL) on March 8, 2024, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) accorded substantial weight to DDOL's findings, dismissed Plaintiff's charge, and issued her a Notice of Right to Sue on September 19, 2024. Defendant contends that it did not discriminate against Plaintiff based on her race or sex, but the specific contentions of the defendant are not detailed in the available information. Plaintiff filed a complaint with the Superior Court for the State of Delaware on October 18, 2024, alleging employment discrimination in the form of constructive discharge, discipline, harassment, and hostile work environment.

Bishop Blanchet High School, a private Catholic high school, is located in a residential, single-family zone in North Seattle. The height limit for institutions in this zone is 30 feet. To better illuminate its athletic field, Bishop Blanchet sought to install four, 70-foot-tall light poles. The City of Seattle's Land Use Code requires institutions to apply for a variance if their proposed structures exceed the height limit. On April 25, 2013, the Director of the Department of Planning and Development (DPD) approved Bishop Blanchet's variance application, subject to 21 conditions addressing impacts such as noise, traffic, and light spill. However, on May 8, 2013, Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, an association of nearby homeowners and residents, appealed the DPD decision to the Hearing Examiner, who subsequently reversed the approval on July 17, 2013.

The City of Seattle has a Special Exception that exempts public schools in residential, single-family zones from the 30-foot height requirement for athletic field lighting. Under this exception, public schools can install higher light poles, up to 100 feet, if they demonstrate that the additional height is necessary for adequate illumination and that impacts from light and glare are minimized. Two public high schools in North Seattle, Nathan Hale High School and Ingraham High School, have utilized this Special Exception to install light poles on their athletic fields. Bishop Blanchet alleges that the City's requirement for a variance, while exempting public schools, violates the Equal Terms provision of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) and deprives Bishop Blanchet of substantive due process under the Washington State Constitution.

Plaintiff Bishop Blanchet contends that it is similarly situated to public schools like Nathan Hale and Ingraham High Schools, which have been allowed to install taller light poles under the Special Exception. Bishop Blanchet argues that the City's distinction between private religious schools and public schools is not justified by any legitimate regulatory purpose. Defendant City of Seattle argues that the Special Exception is justified by the accepted zoning criteria of "fostering the provision of public facilities by governmental agencies." Concerned Blanchet Neighbors, as an interested party, opposes Bishop Blanchet's variance request, citing concerns about noise, traffic, and light pollution. The parties have filed cross-motions for summary judgment, agreeing that there are no material facts in dispute.

President Joseph R. Biden nominated Harris to be a member of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) in January 2022. The Senate confirmed her on May 25, 2022, and she was sworn in on June 1, 2022. Her term expires on March 1, 2028. The Senate later confirmed Harris as Chairman, and she was sworn in as Chairman on March 14, 2024. Harris has been efficient and effective in her role at the MSPB, and when the MSPB's quorum was restored in March 2022, the agency had a backlog of approximately 3,800 cases that had accrued since 2017. By January 2025, however, the MSPB had cleared nearly 99 percent of its backlog. From June 1, 2022, to February 10, 2025, Harris participated in nearly 4,500 decisions.

Plaintiff Harris alleges that on February 10, 2025, she received an email from Trent Morse, Deputy Assistant to the President and the Deputy Director of the White House Presidential Personnel Office, stating that her position on the Merit Systems Protection Board was terminated, effective immediately, on behalf of President Donald J. Trump. Defendants do not dispute that Harris received this email, but they contend that the President has the authority to remove her from her position. Plaintiff alleges that her firing was ultra vires, unconstitutional, and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Harris serving as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, an independent agency responsible for protecting the merit system principles and adjudicating conflicts between federal workers and their employing agencies. The nature of the dispute is Harris's termination from her position, which she claims was unlawful, and the Defendants' contention that the President has the authority to remove her. Relevant pre-litigation events include Harris's nomination, confirmation, and swearing-in as a member and Chairman of the MSPB, as well as her participation in nearly 4,500 decisions during her tenure. The email from Trent Morse to Harris on February 10, 2025, is also a relevant pre-litigation event.

Rola Hamandi, a citizen and national of both France and Lebanon, has lived in the United States since 1990 and has been a legal permanent resident since October 2, 2001. She filed an application for naturalization (form N-400) with the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) on July 31, 2006. In May and July 2007, Hamandi contacted USCIS by telephone about the status of her application, but was given no information. On August 16, 2007, she visited the USCIS Miami District Office in person and was told that her application was delayed because the required FBI name check had not yet been completed. The office followed up with a letter dated September 15, 2007, stating that her case was not yet ready for decision due to the ongoing background investigation.

Hamandi alleges that USCIS failed to schedule her for the requisite interview and test of her language abilities and knowledge of U.S. history and culture. Plaintiff contends that the defendants, including the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, the Director of USCIS, and the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have a nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate her application within a reasonable time. Defendants, on the other hand, contend that they have no clear nondiscretionary duty to complete the adjudication of Hamandi's application prior to the receipt of her name check results and completion of her interview. They also claim that no statute or regulation gives USCIS a nondiscretionary duty to request expedited background checks or imposes any limitations on the FBI's discretion regarding the timetable for conducting name checks.

The FBI performs criminal background checks, including the FBI "name check," with respect to applicants for U.S. citizenship. Hamandi's application has been delayed due to the pending name check. The USCIS has a mandatory, nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate naturalization applications, which includes conducting a background investigation and examination of the applicant. The FBI, however, has no adjudicative responsibilities with respect to naturalization applications, and no statute or regulation cited by Hamandi expressly creates a mandatory duty owed by the FBI to individual naturalization applicants to process background and name checks. Hamandi filed this action seeking to compel defendants to process her naturalization application, which has been pending for over a year.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has required employers with 100 or more employees to file the Employer Information Report EEO-1 since 1966. The EEO-1 report collects data on the number of individuals employed by job category, sex, race, and ethnicity. In 2010, the EEOC began exploring ways to improve enforcement of federal laws prohibiting pay discrimination, including collecting pay data from employers. The EEOC commissioned a study by the National Academy of Sciences (NAS), which recommended collecting pay data through a survey such as the EEO-1. The EEOC also conducted a pilot study to identify the most efficient means to collect pay data.

In 2016, the EEOC published a Federal Register notice proposing a revised EEO-1 data collection, which included a new component (Component 2) to collect data on employees' W-2 earnings and hours worked. The EEOC estimated that the new pay data collection would increase the reporting time per filer by 3.4 hours. After a public comment period, the EEOC published a second Federal Register notice seeking a three-year approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for the revised EEO-1 data collection. OMB approved the proposed collection on September 29, 2016, and issued an OMB control number for the revised EEO-1.

Plaintiff alleges that OMB's subsequent decision to review and stay Component 2 of the EEO-1 report was improper. Defendant contends that the decision was made in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) and was based on a determination that the relevant circumstances related to the collection had changed and that the burden estimates provided by the EEOC were materially in error. Defendant also contends that the EEOC's data file specifications for submitting EEO-1 data were not contained in the Federal Register notices and were not outlined in the supporting statement for the collection of information, and that the public did not have an opportunity to provide comment on the method of data submission. The parties dispute the practical utility and burden of the revised EEO-1 data collection, as well as the adequacy of the EEOC's efforts to address privacy and confidentiality issues.

Bilan Nur, a Muslim woman, immigrated to the United States from Somalia in 1998. In November 1999, she was hired by Alamo as a rental agent at a location on East Washington Street in Phoenix, Arizona. Her duties included renting cars to customers, accepting payment, and answering the telephone, all of which required interaction with clients. Until the events leading to her termination, Ms. Nur's job performance was "fine." Alamo had a "Dress Smart Policy" in place, which aimed to promote a favorable first impression with customers and prohibited employees from wearing certain clothing and accessories, such as more than one earring, open-toe shoes, and half-grown beards. The policy did not explicitly prohibit the wearing of head coverings, but Alamo contends that it prohibited any "garment or item of outer clothing not specifically mentioned in the policy."

In November 2001, during the Muslim holiday of Ramadan, Ms. Nur requested permission from Alamo's City Manager, Victor Bellavia, to wear a head covering at work. Bellavia contacted Alamo's Human Resource Manager, Heather Phillips, who instructed him that Ms. Nur could wear a head covering in the back of the office but would need to remove it while at the rental counter. Alamo did not excuse Ms. Nur from working at the rental counter during Ramadan. On December 1, 2001, Ms. Nur was given a "Counselling Review" for wearing a veil over her hair, and she was told to clock out and discuss the issue with the City Manager. The next day, she received another Counselling Review, was suspended, and was advised to discuss the issue with the City Manager. On December 3, 2001, Ms. Nur received another counselling review, was suspended pending investigation, and was told to return on December 6, 2001, to meet with the City Manager. On December 6, 2001, Alamo terminated Ms. Nur's employment for violating company rules, and the termination form indicated that she was not eligible for re-hire.

Plaintiff alleges that Alamo discriminated against Ms. Nur based on her religion by not accommodating her request to wear a head covering during Ramadan. Alamo contends that it did not discriminate against Ms. Nur and that her religious beliefs did not conflict with her job requirements. Alamo also points to evidence that during Ramadan in 2000, Ms. Nur was asked to remove her head covering and complied without asserting a religious need to object, which Alamo argues raises questions about the sincerity of Ms. Nur's religious beliefs in 2001. The EEOC filed a complaint on September 27, 2002, on behalf of Ms. Nur, asserting a claim of religious discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The matter was stayed due to Alamo's bankruptcy filing but was later lifted, and the EEOC filed a motion for partial summary judgment regarding liability on its religious discrimination claim.

On June 21, 2009, the plaintiff, a middle-aged white woman, was hired as a Senior Case Technician (SCT) in the Social Security Administration's (SSA) Office of Disability Adjudication and Review (ODAR) in Washington, D.C. for a two-year trial period. As an SCT, she assisted in the administrative adjudication of appeals brought by individuals denied Social Security and Social Security Insurance benefits. In addition to her regular SCT work, she performed clerical and technical tasks as a personal clerk to an administrative law judge and frequently filled in as the receptionist at the front desk of ODAR.

Three months after commencing her job, an African American male co-worker physically assaulted her, prompting her to file an informal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint. The co-worker claimed that the plaintiff attacked him. The plaintiff's supervisor, Hariette Hindie, responded to the incident by interrogating the plaintiff in a Weingarten session. When an SSA EEO official told the plaintiff that formal EEO complaints must be filed against "management," the plaintiff decided not to pursue a formal complaint for fear of losing her job. Plaintiff alleges that she did not take any formal action because she feared losing her job, while Defendant contends that the plaintiff had the opportunity to file a formal complaint but chose not to.

The plaintiff earned a promotion to a General Schedule (GS) level seven from a GS level six in June 2010, which was supported by Hindie and based on the plaintiff's job performance during the first year of her probationary period. However, in the following months, Hindie began scrutinizing the plaintiff's work more closely, and in September, she gave the plaintiff a counseling memorandum that identified specific problems with her recent job performance. The plaintiff responded by defending her performance in a rebuttal memorandum. On November 22, 2010, Hindie recommended the plaintiff's termination on the basis of poor work performance during the second year of the plaintiff's probationary period. Plaintiff alleges that Hindie's actions were retaliatory, while Defendant contends that the termination was based on the plaintiff's poor work performance. The plaintiff resigned effective January 5, 2011, to avoid embarrassment, increase her chances of obtaining future employment, and leave a work environment that caused her stress-related illnesses. Following her resignation, the plaintiff filed a formal EEO complaint against SSA management, alleging retaliation and coerced resignation.

Harvey Ross, an African-American man, worked as a general mechanic (grade 5) at the United States Postal Service (Postal Service) since 1987. Prior to joining the Postal Service, Ross worked for 11 years installing, repairing, and maintaining electrical and electronic systems. In August 1989, the Mail Equipment Shops (MES) section of the Postal Service posted a vacancy announcement for a MES technician position. Ross and six other applicants, including four African-Americans, one Caucasian, and one Asian-American, submitted applications for the position. To qualify for an interview, each applicant had to pass the mandatory Postal Test 500 (PT 500), which Ross passed with the highest score.

The selecting panel, consisting of three members, interviewed the six qualified applicants, including Ross, and rated them based on the qualification standards for the position. Ross's interview took place on October 13, 1989, during which he admitted to being ill and nervous. The panel also reviewed Ross's application form and his Supervisory Appraisal form, which showed that his immediate and second-line supervisors, Reginald Carnegie and Steve Cohout, had recommended him only "with reservation" due to his poor attendance and human relations. The appraisal form noted that Ross had "fair human relations and poor attendance." After the interview process, the selecting panel ranked the applicants based on their composite scores, with Arthur Taylor, a Caucasian applicant, receiving the highest score and being selected for the position. Ross was ranked fifth overall and was notified on October 23, 1989, that he had not been selected.

Plaintiff Ross alleges that the Postal Service discriminated against him on the basis of his race when it failed to promote him to the MES technician position. He claims that he was more qualified than the selectee, Arthur Taylor, and that the selection process was flawed. Ross contends that the procedures used during the selection process were in violation of postal regulations and that he was unfairly rated on areas not within the scope of the vacancy announcement, including his past leave record and his experience with heating, air-conditioning, and ventilation. Defendant Postal Service contends that Ross did not receive the promotion because he did not score as well as other applicants during the interview process and had a history of attendance problems at work. The Postal Service also notes that Ross's immediate and second-line supervisors had recommended him only "with reservation" due to his poor attendance and human relations. Ross had filed a formal complaint of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Office of the Post Office, which was initially filed as a national origin discrimination complaint but was later amended to a racial discrimination complaint. The EEOC ultimately found no discrimination, and Ross appealed the decision, which was denied.

Albert Buonanno was employed by AT&T Broadband, LLC from January 10, 1999, to February 1, 2001, initially as a cable dispatcher and later as a quota specialist. He was a Christian who believed in living his life according to the Bible's literal language. In January 2001, AT&T introduced a new "Employee Handbook" that included a section on diversity, which stated that each person at AT&T was responsible for recognizing, respecting, and valuing the differences among all employees. Buonanno questioned the meaning of this language, believing that it would require him to "value" behaviors or beliefs that were repudiated by Scripture, which would compromise his own religious beliefs.

Plaintiff alleges that he could not comply with the challenged language without denying his faith, and therefore, he could not sign the Certificate of Understanding, which was required by AT&T's Certification Policy. Defendant contends that the Diversity Policy was essential to its business development and that permitting an employee to certify anything other than full agreement with all of the language in the Handbook would destroy its competitive advantage. Buonanno's supervisor, Jonathan Dunn, suggested that he seek clarification on the language, and Buonanno wrote a letter to his Human Resources Manager, Susan Batliner, explaining his concerns. 

Buonanno met with Batliner and Dunn to discuss his concerns, but Batliner refused to clarify the meaning of the challenged language, stating that it was not a "philosophical debate." Buonanno reiterated that he supported the Diversity Philosophy but could not disavow his religious beliefs by endorsing behavior or beliefs he considered sinful. Batliner terminated his employment due to his refusal to sign the Certificate, stating that it was a requirement for continued employment. AT&T maintains that its Diversity Philosophy is essential to its business development, and that all employees must agree to it in order to work for the company. Buonanno contends that he was willing to comply with the principles underlying the Diversity Philosophy but could not sign the Certificate due to the ambiguous language.

Yao Etienne Kouakou, an African marketing representative, was employed by New York State Catholic Health Plan, Inc., d/b/a FidelisCare New York, from June 2008 until his involuntary discharge on August 20, 2010. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, he was discriminated against because he was the only African marketing representative in a department where the remainder of the staff was Hispanic. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that his former supervisor, Hector Hernandez, constantly spoke in Spanish with another supervisor, Efrain Vargas, making Plaintiff feel uncomfortable. 

Plaintiff requested a transfer from Hernandez's team in 2008, but was denied. After the transfer request, Plaintiff alleges that Hernandez "turned the marketing department against him" and "falsely accused him of creating a fraudulent application" for a government healthcare program. Plaintiff also alleges that Hernandez forced him to sign a disciplinary letter stating that he did not meet sales quota requirements, which Plaintiff claims was untrue. Defendant terminated Hernandez after Plaintiff showed the letter to the Human Resources Department. 

Plaintiff alleges that, following Hernandez's termination, the marketing department became "angry and retaliated against him." For instance, Vargas allegedly forced Plaintiff to sign documents stating that if he ended up back in Vargas's office, he would be terminated. Another supervisor, Ana Roposo, allegedly continued Plaintiff's mistreatment, and on one occasion, Vargas called Plaintiff an "Africano negro." Other co-workers allegedly "verbally attacked" Plaintiff and were "closer to physically harming him" at work in support of their cause as Spanish speakers. Plaintiff also alleges that he was involved in two specific confrontations with co-workers over gifts that were frequently made available for marketing representatives to give to their clients. In both incidents, Plaintiff was allegedly denied gifts for his clients, while Hispanic applicants received them. Plaintiff notified his supervisor about both incidents, but claims that his supervisor chose to do nothing about them. Plaintiff also alleges that he was investigated for submitting another "fraudulent application," which resulted in his involuntary termination, and that other marketing representatives who were suspected of creating fraudulent applications were not disciplined, investigated, or fired. Defendant contends that there is no evidence that the adverse employment actions against Plaintiff were motivated by his race or national origin.

Richard Vankempen was employed by McDonnell Douglas Corporation until his termination on January 24, 1992. Plaintiff alleges that his employment was wrongfully terminated based on his age. Defendant contends that plaintiff's claim under the Missouri Human Rights Act (MHRA) is untimely, as the two-year statute of limitations would have expired but for defendant's agreement to extend the time for plaintiff to file his MHRA claim until July 1, 1995. Plaintiff filed his original complaint, including an MHRA claim, on June 23, 1995, but did not receive a right-to-sue letter from the Missouri Commission on Human Rights (MCHR) until October 3, 1995. Plaintiff then filed an Amended Complaint on November 2, 1995. 

Defendant contends that receipt of a notice of right to sue is a jurisdictional prerequisite to the maintenance of a civil action for violation of the MHRA, and that plaintiff's MHRA claim was time-barred at the time the Amended Complaint was filed. Plaintiff argues that no federal or state court has held that a right-to-sue letter from the MCHR is a jurisdictional prerequisite to filing an action under the MHRA, and that the statute should be liberally construed. 

Prior to filing the lawsuit, plaintiff had filed a complaint with the MCHR, which had not completed its administrative processing within 180 days. Plaintiff had requested a right-to-sue letter, which was issued on October 3, 1995. The parties had also agreed to extend the time for plaintiff to file his MHRA claim until July 1, 1995. Defendant had moved to dismiss Count III of plaintiff's Amended Complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, arguing that plaintiff's MHRA claim was untimely and that the court lacked jurisdiction over the claim.

Citizens Bank, a small business with a net worth of less than $5,000,000 and fewer than 500 employees, paid an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) deficiency assessment for calendar years 1977 and 1978. The bank then sought recovery of the assessment in a lawsuit against the United States. The IRS opposed the bank's claim, and the case was litigated in the district court. The bank's attorneys spent 70.6 hours working on the case, including 1.5 hours at an evidentiary hearing, at a rate of $75 per hour, and incurred $188.31 in other expenses, such as long distance telephone charges, xerox, and postage. 

Plaintiff alleges that the IRS's position in the case was not substantially justified, as the bank's claim was supported by clear and controlling precedent, specifically the Fifth Circuit's decision in Bank of Coushatta v. United States. Defendant contends that its position was substantially justified, but the attorney who represented the IRS admitted at the evidentiary hearing that the IRS took its position in order to create an "appellate vehicle" to challenge the Bank of Coushatta decision. The IRS had given notice of appeal to the Eleventh Circuit but then voluntarily dismissed its appeal. 

The parties disagree on whether the IRS's position was substantially justified and whether special circumstances make an award of attorneys' fees and expenses unjust. The bank seeks $5,295.00 in attorneys' fees and $188.31 in other expenses, while the United States opposes the motion, arguing that its position was substantially justified. The bank's vice-president and cashier, E.N. Jones, III, submitted uncontroverted affidavits showing that the bank meets the financial eligibility requirements for an award of attorneys' fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA).

Kimberly Guereca was an employee of Sweeping Maids Cleaning Services, a residential and commercial cleaning service in Hobbs, New Mexico, owned and managed by Zulema Cordero and Eduardo Lara, during the second quarter of 2019. As an employee, Guereca performed manual, non-management work, including vacuuming, sweeping, mopping, and scrubbing, alongside other employees who performed similar tasks. These employees, including Guereca, spent the majority of their time performing manual tasks in customers' residences or commercial buildings, handling tools and equipment manufactured outside of New Mexico. Their job functions required little to no official training and did not necessitate a college education or advanced degree.

Plaintiff alleges that she and other employees typically worked in excess of forty hours per week, often working fifty hours or more, but were paid "straight time" for all hours worked without receiving an overtime premium for hours worked over forty per week. Defendants contend that they properly classified cleaning technicians, including Guereca, as exempt from overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) and the New Mexico Minimum Wage Act (NMMWA). However, Plaintiff alleges that Defendants failed to compensate her and other employees at a rate of not less than time-and-one-half their regular rates of pay for hours worked in excess of forty in a workweek.

Defendants had hiring and firing authority over Guereca and other cleaning technicians, and made decisions regarding their pay and classification. Prior to commencing the lawsuit, there is no indication of any settlement discussions or agreements between the parties. On June 20, 2019, Guereca commenced an opt-in collective action against Defendants, alleging violations of the FLSA and NMMWA. Relevant pre-litigation events include Defendants' decisions regarding employee classification and pay, as well as their failure to provide overtime compensation to Guereca and other employees. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Defendants exercising control over Guereca's work and pay. The nature of the dispute centers on whether Defendants properly compensated Guereca and other employees for overtime work under the FLSA and NMMWA.

In February 2017, Hine applied to work as a volunteer firefighter and emergency medical technician (EMT) for the MVFD, a non-profit corporation located in Suitland, Maryland. Hine is deaf and substantially limited in the major life activities of hearing and speaking. Despite this, he had previously served as a volunteer firefighter in Pennsylvania with no restrictions on his duties. As part of the application process, Hine was referred for a physical examination. On March 8, 2018, Defendants informed Hine that he did not meet the standards set by the Prince George's County Fire Department to become a firefighter due to his hearing loss.

Plaintiff alleges that he submitted additional records relating to past hearing test results and requested an opportunity to receive another hearing test. However, on February 23, 2019, the County sent him a denial letter stating that he did not meet the standards to safely perform the essential functions of the position. Hine contends that the County and MVFD are joint employers because they were both involved in the hiring process, and that he would have been hired as a volunteer firefighter if not for Defendants' discriminatory policies, practices, and procedures. Defendant contends that Hine's hearing loss made him ineligible for the position.

On June 12, 2019, Hine filed a charge of discrimination with the United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights (MCCR). The EEOC issued a Notice of Right to Sue on July 28, 2020. Prior to filing the lawsuit, Hine had previously served as a volunteer firefighter in Pennsylvania, and he had applied to work with the MVFD, undergoing a physical examination as part of the application process. The parties' relationship is that of a job applicant and potential employer, with the nature of the dispute being allegations of discrimination based on Hine's disability.

Plaintiff began working for Assurant in 2004 and was promoted to senior quality control specialist around January 2019, while working on manager Brandi Howard's team. On July 25, 2019, Plaintiff had a telephone call with Howard about attending training on the following Saturday, during which Howard allegedly spoke to Plaintiff in a disrespectful manner. Plaintiff reported this incident to Brian Kovach, David Susag, and Christine Bieller, and subsequently met with Kovach on August 8, 2019, to discuss the alleged retaliation and harassment by Howard. 

Plaintiff alleges that after reporting the incident, she was subjected to retaliation, including being assigned additional tasks inconsistent with her job description, which she believes was pretext for discrimination based on her race. Plaintiff filed a Charge of Discrimination with the EEOC on November 22, 2019, alleging retaliation, but did not check the "continuing violation" box. The EEOC dismissed the charge, finding that the facts alleged failed to state a claim under any of the statutes enforced by the EEOC. 

Plaintiff filed a second EEOC charge on March 19, 2020, alleging race-based discrimination and retaliation, stating that her duties had increased substantially and she had been assigned tasks inconsistent with her job description since filing the first charge. Defendant contends that the assignments were part of workflow development and not based on race. The EEOC dismissed the second charge as well, finding insufficient evidence to show a nexus between the previous complaint and the assignment of additional job duties, or that any employee was treated more favorably based on race. Plaintiff sent a formal written complaint to Defendant's executives in June 2020, detailing her concerns of discrimination and retaliation, which was investigated by the then-VP of Employee Relations, Georgie Cummins. Defendant contends that Plaintiff's allegations are unfounded and that the company took appropriate actions to address her concerns.

Harvey Ross, an African-American man, worked as a general mechanic (grade 5) at the United States Postal Service (Postal Service) since 1987. Prior to joining the Postal Service, Ross worked for 11 years installing, repairing, and maintaining electrical and electronic systems. In August 1989, the Mail Equipment Shops (MES) section of the Postal Service posted a vacancy announcement for a MES technician position. Ross and six other applicants, including four African-Americans, one Caucasian, and one Asian-American, submitted applications for the position. To qualify for an interview, each applicant had to pass the mandatory Postal Test 500 (PT 500), which Ross passed with the highest score.

The selecting panel, consisting of three members, interviewed the six qualified applicants, including Ross, and rated them based on the qualification standards for the position. Ross's interview took place on October 13, 1989, during which he admitted to being ill and nervous. The panel also reviewed Ross's application form and his Supervisory Appraisal form, which showed that his immediate and second-line supervisors, Reginald Carnegie and Steve Cohout, had recommended him only "with reservation" due to his poor attendance and human relations. The appraisal form noted that Ross had "fair human relations and poor attendance." After the interview process, the selecting panel ranked the applicants based on their composite scores, with Arthur Taylor, a Caucasian applicant, receiving the highest score and being selected for the position. Ross was ranked fifth overall and was notified on October 23, 1989, that he had not been selected.

Plaintiff Ross alleges that the Postal Service discriminated against him on the basis of his race when it failed to promote him to the MES technician position. He claims that he was more qualified than the selectee, Arthur Taylor, and that the selection process was flawed. Ross contends that the procedures used during the selection process were in violation of postal regulations and that he was unfairly rated on areas not within the scope of the vacancy announcement, including his past leave record and his experience with heating, air-conditioning, and ventilation. Defendant Postal Service contends that Ross did not receive the promotion because he did not score as well as other applicants during the interview process and had a history of attendance problems at work. The Postal Service also notes that Ross's immediate and second-line supervisors had recommended him only "with reservation" due to his poor attendance and human relations. Ross had filed a formal complaint of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Office of the Post Office, which was initially filed as a national origin discrimination complaint but was later amended to a racial discrimination complaint. The EEOC ultimately found no discrimination, and Ross appealed the decision, which was denied.

Leilani Kryzhanovskiy was hired by Amazon in January 2020 as an Onsite Medical Representative at the Stockton, California warehouse location. Her husband, with comparable qualifications and experience, was hired for the same position in April 2020 but was offered substantially more in wages. Kryzhanovskiy and her husband have identical primary responsibilities in their positions. On May 27, 2021, Kryzhanovskiy sent a notification letter to the California Labor & Workforce Development Agency and Amazon, outlining alleged violations of the California Labor Code, including the Equal Pay Act, based on disparate treatment on the basis of gender.

Plaintiff alleges that after her supervisors became aware of her complaint, they began retaliating against her. In May 2021, Kryzhanovskiy had applied for a promotion to the position of Workplace Health & Safety Specialist at the Stockton warehouse. Although an interview was scheduled, her direct supervisor, Brent Butterfield, later told her the position had been filled and her interview was canceled. Kryzhanovskiy contends that Butterfield's actions were in retaliation for her complaints about Amazon's Labor Code violations and gender discrimination. She also alleges that since submitting her complaint, Butterfield has been dismissive of her, including not responding to her request for information about modifying her work schedule and informing her that schedule assignments are based on seniority, despite her being the most senior Onsite Medical Representative at the Stockton warehouse.

Amazon contends that its policies and practices are lawful. The company had uniform written policies and practices for calculating the regular rate of pay, and its wage statements provided to California employees were accurate. Amazon's position is that it did not violate the California Labor Code or engage in gender discrimination. The dispute between Kryzhanovskiy and Amazon involves allegations of unequal pay, retaliation, and violations of California labor laws, with Kryzhanovskiy seeking to represent a class of non-exempt California employees who may have been similarly affected by Amazon's practices. Relevant pre-litigation events include Kryzhanovskiy's notification letter, her application for a promotion, and the subsequent interactions with her supervisor, Brent Butterfield.

Nancy Shaffer was employed at National Can Corporation's Morrisville plant from March 13, 1975, until March 27, 1981, first as a secretary-receptionist and then as a billing clerk. In June 1977, Pat Dettorre was hired as the plant manager, and Shaffer alleges that he engaged in a continuing course of sexual harassment from that point until she left the company. Dettorre allegedly attempted to induce Shaffer to go out with him socially, made verbal sexual advances, and discussed the relative sizes of female employees' chests. When Shaffer refused his advances, Dettorre began to retaliate by mistreating and ignoring her, excluding her from certain luncheons and being overly friendly towards other female employees. Shaffer claims that Dettorre's conduct made it impossible for her to carry out her responsibilities, caused her severe mental anguish, and ultimately led to her resignation on March 27, 1981, which she characterizes as a constructive discharge.

Plaintiff alleges that she sent complaints to both the EEOC and the PHRC, although the exact dates are disputed. National claims that Shaffer's charge was not filed with the PHRC within the 90-day statute of limitations, while Shaffer contends that her charge was received by the PHRC on October 27, 1981, 214 days after her termination. National also argues that Shaffer's common law claims for wrongful discharge and intentional infliction of emotional distress have been supplanted by the remedies provided under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act. Shaffer contends that her claims are valid and that the PHRA does not preclude her from pursuing other remedies.

Shaffer and National have different contentions regarding the timing and filing of her complaints with the EEOC and PHRC. Shaffer alleges that she filed her complaints simultaneously with both agencies, while National claims that the filing date was November 5, 1981, 223 days after termination. The parties also disagree on the applicability of the 300-day exception for filing with the EEOC, with Shaffer arguing that she is entitled to invoke this exception and National arguing that she is not. The dispute centers on the interpretation of the relevant statutes and the timing of the filing of Shaffer's complaints.

On June 21, 2009, the plaintiff, a middle-aged white woman, was hired as a Senior Case Technician (SCT) in the Social Security Administration's (SSA) Office of Disability Adjudication and Review (ODAR) in Washington, D.C. for a two-year trial period. As an SCT, she assisted in the administrative adjudication of appeals brought by individuals denied Social Security and Social Security Insurance benefits. In addition to her regular SCT work, she performed clerical and technical tasks as a personal clerk to an administrative law judge and frequently filled in as the receptionist at the front desk of ODAR.

Three months after commencing her job, an African American male co-worker physically assaulted her, prompting her to file an informal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint. The co-worker claimed that the plaintiff attacked him. The plaintiff's supervisor, Hariette Hindie, responded to the incident by interrogating the plaintiff in a Weingarten session. When an SSA EEO official told the plaintiff that formal EEO complaints must be filed against "management," the plaintiff decided not to pursue a formal complaint for fear of losing her job. Plaintiff alleges that she did not take any formal action because she feared losing her job, while Defendant contends that the plaintiff had the opportunity to file a formal complaint but chose not to.

The plaintiff earned a promotion to a General Schedule (GS) level seven from a GS level six in June 2010, which was supported by Hindie and based on the plaintiff's job performance during the first year of her probationary period. However, in the following months, Hindie began scrutinizing the plaintiff's work more closely, and in September, she gave the plaintiff a counseling memorandum that identified specific problems with her recent job performance. The plaintiff responded by defending her performance in a rebuttal memorandum. On November 22, 2010, Hindie recommended the plaintiff's termination on the basis of poor work performance during the second year of the plaintiff's probationary period. Plaintiff alleges that Hindie's actions were retaliatory, while Defendant contends that the termination was based on the plaintiff's poor work performance. The plaintiff resigned effective January 5, 2011, to avoid embarrassment, increase her chances of obtaining future employment, and leave a work environment that caused her stress-related illnesses. Following her resignation, the plaintiff filed a formal EEO complaint against SSA management, alleging retaliation and coerced resignation.

Plaintiff alleges that after reporting the incident, she was subjected to retaliation, including being assigned additional tasks inconsistent with her job description, which she believes was pretext for discrimination based on her race. Plaintiff filed a Charge of Discrimination with the EEOC on November 22, 2019, alleging retaliation, but did not check the "continuing violation" box. The EEOC dismissed the charge, finding that the facts alleged failed to state a claim under any of the statutes enforced by the EEOC. 

Plaintiff filed a second EEOC charge on March 19, 2020, alleging race-based discrimination and retaliation, stating that her duties had increased substantially and she had been assigned tasks inconsistent with her job description since filing the first charge. Defendant contends that the assignments were part of workflow development and not based on race. The EEOC dismissed the second charge as well, finding insufficient evidence to show a nexus between the previous complaint and the assignment of additional job duties, or that any employee was treated more favorably based on race. Plaintiff sent a formal written complaint to Defendant's executives in June 2020, detailing her concerns of discrimination and retaliation, which was investigated by the then-VP of Employee Relations, Georgie Cummins. Defendant contends that Plaintiff's allegations are unfounded and that the company took appropriate actions to address her concerns.

Albert Buonanno was employed by AT&T Broadband, LLC from January 10, 1999, to February 1, 2001, initially as a cable dispatcher and later as a quota specialist. He was a Christian who believed in living his life according to the Bible's literal language. In January 2001, AT&T introduced a new "Employee Handbook" that included a section on diversity, which stated that each person at AT&T was responsible for recognizing, respecting, and valuing the differences among all employees. Buonanno questioned the meaning of this language, believing that it would require him to "value" behaviors or beliefs that were repudiated by Scripture, which would compromise his own religious beliefs.

Plaintiff alleges that he could not comply with the challenged language without denying his faith, and therefore, he could not sign the Certificate of Understanding, which was required by AT&T's Certification Policy. Defendant contends that the Diversity Policy was essential to its business development and that permitting an employee to certify anything other than full agreement with all of the language in the Handbook would destroy its competitive advantage. Buonanno's supervisor, Jonathan Dunn, suggested that he seek clarification on the language, and Buonanno wrote a letter to his Human Resources Manager, Susan Batliner, explaining his concerns. 

Buonanno met with Batliner and Dunn to discuss his concerns, but Batliner refused to clarify the meaning of the challenged language, stating that it was not a "philosophical debate." Buonanno reiterated that he supported the Diversity Philosophy but could not disavow his religious beliefs by endorsing behavior or beliefs he considered sinful. Batliner terminated his employment due to his refusal to sign the Certificate, stating that it was a requirement for continued employment. AT&T maintains that its Diversity Philosophy is essential to its business development, and that all employees must agree to it in order to work for the company. Buonanno contends that he was willing to comply with the principles underlying the Diversity Philosophy but could not sign the Certificate due to the ambiguous language.

Kimberly Guereca was an employee of Sweeping Maids Cleaning Services, a residential and commercial cleaning service in Hobbs, New Mexico, owned and managed by Zulema Cordero and Eduardo Lara, during the second quarter of 2019. As an employee, Guereca performed manual, non-management work, including vacuuming, sweeping, mopping, and scrubbing, alongside other employees who performed similar tasks. These employees, including Guereca, spent the majority of their time performing manual tasks in customers' residences or commercial buildings, handling tools and equipment manufactured outside of New Mexico. Their job functions required little to no official training and did not necessitate a college education or advanced degree.

Plaintiff alleges that she and other employees typically worked in excess of forty hours per week, often working fifty hours or more, but were paid "straight time" for all hours worked without receiving an overtime premium for hours worked over forty per week. Defendants contend that they properly classified cleaning technicians, including Guereca, as exempt from overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) and the New Mexico Minimum Wage Act (NMMWA). However, Plaintiff alleges that Defendants failed to compensate her and other employees at a rate of not less than time-and-one-half their regular rates of pay for hours worked in excess of forty in a workweek.

Defendants had hiring and firing authority over Guereca and other cleaning technicians, and made decisions regarding their pay and classification. Prior to commencing the lawsuit, there is no indication of any settlement discussions or agreements between the parties. On June 20, 2019, Guereca commenced an opt-in collective action against Defendants, alleging violations of the FLSA and NMMWA. Relevant pre-litigation events include Defendants' decisions regarding employee classification and pay, as well as their failure to provide overtime compensation to Guereca and other employees. The parties' relationship is that of employer and employee, with Defendants exercising control over Guereca's work and pay. The nature of the dispute centers on whether Defendants properly compensated Guereca and other employees for overtime work under the FLSA and NMMWA.

Harvey Ross, an African-American man, worked as a general mechanic (grade 5) at the United States Postal Service (Postal Service) since 1987. Prior to joining the Postal Service, Ross worked for 11 years installing, repairing, and maintaining electrical and electronic systems. In August 1989, the Mail Equipment Shops (MES) section of the Postal Service posted a vacancy announcement for a MES technician position. Ross and six other applicants, including four African-Americans, one Caucasian, and one Asian-American, submitted applications for the position. To qualify for an interview, each applicant had to pass the mandatory Postal Test 500 (PT 500), which Ross passed with the highest score.

The selecting panel, consisting of three members, interviewed the six qualified applicants, including Ross, and rated them based on the qualification standards for the position. Ross's interview took place on October 13, 1989, during which he admitted to being ill and nervous. The panel also reviewed Ross's application form and his Supervisory Appraisal form, which showed that his immediate and second-line supervisors, Reginald Carnegie and Steve Cohout, had recommended him only "with reservation" due to his poor attendance and human relations. The appraisal form noted that Ross had "fair human relations and poor attendance." After the interview process, the selecting panel ranked the applicants based on their composite scores, with Arthur Taylor, a Caucasian applicant, receiving the highest score and being selected for the position. Ross was ranked fifth overall and was notified on October 23, 1989, that he had not been selected.

Plaintiff Ross alleges that the Postal Service discriminated against him on the basis of his race when it failed to promote him to the MES technician position. He claims that he was more qualified than the selectee, Arthur Taylor, and that the selection process was flawed. Ross contends that the procedures used during the selection process were in violation of postal regulations and that he was unfairly rated on areas not within the scope of the vacancy announcement, including his past leave record and his experience with heating, air-conditioning, and ventilation. Defendant Postal Service contends that Ross did not receive the promotion because he did not score as well as other applicants during the interview process and had a history of attendance problems at work. The Postal Service also notes that Ross's immediate and second-line supervisors had recommended him only "with reservation" due to his poor attendance and human relations. Ross had filed a formal complaint of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Office of the Post Office, which was initially filed as a national origin discrimination complaint but was later amended to a racial discrimination complaint. The EEOC ultimately found no discrimination, and Ross appealed the decision, which was denied.

Bilan Nur, a Muslim woman, immigrated to the United States from Somalia in 1998. In November 1999, she was hired by Alamo as a rental agent at a location on East Washington Street in Phoenix, Arizona. Her duties included renting cars to customers, accepting payment, and answering the telephone, all of which required interaction with clients. Until the events leading to her termination, Ms. Nur's job performance was "fine." Alamo had a "Dress Smart Policy" in place, which aimed to promote a favorable first impression with customers and prohibited employees from wearing certain clothing and accessories, such as more than one earring, open-toe shoes, and half-grown beards. The policy did not explicitly prohibit the wearing of head coverings, but Alamo contends that it prohibited any "garment or item of outer clothing not specifically mentioned in the policy."

In November 2001, during the Muslim holiday of Ramadan, Ms. Nur requested permission from Alamo's City Manager, Victor Bellavia, to wear a head covering at work. Bellavia contacted Alamo's Human Resource Manager, Heather Phillips, who instructed him that Ms. Nur could wear a head covering in the back of the office but would need to remove it while at the rental counter. Alamo did not excuse Ms. Nur from working at the rental counter during Ramadan. On December 1, 2001, Ms. Nur was given a "Counselling Review" for wearing a veil over her hair, and she was told to clock out and discuss the issue with the City Manager. The next day, she received another Counselling Review, was suspended, and was advised to discuss the issue with the City Manager. On December 3, 2001, Ms. Nur received another counselling review, was suspended pending investigation, and was told to return on December 6, 2001, to meet with the City Manager. On December 6, 2001, Alamo terminated Ms. Nur's employment for violating company rules, and the termination form indicated that she was not eligible for re-hire.

Plaintiff alleges that Alamo discriminated against Ms. Nur based on her religion by not accommodating her request to wear a head covering during Ramadan. Alamo contends that it did not discriminate against Ms. Nur and that her religious beliefs did not conflict with her job requirements. Alamo also points to evidence that during Ramadan in 2000, Ms. Nur was asked to remove her head covering and complied without asserting a religious need to object, which Alamo argues raises questions about the sincerity of Ms. Nur's religious beliefs in 2001. The EEOC filed a complaint on September 27, 2002, on behalf of Ms. Nur, asserting a claim of religious discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The matter was stayed due to Alamo's bankruptcy filing but was later lifted, and the EEOC filed a motion for partial summary judgment regarding liability on its religious discrimination claim.

Nancy Shaffer was employed at National Can Corporation's Morrisville plant from March 13, 1975, until March 27, 1981, first as a secretary-receptionist and then as a billing clerk. In June 1977, Pat Dettorre was hired as the plant manager, and Shaffer alleges that he engaged in a continuing course of sexual harassment from that point until she left the company. Dettorre allegedly attempted to induce Shaffer to go out with him socially, made verbal sexual advances, and discussed the relative sizes of female employees' chests. When Shaffer refused his advances, Dettorre began to retaliate by mistreating and ignoring her, excluding her from certain luncheons and being overly friendly towards other female employees. Shaffer claims that Dettorre's conduct made it impossible for her to carry out her responsibilities, caused her severe mental anguish, and ultimately led to her resignation on March 27, 1981, which she characterizes as a constructive discharge.

Plaintiff alleges that she sent complaints to both the EEOC and the PHRC, although the exact dates are disputed. National claims that Shaffer's charge was not filed with the PHRC within the 90-day statute of limitations, while Shaffer contends that her charge was received by the PHRC on October 27, 1981, 214 days after her termination. National also argues that Shaffer's common law claims for wrongful discharge and intentional infliction of emotional distress have been supplanted by the remedies provided under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act. Shaffer contends that her claims are valid and that the PHRA does not preclude her from pursuing other remedies.

Shaffer and National have different contentions regarding the timing and filing of her complaints with the EEOC and PHRC. Shaffer alleges that she filed her complaints simultaneously with both agencies, while National claims that the filing date was November 5, 1981, 223 days after termination. The parties also disagree on the applicability of the 300-day exception for filing with the EEOC, with Shaffer arguing that she is entitled to invoke this exception and National arguing that she is not. The dispute centers on the interpretation of the relevant statutes and the timing of the filing of Shaffer's complaints.

Yao Etienne Kouakou, an African marketing representative, was employed by New York State Catholic Health Plan, Inc., d/b/a FidelisCare New York, from June 2008 until his involuntary discharge on August 20, 2010. Plaintiff alleges that during his employment, he was discriminated against because he was the only African marketing representative in a department where the remainder of the staff was Hispanic. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that his former supervisor, Hector Hernandez, constantly spoke in Spanish with another supervisor, Efrain Vargas, making Plaintiff feel uncomfortable. 

Plaintiff requested a transfer from Hernandez's team in 2008, but was denied. After the transfer request, Plaintiff alleges that Hernandez "turned the marketing department against him" and "falsely accused him of creating a fraudulent application" for a government healthcare program. Plaintiff also alleges that Hernandez forced him to sign a disciplinary letter stating that he did not meet sales quota requirements, which Plaintiff claims was untrue. Defendant terminated Hernandez after Plaintiff showed the letter to the Human Resources Department. 

Plaintiff alleges that, following Hernandez's termination, the marketing department became "angry and retaliated against him." For instance, Vargas allegedly forced Plaintiff to sign documents stating that if he ended up back in Vargas's office, he would be terminated. Another supervisor, Ana Roposo, allegedly continued Plaintiff's mistreatment, and on one occasion, Vargas called Plaintiff an "Africano negro." Other co-workers allegedly "verbally attacked" Plaintiff and were "closer to physically harming him" at work in support of their cause as Spanish speakers. Plaintiff also alleges that he was involved in two specific confrontations with co-workers over gifts that were frequently made available for marketing representatives to give to their clients. In both incidents, Plaintiff was allegedly denied gifts for his clients, while Hispanic applicants received them. Plaintiff notified his supervisor about both incidents, but claims that his supervisor chose to do nothing about them. Plaintiff also alleges that he was investigated for submitting another "fraudulent application," which resulted in his involuntary termination, and that other marketing representatives who were suspected of creating fraudulent applications were not disciplined, investigated, or fired. Defendant contends that there is no evidence that the adverse employment actions against Plaintiff were motivated by his race or national origin.

In February 2017, Hine applied to work as a volunteer firefighter and emergency medical technician (EMT) for the MVFD, a non-profit corporation located in Suitland, Maryland. Hine is deaf and substantially limited in the major life activities of hearing and speaking. Despite this, he had previously served as a volunteer firefighter in Pennsylvania with no restrictions on his duties. As part of the application process, Hine was referred for a physical examination. On March 8, 2018, Defendants informed Hine that he did not meet the standards set by the Prince George's County Fire Department to become a firefighter due to his hearing loss.

Plaintiff alleges that he submitted additional records relating to past hearing test results and requested an opportunity to receive another hearing test. However, on February 23, 2019, the County sent him a denial letter stating that he did not meet the standards to safely perform the essential functions of the position. Hine contends that the County and MVFD are joint employers because they were both involved in the hiring process, and that he would have been hired as a volunteer firefighter if not for Defendants' discriminatory policies, practices, and procedures. Defendant contends that Hine's hearing loss made him ineligible for the position.

On June 12, 2019, Hine filed a charge of discrimination with the United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights (MCCR). The EEOC issued a Notice of Right to Sue on July 28, 2020. Prior to filing the lawsuit, Hine had previously served as a volunteer firefighter in Pennsylvania, and he had applied to work with the MVFD, undergoing a physical examination as part of the application process. The parties' relationship is that of a job applicant and potential employer, with the nature of the dispute being allegations of discrimination based on Hine's disability.
